## Khuddaka Nikāya
## Commentary on the Theragāthā
## (Volume I)
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Introduction to the Text
I pay homage to the Buddha, the Protector, who is endowed with the great and noble quality of Mahākaruṇā (Great Compassion), who has reached the further shore of the ocean of all things to be known (ñeyya), who speaks the Dhamma through various subtle, profound, and wonderful methods, and who is the refuge of all beings—humans, devas, and brahmās—within the three realms.

I pay homage to that supreme Dhamma, worshipped continuously by the Sammāsambuddhas (Perfectly Enlightened Ones), which is pure and noble, and by which the virtuous ones, such as the Buddha, who are endowed with the three knowledges, the eight knowledges, and the fifteen conducts (caraṇa), have escaped from the world through the four Paths, the four Fruits, and Nibbāna.

I pay homage to that noble Saṅgha, the assembly of the eight types of noble persons (ariya-puggala), who are endowed with the qualities of virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), liberation (vimutti), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana); who abide in the Paths and Fruits, and who are like an incomparable fertile field for planting the seeds of merit.

Having obtained the merit arising from thus paying homage to the Triple Gem, may I, by the power of that merit, be free from all dangers in all places as I write this commentary.

The Elders (Theras) and Elder Nuns (Therīs), such as Subhūti and others, who had completed their tasks and were endowed with such qualities, being free from worldly attachments (nirāmisa), spoke certain verses (gāthās) in the manner of inspired utterances (udāna). These verses are profound, subtle, and beautiful; they are connected with emptiness (suññatā) and reveal the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma).

Those Great Sages (Mahesī), seekers of special qualities, recited those verses in the Khuddaka Nikāya under the names 'Theragāthā' and 'Therīgāthā' during the Great Councils (Saṅgāyanā).
2:
Because these verses are to be penetrated with profound wisdom, it is indeed difficult for me to provide an explanation of their meaning. Nevertheless, I shall proceed because the Buddha's Dispensation (Sāsana) remains together with its commentaries, and the decisions of the former great teachers (pubbācariya) still stand.

Therefore, relying on those decisions, penetrating the five Nikāyas with wisdom, and following the method of the ancient commentaries (porāṇāṭṭhakathā), I shall respectfully compose a beautiful explanation of the meanings of the Theragāthā and Therīgāthā to the best of my ability. This will be done without contradicting the tradition of the Mahāvihāravāsins, and it will be very pure, unconfused, and contain subtle doctrinal decisions.

For those verses whose meanings are difficult to understand without a sequential explanation, I shall clarify those meanings and illuminate the decisions. 

May the virtuous ones listen to my words as I analyze those meanings, desiring the long-lasting of the True Dhamma (Saddhamma).

Regarding the questions: 'What are these Theragāthās and Therīgāthās?' and 'How did they arise?', although the meaning has already been stated in the verses themselves, I shall speak again for the sake of clarity. Among them, the Theragāthās were first spoken by Elders such as the Venerable Subhūti. Indeed, those Elders, reflecting on the bliss of the Path and Fruit (magga-phala-sukha) they had attained, spoke some verses as inspired utterances (udāna), some by way of reflecting on their meditative attainments (samāpatti-vihāra), some by way of questions, and some at the time of their final passing (parinibbāna) to demonstrate the nature of the Dispensation as a means of deliverance from the round of rebirths. All these verses were collected together at the time of the Council and recited by the redactors of the Dhamma (Dhamma-saṅgāhaka) as the 'Theragāthā'. The Therīgāthās, however, were spoken with reference to the Elder Nuns.

Among the three collections known as the Vinaya Piṭaka, Suttanta Piṭaka, and Abhidhamma Piṭaka, these verses are included in the Suttanta Piṭaka. Among the five Nikāyas—Dīgha Nikāya, Majjhima Nikāya, Saṃyutta Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya, and Khuddaka Nikāya—they are included in the Khuddaka Nikāya. Among the nine factors of the Teacher's Dispensation (navaṅgasatthusāsana), such as Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, and Udāna, they belong to the Gāthā category.
3:
Among the nine factors of the Dispensation—Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla—the Theragāthās are categorized under the Gāthā limb.

(The Venerable Ānanda declared:) "I received eighty-two thousand teachings from the Buddha and two thousand from the monks; thus, eighty-four thousand teachings are present in my heart."

Thus, these verses are included as a small portion of the eighty-four thousand Dhamma aggregates (dhammakkhandha) acknowledged by the Treasurer of the Dhamma (Ānanda).

Among those Theragāthās, they are first organized by way of sections (nipāta), starting from the Ekanipāta (Book of the Ones) and increasing by one verse at a time up to the Cuddasanipāta (Book of the Fourteens), followed by the Soḷasanipāta, Vīsatinipāta, Tiṃsanipāta, Cattālīsanipāta, Paññāsanipāta, Saṭṭhinipāta, and Sattatinipāta, making a total of twenty-one sections. A 'Nipāta' is so called because it is a placement or collection. Where there is a placement (nikkhepa) of single verses, it is called the Ekanipāta. The meaning of the remaining sections should be understood by this same method.

In the Ekanipāta, there are twelve groups (vagga). With ten Elders in each group, there are one hundred and twenty Elders, and the number of verses is the same as the number of Elders. Thus it is said:

"One hundred and twenty Elders, who had completed their tasks and were free from taints (anāsava), were well-recited in the Ekanipāta by the Great Sages (such as Venerable Mahākassapa and others)."

In the Dukanipāta, there are 49 Elders and 98 verses. In the Tikanipāta, 16 Elders and 48 verses. In the Catukkanipāta, 13 Elders and 52 verses. In the Pañcakanipāta, 12 Elders and 60 verses. In the Chakkanipāta, 14 Elders and 84 verses. In the Sattakanipāta, 5 Elders and 35 verses. In the Aṭṭhakanipāta, 3 Elders and 24 verses. In the Navakanipāta, 1 Elder and 9 verses. In the Dasanipāta, 7 Elders and 70 verses. In the Ekādasanipāta, 1 Elder and 11 verses. In the Dvādasanipāta, 2 Elders and 24 verses. In the Terasanipāta, 1 Elder and 13 verses. In the Cuddasanipāta, 2 Elders and 28 verses. There is no Pannarasanipāta (Book of the Fifteens). In the Soḷasanipāta, 2 Elders and 32 verses. In the Vīsatinipāta, 10 Elders and 245 verses. In the Tiṃsanipāta, 3 Elders and 105 verses. In the Cattālīsanipāta...
4:
(One monk, 42 verses.) In the Paññāsanipāta, there is one monk and 55 verses. In the Saṭṭhinipāta, one monk and 68 verses. In the Sattatinipāta, one monk and 71 verses. Summing them all up, there are 264 monks and 1,360 verses. It has also been said: "These verses are one thousand three hundred and sixty; and two hundred and sixty-four monks have been proclaimed."

As for the Therīgāthā, there are sixteen collections (nipātas): from the Ekanipāta increasing by one up to the Navanipāta, then the Ekādasanipāta, Dvādasanipāta, Soḷasanipāta, Vīsatinipāta, Tiṃsanipāta, Cattālīsanipāta, and Mahānipāta. Among these, in the Ekanipāta, there are 18 nuns and 18 verses. In the Dukanipāta, 10 nuns and 20 verses. In the Tikanipāta, 8 nuns and 24 verses. In the Catukkanipāta, 1 nun and 4 verses. In the Pañcakanipāta, 12 nuns and 60 verses. In the Chakkanipāta, 8 nuns and 48 verses. In the Sattanipāta, 3 nuns and 21 verses. From the Aṭṭhanipāta up to the Soḷasanipāta, there is one nun each, with verses corresponding to the measure of each nipāta. In the Vīsatinipāta, there are 5 nuns and 1,800 verses. In the Tiṃsanipāta, 1 nun and 34 verses. In the Cattālīsanipāta, 1 nun and 48 verses. In the Mahānipāta, there is also 1 nun and 75 verses. In this way, the extent and quantity of the nipātas, vaggas, and verses in this [Therīgāthā] should be understood.
5:
## Commentary on the Introductory Verses

These Theragāthā, whose extent has been thus defined, are the beginning. Among those Theragāthā:

"Like lions roaring, fanged, in a mountain cave, listen to the verses of those with developed selves, which lead to the goal."

This is the opening verse spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council for the purpose of praising those elder monks. In that verse, in the word "sīhānaṃ," the term sīha (lion) appears in the sense of the king of beasts in such passages as, "Monks, the lion is the king of beasts..." (A.N. 4.33). It appears as a designation (a person's name) in such passages as, "Then the general Sīha approached the Blessed One..." (A.N. 5.34). It appears in the sense of the Tathāgata, the Blessed One, in such passages as, "Monks, 'Lion' is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One..." (A.N. 5.99, 10.21).

Just as it appears in those passages in reference to the Blessed One by way of a comparison of similarity, so too in this verse, it should be understood only by way of a comparison of similarity. Therefore, "sīhānaṃva" means "sīhānaṃ iva" (like the roar of lions). There is a loss of a vowel through the power of euphonic combination (sandhi), as in "evaṃsa te" and so on. There, "iva" is an indeclinable (nipāta). "Suṇātha" is a verb (ākhyāta). The remaining words are nouns (nāma). In the word "sīhānaṃva," the genitive case is used in the sense of connection (sambandha). Although the object of connection (sambandhī) is not explicitly stated in form, it is indeed stated by way of meaning.

For example, when it is said, "This person's face is like a camel's," the meaning "a face like a camel's face" is already expressed; similarly here, when "sīhānaṃva" is said, the meaning "like the roar of lions" is already expressed. If it is asked why, it is because in the [camel] example, the word "mukha" (face) is in proximity, and here too, the word "nadantānaṃ" (roaring) is in proximity. Therefore, "sīhānaṃva" is a comparative statement (nidassanavacana). "Nadantānaṃ" shows the connection with what is being compared. "Dāṭhīnaṃ" is its qualifier (visesana). "Girigabbhare" shows the place where that roaring occurs. "Suṇātha" is an exhortation to listen. "Bhāvitattānaṃ" shows the source (the persons) of what is to be heard. "Gāthā" shows the object to be heard. "Atthūpanāyikā" is its qualifier.

Although "sīhānaṃ nadantānaṃ dāṭhīnaṃ" appears here in the masculine gender, the meaning should also be understood in the feminine gender by changing the gender to "sīhīnaṃ" and so on. Or, by way of the inclusive plural (ekasesa), "lions" means both male lions and female lions, and thus it should be understood as "of those [elders and elder nuns]."
6:
These three introductory verses (nidāna-gāthā) beginning with "Sīhānaṃ" are common (sādhāraṇa) to both the Theragāthā and the Therīgāthā.

Among those words, the term "Sīha" (lion) is used because of the meanings of endurance (sahana) and killing (hanana). How so? Because the lion, the king of beasts, is endowed with exceptional strength, it has no danger from creatures such as the sarabha deer or the noble rutting elephant. It also endures all dangers such as wind and heat. When it goes out for food, because of its great majesty and power, even if it encounters rutting elephants or wild buffaloes, it is fearless, undaunted, and overcomes them. Having overcome them, it truly kills them and lives happily, eating the tender meat. In the same way, these Great Elders (Mahātheras), because they are endowed with exceptional noble power (ariya-bala), are able to endure all dangers. Because they can overcome, kill, and abandon the power of defilements (kilesas) such as lust (rāga), and because their majesty and power are sharp, they dwell in the bliss of jhāna and so forth, fearless and undaunted by any danger. Thus, they are called "Sīha" because they are like lions in their ability to endure and to kill.

According to the linguistic meaning—just as the word "takka" is formed from the word for weaving (kantana) by reversing the beginning and the end—similarly, "Sīha" should be understood through the meaning of harming or killing (hiṃsana). Likewise, it is called "Sīha" because of the meaning of endurance (sahana). If it is stated according to the method of Nirutti by placing it in the Pisodarādi group, there is nothing more to be said.

Alternatively, just as the king of beasts, the maned lion (kesara-sīha), wanders alone due to its great majesty and power and does not desire any companion, so too these Great Elders wander alone because of their sharp power and their delight in seclusion (viveka). They are called "Sīha" because they are like lions in the sense of wandering alone. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Like a lion wandering alone, like a great tusker."

Alternatively, these Great Elders are called "Sīha" because they are like lions, being endowed with special qualities such as fearlessness, speed, and effort. Regarding this, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these two who do not tremble at the sound of a crashing thunderbolt. Which two? A monk whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) and the lion, the king of beasts."

The speed of a lion is also extraordinary compared to others; so is its effort. For instance, that lion can leap over even a hundred bulls and pounce upon wild buffaloes and such. Even as a lion cub, it can face and rival even noble rutting elephants. The speed of the Noble Path (ariya-magga) and the effort of these Great Elders are also extraordinary compared to others. "Sīhānaṃ" refers to the Great Elders who are like lions, and here the metaphor (rūpaka) of the lion should be understood. This is because of the meanings such as supreme endurance. "Nadantānaṃ" means: just as lions come out from their dwelling cave to seek food, stretch their bodies, and fearlessly let out a roar, so too these Great Elders let out this roar (the sound of Dhamma) on occasions such as reflection and inspired utterances (udāna). Therefore, it is said "Sīhānaṃ".
7:
(The lion) bites and eats (its prey) as if penetrating a young tree. The speed of the Noble Path (ariya-magga) and the speed of psychic power (iddhi) of these Great Elders are incomparable to others, and their right effort (sammappadhāna) is also supreme and unsurpassed. Therefore, in the phrase "Sīhānaṃ va," it means "like the Great Elders who are similar to lions." In this context, the lion should be regarded as an inferior comparison (hīnūpamatā), because the most excellent meanings such as endurance are found only in the Elders.

"Nadantānaṃ" means those who roar (or thunder). Just as lions come out from their dwelling cave, stretch their bodies, and let out a fearless lion's roar at times such as seeking food, making effort, or when they are joyful, so too these Great Elders uttered this fearless roar at times such as reflecting on their internal objects or making inspired utterances (udāna). Therefore, it is said: "Sīhānaṃ va nadantānaṃ." "Dāṭhīnaṃ" means those with tusks (or fangs), those with praised tusks, or those with exceptionally great tusks. Just as lions overcome their enemies by the power of their four very firm and sharp fangs and fulfill their heart's desire to the end, so too these Great Elders, by the power of the four fangs of the Noble Path, overcame the enemies such as lust (rāga) that had never been overcome before in the beginningless Saṃsāra, and reached the end of their heart's desire. Here too, the meaning should be understood through the comparison of similar qualities, as they are called "tusks" because they are like tusks.

"Girigabbhare" means in a mountain cave; it is a locative case (bhūmma-vibhatta) in the sense of proximity. Some read it as "girigavhare." It means in a forest thicket or a dense grove of trees in the mountains. This shows the place where those lions shine and the suitable ground for the lion's roar. It should be read in connection as "nadantānaṃ girigabbhare." Just as lions generally live in mountain caves that are difficult for others to approach and are secluded from people, and they let out a lion's roar when going for food to dispel the fear of small animals that might arise upon seeing them, so too these Great Elders dwelt in secluded places like mountain caves that are difficult for others to approach, and they uttered the fearless roar known as the verses to be spoken, in order to avoid the fear of craving and views (taṇhā-diṭṭhi) in worldlings (puthujjanas) who are small in terms of virtue. Therefore, it is said: "Sīhānaṃ va nadantānaṃ, dāṭhīnaṃ girigabbhare."

"Suṇātha" is an exhortation meaning "Listen!" By that word, he arouses the desire to listen in the assembly gathered for the verses to be spoken, creates attentiveness in listening, and establishes respect and high esteem while well-arousing effort. Or else (another way is)...
8:
The meaning of the words beginning with "Sīhānaṃ" should be understood in their primary sense, without metaphorical interpretation. Therefore, the meaning is: listen to the verses which are like the fearless roar of those great elders—verses that resemble the lion's roar of the lion-kings, the lords of beasts, who possess noble fangs praised for their firm and sharp nature and who roar in mountain caves. This is what is meant: just as the lion-kings, the lords of beasts, roaring a lion's roar, have no fear from any direction, and that fearless roar causes terror in other animals; so too, listen to the verses of the diligent elders with cultivated minds, which are like a lion's roar, being fearless sounds because all causes of fear have been entirely abandoned, and which cause terror in the negligent.

"Bhāvitattānaṃ" means those with cultivated minds (bhāvitacittānaṃ). For the mind is called "atta" (self) in such passages as "The self (mind) is indeed difficult to tame" (Dhammapada 159), "He who has a steady mind is as straight as a shuttle" (Sutta Nipāta 217), and "The right direction of one's self" (Khuddakapāṭha 5.4). Therefore, it means those whose minds are developed through Samatha and Vipassanā by repeatedly practicing the training of higher mind (adhicittasikkhā), and who remain having reached the summit of Samatha and Vipassanā meditation. Alternatively, "Bhāvitattānaṃ" means those who have cultivated their nature, meaning those who have cultivated qualities such as virtue (sīla).

It is called "Gāthā" because it is recited. It is a speech consisting of four or six feet (lines) produced by seers through the power of the Anuṣṭubh meter and so forth. Other speeches are also called so because of their similarity to it. They are called "Atthūpanāyikā" because they bring about various benefits such as one's own benefit (attattha), or because they lead beings to those benefits.

In another way, "Bhāvitattānaṃ" refers to those whose self-identity (attabhāva) is thoroughly infused with the cultivation of body and mind. Because the conceit "I" adheres to this body, it is called "atta". That self-identity has been cultivated by those elders through the meditation of diligence (appamāda-bhāvanā) and faultless meditation (anavajja-bhāvanā), thus being well-made to take on the fragrance of virtue. By this, he shows the fulfillment of all four types of cultivation: cultivation of the body (kāya-bhāvanā), cultivation of virtue (sīla-bhāvanā), cultivation of the mind (citta-bhāvanā), and cultivation of wisdom (paññā-bhāvanā).

In this context, "Bhāvanā" refers to the practice that is the cause for realizing the Four Noble Truths (sambodhipaṭipadā). Where there is the realization of the truths (saccasambodhi), that realization is of two kinds: by way of penetration (abhisamaya) and by way of the requisite knowledge for that purpose (tadattha). Furthermore, enlightenment (sambodhi) is of three kinds: Perfect Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi), Individual Enlightenment (paccekasambodhi), and Disciple's Enlightenment (sāvakasambodhi). Among these, "Sammāsambodhi" is so called because of knowing all phenomena rightly and by oneself, and because of making them known. The Path-knowledge (maggañāṇa) which is the proximate cause of Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa), and the Omniscience which is the proximate cause of Path-knowledge, are called "Sammāsambodhi". Therefore, it is said:

"That Blessed One who, without a teacher, by himself penetrated the truths in things not heard before, and reached omniscience therein, and mastery over the powers, is called 'Buddha'."

That Blessed One who, without a teacher, by himself penetrated the truths in things not heard before, and reached omniscience therein, and mastery over the four truths, and reached mastery over the four fruits. Indeed, he is called a "Paccekasambuddha" because he reached mastery over the four fruits, because he knows the four truths that should be known, and because he knows them only by himself. The special realization of the four truths through the knowledge of a disciple's enlightenment (sāvakabodhiñāṇa) after being made to know by another is called "Sāvakabodhi".
9:
"Buddha" refers to that Blessed One who is self-become (sayambhū), without a teacher, who by himself penetrated the truths in things not heard before, and reached omniscience therein, and mastery over the powers (valesu vasībhāvaṃ).

Indeed, mastery over the powers means the state of enlightening those who are capable of being enlightened. "Paccekasambodhi" means enlightenment by oneself individually; it means the realization of the truths through self-become knowledge (sayambhūñāṇa) without being taught. For the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas, although the realization of the truths occurs by themselves through self-become knowledge, it is "with followers" (sānubuddha) because it becomes the cause for the realization of the truths by countless beings. However, the realization of the truths by these [Paccekabuddhas] does not become the cause for the realization of the truths by even a single other being. Those who are born at the end of hearing the Dhamma teaching of the Teacher are called "disciples" (sāvaka). The realization of the truths by those disciples is "Sāvakasambodhi".

This enlightenment is of three types. It should be understood as the fulfillment of the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma), such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), by the three types of Bodhisattas reaching the summit through their respective appropriate practices. This is because other types of penetration (abhisamaya) are inseparable from that enlightenment. Without the penetration of realization (sacchikiriyābhisamaya), the penetration of cultivation (bhāvanā-abhisamaya) cannot occur. When there is the penetration of cultivation, the penetration of abandoning (pahānābhisamaya) and the penetration of full understanding (pariññābhisamaya) are also accomplished.

In truth, the Great Bodhisatta, having fulfilled the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra), having performed the necessary duties in his final birth, ascended the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and made the vow: "I shall not break this cross-legged posture as long as my mind is not liberated from the taints (āsava) without clinging." Sitting on the unconquerable seat (aparājitapallaṅka), even as the sun was setting, he defeated the host of Māra. In the first watch of the night, through the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa), he recollected the aggregates previously inhabited in many modes and details. In the middle watch, by purifying the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), he attained the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (cutūpapātañāṇa) and the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa). In the last watch, thinking, "Alas, this world has fallen into suffering; it is born, it ages, it dies, it passes away, and it is reborn, yet it does not know the escape from this suffering, from aging and death," he applied himself to insight (vipassanā) by way of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), starting from aging and death. Just as one whets an axe on a grindstone to cut down a great forest, the Lord of the World, whetting the axe of knowledge to cut down the forest of defilements, in order to reach Buddhahood, having fulfilled the requisites of merit and knowledge (puñña-ñāṇa-sambhāra), and because of having reached perfection (pāramī), he took up the course of insight to attain omniscience. Entering into various attainments (samāpatti) in between, and contemplating the delimited mental and material phenomena by attributing the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa), he purified the cycles of contemplation through three million six hundred thousand modes of contemplating dependent origination in many ways. When the great insight-knowledge (mahāvipassanāñāṇa) became sharp and clear in those three million six hundred thousand modes, it arose as insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā). While performing that insight leading to emergence with all effort, at that time, through the sequence of the Path, the defilements...
10:
Due to the maturation of the fulfillment of causes (hetusampatti), for the sake of attaining Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññutañāṇa), taking up the course of insight (vipassanā), and entering into various meditative attainments (samāpatti) at intervals, he applies the three characteristics to the mind and matter (nāmarūpa) as they have been defined. By the power of insight into states one by one (anupadadhamma-vipassanā), while contemplating the numerous and diverse formations (saṅkhāra), he extensively purifies the turns of contemplation through three million six hundred thousand modes. At that time, while the insight knowledge known as the Great Vajira Knowledge (mahāvajirañāṇa)—which is sharp, courageous, and clear—is proceeding as emergence-leading insight (vuṭṭhānagāminī), whenever he connects that insight with the Path, he then exhausts the one thousand five hundred defilements through the sequence of the Paths. He is said to attain Supreme Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi) at the moment of the Path of Arahantship, and is said to have attained it from the moment of the Fruition of Arahantship. Due to reaching the state of a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha (sammāsambuddha), the Ten Powers (dasabala), the Fourfold Intrepidity (vesārajja), and so on, also come into the possession of that Blessed One at that time. This is the practice leading to Supreme Enlightenment in terms of realization (abhisamaya).

In terms of its meaning, however, it refers to the accumulation of the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) occurring within the interval from the Great Resolve (mahābhinīhāra) up to the rebirth in the Tusita heaven. Everything that should be said in this regard has been stated in detail and in all its aspects in the Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary, and should be understood according to the method stated there.

Paccekabodhisattas also, having made the resolve for Paccekabodhi and gradually accumulating the requisites for Paccekasammāsambodhi, remain in their final existence at such a time. Due to their knowledge reaching maturity, they take up the sign of spiritual urgency (saṃveganimitta) that appears before them, and seeing the danger specifically in existence and so on, they distinguish through their self-evolved knowledge the process of becoming (pavatti), the cause of the process, the cessation of the process (nivatti), and the cause of cessation. By the method beginning with "He wisely attends, 'This is suffering'," they develop the meditation on the Four Noble Truths. Subduing the formations in accordance with their own resolve, they gradually arouse insight and, reaching the Path of Arahantship through the sequence of the Paths, they are said to realize Paccekasammāsambodhi. From the moment of the Fruition of Arahantship, they are known as Paccekabuddhas and become the supreme recipients of offerings (aggadakkhiṇeyya) for the world including the devas.

As for the disciples (sāvaka), having heard the discourse on the meditation of the Four Noble Truths from the Teacher or from their fellow practitioners, they follow the practice appropriate to that teaching at that very moment or at another time. Striving and exerting themselves, they arouse insight, and if, through the development of the practice, they [realize] the Truths...
11:
When they realize the Four Noble Truths by practicing to reach the stage of a Chief Disciple, a Great Disciple, or an Ordinary Disciple in accordance with their own resolve, they are said to attain Disciple Enlightenment (sāvakabodhi) at the moment of the Path of Arahantship. From that moment of the Fruition of Arahantship, they are known as Disciple-Buddhas (sāvakabuddha), the supreme recipients of offerings in the world including the devas. Thus, Paccekasammāsambodhi and Sāvakasambodhi should be understood in terms of realization (abhisamaya).

Regarding the realization of those Four Noble Truths, for the Great Bodhisattvas, the accumulation of the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) should be desired for a minimum duration of four incalculables (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand eons (kappa); for a medium duration, eight incalculables and a hundred thousand eons; and for a maximum duration, sixteen incalculables and a hundred thousand eons. These differences should be understood by way of those who emphasize wisdom (paññādhika), those who emphasize faith (saddhādhika), and those who emphasize energy (vīriyādhika). For the wisdom-emphasizing Bodhisattvas, faith is weak and wisdom is sharp; therefore, due to the clarity and subtlety of their wisdom in skill in means (upāyakosalla), their perfections (pāramī) reach fulfillment in a short time. For the faith-emphasizing Bodhisattvas, wisdom is moderate; therefore, their perfections reach fulfillment neither too quickly nor too slowly. For the energy-emphasizing Bodhisattvas, however, wisdom is weak; therefore, their perfections reach fulfillment only after a long time.

It is not so for the Paccekabodhisattas. For them, even if they are wisdom-emphasizing, the accumulation of the requisites for Paccekabodhi should be desired for two incalculables and a hundred thousand eons, and not less than that. The faith-emphasizing and energy-emphasizing Paccekabuddhas also realize Paccekasammāsambodhi only after passing a few more eons beyond the stated duration, but they do not reach the third incalculable.

Among the Disciple-Bodhisattvas, those who resolve for the state of a Chief Disciple must accumulate the requisites for one incalculable and a hundred thousand eons. For those who resolve for the state of a Great Disciple, as well as for the Mother, Father, Attendant, and Son of a Buddha, the requisites must be accumulated for only a hundred thousand eons.

In this regard, it is said:
"Humanity, the male sex, the cause (merit), the sight of a Teacher,
Going forth, the attainment of virtues, great dedication, and strong desire—
By the combination of these eight factors, the Resolve succeeds."

For the Great Bodhisattvas who have made their aspiration by combining these eight stated factors, from the time they make the Great Resolve, they are constantly devoted to acts such as giving (dāna). Even if they give great gifts daily like the gift of King Vessantara, or accumulate all the perfections such as virtue (sīla) appropriate to that giving, before reaching the aforementioned time limits, in the interval...
12:
There is no such thing as attaining Buddhahood [without the maturation of knowledge]. Why is that? Because the knowledge has not yet matured. Just as a crop that is to be completed in a specific time does not reach growth, prosperity, and abundance, nor does it bear grain and reach ripeness before that time; in the same way, the Buddha's knowledge reaches growth, prosperity, and abundance only through the aforementioned determined time, and reaches maturation by taking the 'embryo' of insight (vipassanā).

It is said: "Being human, perfection of gender, the sight of a passionless one (an Arahant), great dedication, and strong desire [for Bodhi]—these are the causes for the fulfillment of the aspiration (abhinīhāra)."

For the Paccekabodhisattas who have made their aspiration by combining these five factors, and for the Sāvakabodhisattas who have made their resolution (paṇidhāna) by virtue of an aspiration endowed with the two factors of "great dedication and desire for Bodhi," there is no such thing as attaining Paccekasambodhi-knowledge or the aforementioned Sāvakasambodhi-knowledge in the interval without reaching the time periods specified for each. Why is that? Because the knowledge has not yet matured. For these individuals, just as the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī) nurtured by the perfections of giving (dāna) and so forth for the Mahābodhisattas gradually takes the embryo of insight and reaches maturation to fulfill the Buddha's knowledge; in the same way, the perfection of wisdom nurtured by giving and so forth gradually takes the embryo of insight according to its capacity and reaches maturation to fulfill Paccekabodhi-knowledge and Sāvakabodhi-knowledge.

Indeed, those aspirants, through practice in giving, possess a disposition free from greed in their various existences, having a mind unattached to all sensual pleasures and a mind free from longing. Through practice in virtue (sīla), they have well-guarded bodies and speech, possessing extremely pure bodily and verbal actions, pure livelihood, guarded sense-doors, and moderation in eating; and by devotion to wakefulness, they concentrate their minds. Their devotion to wakefulness should be understood by way of the 'duty of going and returning' (gatapaccāgatikavatta).

For those practicing in this way, because they are endowed with the momentum of merit, the eight attainments (samāpatti), the five supernormal knowledges (abhiññā), the six supernormal knowledges, and the preliminary insight which is the foundation, come into their hands without difficulty. Energy (vīriya) and the others are included within these [practices of dāna, sīla, and bhāvanā]. Indeed, the great exertion in accumulating the merit of giving and so forth for the sake of Paccekabodhi or Sāvakabodhi is energy (vīriya). The endurance of what is contrary to that Bodhi is patience (khanti). The non-deviation in the undertaking of giving and virtue is truthfulness (sacca). The unshakable and firm resolution in all matters is determination (adhiṭṭhāna). The desire for the welfare of beings who are the objects of giving and virtue is loving-kindness (mettā). The equanimity toward the wrongdoings committed by beings...
13:
...this is the perfection of equanimity (upekkhā). In this way, when giving, virtue, and mental development (bhāvanā), as well as virtue, concentration, and wisdom, are accomplished, energy and the other perfections are also accomplished. That very practice of giving and so forth is called 'bhāvanā' (development) because it develops and permeates the mental continuum of those Bodhisattas for the sake of Paccekabodhi and Sāvakabodhi. Specifically, the practice of calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) occurring in a continuum well-prepared by giving, virtue, and so forth is called bhāvanā. Because of such exertion, those Bodhisattas become endowed with the attainment of the practice of calm and insight performed in the past. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Ānanda, there are these five benefits for one who has practiced meditation in the past (pubbayogāvacara). What are the five? Here, Ānanda, a person who has previously practiced meditation in this Dispensation attains the fruit of Arahantship early in this very life. If he does not attain it early in this life, then he attains it at the time of death. If not then, being a deva, he attains it. If not then, he becomes one of quick intuition (khippābhiñña) in the presence of the Buddhas. If not then, in the final period, he becomes a Paccekabuddha." (Thus it is stated in the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta Commentary of the Sutta Nipāta).

In this way, because they have a mind developed by the development of calm and insight, which is the preliminary practice permeated by the perfections, and by the development of the Path (maggabhāvanā) known as realization (abhisamaya), which is the practice leading to cessation (nirodha), the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha (Buddhasāvakas) are called 'bhāvitatta' (those of developed self/mind). Among them, the disciples of the Buddha (the Elders) are intended here.

Furthermore, by the phrase "sīhānaṃva" (like lions), the Theras' lion-like conduct is shown, demonstrating their invincibility by opposing states and their prevalence over them. By the phrase "sīhānaṃva nadantānaṃ... pe... gāthā" (the verses of those roaring like lions...), the lion's roar-like nature of the Elders' verses is shown, demonstrating that those verses cannot be overcome by other doctrines and that they prevail over those doctrines. By the word "bhāvitattānaṃ," the cause of both is explained. Because of their state of having a developed mind, the Elders are here called lion-like, and their verses are like a lion's roar. By the word "atthūpanāyikā," the benefit in overcoming is shown. In that context, the 'opposing states' of the Elders are the defilements (saṃkilesa). Overcoming those defilements is abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna) along with abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna) and abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna). When there is abandonment by eradication, abandonment by tranquilization (paṭipassaddhi-pahāna) and abandonment by deliverance (nissaraṇa-pahāna) are also accomplished. Because those Elders...
14:
Because of having a developed mind, they (the elders) are called 'Bhāvitatta'. Indeed, the Noble Ones (Ariyas) are said to be developing the meditation of heedfulness (appamāda-bhāvanā) at the moment of the Path (magga-khana); from the moment of the Fruition of Arahantship (arahatta-phala-khana) onwards, they are called 'Bhāvitatta' (those who have developed themselves). This is the intended meaning.

Among those (five types of abandonment), through abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna), their perfection of virtue (sīla-sampadā) is shown; through abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna), the perfection of concentration (samādhi-sampadā) is shown; through abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna), the perfection of wisdom (paññā-sampadā) is shown; and through the remaining two (abandonment by tranquilization and abandonment by escape), the fruits of those perfections are shown. Through virtue, the goodness in the beginning (ādi-kalyāṇa) of their practice is shown. According to the words, "What is the beginning of wholesome states? It is virtue that is well-purified," and "Established in virtue," and "The non-doing of all evil," virtue is indeed the goodness in the beginning of the practice because it brings about qualities such as non-remorse (avippaṭisāra). Through concentration, the goodness in the middle (majjhe-kalyāṇa) is shown. According to the words, "Developing the mind," and "The attainment of the wholesome," concentration is indeed the goodness in the middle of the practice because it brings about qualities such as the various supernormal powers (iddhividha). Through wisdom, the goodness in the end (pariyosāna-kalyāṇa) is shown. According to the words, "Purifying one's own mind," and "Developing wisdom," wisdom is indeed the end of the practice. Because wisdom is supreme among wholesome states and because it brings about the quality of steadfastness (tādi-bhāva) amidst the desirable and the undesirable, that wisdom alone is most excellent.

"Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the wind,
Even so, the wise are not shaken by blame and praise."
Thus it was taught.

Likewise, through the perfection of virtue, the state of possessing the three knowledges (tevijjā) is shown. Indeed, depending on the perfection of virtue, they reach the three knowledges. Through the perfection of concentration, the state of possessing the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā) is shown. Indeed, depending on the perfection of concentration, they reach the six supernormal powers. Through the perfection of wisdom, the state of possessing the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) is shown. Indeed, depending on the perfection of wisdom, they reach the four analytical insights. By saying they are endowed with virtue, concentration, and wisdom, it should be understood that this shows how among those elders, some possess the three knowledges, some possess the six supernormal powers, and some have reached the analytical insights.

Likewise, through the perfection of virtue, the avoidance of the extreme called devotion to sensual pleasure (kāmasukhallikānuyoga) is shown. Through the perfection of concentration, the avoidance of the extreme called devotion to self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga) is shown. Through the perfection of wisdom, the practice of the Middle Way (majjhimā-paṭipadā) is shown. Likewise, through the perfection of virtue, the abandonment of the transgressive defilements (vītikkama-kilesa) of those elders is shown. Through the perfection of concentration...
15:
(Through the perfection of concentration), the abandonment of obsessive defilements (pariyuṭṭhāna-pahāna) is shown; through the perfection of wisdom, the abandonment of latent tendencies (anusaya-pahāna) is shown. Or, through the perfection of virtue, the purification of the defilement of misconduct (duccarita-saṅkilesa) is shown; through the perfection of concentration, the purification of the defilement of craving (taṇhā-saṅkilesa) is shown; through the perfection of wisdom, the purification of the defilement of views (diṭṭhi-saṅkilesa) is shown. Alternatively, through abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna), their transcendence of the four woeful planes (apāya) is shown. Through abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna), the transcendence of the sense sphere (kāmadhātu) is shown; and through abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna), the transcendence of all existence (sabbabhava) is shown. This is how it should be understood.

In this term "Bhāvitattānaṃ," the three types of development—the development of virtue (sīla-bhāvanā), the development of the mind (citta-bhāvanā), and the development of wisdom (paññā-bhāvanā)—should be understood, as the development of the body (kāya-bhāvanā) is included within these three. The entire statement that the development of virtue is the beginning of the noble practice is similar to what was said before. Just as other groups of animals cannot endure the roar of lions, let alone overcome it—on the contrary, the lion's roar alone overcomes them—even so, the doctrines of outside sectarians (titthiya) cannot endure the doctrine of the elders, let alone overcome it; on the contrary, the doctrine of the elders (Theravāda) alone overcomes and suppresses those sectarian doctrines. Why is that? Because it proceeds as: "All conditioned things are impermanent; all conditioned things are suffering; all phenomena are non-self," and as "the element of Nibbāna." Indeed, by the nature of things, no one can make it otherwise, for it is irreversible. What should be said here will become clear later. Thus, the explanation of the meaning of the first verse should be understood in brief.

In the second verse, however, the following is the explanation of the meaning by way of showing the connection. Therein, the Venerable Ānanda, wishing to make known the verses of those elders, spoke the words beginning with "yathānāma" to praise those elders generally by name, by clan, and by quality. Specifically, however, it will become clear in the respective verses. In that second verse, "yathānāma" means those who are well-known by name, such as Subhūti, Mahākoṭṭhika, and so on. "Yathāgotta" means those who are well-known by their clan or birth, such as Gotama, Kassapa, and so on. "Yathādhammavihārī" means those who, not stopping at the mere limit of scriptural study (pariyatti), dwell having become frequent attainers of meditative attainments (samāpatti) as is appropriate. Alternatively, "yathādhammavihārī" means those who possess such qualities and who dwell in such a way; those who possess such qualities as virtue and so on, and who dwell in the divine abidings (dibba-vihāra) and so forth...
16:
The meaning is that they lived constantly and in such a dwelling (vihāra). Regarding the term "yathādhimuttā," it refers to those who have such an inclination; among the inclinations of faith (saddhādhimutti) and wisdom (paññādhimutti), they are called "yathādhimuttā" because they are inclined towards Nibbāna through the doors of emptiness (suññatamukha) and so forth, in the manner already described. Indeed, it is stated in the Dhammapada: “For those inclined towards Nibbāna, the taints (āsavas) come to an end” (Dhp. 226). Both of these should be understood by the power of the preliminary stage of meditation (pubbabhāga) before the attainment of Arahantship. This is because the aforementioned inclination occurs only in the stage prior to reaching Arahantship and not after. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “The man who is not credulous (who knows by himself), who knows the unmade (Nibbāna), who has cut the link (of saṃsāra)...” (Dhp. 97).

There is also a variant reading "yathāvimuttā," which means having such liberation among the liberations of wisdom (paññāvimutti) and liberation in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutti). "Sappaññā" refers to the wise who are endowed with the three types of wisdom: the wisdom of triple-rooted rebirth-linking (tihaituka-paṭisandhi-paññā), the wisdom of maintenance (pārihārika-paññā), and the wisdom of mental development (bhāvanā-paññā). "Vihariṃsu" means that because of being so wise, they lived in whatever comfortable dwelling they had obtained. "Atanditā" means being untiring, possessing the necessary energy and exertion to the best of one's ability in practicing for both one's own welfare and the welfare of others.

In this verse, by mentioning their names and clans, their state of being well-known and famous is shown. By mentioning the dwelling in the Dhamma (dhammavihāra), the fulfillment of virtue (sīlasampadā) and the fulfillment of concentration (samādhisampadā) are shown. By the phrase "yathādhimuttā sappaññā," the fulfillment of wisdom (paññāsampadā) is shown. By the word "atanditā," the fulfillment of energy (vīriyasampadā), which is the cause of the fulfillment of virtue and so forth, is shown. By the phrase "yathānāmā," the fact that these elders have well-known names is shown. By the phrase "yathāgottā," the attainment of the fulfillment of the lineage of a faith-follower (saddhānusārī) and a Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī) is shown. By the phrase "yathādhammavihārino" and so forth, the attainment of the qualities of virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation (sīla, samādhi, paññā, vimutti, vimuttiñāṇadassana) is shown. By the word "atanditā," the practice for the welfare of others by those elders who are established in the fulfillment of their own welfare is shown.

Alternatively, the word "yathānāmā" shows the names given to those elders by their teachers, as it mentions only the names. The word "yathāgottā" shows their status as true sons of noble family (kulaputta) by referring to their lineage. By mentioning the lineage in this way, their state of having gone forth out of faith is shown...
17:
(Continued from the previous page) ...is shown. The phrase "yathādhammavihārino" shows the fulfillment of conduct (caraṇa-sampadā) because it illustrates being endowed with the restraint of virtue (sīlasaṃvara) and so forth. The phrase "yathādhimuttā sappaññā" shows their fulfillment of knowledge (vijjā-sampadā) because it illustrates the attainment of the fulfillment of knowledge ending in the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya). The word "atanditā" shows the means (upāya) for attaining the fulfillment of knowledge and conduct. Alternatively, by the phrase "yathānāmā," only the fact that those elders have well-known names is shown. By the phrase "yathāgottā," the fulfillment of the latter two wheels (pacchimacakka-dvaya) is shown. Indeed, for a person who does not have a well-directed mind and who has not performed merit in the past, the attainment of the lineage of a faith-follower or a Dhamma-follower is not possible. By the phrase "yathādhammavihārino," the fulfillment of the former two wheels (purimacakka-dvaya) of those noble persons is shown. Indeed, for one living in an unsuitable place and for one lacking reliance on superior persons (sappurisūpanissaya), such special qualities are not possible. By the phrase "yathādhimuttā," the fulfillment of hearing the True Dhamma (saddhammasavana) is shown. Indeed, without the voice of another (paratoghosa), the penetration of the Four Noble Truths by disciples (sāvakas) is not possible. By the phrase "sappaññā atanditā," the unfailing cause of the aforementioned special qualities is shown, as it illustrates the beginning of the right method.

Another method: In the phrase "yathāgottā," by mentioning the lineage, the fulfillment of wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra) of those elders is shown, because wise reflection is possible for one endowed with the aforementioned lineage. In the phrase "yathādhammavihārino," by taking the dwelling in the Dhamma, the fulfillment of hearing the True Dhamma (saddhammasavana) is shown, because without hearing the True Dhamma, that dwelling is not possible. By the phrase "yathādhimuttā," the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhamma-paṭipadā) that has reached its peak is shown. By the word "sappaññā," the state of acting with clear comprehension (sampajāna-kāritā) in all matters is shown. By the word "atanditā," the untiring nature in the practice for the welfare and happiness of others by those elders who have already fulfilled their own welfare according to the stated method is shown. Furthermore, by the phrase "yathāgottā," the fulfillment of going for refuge is shown, as it mentions the lineage following faith. By the phrase "yathādhammavihārino," the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha) preceded by virtue is shown. By the phrase "yathādhimuttā sappaññā," the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha) and so forth are shown. Taking refuge is the beginning of the qualities of a disciple, concentration is the middle, and wisdom is the end; thus, by showing the beginning, middle, and end, all the qualities of a disciple are shown.

To show the practice by which those elders attained such an abundance of qualities, the words beginning with "tattha tattha vipassitvā" were spoken. "Tattha tattha" means in those various secluded places such as the foot of trees, mountain clefts, and so forth.
18:
In those various secluded places such as the foot of trees and mountain clefts. "Tattha tattha" means at those various times, such as when uttering the verses of inspiration (udāna) and so forth. "Vipassitvā" means having contemplated. Having fulfilled the Purification of View (diṭṭhivisuddhi) and the Purification by Overcoming Doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi) through the discernment of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa-vavatthāna) and the grasping of causes (paccaya-pariggaha); having reached the fifth purification, the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is and Is Not the Path (maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi), through the sequence of comprehension by groups (kalāpasammasana) and so forth; and having exerted effort in insight (vipassanā) by way of bringing it to the culmination of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way (paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi); "Phusitvā" means having reached and realized.

"Accutaṃ padaṃ" refers to Nibbāna. That Nibbāna is called "accuta" (deathless/unfailing) because it does not possess the nature of passing away itself, because it is the cause of non-passing away for those who have attained it, and because there is no passing away (cuti) in this Nibbāna. It is also called "pada" (state/path) because it is unmixed with conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhamma) and because it is that which should be attained by those who desire it.

"Katantaṃ" means the end of what was to be done, the end of the Noble Path (ariya-magga). The Noble Path attained by those Elders is called "kata" (done/made) because it is produced by its own causes. The Fruit (phala) which is the finality of that Noble Path is intended as "katanta." That "katanta" is the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). Alternatively, conditioned phenomena are called "kata" because they are produced and accomplished by causes; Nibbāna is called "katanta" because it is the state of escape from those conditioned phenomena. Reflecting on that Nibbāna, they contemplate their practice through the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana) regarding the Noble Fruit and Nibbāna, thinking: "Indeed, by attaining the Noble Path, I have attained this Noble Fruit; I have attained the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu)."

Alternatively, by way of the penetration of the Truths, the sixteen-fold task such as full understanding (pariññā) and so forth, which is to be done by a Noble One, is called "kata" because it has been accomplished and finalized by one standing in the Fruit of Arahantship; thus they reflect on that which has been done. By this term "katanta," the reflection on the abandoned defilements is shown. According to the previous method, the remaining reflections are shown, and thus the nineteen types of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā) are indicated.

In the phrase "imam-atthaṃ," the word "imaṃ" (this) is said because the meaning of all the verses of the Elders and Elderesses was present and manifest in the wisdom of himself and the other Great Elders, the reciters of the Dhamma (dhamma-saṅgāhaka), who had assembled there. "Atthaṃ" (meaning) refers to the meaning connected with the mundane and supramundane, which brings benefit to oneself and others, as expressed by the verses beginning with "My little hut is roofed."

"Abhāsisuṃ" means they spoke by way of composing verses. The connection is: "Listen to the verses of those who have developed themselves, which I am about to speak, which clarify that benefit and bring benefit to oneself." And those Great Elders thus...
19:
The Venerable Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, clarifies this meaning: that those Great Elders, through verses expressing their own right practice, manifest the state of the Sasana as being definitely leading out of suffering (niyyānika), and thereby urge others also toward that right practice. In so clarifying, it should be understood that he shows that praising those Elders with these verses and establishing them as the introduction (nidāna) to their words is indeed appropriate.

## The Explanation of the Introductory Verses is Finished.

## 1. The Book of the Ones (Ekakanipāta)

## 1. The First Chapter (Paṭhamavagga)

## 1. The Explanation of the Verses of Elder Subhūti

Now follows the explanation of the meaning of the Elders' verses proceeding in the manner beginning with "My little hut is roofed" (channā me kuṭikā). That explanation of meaning will be clear and easy to understand only if it is spoken after revealing the circumstances of the origin (atthuppatti) of those various verses. Therefore, I shall provide the explanation of meaning after revealing the circumstances of the origin in each instance.

In this regard, what is the origin of the verse "My little hut is roofed"? It is said—it is said that a hundred thousand aeons ago, before the Blessed One Padumuttara, the Protector of the World, had arisen, a son was born to a certain wealthy brahmin in the city named Haṃsavatī. They named the boy "Nanda the Youth" (Nanda Māṇava). When he reached the proper age, he studied the three Vedas, but seeing no essence in those Vedas, he went forth into the ascetic life of a seer (isi-pabbajjā) at the foot of a mountain together with his retinue of forty-four thousand youths. He produced the eight attainments (samāpatti) and the five mundane direct knowledges (abhiññā). He also taught the subjects of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) to his disciples. They too, before long, became attainers of jhāna.
20:
At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara, having arisen in the world, was staying near the city of Haṃsavatī. One day, at dawn, while surveying the world, he saw the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for the attainment of Arahatship of the matted-hair ascetic disciples of the ascetic Nanda, as well as the ascetic Nanda’s aspiration for the position of a disciple, being endowed with two qualities. Having attended to his physical needs early in the morning, he took his bowl and robes and, without consulting anyone else, wandered alone like a lion. While the disciples of the ascetic Nanda had gone to search for various fruits, the Buddha, thinking 'Let him know my Buddhahood,' descended from the sky and stood upon the earth right before the eyes of the ascetic Nanda who was watching.

The ascetic Nanda, seeing the power and majesty of the Blessed One and the perfection of his major and minor marks, reflected on the Vedic texts concerning marks and thought: 'A person endowed with such marks, if he lives the household life, will become a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch); if he goes forth into homelessness, he will become an Omniscient Buddha who has removed the veil of defilements in the world. This man is a Great Man (purisājāniya) and is undoubtedly a Buddha.' Having realized this, he went out to welcome him, paid homage with the five-point prostration, prepared a seat, and offered it. The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. The ascetic Nanda also took a seat suitable for himself and sat in a proper place.

At that time, forty-four thousand matted-hair ascetics returned to their teacher, bringing various exquisite and nutritious fruits. Seeing the Teacher and their own master seated, they said: 'Teacher, we have wandered thinking that there is no one greater than you in this world, but we think this man is even greater than you.' The ascetic Nanda replied: 'Dear sons, what are you saying? Do you wish to compare a mustard seed with Mount Sineru, which is one hundred and sixty-eight thousand yojanas high? Do not compare me with the Omniscient Buddha.'

Then those ascetics thought: 'If this person were inferior, our teacher would not have used such a comparison. How great indeed is this Great Man!' and they prostrated at his feet, paying homage with their heads. Then their teacher said: 'Dear sons, we do not have offerings suitable for Buddhas, and the Blessed One has arrived here at the time for alms-round. Therefore, let us offer what we can. Bring whatever exquisite fruits you have gathered.' Having had them brought, he washed his hands and personally placed them in the Tathāgata’s bowl.
21:
As soon as the Teacher accepted the fruits, the deities infused them with divine essence (ojā). The ascetic himself filtered the water and offered it. After the meal was finished and while the Teacher was seated, the ascetic called all his disciples and sat near the Teacher, engaging in pleasant conversation. The Teacher thought, 'Let the Saṅgha of monks come.' Knowing the Teacher’s thought, about one hundred thousand monks who were Arahants (khīṇāsava) arrived, paid homage to the Teacher, and stood in a suitable place.

The ascetic Nanda addressed his disciples: 'Dear sons, the seat where the Buddhas are sitting is low, and there are no seats yet for the hundred thousand monks. Today, it is proper for you to make a grand offering to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks. Bring flowers of beautiful color and fragrance from the foot of the mountain.' Because the range of psychic power is inconceivable, they brought flowers of beautiful color and fragrance in just a moment and prepared a flower-seat for the Buddhas measuring one yojana. For the chief disciples, it was three gāvutas; for the remaining monks, it varied from half a yojana downwards; and for the most junior monk, the flower-seat was one usabha in size.

When the seats had been thus prepared, the ascetic Nanda stood before the Blessed One with palms joined in reverence and said: 'Venerable Sir, for my long-term welfare and happiness, please ascend this flower-seat.' The Blessed One sat upon the flower-seat. When the Blessed One was thus seated, the monks, knowing the Teacher’s manner, sat in their respective appropriate seats. The ascetic Nanda took a large flower-umbrella and stood holding it over the Tathāgata’s head. The Blessed One, thinking 'May this offering of the ascetics be of great fruit,' entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Knowing that the Blessed One had entered the attainment, the monks also entered it.

While the Blessed One remained in the attainment of cessation for seven days, the disciples, at the time for alms-round, ate wild roots and fruits, and at other times, they stood with palms joined before the Buddhas. The ascetic Nanda, however, did not even go for alms but spent the seven days in the bliss of rapture (pīti-sukha) while holding the flower-umbrella.

The Blessed One, having emerged from the attainment of cessation, commanded a disciple who was endowed with two qualities—the factor of dwelling in peace (araṇavihāri) and the factor of being worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya)—saying: 'Give a discourse of appreciation for the flower-seats to the assembly of hermits.' That disciple, with a joyful heart like a great warrior who has received a great reward from a Universal Monarch, his own...
22: That disciple, remaining in his place, reflected upon the word of the Buddha known as the Tipiṭaka and performed the act of appreciation (anumodanā). At the conclusion of his discourse, the Teacher himself preached the Dhamma. At the end of the discourse, all forty-four thousand ascetics attained Arahantship. The Teacher stretched out his hand and said, "Come, monks (Etha bhikkhavo)." At that very moment, their hair and beards disappeared. The eight requisites appeared on their bodies, and they surrounded the Teacher like elders of sixty years' standing. However, Nanda the ascetic did not attain any distinction because his mind was distracted. From the time he began to listen to the Dhamma in the presence of that Elder Araṇavihārī, the thought arose: "Indeed, how wonderful! May I also, in the future, in the dispensation of a Buddha yet to arise, obtain the position attained by this disciple." Because of that thought, he was unable to penetrate the paths and fruits. Having paid homage to the Buddha and standing before him, he asked: "Venerable Sir, who is this monk in your dispensation who performed the appreciation for the flower-seats for the group of ascetics?" "This monk has attained the foremost rank (etadagga) both in the quality of dwelling in peace (araṇavihārī) and in the quality of being worthy of offerings," the Buddha replied. "Venerable Sir, by this merit of honor performed by me in holding the flower-parasol for seven days, I do not wish for any other prosperity. In the future, in the dispensation of a Buddha, may I become a disciple endowed with these two qualities like this Elder," he made the aspiration. The Teacher, sending forth his knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa) to see if the ascetic's aspiration would be fulfilled, saw that it would be fulfilled after one hundred thousand aeons. He said to Nanda the ascetic: "This aspiration of yours will not be in vain. In the future, after one hundred thousand aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. In the presence of that Buddha, it will be fulfilled." Having said this and preached a Dhamma talk, he departed into the sky surrounded by the community of monks. Nanda the ascetic stood with joined palms directed towards the Teacher and the community of monks until they were out of sight. Later, he approached the Teacher from time to time to listen to the Dhamma. Having maintained his meditative absorptions (jhāna) without decline, he was reborn in the Brahma realm upon passing away. After passing away from the Brahma realm, he became a forest-dweller (āraññaka) who practiced as an ascetic for another five hundred lives. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, he also ordained and lived in the forest, fulfilling the duty of going and returning (gatapaccāgata-vatta). It is said that without fulfilling this duty...
23:
...there is no one who reaches the status of a Great Disciple (Mahāsāvaka) without fulfilling the gatapaccāgata-vatta. The gatapaccāgata-vatta should be understood according to the method stated in the Sutta Commentaries. Having fulfilled the gatapaccāgata-vatta for twenty thousand years, he passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, a celestial realm of the sense sphere. This matter is stated in the Apadāna:

Not far from the Himālaya mountains, there is a mountain named Nisabha.
My hermitage was well-constructed, and a leaf-hut was well-fashioned.
At that time, I was an ascetic named Kosiya, of fierce austerity,
Living alone without a companion on Mount Nisabha.
Then, I did not eat fruits, roots, or leaves;
I lived only on fallen leaves.
Even if I were to lose my life, I would not corrupt my livelihood;
I gladdened my own mind and avoided wrong means of search.
Whenever a thought associated with lust arose in my mind,
I myself reflected upon it and subdued that lustful thought with a concentrated mind.
'You are lustful for objects of lust, angry at objects of anger,
And deluded by objects of delusion. Depart from this forest!
This is the dwelling of the pure, of ascetics free from stain.
Do not defile this pure place; depart from this forest!
If you become a householder and have a son,
Do not fail in both; depart from this forest!
Just as a torch from a funeral pyre (chavālāta) is of no use anywhere,
And is not regarded as wood in either village or forest,
So you are like that funeral torch. You are neither a layman nor a restrained monk.
Today, being free from both sides, depart from this forest!
Could such a thought occur to you? Who can know this thought of yours?
You are carrying the burden of my faith with much laziness.'
24:
'Wise men will loathe you as a city-dweller loathes excrement; the ascetics will always pull you back and urge you on.

The wise will speak of you as one who has transgressed the teaching; if you do not find companionship, how will you live?

Just as a powerful bull elephant approaches a sixty-year-old elephant in rut, leaking from three places, and drives him out of the herd—

Having been driven from the herd, he finds no happiness or pleasure, but becomes miserable and dejected, trembling as he broods—

Even so, the ascetics will drive you out, you of poor wisdom; having been driven out by those ascetics, you will not find happiness.

Like an elephant driven from the herd, whether by day or by night, pierced by the dart of grief, you will burn with distress.

Just as counterfeit gold does not shine in any way, so you, devoid of virtue, will not be able to meditate on any object.

Even if you live in a house, how will you live? You have no wealth stored up as an inheritance from your mother or father.

You would have to live in a house by doing work yourself and letting sweat pour from your body; such a life would not please you. (Practicing Dhamma) is better for you.'

In this way, I restrained the mind that had fallen into defilement on that Mount Nisabha; by speaking various Dhamma discourses, I prevented the mind from evil.

As I lived in this way, dwelling in heedfulness, thirty thousand years passed for me in the forest.

Seeing me delighting in heedfulness and seeking the highest goal, the Buddha Padumuttara came into my presence.

The Buddha, whose radiance was like the color of a golden ebony fruit, immeasurable and incomparable, peerless in appearance, then walked in the air.
25:
Like a Sāla tree in full bloom, like a streak of lightning amidst a dense cloud, the Buddha, peerless in wisdom, then walked in meditation in the sky.

Fearless like a lion, majestic like a noble elephant, and graceful like a king of tigers, He then walked in meditation in the sky.

With a complexion like pure gold, resembling glowing khadira embers, like a brilliant radiant gem, He then walked in meditation in the sky.

Resembling a pure silver mountain, like the full moon, and like the sun at midday, He then walked in meditation in the sky.

Seeing Him walking in meditation in the sky, I then thought: "Is this being a deva, or is he a human?"

"I have never heard of nor seen such a man on this earth. Surely, there are sacred verses; this person must be the Buddha."

Having thought thus, I clarified my mind and then gathered various flowers and scents.

Having prepared a pleasant and delightful seat of flowers, I spoke these words to the Buddha, the supreme trainer of men:

"O Hero, this seat suitable for You has been prepared by me. Gladdening my heart, please sit upon this seat of flowers."

Like a fearless lion, the Blessed One sat upon that noble seat of flowers for seven days and nights.

I remained standing in homage for seven days and nights. Having emerged from meditative absorption, the Teacher, supreme in the world, spoke these words in praise of my merit:

"Develop the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati), the supreme among meditations. By developing this mindfulness, you will fulfill the desires of your heart."
26:
"For thirty thousand aeons, you will delight in the deva realm. Eighty times you will be Sakka, the king of devas, and exercise divine sovereignty. A thousand times you will be a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch) in the land.

"You will enjoy the vast status of a regional king for an uncountable number of times. All this prosperity is the fruit of the recollection of the Buddha.

"While wandering through various lives, you will obtain great wealth. There will be no lack in your wealth; this is the fruit of the recollection of the Buddha.

"In one hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gautama by lineage, born of the Okkāka clan, will arise in the world.

"Renouncing eighty crores of wealth and many servants and workers, you will go forth into the dispensation of the Blessed One Gautama.

"Having pleased the Fully Enlightened One Gautama, the Bull of the Sakyans, you will become a disciple of the Teacher, known by the name Subhūti.

"Sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, He will place you in the foremost position in two things: in being worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya) and in the dwelling of peace (araṇavihāra)."

Having spoken these words, the Fully Enlightened One named Padumuttara, the Great Hero, rose into the sky like a king of swans in the air.

Instructed by the Protector of the World, I paid homage to the Tathāgata and, filled with joy, always developed the supreme recollection of the Buddha.

Due to that well-performed wholesome deed and my intentional aspiration, I left the human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Eighty times I was Sakka, the king of devas, and exercised divine sovereignty. A thousand times I was also a Cakkavatti king.

I enjoyed the vast status of a regional king for an uncountable number of times, experiencing excellent prosperity. This is the fruit of the recollection of the Buddha.
27:
"While wandering through various lives, I obtained great wealth and prosperity. There was no lack in my wealth; this is the fruit of the recollection of the Buddha.

"In the hundred thousand aeons since I performed that wholesome deed, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of the recollection of the Buddha.

"The four analytical insights, the eight liberations, and the six higher powers have been realized. The instruction of the Buddha has been carried out."

Thus the Venerable Subhūti Thera recited these verses.

In this way, after experiencing divine prosperity by being reborn repeatedly in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and upon passing away from there, he became a Cakkavatti king and a regional king many hundreds of times in the human world, enjoying grand human prosperity. Then, in the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn in the house of the merchant Sumana in Sāvatthī as the younger brother of Anāthapiṇḍika, and he was named "Subhūti."

At that time, our Blessed One had arisen in the world and, having set in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma, gradually went to Rājagaha. There, while benefiting the world through the acceptance of the Veḷuvana monastery and other acts, He resided in the Sītavana forest near Rājagaha. At that time, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika took trade goods from Sāvatthī and went to the house of his friend, the merchant of Rājagaha. Hearing of the arising of the Buddha, he approached the Teacher residing in the Sītavana forest. Upon the very first meeting, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and invited the Teacher to come to Sāvatthī. Subsequently, along the forty-five yojana path, he established monasteries at every yojana, spending one hundred thousand coins per yojana. In Sāvatthī, he purchased the garden land of Prince Jeta, measuring eight karīsas by the royal standard, by covering the ground with ten million coins, and there he built and offered a monastery for the Blessed One.

On the day the monastery was accepted, this householder Subhūti went together with the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika and, while listening to the Dhamma, gained faith and went forth as a monk. After his higher ordination, he mastered the two Mātikās, requested a meditation subject, and practiced the Dhamma of a recluse in the forest. By developing insight (vipassanā) based on the absorption of loving-kindness (metta-jhāna), he attained Arahantship. That Elder [preached] the Dhamma...
28:
When teaching the Dhamma, the Elder Subhūti taught without specific designation, following the method taught by the Teacher. Therefore, he became the foremost among those who dwell in peace (araṇavihārī). When wandering for alms, he would enter into the absorption of loving-kindness (mettā-jhāna) at every house, and upon emerging, he would accept the alms, thinking, "In this way, the giving will be of great fruit for the donors." Therefore, he became the foremost among those worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya). Thus the Blessed One said: "Monks, among my monk disciples who dwell in peace, Subhūti is the foremost; among those worthy of offerings, Subhūti is the foremost."

In this way, this Great Elder, established in the fruit of Arahantship and having reached the pinnacle of the results of the perfections (pāramīs) he had fulfilled, became well-known and distinguished in the world. Wandering through the countryside for the benefit of many, he eventually arrived at Rājagaha.

King Bimbisāra, hearing of the Elder's arrival, approached and paid homage to him, saying, "Venerable Sir, please stay right here; I will build a dwelling place for you." Having made this promise, he departed and then forgot. The Elder, not obtaining a dwelling, spent his time in the open air. Due to the Elder's spiritual power, it did not rain. The people, oppressed by the lack of rain, cried out at the gate of the King's palace. The King, investigating the reason why it was not raining, thought, "I suppose it is not raining because the Elder is staying in the open air." He then had a leaf-roofed hut built for the Elder and said, "Venerable Sir, please stay in this leaf-roofed hut," paid homage, and departed.

The Elder entered the small hut and sat down cross-legged on a grass mat. At that time, the rain began to drizzle slightly, but it did not yet fall in a steady stream. Then the Elder, wishing to allay the people's fear of drought and wanting to make known the absence of danger in his internal and external affairs, uttered this verse:

"My little hut is roofed, pleasant, and sheltered from the wind; rain, O sky-deva, as you please!
My mind is well-concentrated and liberated; I dwell with ardent effort; rain, O sky-deva!"

Thus he spoke this verse.
29:
In that verse, the word 'channa' first appears in the sense of 'suitable' or 'appropriate' in such passages as "That maiden is suitable (channā) for this youth" and "It is not suitable, it is not proper." In passages such as "Only the six sense bases (channaṃ), Phagguna," it appears in a specific numerical sense as a distinction of speech. In passages such as "Rain leaks through what is covered (channaṃ), it does not leak through what is open," it appears in the sense of a roof or covering. In passages such as "How shall I perform the dressing (nacchannopi) for you with that robe?" it appears in the sense of wearing or clothing. In passages such as "The Venerable Channa practices improper conduct," it appears as a designation (a name). In passages such as "Entirely covered, entirely enclosed," and "The hut is roofed (channā), the fire is kindled," it appears in the sense of covering with grass and so on. Here too, it should be understood only in the sense of covering with grass and so on. Therefore, it means it is well-covered with grass or leaves so that it does not rain in, there is no falling of rainwater, and it does not leak.

The word 'me' appears in the instrumental sense (karaṇa) in such passages as "The Dhamma attained by me (me) with difficulty is not fit to be taught now," meaning "by me" (mayā). In passages such as "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma in brief to me (me)," it appears in the dative sense (sampadāna), meaning "to me" (mayhaṃ). In passages such as "Monks, before my (me) enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta," it appears in the genitive sense (sāmi). Here too, it should be understood in the genitive sense, meaning "my." Although for the Arahants there is nothing to be cherished as "mine" because they are untainted by worldly conditions, they use the mere expression "I" and "mine" according to worldly convention. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "How then, monks, may my disciples be heirs of the Dhamma, not heirs of material things?"

The word 'kuṭikā' refers to the mother's womb, the physical body, and a shelter roofed with grass and leaves. This is true. In passages such as "You call the mother a little hut (kuṭikā), you call the wife a nest, you call the sons a cobweb, and I call craving a bond," the mother's womb is called 'kuṭikā'.
30:
“In the small hut which is a skeleton, sewn together with flesh and sinews; fie upon the foul-smelling thing, why do you cherish another's body?” (Theragāthā 1153)—in such verses, the physical body (karajakāya) is called a “little hut” (kuṭikā) because it is a collection of hair and so forth. In passages like “The hut of the sister of the Blessed One Kassapa leaks” and “A hut is either plastered inside or plastered outside,” it refers to a shelter thatched with grass, leaves, and so forth. Here too, it should be understood as such, since a leaf-hut (paṇṇasālā) is intended. Kuṭi itself is kuṭikā; an inconspicuous hut is called “kuṭikā.”
