The word sukha (happiness/pleasant), however, appears in the sense of pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) in passages such as “Having left behind both pleasure and pain, and even earlier, joy and grief.” It appears as the root of happiness (sukha-mūla) in “Happy is the arising of the Buddhas, happy is the teaching of the True Dhamma.” It appears as the cause of happiness (sukha-hetu) in “Monks, ‘merit’ is a name for happiness.” It appears as a pleasant object (sukhārammaṇa) in “Mahāli, because form is pleasant, follows after pleasure, and is immersed in pleasure.” It appears as non-affliction (abyāpajja) in “Cunda, these are dwellings in happiness in the present life in the discipline of the Noble One.” It appears as Nibbāna in “Nibbāna is the supreme bliss.” It appears as a place that is a condition for happiness (sukha-paccayaṭṭhāna) in “Monks, to the extent that it is not easy to describe by speech how happy the heavens are.” It appears in the sense of what is desirable, dear, and agreeable (iṭṭha, piya, manāpa) in “Having a happy result in the heavens, leading to the heavens.” Here too, it should be understood as a desirable object or a condition for happiness. That hut is called “pleasant” (sukhā) because it is prepared agreeably inside and out, making it comfortable for dwelling. Likewise, it is called sukhā because it is endowed with a pleasant climate—neither too cold nor too hot—and thus serves as a condition for physical and mental ease.

Nivātā means windless, or having windows closed with well-fitted shutters, thus free from the danger of wind. This explains the “pleasantness” of that hut. For in a drafty dwelling, a suitable climate cannot be obtained, whereas in a windless one, such a suitable climate (utu-sappāya) is obtainable.

Vassa means “Rain down well a stream of water repeatedly.” In the word devā, this term deva appears in the sense of a king, known as a conventional god (sammuti-deva), in the passage: “Great King, these eighty-four thousand cities, headed by the royal capital Kusāvatī, belong to you.”
31:
In this context, in passages such as “O King (deva), generate the desire and have regard for life,” the word deva refers to a king (khattiya) who is a conventional god (sammuti-deva). In passages such as “The gods of the Four Great Kings are beautiful and have much happiness,” it refers to gods by rebirth (upapatti-deva). In passages such as “The teaching of that God of gods (devātideva), the All-Seer,” it refers to gods by purity (visuddhi-deva). For when the Blessed One is called a god superior to the gods of purity (atideva), it is already stated that He is superior to the other [types of] gods. In passages such as “In the clear sky free from clouds,” it refers to the sky (ākāsa). In passages such as “The rain god (deva) does not rain down a stream of water properly from time to time,” it refers to a cloud or the rain god (pajjuñña). Here too, deva should be understood as a cloud or the rain god. For the Elder addresses the rain god, commanding it, “Rain!” Yathāsukhaṃ means as you please (at will). “Because of your raining, there is no external danger to me; therefore, rain as you wish,” he says, wishing to favor the beings who depend on rain for their livelihood.

Now, to show the absence of internal dangers, he said “Cittaṃ” and so forth. Therein, “My mind is well-concentrated” (cittaṃ me susamāhitaṃ) means my mind is very well and properly placed on the object with one-pointedness. And that concentration is not merely by the suppression (vikkhambhana) of the hindrances and so forth. Rather, it is specially liberated from all fetters included in the lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana) and the higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana), and from all defilements. It means it remains having abandoned them through abandonment by destruction (samuccheda-pahāna) and abandonment by tranquilization (paṭipassaddhi-pahāna). Ātāpī means one who possesses energy. He dwells having aroused energy for the sake of Fruition Attainment (phala-samāpatti) and for the sake of dwelling happily in the present life (diṭṭhadhamma-sukha-vihāra) through the practice of insight (vipassanā). He maintains his existence through divine dwellings (dibba-vihāra) and so forth, but not for the sake of abandoning defilements, because there are no defilements left to be abandoned. To show the meaning, “O rain god, just as I urged you to rain because of the absence of external dangers, so too [I urge you] because of the absence of internal dangers,” the Elder said again, “Rain, O god!”

Another method: Channā means covered or closed. Kuṭikā means the individual form (attabhāva). For that individual form is referred to by the name “body” (kāya) in passages such as: “Monks, for the person who is a collection of many parts, hindered by ignorance and joined with craving, this very body has arisen, and externally there is name-and-form.” “Monk, [bail out] this...”
32:
In verses such as, "O monk, bale out this boat [of the physical body]; when baled out, it will go lightly for you" (Dhammapada 66), it appears under the name "boat." In verses such as, "O house-builder [craving], you are seen; the ridge-pole is broken" (Dhammapada 154), it appears under the name "house." In verses such as, "A being, covered by many defilements, staying in a cave, is immersed in the delusive sensual pleasures" (Sutta Nipāta 778), it appears under the name "cave." In verses such as, "Faultless, with a white canopy, the one-wheeled chariot rolls on" (Udāna 65), it appears under the name "chariot." In verses such as, "You shall not build the house again" (Dhammapada 154), it appears under the name "house." In verses such as, "The hut is open, the fire is extinguished" (Sutta Nipāta 19), it appears under the name "house/hut." Therefore, here too, this physical body is called a "small hut" (kuṭikā).

Indeed, just as a small hut named "house" is obtained depending on wood and so forth, the physical body, which is obtained depending on the earth element and so forth designated as bones and so forth, and on phenomena such as contact (phassa) and so forth, is called a "small hut" because it is the dwelling place of the monkey-like mind. As it is said:

"An appearance like a hut of a skeleton, thus is the monkey's dwelling;
The monkey-like mind, having entered the small hut with five doors,
Goes around the doors, knocking again and again."

That small hut of the physical body is said to be "thatched" (channā) because it is well-closed and protected by the wisdom of the Elder, who is not leaked into by lust and so forth, which can pierce through by means of the three, six, or eight doors of non-restraint. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "I declare the restraint of the streams; they are closed by wisdom" (Sutta Nipāta 1041). Because it is thatched in the manner described, it is pleasant (sukhā) and has reached happiness because of the absence of the suffering of defilements and because of being endowed with spiritual happiness (nirāmisa-sukha). For that very reason, it is "windless" (nivātā), meaning it has a humble conduct because pride, intoxication, stubbornness, and rivalry have been destroyed. This method also shows: "For me, it is not accomplished merely by closing the defiling phenomena (saṃkilesa-dhamma); rather, it is accomplished because the mind is well-concentrated through the concentration of the Path of Arahatship, and because the mind is liberated from all fetters through the wisdom of the Path of Arahatship." Thus he said: "My mind is well-concentrated and liberated."

Even though this is so, he does not remain indifferent, thinking, "Now I have done what was to be done." Rather, he dwells with effort that burns away defilements (ātāpī), and being energetic in bringing welfare and happiness to the world including the devas, even during the time of wandering for alms, he dwells in every house only with the Brahma-vihāras. Therefore, "O King Pajunna, whether out of a desire to do what is pleasing to me or out of compassion for beings who live depending on rain, rain down well; let the stream of rain fall." In this way, the meaning should be understood here.
33:
In this verse, by the words "My small hut is thatched, pleasant, and windless," the Elder shows his training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), which is divided into mundane and supramundane. By the words "My mind is well-concentrated," he shows the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā). By the word "liberated," he shows the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). By the words "I dwell with effort," he shows the dwelling in happiness in the present life.

Alternatively, by the words "My small hut is thatched, pleasant, and windless," he shows the signless dwelling (animitta-vihāra) by way of removing signs such as permanence, etc., through the closing of the rain of defilements. By the words "My mind is well-concentrated," he shows the desireless dwelling (appaṇihita-vihāra). By the word "liberated," he shows the emptiness dwelling (suññata-vihāra). By the words "I dwell with effort," he shows the means of attaining those three dwellings. Or, by the first statement, he shows the abandonment of hatred; by the second, the abandonment of lust; and by the third, the abandonment of delusion. Likewise, by the second statement, or by the first and second, he shows the attainment of dwelling in the Dhamma (dhamma-vihāra). By the third, he shows the attainment of liberation (vimutti). By the words "I dwell with effort," it should be understood that he shows his tirelessness in practicing for the welfare of others.

Thus, because the dwellings in the Dhamma and so forth mentioned in the verse beginning with "Yathānāma" have been shown by this verse, in order to show the name among the name and clan not yet shown in that verse, it is said: "Thus [it was said] by the Venerable Subhūti..." and so forth. Elders who are well-known by name alone will be shown by name; those well-known by clan alone, by clan; and those well-known by both, by both. This Elder, however, is characterized by name and not so much by clan; therefore, it is said: "Thus [it was said] by the Venerable Subhūti." In that text, "itthaṃ" means in this way, in this manner. "Sudaṃ" is "su idaṃ," where the letter "i" is elided due to euphonic combination (sandhi). "Su" is a mere particle, and it should be connected as "this verse." "Āyasmā" is a term of endearment, a term of respect, reverence, and deference. "Subhūti" is the mention of the name. That Elder was pleasant to look at and inspiring because of his physical perfection, and also because of his perfection of qualities. Thus, because he was endowed with the beauty of physical parts and the beauty of the perfection of virtue and so forth, he was known as "Subhūti." Because of his association with firm qualities such as the essence of virtue, he is called "Thera" (Elder). "Abhāsittha" means he spoke.

Why do these Great Elders declare their own qualities? Having reflected on the supramundane Dhamma attained by themselves—which had never been attained before in this long journey of saṃsāra, which is extremely profound, exceedingly peaceful, and sublime—they do so by way of an inspired utterance (udāna) prompted by the surge of joy, and by way of manifesting the state of the Dispensation as leading out of suffering, being of very few desires...
35:
"...'I shall aspire.' (Thinking thus), that young man of good family, having given great offerings for seven days in that very manner, and after the meal was finished, opened his storehouse of cloth and placed excellent, fine cloth sufficient for a set of triple robes at the feet of the Blessed One. Having also offered triple robes to the hundred thousand bhikkhus, he approached the Blessed One and said: 'Venerable Sir, seven days ago from today, you appointed a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position. I, too, like that bhikkhu, wish to become the foremost among those who have attained the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) after ordaining in the Dispensation of a Buddha who will arise in the future.' Having said this, he prostrated at the feet of the Teacher and made his aspiration.

The Teacher, seeing that the young man's aspiration would be fulfilled, prophesied: 'In the future, a hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise in the world. In the Dispensation of that Buddha Gotama, your aspiration will be fulfilled.' This is also stated in the Apadāna (Ap. Thera. 2.54.221-250):

The Conqueror named Padumuttara, the Sage who knew all the worlds, the One with Vision, arose a hundred thousand aeons ago.
The Buddha, the advisor, the instructor, the savior of all living beings, and the one skilled in teaching, saved many people.
The compassionate one, the merciful one, the seeker of welfare for all living beings, established all the heretics who came to him in the Five Precepts.
Thus, the Dispensation was free from disturbance and devoid of heretics; it was adorned with Arahants who were such as those who had attained mastery (vasībhāva).
That Great Sage, who was fifty-eight cubits in height, resembled a golden pillar and was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
At that time, the lifespan was a hundred thousand years. Remaining for that long, the Buddha Padumuttara saved many people.
At that time, I was a Brahmin in the city of Haṃsāvatī, a master of the Vedas. Approaching the Supreme One of the World, I heard the Dhamma teaching.
Then the Hero, the Buddha, appointed a disciple who was proficient in the field of analytical insights (paṭisambhidā)—skilled in the analytical insights of meaning (attha), law (dhamma), language (nirutti), and intellect (paṭibhāna)...
36:
(The Buddha) placed that disciple in the foremost position (Etadagga); hearing those words, I was delighted and then served the excellent Conqueror (Jina) along with his disciples for seven days.

Having covered the Buddha, the Ocean of Wisdom, along with the Saṅgha, with cloths, I prostrated at his feet and aspired for that position (of Etadagga).

After I had so aspired, the Foremost of the World said: "Monks, look at this excellent brahmin, bowing at my feet, with a radiance like the interior of a lotus."

"This man aspires for the position of a monk (Etadagga) in the presence of the Buddha. Because of that faith, generosity, and hearing of the True Dhamma...

...he will be happy in all existences, and after wandering through various lives, in the future time, he will attain his heart's desire.

One hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka family, will arise in the world.

He will be an heir to that Buddha's Dhamma, a breast-born son, a true son of the Dhamma, a disciple of the Teacher named Koṭṭhika."

Hearing that prophecy, I was delighted; for the rest of my life, with a mind of loving-kindness, mindful, wise, and composed, I served the Conqueror.

By the result of that meritorious deed, and by my intention and aspiration, after leaving the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Three hundred times I exercised the kingship of the gods; five hundred times I was a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti).

I obtained vast regional kingship beyond counting; by the power of that merit, I was happy everywhere.

I wandered only in these two states of existence: as a god or as a human. I did not go to any other destination (gati); this is the fruit of well-performed merit.

I was born only in these two noble clans: Khattiya or Brahmin. I was never born in a low clan; this is the fruit of well-performed merit.
37:
When I reached my final birth, I was born in a wealthy Brahmin family in the city of Sāvatthī. My mother was named Candavatī, and my father was named Assalāyana. When the Buddha disciplined my father with complete purity, I then gained faith in the Sugata, left the household life, and ordained. The Venerable Moggallāna was my teacher, and the Venerable Sāriputta was my preceptor. Even while my hair was being shaved, wrong view was cut off along with its roots. While I was putting on the saffron robes, I attained the fruit of Arahantship. My wisdom became distinct and clear in the analytical knowledges of meaning (attha), doctrine (dhamma), language (nirutti), and perspicuity (paṭibhāna). Because of such qualities, the Buddha, the Chief of the World, placed me in the foremost position. When questioned by the Venerable Upatissa (Sāriputta), I was able to answer without doubt. Because of that quality, I am the foremost among those with the four analytical knowledges in the Buddha's Dispensation. My defilements have been burnt away; all existences have been uprooted. Like an elephant that has broken its bonds, I live without taints (āsavas). My coming into the presence of the Buddha was indeed a good coming. I have attained the three true knowledges; I have fulfilled the Buddha's Dispensation. I have realized the four analytical knowledges, the eight liberations, and the six higher powers; I have fulfilled the Buddha's Dispensation.

Thus, that noble son, accumulating the requisites of merit and wisdom in various lives and wandering among devas and humans, was born in a wealthy Brahmin family in Sāvatthī when our Buddha appeared. They named him Koṭṭhika-tissa. When he came of age, he studied the three Vedas and mastered the brahminical arts. One day, he went to the presence of the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and ordained. From the time he became a monk, he practiced insight meditation (vipassanā) and attained the fruit of Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Being one who had mastered the four analytical knowledges, whenever he approached famous Great Elders or the Buddha to ask questions, he asked questions only regarding the analytical knowledges. Thus, this Elder became the foremost among those who attained the analytical knowledges, both because of the special merit he had performed in the presence of previous Buddhas and because of his mastery through practice. Then, the Buddha, on the occasion of the arising of the Mahāvedalla Sutta, placed that Elder in the foremost position among those who have attained the analytical knowledges. He said, "Monks, among my disciples who have attained the analytical knowledges, Mahākoṭṭhika is the foremost." Later, while experiencing the bliss of liberation, the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika uttered this inspired verse: "He is calm in faculties, restrained from evil, speaks with wisdom and reflection, and is not distracted, standing firm in pure virtue. Such a person can shake off evil unwholesome states as the wind shakes off leaves." This is the meaning of the verse beginning with "Upasanto".
38: Mahākoṭṭhika Thera became the foremost among those who had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) because of his past merit and his mastery through practice. Then, the Teacher, having made the Mahāvedalla Sutta the occasion for his appointment, placed him in the foremost position among those who had attained the analytical knowledges: "Monks, among my monk disciples who have attained the analytical knowledges, this Mahākoṭṭhika is the foremost." At a later time, while experiencing the bliss of liberation, he uttered this verse as an inspired utterance (udāna): "Calm, ceased, speaking with wisdom, not restless, he shakes off evil states as the wind shakes leaves from a tree." Thus did the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika Thera speak this verse. Therein, 'upasanto' (calm) means one who is calm because of the calming of the six sense bases, mind being the sixth, making them free from indulgence. 'Uparato' (ceased) means one who has desisted and abstained from all evil-doing. 'Mantabhāṇī' (speaking with wisdom): wisdom is called 'mantā'; he is 'mantabhāṇī' because he speaks after investigating with that wisdom. The meaning is that he speaks without abandoning the quality of being a speaker at the right time (kālavādī) and so forth. Or, he is 'mantabhāṇī' because he speaks by way of wise speech; the meaning is that, apart from poorly spoken words, he speaks only well-spoken words endowed with the four factors by virtue of his own speech. 'Anuddhato' (not restless) means not puffed up because of not exalting himself by way of birth and so forth. Alternatively, he is 'upasanto' through the calming of the three bodily misconducts and abstaining from them; 'uparato' through the ceasing and abandoning of the three mental misconducts; 'mantabhāṇī' through the non-occurrence of the four verbal misconducts and by being a speaker of measured words; 'anuddhato' due to the absence of restlessness (uddhacca) that arises because of the three types of misconduct. Thus, established in pure virtue by abandoning the three types of misconduct, and concentrated by abandoning restlessness, and making that very concentration the proximate cause, he develops insight and, through the sequence of the path, shakes off evil states. Or, he discards all defiling states, which are called 'evil' (pāpaka) in the sense of being base, through the power of eradication (samuccheda). How? "As the wind shakes leaves from a tree." Just as the wind shakes off the old, withered leaves of a tree, removing them by separating them from their bond, so too, standing in the aforementioned practice, he removes evil states from his own continuity. It should be understood that this verse is also an explanation of his attainment of Arahantship (aññābyākaraṇa) by way of referring to another.
39:
In this verse, by mentioning the abandoning of bodily and verbal misconduct, he shows the purity of application (payogasuddhi); by mentioning the abandoning of mental misconduct, he shows the purity of intention (āsayasuddhi). For one whose application and intention are thus purified, by the word "anuddhato" (unagitated), which signifies the absence of restlessness (uddhacca), he shows the abandoning of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) that occur together with it. Among these, through the purity of application, the perfection of virtue (sīla) is clarified; through the purity of intention, the acquisition of states helpful to the development of serenity (samatha) is clarified; through the abandoning of hindrances, the development of concentration (samādhi) is clarified; and by the words "dhunāti pāpake dhamme" (he shakes off evil states), the development of wisdom (paññā) is clarified.

In this way, the three trainings such as the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the Dispensation (Sāsana) which is good in three ways, the three types of abandoning such as abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna), the practice of the Middle Way (majjhima-paṭipadā) by avoiding the two extremes, and the means of transcending the realms of misery and so forth, should be extracted and applied accordingly. In this same manner, the application of meaning in the remaining verses should also be understood accordingly. However, I shall only explain the meanings that have not been mentioned before in those various verses. The words "itthaṃ sudaṃ āyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko" (thus the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika...) are words of praise, just like the words "yathā taṃ mahāmoggallāno" (as did the Great Moggallāna).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Mahākoṭṭhika is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kaṅkhārevata

The verse beginning with "Paññaṃ imaṃ passa" (Behold this wisdom) belongs to the Venerable Elder Kaṅkhārevata. What is its origin? This Elder was also born into a wealthy Brahmin family in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara. One day, while the Buddha was teaching the Dhamma, he went to the monastery with a great crowd as mentioned above. Standing at the edge of the assembly and listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those who delight in meditation (jhāna). He thought, "It would be good if I too could become such a person in the future." At the end of the teaching, he invited the Teacher and, having performed a great act of honor as mentioned above, he said to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, I do not aspire to any other fortune through this meritorious deed. Just as that monk was appointed by you seven days ago to the foremost position among those who meditate, may I also become the foremost among those who meditate in the Dispensation of a future Buddha."

The Teacher, looking into the future and seeing that his wish would be fulfilled, said, "In the future, at the end of a hundred thousand aeons..."
40:
“The Buddha named Gotama will arise; in the dispensation of that Blessed One, you will be the foremost among those who practice jhāna,” he prophesied and then departed.

Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, he was reborn in a wealthy family in the city of Sāvatthī during the time of our Blessed One. Later, in the afternoon, he went to the monastery along with a great crowd of people going to listen to the Dhamma. Standing at the edge of the assembly, he heard the Dhamma discourse of the Dasabala, gained faith, went forth, and received the higher ordination (upasampadā). Having learned the meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) and practiced the preliminary exercises for jhāna, he became an attainer of jhāna. Using jhāna as a basis, he attained Arahantship.

That elder mostly entered the attainments (samāpatti) that the Blessed One entered, and became one who had mastered the jhānas throughout the day and night. Then the Teacher placed him in the foremost position among those who practice jhāna, saying: “Monks, among my monk disciples who practice jhāna, this Kankhārevata is the foremost.” This is also stated in the Apadāna:

Padumuttara, the Victor, the Visionary in all things,
The Leader, arose a hundred thousand aeons from now.

With a jaw like a lion's, a voice like Brahmā's,
A sound like a swan's or a drum's, a gait like a noble elephant's,
And a radiance exceeding that of the moon and sun.

Of great wisdom, great effort, great jhāna, great power,
Of great compassion, the Protector, the dispeller of great darkness.

Once, that Supreme One of the three worlds, the Buddha,
The Sage who knows the dispositions of beings, preached the Dhamma
While disciplining many who were to be tamed.

Praising a monk who was a meditator, delighted in jhāna, heroic,
Peaceful, and undisturbed, the Victor delighted the people in the assembly.

At that time, I was a brahmin in Haṃsavatī, a master of the Vedas.
Having heard the Dhamma, I was joyful and aspired to that position.

Then the Victor, the Leader, prophesied in the midst of the Saṅgha:
“Be joyful, O Brahmin, you shall obtain that heart's desire.”
41:
“A hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan,
Born of the Okkāka family, will arise in the world.

His heir in the Dhamma, his legitimate son, created by the Dhamma,
A disciple of the Teacher named Revata, will come to be.”

Due to that well-performed deed, and through my intention and aspiration,
I abandoned the human body and went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Now, in my final birth, I was born in the prosperous and wealthy Koliyan clan,
Endowed with noble lineage.

When the Buddha preached the Dhamma in Kapilavatthu,
I then gained confidence in the Sugata and went forth into homelessness.

I had many doubts regarding various matters of what is allowable and what is not.
The Buddha dispelled all those doubts by preaching the supreme Dhamma.

Then, having crossed over the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra), I dwelt delighting in the bliss of jhāna.
At that time, the Buddha saw me and spoke these words:

‘Whatever doubts there are, whether here or elsewhere, whether known by oneself or known by others;
Those who practice jhāna, being ardent and living the holy life, abandon them all.’

The meritorious deed performed a hundred thousand aeons ago shows its fruit to me here.
Like an arrow released with great speed, I have burnt up my defilements.

Then, seeing my delight in jhāna, the Buddha, the Sage who has reached the end of the world,
Who knows the entire world and possesses great wisdom, designated me
As the foremost among the monks who practice jhāna.

My defilements are burnt up; all births are uprooted.
Like an elephant that has broken its bonds, I live without taints (anāsava), having cut the bond of defilements.

Indeed, my coming to the presence of the Buddha was good.
I have attained the three knowledges; the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.
42:
In this world of humans and in other worlds of devas, all doubts exist. Those who are habitually meditative, through their own wisdom or the wisdom of others, can abandon all those doubts. Possessing effort that burns away defilements, they practice the holy life. The wholesome kamma performed a hundred thousand aeons ago bears fruit in this final birth. Like the momentum of a well-released arrow, I have destroyed the defilements.

Having thus destroyed the defilements, seeing me delighting in meditation, the Blessed One—who has reached the end of the world, who knows the entire world, and who possesses great wisdom—declared me the foremost among the monks who enter into meditative absorption. My defilements are destroyed; all existences are uprooted. Like an elephant freed from its bonds, I live without taints (āsavas), having cut the bond of defilements.

My coming to the presence of the Blessed One was a good coming. In the presence of the Blessed One, I have attained the three knowledges (tevijjā) and carried out the Buddha's instruction. The four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), the eight liberations (vimokkha), and the six supernormal powers (abhiññā) have been realized; the Buddha's instruction has been carried out.

The Great Elder, whose task was thus completed, reflected on how his mind was formerly oppressed by doubt for a long time, and how he is now entirely free from doubt. Thinking, 'How wonderful is the power of my Teacher's teaching! Because of that power, I am now free from doubt and have a peaceful mind within,' he felt great reverence. Desiring to praise the Blessed One's wisdom, he uttered this verse: 'Look at this wisdom!'

In that verse, 'paññā' (wisdom) is so called because it knows in various ways (pakārena jānāti) and makes others know in various ways (pakārehi ñāpeti). It means He knows the various inclinations (āsaya), underlying tendencies (anusaya), temperaments (carita), and dispositions (adhimutti) of beings to be guided, as well as the various aspects of ultimate realities such as wholesome states and aggregates to be taught. He penetrates them according to their true nature and makes them known through those various ways. Here, the Teacher's knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa) is intended; therefore, he said 'this wisdom.' He spoke of 'this' by taking that knowledge of teaching, which was accomplished in him through the power of the teaching, as if it were manifest before his eyes through the grasp of the method. Or, to the extent that the Teacher's knowledge of teaching is grasped by the disciples through the method, to that same extent, the knowledge of penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa) in one's own sphere is also grasped through the method. Therefore, the Venerable Sāriputta said: 'Moreover, Bhante, the sequence of the Dhamma (dhammanvaya) is known by me.'

'Look!' (passa) is an exclamation made out of wonder without a specific addressee, or it is addressing one's own mind. Just as the Blessed One, when uttering an inspired utterance (udāna), said: 'Look at this world, oppressed by ignorance, being that delights in being, not yet released from existence.'

'Tathāgatānaṃ' means the wisdom of the Buddhas, who are called 'Tathāgata' because of meanings such as coming truly. He is called 'Tathāgata' for eight reasons: because He has come thus (tathā āgato), because He has gone thus (tathā gato), because He has arrived at the true characteristic (tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato), because He has awakened to the true dhammas as they really are (tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddho), because of seeing truly (tathadassitāya), because of speaking truly (tathavāditāya), because of acting truly (tathākāritāya), and because of overcoming (abhibhavanaṭṭhena). Furthermore, He is called 'Tathāgata' because He has come in a true manner, gone in a true manner, arrived at the true characteristic, reached true dhammas, is of such a nature, has proceeded in such a manner, has arrived through such causes, and is of a true nature. This is the summary found in the Commentary on the Theragāthā. The detailed explanation should be understood in this same way in the Udāna Commentary and the Itivuttaka Commentary named Paramatthadīpanī.

Now, to show the supreme quality of the Venerable Vakkali's wisdom, the words beginning with 'How is fire?' are spoken. There, the word 'How' is a term of comparison. This word 'How' indicates the state of being a simile for the object of comparison. The word 'burnt' shows the connection with the object of comparison. The word 'extinguishes' indicates the time of the action performed. This is the intended meaning in this verse.
43:
The Blessed One is called Tathāgata for eight reasons: because he has come in such a way, because he has gone in such a way, because he has such characteristics, because he has arrived in such a way, and because he has an unerring nature. What is stated here is only a brief summary. The detailed explanation should be understood according to the method already mentioned in the Udāna Commentary and the Itivuttaka Commentary, both titled Paramatthadīpanī.

Now, to show the unique and extraordinary quality of his wisdom, the words beginning with "Aggī yathā" are spoken. "Yathā aggī" is a metaphorical expression. The word "yathā" indicates the nature of the simile. The word "pajjalito" (blazing) shows the connection with the object of comparison. The word "nisīthe" (at midnight) shows the time when the action occurs. The meaning here is: just as a fire blazing on high ground in the fourfold darkness of the night remains dispelling the mass of darkness in that place, even so, behold this wisdom of the Tathāgatas, known as the knowledge of teaching, which completely dispels the darkness of doubt in beings who are to be guided (veneyya).

Because they give the light of knowledge through the elegance of their teaching, they are called "Ālokadā" (Givers of Light). Because they give the eye of wisdom, they are called "Cakkhudadā" (Givers of Sight). Wishing to show both of these as the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for dispelling doubt, it is said: "Those [Tathāgatas] dispel the doubts of those who have come to them." Those Tathāgatas, by the power of their teaching, completely dispel and destroy the sixteen types of doubt that arise in the veneyya beings who have approached them, such as "Was I in the past?", as well as the eight types of doubt (vicikicchā) such as "He doubts the Buddha, he doubts the Dhamma." As for the doubts known as vinaya-kukkucca (scrupulousness regarding discipline), they are removed only by the removal of those [specific] disciplinary issues.

Another method: Just as a fire blazing in the night with very sharp flames, standing on a high place, dispels darkness and makes clear what is even and uneven merely by providing radiance, thus being a giver of light; but for those standing very near, it is called a giver of sight because it performs the function of the eye by making the fire itself very clear. Even so, the Tathāgatas are "Ālokadā" for those who stand far from their Dhamma-kāya and have not performed prior merit, dispelling the darkness of delusion (moha) with the light of wisdom and making clear the unevenness and evenness of bodily conduct, etc. For those standing near who have performed prior merit, they are "Cakkhudadā" by arising the Dhamma-eye. Those...

## The explanation of the verse of Venerable Kankhārevata is finished.
44:
The construction of the meaning is: "Behold the extraordinary wisdom of those Tathāgatas, who dispel the doubts of those like me who are full of doubt and have come into the range of their speech, by arising the Noble Path (ariya-magga)." Thus, this verse is also an Aññābyākaraṇa-gāthā (a verse declaring the attainment of Arahatship) as the Elder demonstrates the dispelling of his own doubts. Indeed, during his time as a worldling (puthujjana), that Elder was scrupulous even in matters that were allowable, and because he was full of doubts, he was known as "Kankhārevata" (Revata the Doubter). Later, even at the time of being an Arahant, he was still referred to by that same name. Therefore, it is said: "Thus the Venerable Kankhārevata spoke this verse." The meaning of those words is just as already stated.

## The commentary on the verse of Venerable Kankhārevata is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Verse of Venerable Puṇṇa

The verse beginning with "Sabbhireva samāsetha" is the verse of Venerable Puṇṇa. What is the background story? It is said that before the appearance of the Buddha Padumuttara, he was born into a wealthy Brahmin family in the city of Haṃsavatī. Gradually reaching the age of discretion, when the Buddha appeared in the world, he went to the monastery one day with a great crowd during the time of the Buddha's Dhamma teaching. Sitting at the edge of the assembly while listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position (aggaṭṭhāna) among the preachers of Dhamma (dhammakathika). He thought, "It is proper for me also to become like this in the future."

When the assembly departed at the end of the teaching, he approached the Teacher, invited him, and after performing a great offering in the manner already described, he said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, by this meritorious deed of service, I do not aspire for any other prosperity. Just as that monk was appointed to the foremost position among the preachers of Dhamma seven days from now, may I also become the foremost among the monks who are preachers of Dhamma in the dispensation of a future Buddha." Thus he made his aspiration. The Teacher, looking into the future and seeing the fulfillment of his aspiration, prophesied: "One hundred thousand aeons (kappa) from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. In his dispensation, you will ordain and become the foremost among the preachers of Dhamma."
45: That man, having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life in that existence, passed away from there. While accumulating the requisites of merit and knowledge for a hundred thousand aeons and wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he was reborn during the time of our Blessed One in a wealthy Brahmin family in the Brahmin village named Doṇavatthu, not far from the city of Kapilavatthu, as the nephew of the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña. On the day of his naming ceremony, they gave him the name "Punna." After the Teacher attained Enlightenment and set the noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion, Punna eventually went to Rājagaha. While the Teacher was residing there, Punna went forth in the presence of the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña and received higher ordination. Having performed all the preliminary duties of a monk and applying himself to meditation, he thought, "I will go to the Blessed One only after reaching the goal of the monkhood." Thus, he did not go to the Teacher with his uncle but remained near Kapilavatthu. Practicing with wise reflection and exerting himself in insight meditation, he attained Arahantship before long. This account is also stated in the Apadāna: "I was once a teacher, a master of the mantras, who had reached the further shore of the three Vedas. Surrounded by my disciples, I approached the Best of Men. Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, the Recipient of Offerings, praised my meritorious deeds in brief, O Great Sage. Having heard that Dhamma and having paid homage to the Teacher, I raised my joined palms and departed towards the south. Having heard the Dhamma taught in brief, I explained it in detail to my disciples. All my disciples were delighted upon hearing my speech. Dispelling their own views, they gained confidence in the Buddha. I also teach in that same manner, both in brief and in detail. I am an expert in the method of Abhidhamma, and through the purity of the Kathāvatthu, I make all people understand; I dwell free from the taints."
46: "Five hundred aeons ago, there were four Universal Monarchs named Suppakāsaka, endowed with the seven treasures, who ruled over the four great islands. I have realized the four analytical insights, the eight liberations, and the six higher powers; I have fulfilled the teaching of the Buddha." There were five hundred young men of good family who went forth under the Elder Punna. Since the Elder himself was a possessor of the ten subjects of talk, he also instructed those five hundred disciples with the ten subjects of talk. Abiding by his instruction, they all attained Arahantship. Realizing that they had reached the summit of the monk's life, they approached their preceptor and said, "Venerable Sir, our task has reached its summit, and we have also mastered the ten subjects of talk. Now is the time for us to see the One of Ten Powers." Hearing their words, the Elder thought, "The Teacher knows that I possess the ten subjects of talk. When I teach the Dhamma, I do so without omitting the ten subjects of talk. If I go, all these monks will surround me as I travel. It is not appropriate for me to go and see the Blessed One in such a large group. Let these monks go and see Him first." He then told those monks, "Friends, you go ahead and see the Tathāgata. Pay homage to His feet in my name. I will follow later by the same path you take." All those elders, who were residents of the Blessed One's birthplace, were Arahants who had destroyed the taints and were masters of the ten subjects of talk. Accepting their preceptor's instruction and paying homage to him, they gradually wandered on dhutanga and, after traveling a distance of sixty yojanas, arrived at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha. They paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down at a respectful distance. It is the custom of the Blessed Buddhas to exchange pleasantries with visiting monks. Therefore, the Blessed One engaged in sweet conversation with them, saying, "Monks, is it tolerable? Is it maintainable?" and so on. Then He asked, "Monks, from where have you come?" When they replied, "From the birthplace," He asked about the monk who possessed the ten subjects of talk: "Monks, who among the fellow practitioners living in the birthplace is so highly regarded that it is said, 'He is himself of few desires and speaks to the monks about fewness of desires'?" They reported, "Venerable Sir, it is the Venerable Punna, the son of the Brahmin lady Mantāṇī." Upon hearing this account, the Venerable Sāriputta desired to see the Elder. Then the Teacher went from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī...
47:
The Blessed One went to Sāvatthī. Elder Puṇṇa, hearing that the Blessed One had arrived there, thought, "I will see the Teacher," and went, reaching the Tathāgata right inside the Gandhakuti. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. After hearing the Dhamma, the Elder paid homage to the Blessed One and went to the Andhavana forest for seclusion, sitting at the foot of a certain tree for the day's abiding.

Venerable Sāriputta, hearing of his arrival, went looking ahead, noted the opportunity, approached the Elder sitting at the foot of the tree, exchanged pleasantries, and asked him about the sequence of the Seven Stages of Purification (Satta-visuddhi). Elder Puṇṇa, answering every question asked by Venerable Sāriputta, delighted his mind with the simile of the seven relay chariots (Rathavinīta). Both Elders rejoiced in each other's well-spoken words. Later, the Teacher, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, declared: "Monks, among my monk disciples who are Dhamma preachers, this Puṇṇa is the foremost," thus placing Elder Puṇṇa in the pre-eminent position of Dhamma preachers. One day, reflecting on his attainment of liberation, the fruit of Arahantship, he thought: "Depending on the Teacher, I and many other beings have been liberated from the suffering of the round of rebirths; indeed, association with the virtuous is of great benefit." Filled with joy and happiness, by the power of inspired utterance, he recited the verse beginning with "Sabbhireva samāsetha" (One should associate only with the virtuous).

In that verse, "Sabbhireva" means only with the virtuous (sappurisa). Here, by the word "Santo", the Noble Ones (ariyas) such as the Buddha are intended. These Buddhas and Noble Ones are called "Santa" (peaceful) and "Sappurisa" (virtuous) because they have completely abandoned the practices of the unvirtuous, reached the pinnacle of the True Dhamma, and are exceedingly praiseworthy. "Samāsetha" means one should associate well, one should live together. It means that by attending on those virtuous ones, desiring to hear their words, and following their observed conduct, one should live in association with them.

"Paṇḍitehatthadassibhi" is praise for those virtuous ones. Wisdom is called "paṇḍā"; because this wisdom has arisen in these persons, they are called "paṇḍita" (wise). For that very reason, because they see the various benefits such as one's own benefit correctly and without distortion, they are called "atthadassī" (seers of the benefit). One should associate with those wise seers of the benefit. Why should one associate? Because those virtuous wise ones—or because for those who associate well with those wise ones—it is of certain benefit; because it is called "attha" (benefit/meaning) as it is to be attained only through the knowledge of the path and so on; because it is called "mahanta" (great) due to having great qualities and being peaceful; because it is called "gambhīra" (deep) due to its nature of being difficult to penetrate and being the object of deep knowledge; because it is called "duddasa" (difficult to see) as it cannot be seen by those with low desires and is to be seen with difficulty by others...
48:
...The Four Noble Truths are subtle (nipuṇa) because of their subtle nature and because they are the object of subtle knowledge. Because of such a subtle and fine nature, Nibbāna is called "aṇu" (minute/subtle). Or, it is called "attha" (ultimate meaning) because of its undistorted ultimate nature. It is called "mahanta" (great) because it brings about the state of a Noble One and because it is a sign of greatness. It is called "gambhīra" (deep) because of its non-obvious nature. It is called "duddasa" (difficult to see) because it is seen with hardship and cannot be seen through mere ease. The Four Noble Truths are said to be difficult to see because they are deep, and deep because they are difficult to see. The wise (dhīra) thoroughly attain these Four Noble Truths, especially the subtle Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). The wise, endowed with fortitude, having applied themselves to the meditation on the Four Noble Truths, attain them perfectly.

"Appamatta" (diligent) means fulfilling the practice of diligence without being devoid of mindfulness in all postures. "Vicakkhaṇā" (discerning) means being skilled and proficient in the development of insight (vipassanā-bhāvanā). Therefore, the connection is: "One should associate only with the virtuous". Alternatively, the term "Paṇḍitehatthadassibhi" is in the ablative case. The connection is: because the wise, diligent, and discerning ones thoroughly attain the benefit endowed with great distinctions together with the wise seers of the benefit, therefore "one should associate only with such virtuous ones". Thus, this verse was also an "Aññābyākaraṇa" verse (a declaration of gnosis) by showing the Elder's penetration of the truth.

## The Commentary on the Verse of Elder Puṇṇa is Finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Verse of Elder Dabba

The verse beginning with "Yo duddamiyo" is the verse of Venerable Elder Dabba. What is its origin? This Elder also, having been reborn in a respectable family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, and having reached maturity, heard a Dhamma teaching as mentioned above. He saw the Teacher placing a certain monk in the foremost position among those who assign lodgings (senāsanapaññāpaka). Having performed a special deed and aspiring for that position, he received a prophecy from the Teacher. He performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and went forth as a monk when the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha was declining.

At that time, six others went forth with him. These seven monks, being of one mind, saw others being disrespectful toward the dispensation and thought: "What shall we do by staying here? Let us practice the Dhamma of a recluse in a secluded place and make an end of the suffering of the round of rebirths." They made a ladder, climbed a high mountain peak, and said: "Let those who know the strength of their own minds push down the ladder; let those who have attachment to life go down; do not be regretful later." They all pushed down the ladder with one mind. Admonishing each other, "Friends, do not be negligent," they sat in places suitable for their minds and practiced the Dhamma of a recluse. Among those seven monks, one Elder reached the fruit of Arahantship on the fifth day. Thinking, "My task is done; what shall I do here?", he brought almsfood from the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) by psychic power and said: "Friends, partake of this almsfood; let the matter of seeking alms concern only me; you just apply yourselves to your own meditation." Then the others said: "We have pushed down the ladder; he who first attains the Dhamma, that person..."
49:
“Do not be full of regret later,” they said. All seven monks, being of one mind, pushed down the ladder and exhorted one another, saying, “Friends, be diligent.” They then sat in places suitable for their minds and began to practice the Dhamma of a recluse.

Among them, one elder attained the fruit of Arahantship on the fifth day. Thinking, “My task is finished; what shall I do in this place?” he brought alms-food from Uttarakuru by psychic power and said, “Friends, partake of this alms-food. Let the duty of seeking alms be mine alone; you just perform your task of meditation.” Then the other monks asked, “Friends, when we pushed down the ladder, did we say, ‘Let the one who first realizes the Dhamma bring alms-food, and the rest of us will partake of the food brought by him and practice the Dhamma of a recluse’?” “We did not say so, venerable sir,” they replied. “Venerable sir, you have obtained this because of your past causes. We, too, shall make an end of the cycle of suffering as much as we can. Please go, venerable sir.” The elder, unable to convince those monks, partook of the alms-food in a suitable place and departed.

Another elder attained the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi) on the seventh day and, after passing away from that life, was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa Brahma realm. The remaining five elders wandered through the realms of gods and humans for the interval between two Buddhas and were reborn in various families. One was reborn in the royal house of Takkasilā in the Gandhāra kingdom. One was reborn in the womb of a female wandering ascetic in the Majjhantika kingdom. One was reborn in a house of a householder in the Bāhiya kingdom. One was born in the quarters of the bhikkhunīs.

As for this Elder Dabba, he took conception in the house of a Malla king in the city of Anupiya in the Malla kingdom. His mother passed away just as she was about to give birth. They took the corpse to the cemetery, placed it on a wooden pyre, and set it on fire. Due to the intense heat of the fire, her abdomen split into two. By the power of his own merit, the child sprang up and fell onto a bundle of wood (dabba). They took the child and gave him to his grandmother. When naming him, because he had survived by falling onto a bundle of wood, she named him “Dabba.” When the boy was seven years old, the Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, was wandering through the Malla kingdom and stayed in the Anupiya Mango Grove.

As soon as the boy Dabba saw the Teacher, he felt devotion and desired to ordain. Thinking, “I will ordain in the presence of the Teacher,” he asked permission from his grandmother. She said, “Dear child, very well,” and taking the boy Dabba, she went to the Teacher and said, “Venerable Sir, please ordain this boy.” The Teacher gave a sign to a certain monk, saying, “Monk, ordain this child.” Hearing the Teacher's words, that elder, while ordaining the boy Dabba, taught him the meditation on the five parts of the body ending in skin (taca-pañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna). A being who is endowed with past causes and has made previous aspirations, at the very first—
50:
As soon as the boy Dabba saw the Teacher, he felt devotion and desired to ordain. Thinking, “I will ordain in the presence of the Ten-Powered One,” he asked permission from his grandmother. She said, “Very well, dear,” and taking the boy Dabba, she went to the Teacher and said, “Venerable Sir, please ordain this boy.” The Teacher gave a sign to a certain monk, saying, “Monk, ordain this child.” Hearing the Teacher's words, that elder, while ordaining the boy Dabba, taught him the meditation on the five parts of the body ending in skin (taca-pañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna). The boy, who was endowed with past causes and had made previous aspirations, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) at the very moment the first lock of hair was shaved. When the second lock of hair was being shaved, he was established in the fruit of Once-returning (sakadāgāmiphala); at the third lock, in the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala). The completion of shaving all his hair and the realization of the fruit of Arahantship occurred simultaneously, neither before nor after the other. The Teacher, after staying in the Malla kingdom as long as he pleased, went to Rājagaha and took up residence in the Veḷuvana Monastery.

There, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, having gone into seclusion and reflecting on the completion of his task as an Arahant, desired to devote his body to performing services for the Saṅgha. He thought, “What if I were to assign lodgings for the Saṅgha and distribute meals?” He went to the Teacher and informed him of his thought. The Teacher gave him his approval and accepted him as the assigner of lodgings and the distributor of meals. Then, saying, “This Dabba, though young, stands in a great position,” the Buddha gave him higher ordination (upasampadā) even though he was only seven years old. From the time of his higher ordination, the elder assigned lodgings and distributed alms-food to all the monks residing in and around Rājagaha. His reputation as an assigner of lodgings became well-known in all directions: “It is said that Dabba Mallaputta assigns lodgings to monks of similar temperament in the same place; he assigns lodgings whether they are near or far; and he leads those who are unable to go by psychic power.”

Then, at both proper and improper times, monks would have him assign lodgings, saying, “Friend Dabba, assign us a lodging in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove; assign us a lodging in the Maddakucchi Deer Park,” and they would go while watching the elder's psychic power. The elder, too, would create mind-made bodies through psychic power, providing each elder with a monk similar to himself. With his finger glowing with light, he would walk ahead and say, “This is the couch, this is the chair,” and so on. After assigning the lodgings, he would return to his own dwelling...
51:
(He) returns (to his usual place). This is just a summary here; in detail, this story has already appeared in the Pāḷi. The Blessed One, taking this very matter as the occasion, later while seated in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha, placed the Elder Dabba in the foremost position among the monks who assign lodgings, saying: "Monks, among my disciple monks who assign lodgings, this Dabba Mallaputta is the foremost." This is also stated in the Apadāna:

"A Conqueror named Padumuttara, a Sage who knew the whole world, a Visionary, arose one hundred thousand aeons from now.

He was an advisor, an instructor, one who crossed all beings over (to Nibbāna), a Buddha skilled in preaching, who saved many people.

Compassionate, merciful, and seeking the welfare of all beings, that Blessed One established all those who had reached the views of heretics in the five precepts.

Thus, the Sasana was free from confusion and void of heretics; it was adorned with such noble Arahants who had attained mastery.

That Great Sage, who was like a golden pillar and endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, rose fifty-eight cubits (into the sky).

At that time, the lifespan was one hundred thousand years; remaining for that long, He saved many people.

Then, I was a famous son of a wealthy merchant in the city of Haṃsavatī; approaching the Lamp of the World, I heard the preaching of the Dhamma.

Hearing the words of praise (for the foremost position) for a disciple who assigned lodgings for the monks together with the Buddha, I was filled with joy.

Having performed a great deed of merit for that Great Sage together with the Saṅgha, I prostrated at His feet and aspired for that position.

Then that Great Hero, praising my deed, said: 'This merchant's son has fed the Leader of the World together with the Saṅgha for seven days.'"
52: "That noble son, who has eyes like lotus petals, shoulders like a lion, and skin like the color of gold, prostrates at my feet, wishing for the supreme position. In one hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama by clan, born in the Okkāka family, will arise in the world. A disciple of that Buddha, famous by the name Dabba, will then be the foremost among those who assign lodgings in the monasteries. Due to that well-performed meritorious deed, and because of my intentions and aspirations, I left the human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. I have been the king of deities three hundred times. I have been a Wheel-turning Monarch five hundred times. I obtained the position of a regional king so many times that it cannot be counted by numbers. Due to the power of that meritorious deed, I was happy in all my lives. Ninety-one aeons ago, the Buddha named Vipassī, who was beautiful to behold and saw all phenomena, arose. Having a mind of malice, I insulted a disciple of that Buddha, even though I knew he was pure and had destroyed all taints. I also took the voting ticket (salāka) of the disciples who sought the virtues of the Buddha, the best among men, and offered milk-rice. In this Bhadda-kappa, the famous Buddha named Kassapa by clan, of Brahman lineage, the best among those who speak, arose. Having made the Sasana shine, subduing the lowly heretics, and disciplining those who should be disciplined, He attained Parinibbāna together with His disciples. When the Protector together with His disciples had attained Parinibbāna and the Sasana was reaching its disappearance, the deities, with agitated minds, lamented with disheveled hair and tearful faces. 'The eye of Dhamma will disappear; we shall no longer see the monks of good practice; we shall no longer hear the True Dhamma; alas, our merit is so little!' (Thus they cried)."
53:
"Then all this earth, which is usually unshakable, shook. The ocean, as if in sorrow with the world of deities, wailed with a piteous sound.

In the four directions, the drums of the deities sounded without command. From all around, the terrifying thunderbolts of the deities also roared.

Torches fell from the sky. Comets were also seen. Flames along with smoke were manifest. All the beasts wailed piteously.

Seeing the terrifying omens indicating the disappearance of the Sasana, we seven monks at that time were struck with agitation and thought thus:

'There is no use for us to live without the Sasana. Let us enter the great forest and strive in the teaching of the Conqueror.'

Then, seeing a high and noble mountain in the forest, we climbed that mountain by a ladder and then threw the ladder down.

Then the Elder admonished us: 'Friends, the appearance of a Buddha is very rare. The very rare faith has also been obtained. The remaining Sasana is but a little.'

'Those who miss the right opportunity (khana) fall into the infinite ocean of suffering. Therefore, one should strive as long as the teaching of the Sage remains.'

That Elder became an Arahant. The second monk who followed him became an Anāgāmī. The other five of us, being endowed with virtue and striving, went to the deva world.

There is one who has crossed over Saṃsāra and attained Parinibbāna. There is also one who is alone in the Suddhāvāsa realm. Myself, along with Pukkusāti, Sabhiya, and Bāhiya,

As well as Kumārakassapa, have reached various realms. We have been liberated from the bonds of Saṃsāra, having received the compassion of the Buddha Gotama.

While I was in my mother's womb in Kusinārā of the Malla country, my mother died, and when she was placed on the funeral pyre to be cremated, I fell from there.

Because I fell onto a heap of grass (dabba), I became famous as 'Dabba'. By the power of the holy life, I was liberated from defilements at the age of seven."
54:
I am endowed with the five factors due to the power of having offered milk-rice. Due to the unwholesome deed of having once accused an Arahant, I have been subjected to many accusations by evil-minded people.

Now, I have transcended both merit and demerit; having reached the supreme peace of Nibbāna, I dwell free from taints (āsavas).

I prepared lodgings, bringing joy to those of good conduct. The Victor (Jina), being pleased with that quality, placed me in the foremost position (Etadagga).

My defilements are burnt away, and all existences are completely uprooted. Like a great elephant that has broken its bonds, I dwell free from taints.

My coming to the presence of the Buddha was indeed a good coming. The three knowledges have been attained, and the teaching of the Buddha has been carried out.

The four analytical insights... (and so on) ...the teaching of the Buddha has been carried out.

Despite being such a person, due to an evil deed committed in a past life—the slander of an Arahant Elder—he suffered in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years. Due to the remnants of that kamma (kammapilotika), the monks Mettiya and Bhummajaka, holding a wrong view that 'this Elder Dabba has caused a rift between us and the householders who provide us with good food,' accused him with a baseless charge of a Pārājika offense. When that legal issue (adhikaraṇa) was settled by the Saṅgha through the 'verdict of mindfulness' (sativinaya), this Elder, out of compassion for the world and wishing to make his qualities known, recited this verse beginning with 'Yo duddamiyo.'

In that verse, the word 'Yo' (whoever) is an indefinite designation, which should be understood as definite by the word 'So' (he). Although speaking as if referring to another person by using both, he is referring only to himself. 'Duddamiyo' means one who is difficult to tame, or impossible to tame. He says this considering the agitation of the mind intoxicated by the defilements associated with wrong views during his time as a worldling (puthujjana), and the lack of calm in the sense faculties. 'Damena' means by the supreme taming of the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga). Indeed, one tamed by that Path deserves to be called 'tamed' (danta) because there is no further need for taming; one does not deserve it by any other taming. Alternatively, 'damena' means by the Buddha, the Charioteer of men to be tamed (purisadammasārathi)...
55:
...who has tamed [him]. 'Dabba' means 'drabya' or 'bhabba' (worthy/capable). Therefore, the Blessed One, referring to this very Elder, said: 'Dabba, even those named Dabba who are famous among men cannot resolve it thus.'

'Santusito' means one who is content through contentment with whatever requisites are received, contentment with the meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti), and contentment with the Path and Fruit. 'Vitiṇṇakaṅkho' means one who has crossed over doubt, because doubts based on the sixteen grounds and the eight grounds have been completely uprooted by the first Path (Stream-entry) alone. 'Vijitāvī' is called a conqueror because he has conquered and destroyed all the side of defilements that should be conquered by a noble man of breeding (purisājānīya). 'Apeta-bheravo' means one who is free from terrifying objects of fear, one who has reached the cessation of fear, because the twenty-five types of fear have been entirely removed.

The mention of 'Dabba' again is the proclamation of his name. 'Parinibbūto' (fully extinguished): there are two kinds of Parinibbāna—extinction of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna), which is the Nibbāna element with residue remaining (saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu), and extinction of the aggregates (khandha-parinibbāna), which is the Nibbāna element without residue remaining (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). Here, the extinction of defilements is intended. Therefore, it means he is extinguished through the extinction of defilements, because the states that should be abandoned have been entirely abandoned by the Path. 'Ṭhitatto' means one of a firm nature, unshakable, one who cannot be moved by worldly conditions (lokadhamma) due to having attained the state of 'tādibhāva' (equanimity/suchness) towards desirable objects and so on.

The word 'hi' is a particle indicating a reason. Therefore, although he was difficult to tame in the past, when he became the Elder Dabba, he was tamed by the Teacher with the supreme taming, and thus became content, one who has crossed over doubt, a conqueror, and free from fear. Therefore, that Dabba is one whose defilements are extinguished, and because of that very extinction, he is of a firm nature. One should only have confidence (pasāda) in such an Elder Dabba; one should not let that confidence change into another state. Out of compassion for beings whose wisdom follows the lead of others, the Elder explained his attainment of the Fruit of Arahantship.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Dabba Thera is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Verses of Sītavaniya Thera

The verse beginning with 'Yo Sītavanaṃ' is the verse of the Venerable Sambhūta Thera. How did this matter arise? It is said that one hundred and eighteen aeons ago from now, the Buddha named Atthadassī appeared in the world. While he was rescuing the world including the devas from the great flood of saṃsāra, one day he approached the bank of the Ganges river together with a large Saṅgha of monks. At that time, this [Sambhūta Thera] was born in a householder's family. Seeing the Blessed One there, with a heart full of faith, he approached, paid homage, and asked, 'Venerable Sir, do you wish to go to the other shore?' The Blessed One said, 'We shall go.' At that very moment, that young man of good family...
56:
Having joined boats and rafts together, he caused them to approach the Blessed One. The Blessed One, out of compassion for him, boarded the boat along with the community of monks. He also boarded it himself and, having safely reached the opposite bank, provided a great offering to the Blessed One and the community of monks on the second day. He followed them for some distance and, after paying homage with a devoted heart, returned.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. One hundred and thirteen aeons (113) ago from now, he was reborn into a khattiya family and became a Cakkavatti, a righteous king, a king of Dhamma. Having established beings on the path to a happy destination, he passed away from there. Ninety-one aeons (91) ago, he was ordained in the dispensation of Vipassī Buddha; undertaking the dhutanga practices, he dwelt in a cemetery and practiced the recluse's Dhamma. Again, in the time of Kassapa Buddha, he was ordained in that dispensation along with three friends and practiced the recluse's Dhamma for twenty thousand years. Having wandered through the realms of devas and humans during the interval between Buddhas, he was reborn in this Buddha's era as the son of a wealthy Brahmin in the city of Rājagaha. They named him "Sambhūta." When he reached maturity, he attained mastery in the arts of the Brahmins. Along with three friends—Bhūmija, Jeyyasena, and Abhirādhana—he went to the Blessed One, and upon hearing the Dhamma, he gained faith and was ordained. Referring to them, it was said:

"Bhūmija, Jeyyasena, Sambhūta, and Abhirādhana—these have penetrated the Dhamma in the dispensation of the One of Noble Conduct."

Thereafter, Sambhūta took the meditation subject of mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati) from the Blessed One and dwelt constantly in the Sītavana forest. Because of this dwelling, that venerable one became known as "Sītavaniya." At that time, Vessavaṇa, the Great King of Devas, was traveling through the air toward the southern region of Jambudīpa on some business. Seeing the Elder sitting in the open air and reflecting on his meditation subject, he descended from his celestial mansion, paid homage to the Elder, and gave orders to two yakkhas: "When the Elder emerges from concentration, inform him of my arrival and provide him with protection," and then he departed. Those yakkhas stood near the Elder, and when he had withdrawn from his reflection and was sitting, they informed him. Hearing this, the Elder said, "You should tell the Great King Vessavaṇa in my words: 'The Blessed One has established the protection called "mindfulness" for those who stand in His dispensation. That very mindfulness protects one like me. You may remain free from concern in this matter. There is no need to provide such protection for those who stand in the instruction of the Blessed One.'" Having dismissed the two yakkhas, he developed insight at that very moment and realized the Three Knowledges. Later, when Vessavaṇa returned and approached the Elder, he recognized by the expression on his face that the task of the recluse had been completed...
57:
"There is no need for such protection," he said, and having dismissed those yakkhas, he developed insight at that very moment and realized the Three Knowledges. Then, Vessavaṇa, while returning, approached the Elder and, knowing by the expression on his face that his task was completed (that he had become an Arahant), went to Sāvatthī and informed the Blessed One. In the presence of the Teacher, he praised the virtues of the Elder with this verse:

"Endowed with the protection of mindfulness, possessed of steadfastness, and concentrated with energy; Sambhūta, born following the Teacher's instruction, is a possessor of the Three Knowledges who has reached the further shore of death."

Thus he praised the Elder's virtues. This matter was also stated in the Apadāna:

"The Blessed One Atthadassī, the Lord of bipeds, the Bull among men, surrounded by his disciples, approached the bank of the Ganges.

The Ganges was full to the brim, so that a crow could drink from it, and was very difficult to cross. I caused the community of monks and the Buddha, the Supreme among bipeds, to cross over (to the other side).

In the hundred and eighteen aeons since I performed that deed, I have not known a miserable state; this is the fruit of that crossing.

Thirteen aeons ago, I was a Cakkavatti of great power, endowed with the seven treasures, for five times.

In this final birth, I was born into a Brahmin family and was ordained in the Teacher's dispensation along with three friends.

My defilements have been burnt away... (pe)... the Buddha's dispensation has been fulfilled."

Then, when the Venerable Sambhūta saw monks who were going to see the Blessed One, he said, "Friends, pay homage to the Blessed One's feet with your heads in my name, and speak thus." Desiring to make known that he had not troubled his Teacher, the Blessed One, because of the Dhamma, he uttered the verse beginning with "Yo Sītavanaṃ." Those monks approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and wishing to properly convey the message of the Venerable Sambhūta, said, "Venerable Sir, the Venerable Sambhūta pays homage to the Blessed One's feet with his head and speaks thus," and they reported that verse. Hearing those words, the Blessed One said, "Monks, Sambhūta is wise..."
58:
“The monk Sambhūta has attained the Dhamma (the Path and Fruit) in accordance with the Dhamma; he does not trouble me on account of the Dhamma. Vessavaṇa has informed me of this matter concerning that elder,” the Buddha said.

The monks reported the verse beginning with “Yo Sītavanaṃ,” spoken by the Elder Sambhūta, to the Blessed One. In that verse, “Sītavana” is the name of a large and fearsome cemetery forest near Rājagaha. “Upagā” means he approached it for the purpose of residing there. By this, the Blessed One shows a dwelling place suitable for a monk, as permitted by the Blessed One. “Bhikkhu” means a monk, so-called because he sees danger in the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra) and because he has destroyed the defilements. “Eko” means alone, without a companion; by this, physical seclusion (kāya-viveka) is shown. “Santusito” means content; by this, the lineage of the noble ones (ariyavaṃsa) characterized by contentment with the four requisites is shown. “Samāhitatto” means having a mind concentrated through the distinctions of access concentration and absorption concentration; by this, the lineage of the noble ones who delight in meditation (bhāvanārāma) is shown through the means of mental seclusion (citta-viveka) and meditation. “Vijitāvī” means one who stands having conquered the host of defilements that should be conquered by practicing rightly in the Dispensation; by this, seclusion from the substrata of existence (upadhi-viveka) is shown. “Apeta-lomahaṃso” means one whose hair does not stand on end because the defilements, which are the causes of fear, have departed; by this, the fruit of right practice is shown. “Rakkhanti” means guarding. “Kāyagatāsati” means mindfulness directed toward the body; it is the non-abandoning of the meditation subject of mindfulness of the body by way of development. “Dhitimā” means one possessing firm wisdom; this is a description of practice based on having a concentrated mind or being a conqueror.

The summary of the meaning here is: That monk, looking toward the bliss of seclusion, went alone to the Sītavana forest. Having arrived, being content due to the absence of fickleness and possessing firm wisdom, he developed the meditation subject of mindfulness of the body. Making the jhāna thus attained a basis, he increased his effort in insight (vipassanā). Through the attained highest path (arahatta-magga), he became concentrated and a conqueror. Having completed his task, because the causes of fear were entirely removed, he became one whose hair does not stand on end.

## The Commentary on the Verse of Sītavaniya Thera is finished.
59:
The verse beginning with “Yo pānudi” is the verse of the Venerable Bhalliya. What is its origin? It is said that thirty-one aeons ago, before the Buddhas had arisen, this elder, with a heart full of faith, gave various fruits to a Paccekabuddha named Sumana. Wandering only in happy realms, he was born into a Brahmin family in the city of Aruṇavatī during the time of Sikhī Buddha. Hearing that “the two merchant sons named Ujita and Ojita gave the first meal to the Blessed One Sikhī, the first to attain full enlightenment,” he approached the Blessed One with his friend, paid homage, and invited Him for the next day. After providing a great gift, they made an aspiration: “Venerable Sir, may we both be the first meal-givers to a Buddha like you in the future.”

Having performed meritorious deeds in various births and wandering among gods and humans, they were born as brothers, the sons of a wealthy merchant named Gopālaka, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa. For many years, they served the Saṅgha of monks with milk-rice. In the time of our Blessed One, they were born as brothers, the sons of a caravan leader in the city of Pokkharavatī. Among them, the elder was named Tapussa and the younger was named Bhalliya. While they were traveling for trade with five hundred wagons filled with merchandise, the Blessed One, having recently attained enlightenment, spent seven weeks reflecting on the Dhamma of the bliss of liberation. In the eighth week, while He was staying at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree, they were passing along the main road not far from the Rājāyatana tree. At that time, although the ground was level and free of mud and water, their wagons would not move forward and stopped. While they were wondering, “What could be the reason?”, a deity who had been an old relative showed herself in the fork of a tree and said: “Friends, this Blessed One has recently attained enlightenment. He has been without food for seven weeks, experiencing the bliss of liberation, and is now sitting at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree. Honor that Blessed One with food; such an offering will be for your long-term welfare and happiness.”

Hearing this, they experienced great joy and happiness. Thinking that “preparing food would take too long,” they offered fried cakes and honey balls to the Blessed One. They took the two-word refuge, received hair relics, and departed. They were the first lay disciples (upāsakas). Then, after the Blessed One went to Vārāṇasī, set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, and was staying in Rājagaha in due course, Tapussa and Bhalliya [went] to Rājagaha...
60:
The brothers Tapussa and Bhalliya, who had arrived at the city of Rājagaha, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. The Blessed One preached the Dhamma to them. Of those two brothers, Tapussa was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) and became a lay follower (upāsaka). Bhalliya, however, went forth and became an Arahant endowed with the six higher powers (chaḷabhiññā). This matter is stated in the Apadāna as follows—

“The Buddha named Sumana was then residing in the city of Takkarā. At that time, I took a vallikāra fruit and offered it to that Self-Enlightened One.

Thirty-one aeons ago from now, I gave that fruit. Due to the merit of that gift of fruit, I have never known a woeful state; this is the fruit of the gift of fruit.

My defilements have been burnt away... (etc.) ... I have fulfilled the teaching of the Buddha.”

Then one day, Māra displayed a terrifying form to frighten the Elder Bhalliya. The Elder, wishing to manifest his transcendence of all fears, recited the verse beginning with “Yo pānudī.”

In that verse, “Yo pānudī” means he who dispelled, cast away, abandoned, or destroyed. “Maccurājassa” refers to the King of Death; death is the breaking up of the aggregates (khandhas), and because it causes beings to follow its will, it is called a king in the sense of lordship—thus, the King of Death (Maccurāja). “Senaṃ” refers to old age, sickness, and so forth; since these are factors in bringing one under the power of death, they are called the army (senā). That King of Death is called “Mahāsena” because he has a great, diverse, and extensive army. As it is said: “Indeed, there is no bargaining with that Death, who has a great army.” Alternatively, in the sense of killing virtues, “Maccu” here refers to Devaputta Māra, and because they are his companions, sensual desires and the like are his armies. Thus it is said—
