“Sensual desires are your first army; the second is called discontent (arati). Hunger and thirst are your third army; the fourth is called craving (taṇhā).

Sloth and torpor are your fifth army; the sixth is called fear (bhīru). Doubt (vicikicchā) is your seventh army; conceit (māna) and ingratitude (makkha) are the eighth.”
61:
“Like a very weak reed bridge (naḷasetu)”: Because it is devoid of essence, the army of defilements is like a reed bridge; because it is extremely weak, it is very feeble. The Elder Bhalliya destroyed it with the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga), which is like a great flood (mahogha) due to the powerful nature of the nine supramundane states (nava lokuttara dhamma). Thus, the construction of the meaning is: he who has conquered defilements, is free from dread, is tamed, has attained the extinction of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna), and remains unshaken by worldly conditions. Hearing this, the wretched Māra thought, “This ascetic knows me,” and vanished on the spot.

## The Commentary on the Verse of Elder Bhalliya is Finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Verse of Elder Vīra

“Yo duddamiyo” and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Elder Vīra. What is its origin? It is said that ninety-one aeons ago from this present one, this Elder had cleaned the monastery where the Buddha Vipassī resided. One day, he took nigguṇḍhi flowers, which resemble sindhuvāra flowers, and offered them to the Blessed One. Due to that meritorious deed, wandering through the worlds of gods and humans, thirty-five aeons ago from now, he was born into a kshatriya family and became a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) named Mahāpatāpa. Ruling with righteousness and justice, he established beings on the path to heaven. Again, in this very aeon, during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, he became a wealthy merchant and gave alms to the poor and travelers, and offered milk-rice to the Saṅgha. Thus, performing such accumulations of merit through giving in various births and aspiring for Nibbāna, he wandered through the worlds of gods and humans. In this Buddha-era, he was born in the city of Sāvatthī into the family of a minister of King Pasenadi Kosala and was named “Vīra” (Hero). When he reached maturity, he was endowed with strength, speed, and other qualities consistent with his name, becoming a brave warrior on the battlefield. At the urging of his parents, he married and had one son. Later, prompted by past causes, he saw the danger in sensual pleasures and in Saṃsāra. Being stirred by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he went forth, and by striving and exerting effort, he soon became an Arahant endowed with the six higher powers. This matter is stated in the Apadāna as follows—

“I was a park-keeper for the Blessed One Vipassī;
Having raised up a nigguṇḍhi flower, I offered it to the Buddha.”
63:
## 9. Pilindavacchattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with “Svāgataṃ” is that of the Venerable Pilindavaccha Thera. What is the account of his origin? This Elder, it is said, was born into a wealthy family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. As mentioned previously, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position (etadagga) of being dear and pleasing to the deities. Aspiring to that position, he performed meritorious deeds for the rest of his life. Passing away from that life, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the time of Sumedha Buddha, he was born in the human world, and when the Buddha attained Parinibbāna, he made offerings to the Teacher's stupa and gave great alms to the Saṅgha. Passing away from that life, he continued to wander among devas and humans. During a period when no Buddha had arisen, he became a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) and established the people in the five precepts, leading them to the heavenly realms.

Before our Buddha had arisen, he was born into a Brahmin household in the city of Sāvatthī. They named him “Pilinda.” “Vaccha,” however, was his clan name (gotta). Because of that clan, he later became known as “Pilindavaccha.” Due to having much spiritual urgency (saṃvega) regarding saṃsāra, he ordained as a wandering ascetic (paribbājaka) and mastered the science known as Cūḷagandhāra. Through that science, he became capable of flying through the air and knowing the minds of others, and he lived in Rājagaha, having reached the pinnacle of gain and fame.

Then, when our Blessed One attained Enlightenment and in due course arrived at Rājagaha, from that time on, by the power of the Buddha, his science no longer worked and could not accomplish its purpose. He thought: “I have heard this said by teachers of old: ‘Where the Mahāgandhāra science is present, there the Cūḷagandhāra science cannot succeed.’ Since the time the ascetic Gotama arrived, this science of mine has not succeeded. Undoubtedly, the ascetic Gotama knows the Mahāgandhāra science. What if I were to attend upon him and learn that science in his presence?” 

He approached the Blessed One and said: “Great Ascetic, I wish to learn a certain science in your presence; please grant me the opportunity.” The Blessed One said: “In that case, ordain.” Thinking, “Ordination must be the preliminary preparation for the science,” he ordained. The Blessed One taught him the Dhamma and gave him a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suited to his temperament. Because he was endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), he developed insight (vipassanā) before long and attained Arahatship. Furthermore, the deities who, in previous lives, had stayed in his admonition and were born in the deva realms, used to visit the Elder in the evening and morning out of gratitude. Therefore, the Elder reached the foremost position among those who are dear and pleasing to the deities.
64:
In a previous life, the deities who had lived according to his advice and were reborn in the celestial realm, out of gratitude and great reverence, would visit the Elder in the evening and morning before departing. Therefore, the Elder attained the foremost position among those who are dear and pleasing to the deities. This is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

"When the Lord of the World, the Supreme Person, the Buddha Sumedha, had attained Parinibbāna,
With a clear and joyful heart, I performed an act of worship to the stupa.

In that assembly, there were Arahants who had destroyed the taints,
Who were endowed with the six supernormal powers and great psychic potency.
Having invited them there, I offered a meal to the Saṅgha.

At that time, the attendant of the Blessed One Sumedha was named Sumedha.
He then gave the words of appreciation (anumodanā).

Through that clarity of mind, I was reborn in a celestial mansion,
Where eighty-six thousand nymphs delighted me.

They always followed my will in all sensual pleasures,
I surpassed other deities; this is the fruit of meritorious action.

Twenty-five aeons ago, I was a Khattiya king named Varuṇa,
A Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) who possessed pure food.

At that time, people did not sow seeds, nor did they lead the ploughs;
They enjoyed Sāli rice that grew and ripened on its own without tilling.

Having exercised sovereignty there, I went again to the state of a deity;
Even then, such perfection of wealth and enjoyment arose for me.

Neither friends nor enemies, nor any living beings, harmed me;
I was dear to all beings; this is the fruit of meritorious action.

Thirty thousand aeons ago, I gave that gift;
I have not known a woeful state since; this is the fruit of the offering of scented paste.

In this Bhadda Kappa, I was a lord of men,
A powerful Universal Monarch of great majesty."
65:
"I established many people in the five precepts,
Leading them only to the heavenly realms, and I became dear to the deities.

My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Because he was so exceedingly beloved by the deities, the Blessed One placed this Elder in the foremost position among those dear and pleasing to the deities: "Monks, among my monk disciples who are dear and pleasing to the deities, Pilindavaccha is the foremost." One day, while sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, the Elder reflected on his own virtues and, wishing to praise his coming to the Blessed One as the cause of his higher knowledge (vijjā), he recited the verse beginning with "Svāgataṃ nāpagataṃ."

In that verse, "svāgataṃ" means a good coming; this is to be connected with the word "mine." Alternatively, "svāgataṃ" means "I have come well," which should be understood by changing the grammatical case. "Nāpagataṃ" means not a bad going, not departing from benefit and prosperity. "Nayidaṃ dummantitaṃ mama" means this speaking or reflecting of mine is not badly spoken or badly thought. The meaning is: my coming to the presence of the Blessed One is a good coming, and because it is a good coming, it is not a bad coming. My thought or speech, "I will listen to the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One and ordain," or my reflection with the mind, is also not a bad thought.

Now, showing the reason for this, he said the words beginning with "saṃvibhattesu." "Saṃvibhattesu" means well-analyzed. "Dhammesu" refers to things to be known (ñeyya-dhamma) or things that calm defilements (samatha-dhamma), which are analyzed and taught by various heretics in terms of primordial nature (pakati) etc., and by the Buddhas in terms of suffering (dukkha) etc. Among those, that which is the best is the Four Noble Truths, or the Teaching (Sāsana) that makes them known; I have approached that teaching, thinking, "This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya." Or, among the natural phenomena (sabhāva-dhamma) which are well-analyzed by the Buddhas according to their true nature as wholesome etc., or as aggregates (khandha) etc., that which is the best, most excellent, and supreme is the Dhamma of the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna; I have approached that through personal realization and have realized it. Therefore, the connection is: "My coming is a good coming and not a bad coming; it is a good thought and not a bad thought."

## The Commentary on the Verses of Pilindavaccha Thera is finished.
66:
## 10. Puṇṇamāsattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with "Vihari apekkhaṃ" is that of the Venerable Elder Puṇṇamāsa. What is the story of its origin? It is said that during the time of the Blessed Buddha Vipassī, he was reborn as a ruddy goose (cakka-vaka). Seeing the Blessed One walking, he was filled with devotion and, taking a sāla flower in his beak, he made an offering. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and seventeen aeons ago, he became a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) eight times.

In this very Bhadda-kappa, when the dispensation of the Blessed Buddha Kassapa was declining, he was reborn in a wealthy family, ordained, and practiced the Dhamma of a recluse. Passing away from there, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this present Buddha-era, he was reborn in the city of Sāvatthī as the son of a Brahmin named Samiddhi. On the day of his birth, all the empty pots in that house became filled with gold coins (suvaṇṇamāsa). For that reason, they named the boy "Puṇṇamāsa."

When he reached maturity, he mastered the Brahmin sciences, married, and had a son. Being endowed with the supporting conditions of past perfections (pāramī-upanissaya), he became disgusted with household life. He approached the Blessed One, heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and ordained. Having attained full ordination, he fulfilled the preliminary duties and, being devoted to the meditation on the Four Noble Truths, he developed insight (vipassanā) and attained Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"At that time, I was a ruddy goose on the banks of the Sindhu River; I lived on pure moss and was well-restrained from evil.

I saw the stainless Buddha walking through the air; taking a sāla flower in my beak, I offered it to Vipassī.

Whosoever's faith in the Tathāgata is unshakable and well-established, through that devotion of mind, he does not go to a woeful state.

Welcome indeed was my coming to the presence of the Best of Buddhas; as a peaceful bird, I have sown a good seed.

In the ninety-one aeons since I offered that flower, I have not known a woeful state; this is the fruit of Buddha-pūjā."

Due to the merit of honoring the Buddha, eight Universal Monarchs named Suchārudassana, Kanaka, and Bala arose seventeen aeons ago. My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

At that time, the former wife of the Elder Puṇṇamāsa, desiring to seduce him, adorned herself with garments and ornaments and approached him with their son. She began to attempt to reveal her lustful disposition through sweet talk and so on. The Elder, seeing her behavior and wishing to demonstrate his lack of attachment to any object, uttered the verse beginning with "Vihari apekkhaṃ."

In that verse, "Vihari" means specifically abandoned or removed. "Apekkhaṃ" refers to having no longing in this present world or in this individual existence. "Huraṃ" refers to the future time or another existence. Alternatively, "this world" refers to the six internal bases (ajjhattika-āyatana) within oneself, and "huraṃ" refers to the six external bases (bāhira-āyatana) such as visual forms.
67:
The eight Universal Monarchs named Suchārudassana, Kanaka, and Bala, who lived seventeen aeons ago, shared the same names and possessed great power.

"My defilements are burnt up..." (and so on), the instruction of the Buddha has been carried out.

At that time, the former wife of the Elder Puṇṇamāsa, desiring to seduce him, adorned herself with ornaments and approached him with their son, attempting to reveal her lustful disposition through sweet speech and other means. The Elder, seeing the woman's behavior and wishing to make clear his lack of attachment to any sense object, uttered the verse beginning with "Vihari apekkhaṃ."

In that verse, "Vihari" means specifically abandoned or removed. "Apekkha" refers to craving (taṇhā). "Idha" refers to either this present world or this individual existence. "Huraṃ" refers to either the future time to come or another individual existence. Alternatively, "idha" refers to the six internal bases within oneself, and "huraṃ" refers to the six external bases. The word "vā" (or) expresses a connective sense, as in "apadā vā dipadā vā" (whether footless or two-footed). By the word "yo" (who), he refers to himself as if he were another. "Vedagū" means one who has reached Nibbāna through Path-knowledge, or one who knows. Or, it refers to one who stands having penetrated the Four Noble Truths by way of full understanding (pariññā) of the truth of suffering, abandoning (pahāna) of the truth of origin, realization (sacchikiriya) of the truth of cessation, and development (bhāvanā) of the truth of the path. "Yatatto" means one whose nature is restrained by Path-restraint (magga-saṃvara), or one whose nature is restrained by Right Effort (sammā-vāyāma). "Sabbesu dhammesu anūpalitto" means one who is not stained by the stains of craving and views (taṇhā-diṭṭhi) regarding all objective phenomena. By this term, he shows the transcendence of worldly conditions (lokadhamma) such as gain and loss. "Lokassa" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha). Indeed, they are called "loka" (world) in the sense of disintegrating and crumbling. "Jaññā" means having known. "Udayabbayañca" refers to arising and passing away. By knowing this, he shows the preliminary practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā) of the aforementioned qualities.

The meaning here is this: The Elder Puṇṇamāsa, having known the arising and passing away of the entire world of aggregates and so on through fifty modes, has reached Nibbāna through Path-knowledge, is restrained in nature, and is unstained by craving and views in any object. Having removed longing in all respects and being content, he is not moved in the least by such perversions. Therefore, "O blind fool, go back by the very way you came." Then that woman, thinking, "This recluse is without longing for me or for his son; it is not possible to seduce him," departed.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Puṇṇamāsa is finished.
## In the Commentary on the Theragāthā of the Paramatthadīpanī,
## the Commentary on the First Group (Paṭhamavagga) is finished.
68:
## 2. The Second Group (Dutiya Vagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Cūḷavaccha

The verse beginning with "Pāmojjabahulo" is that of the Venerable Elder Cūḷavaccha. What is its origin? It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was born into a poor family and made a living as a hired laborer for others. Seeing the Elder named Sujāta, a disciple of the Buddha, searching for rag-robes (paṃsukūla), he approached with a devoted heart, offered a cloth, and paid homage with the five-point prostration. Due to that meritorious deed, he ruled as the king of gods thirty-three times. He became a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) seventy-seven times. He was a regional king many times. Thus, after wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he ordained and practiced the ascetic life during the decline of the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha. Having wandered back and forth between the realms of gods and humans for the duration of one Buddha-interval, he was born into a Brahmin family in Kosambī during the time of our Buddha. He was given the name Cūḷavaccha. When he reached maturity, he attained mastery in the Brahmin arts. Hearing of the Buddha's virtues, he approached the Buddha with a devoted heart. The Buddha preached the Dhamma to him. Having gained faith, he ordained and received higher ordination. After performing the preliminary duties, he dwelt developing a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable to his temperament. At that time, the monks of Kosambī were engaged in quarrels. Then, the Elder Cūḷavaccha, without taking the side of either group of monks, remained steadfast in the advice given by the Buddha, cultivated insight (vipassanā), and attained Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"A disciple of Padumuttara Buddha, named Sujāta,
Was then wandering through the rubbish heaps, searching for rag-robes.
In the city of Haṃsavatī, I was a hired laborer for others;
Having offered half a garment, I paid homage with my head.
By that well-performed deed, and by my intention and aspiration,
Having abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Thirty-three times I was the lord of gods, exercising the sovereignty of gods;
And seventy-seven times I was a Universal Monarch."
69:
"I obtained the position of a regional king, vast and beyond counting;
Through the gift of half a garment, I rejoice, free from fear, being liberated (from the round of suffering).

If I so desire today, I could cover this region, including forests and mountains,
With linen cloths; this is the fruit of half a garment.

In the hundred-thousandth aeon past, I gave that gift of half a garment;
Due to the fruit of that meritorious deed, I have not known the four woeful states.
This is the fruit of the gift of half a garment.

My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

Then, the Elder Cūḷavaccha, having attained Arahantship and seeing the destruction of their own welfare by those monks who delighted in quarreling, was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Reflecting on his own special attainment, he spoke the verse beginning with "Pāmojjabahulo" by the power of joy and gladness (pīti-somanassa).

In that verse, "Pāmojjabahulo" means one who abounds in joy by the power of delighting in the most noble wholesome states, being free from remorse (vippaṭisāra) due to the extreme purity of his virtue. Therefore, he said, "Dhamme buddhappavedite" (In the Dhamma proclaimed by the Buddha). There, "Dhamme" refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) or the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (lokuttaradhamma). Indeed, because they were manifested by the Omniscient Buddha through His pre-eminent teaching, they are called "Buddhappavedita" (proclaimed by the Buddha) in an exceptional sense. However, since it is the means of attainment, the Dhamma of the teachings (pariyatti) is also included here. "Padaṃ santaṃ" refers to Nibbāna. A monk of such a nature attains and experiences Nibbāna, the peaceful state, the peaceful portion, which is the highest bliss because it is the state of the subsiding of all formations (saṅkhāra). For a monk of pure virtue, being abundant in joy due to the absence of remorse, and being devoted to the true Dhamma, attains all successes (sampatti) culminating in liberation. As it was said: "Ananda, wholesome virtues have non-remorse as their purpose; non-remorse has joy as its purpose," and so forth.

Alternatively, "Pāmojjabahulo" means abounding in joy by focusing on the Triple Gem: the Buddha is the Fully Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed, and the Saṅgha is well-practiced. As for what that person abounding in joy does, he said, "Dhamme buddhappavedite," and so on. For a person endowed with faith, because the association with the wise, hearing the true Dhamma, wise reflection, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma occur with ease, all successes come into his hands.
70:
All forms of prosperity come into one's possession. It is as the Blessed One said: "One who has faith approaches; one who approaches, attends frequently," and so forth.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Cūḷavaccha Thera is finished.

## 2. The Commentary on the Verses of Mahāvaccha Thera

"Paññābalī" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Mahāvaccha Thera. What is its origin? It is said that this Elder offered a gift of drinking water to the Blessed One Padumuttara and the Saṅgha of monks. Again, in the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, he became a lay devotee (upāsaka) and performed many meritorious deeds that serve as a support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya). Due to those meritorious deeds, he wandered only in happy realms (sugati) and, during the appearance of this Buddha, was reborn in the village of Nāḷaka in the kingdom of Magadha as the son of a Brahmin named Samiddhi. His name was Mahāvaccha.

When he reached maturity, he heard that the Venerable Sāriputta was a disciple of the Blessed One and thought, "That Elder is indeed of great wisdom. He has become a disciple of someone; that person must surely be the supreme individual in this world." Thus, having developed faith in the Blessed One, he went forth in the presence of the Teacher. While practicing meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), he attained Arahantship before long. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"In the Saṅgha of monks of the peerless Padumuttara Buddha,
With a confident and joyful mind, I filled a water pot.

Whether on a mountain top, on a tree top,
In the sky, or on the ground,
Whenever I desire drinking water,
It quickly appears for me.

In the hundred thousandth aeon ago, I gave that gift;
Since then, I have not known a woeful state. This is the fruit of the gift of water.

My defilements are burnt away... (etc.)... all existences are uprooted,
The six higher powers (abhiññā) have been realized, and the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Thus, having attained Arahantship and experiencing the bliss of liberation (vimuttisukha), he uttered the verse beginning with "Paññābalī" to inspire his fellow practitioners by demonstrating the liberating nature of the Dispensation.
71:
In that verse, "Paññābalī" means being endowed with an exceptionally great power of wisdom through the influence of preservative wisdom (parihāriya-paññā) and insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā). "Sīlavatūpapanno" means being endowed with the supreme fourfold purification virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) and the practices known as ascetic qualities (dhuta-dhamma). "Samāhito" means being composed through concentration, categorized into access (upacāra) and absorption (appanā) concentration. "Jhānārato" means, because of being so composed, delighting in and being constantly devoted to the contemplation of objects (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and the contemplation of characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). He is one who is mindful through the power of never being without mindfulness at all times.

"Yadatthiyaṃ" refers to being beneficial, not devoid of purpose. That which is beneficial for a certain reason is called "yadatthiyaṃ". Just as the use of the four requisites by a consumer is beneficial, so is one who consumes food in that manner. Such consumption is beneficial either through "ownership-use" (sāmiparibhoga) or "inheritance-use" (dāyajjaparibhoga). It cannot be beneficial in any other way. The word "bhojanaṃ" (food) should be understood as a mere illustration. It is called "bhojana" because it is eaten or consumed; it refers to all four requisites. There is also a variant reading "yadatthikaṃ". For whatever purpose the Teacher allowed the four requisites—for the purpose of the maintenance of the body and for the purpose of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna)—that purpose exists. Therefore, while using the requisite of food for the sake of Nibbāna without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna), one should, through that very use, await the time of one's own final Nibbāna (anupādā-parinibbāna). This refers to an Arahant who is free from lust (vītarāga) in this Dispensation. The meaning is that such a practice does not exist among those outside the Dispensation who are free from lust for sensual pleasures.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Mahāvaccha Thera is finished.

## 3. The Commentary on the Verses of Vanavaccha Thera

"Nīlabbhavaṇṇā" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Vanavaccha Thera. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī, he was reborn in the species of a turtle and lived in the river named Vinatā. That turtle had a body the size of a small boat. One day, seeing the Blessed One standing on the riverbank, he thought, "The Blessed One likely wishes to go to the other side." Intending to carry Him on his back, he lay down at the Buddha's feet. The Blessed One, knowing the turtle's intention and out of compassion for him, mounted the turtle. The turtle, filled with joy and happiness, crossed the river current like an arrow shot with the force of a bowstring, reaching the other bank in that very moment. The Blessed One, having predicted the fruit of that merit and the future prosperity that would arise, departed.
72:
Through that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, he became an ascetic many hundreds of times and lived only in the forest. Again, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, he was reborn as a pigeon. Seeing a monk who lived in the forest dwelling in loving-kindness (mettā-vihārī), he felt a clear devotion in his heart.

Passing away from that life as a pigeon, he was reborn into a family in Vārāṇasī. Upon reaching adulthood, he felt spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and ordained, accumulating many meritorious deeds that serve as a support for liberation from the round of suffering. Thus, wandering through various deva and human realms, during the time of this Buddha's appearance, he took rebirth in the house of a Brahmin named Vacchagotta in the city of Kapilavatthu. His mother, being heavily pregnant, developed a craving to see the forest. While she was wandering in the forest, the kamma-born winds (labor pains) were stirred within her at that very moment. Her attendants surrounded her with a curtain. She gave birth to a son endowed with the marks of great merit and wisdom. This noble son became a childhood playmate of the Bodhisatta. He was named "Vaccha." Due to his delight in the forest, he became known as "Vanavaccha."

Later, when the Great Being went forth in the Great Renunciation and strove in the great exertion, Vaccha thought, "I too will live in the forest with Prince Siddhattha." He went forth, became an ascetic, and while living in the Himalayas, he heard of the attainment of Buddhahood. He approached the Blessed One, ordained, took a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), and while living in the forest, he soon developed insight (vipassanā) and realized the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

The Blessed One Atthadassī, the Self-Awakened, the Leader of the World—that Tathāgata approached the bank of the Vinatā River.
Coming out of the water, I, a turtle dwelling in the water, desiring to help the Leader of the World cross, approached the Buddha.
"May the Buddha, the Great Sage Atthadassī who knows the Four Noble Truths, climb upon my back. I shall carry you across; you are the one who brings an end to the suffering of saṃsāra."
Knowing my intention, the famous Atthadassī, the Leader of the World, climbed upon my back and stood there.
73:
"From the time I could remember myself, from the time I reached the age of discretion, I have never known such happiness as that which I felt when touching the soles of the Buddha's feet.

Having crossed over, the Blessed One Atthadassī, of great fame, stood on the riverbank and spoke these verses:

'As long as my mind flows like the current of the Ganges, I cross. And this wise turtle king has carried me across.
By this act of carrying the Buddha across, and by his heart of loving-kindness, he will delight in the deva world for one hundred and eighty eons.
Coming from the deva world to this world, urged by his root of merit, sitting on a single seat, he will cross the stream of doubt (vicikicchā).
Just as in a good field, even if a small seed is sown, when a good shower of rain falls, the harvest delights the farmer;
Even so, in this Buddha-field taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One, when the good shower of rain falls, the fruit (mundane and supramundane) will delight me.'

'I have a mind directed toward Nibbāna through exertion, I am peaceful and free from substrates (upadhi). Having fully understood all taints (āsavas), I live taintless.
One hundred and eighty eons ago, I performed that deed of carrying the Buddha across. Because of the merit of that crossing, I do not know a miserable rebirth (duggati).
My defilements are burnt... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.'

Thus, having attained Arahantship, while the Blessed One was staying in Kapilavatthu, he went there, paid homage to the Teacher, and met with the monks. When asked as a friendly greeting, 'Friend, do you live comfortably in the forest?' he replied, 'Friend, the mountains in the forest are delightful.' Wishing to praise the mountains where he had lived, he recited the verse beginning with 'Nīlabbhavaṇṇā.'

In that verse, 'Nīlabbhavaṇṇā' means (mountains) that resemble dark clouds or have the shape of dark clouds. 'Rucirā' means radiant and brilliant, suffused with light. 'Sīta-vārī' means having cool waters. 'Sucindharā' means because of having pure ground, or [the abode] of the Noble Ones (Ariyas) who have minds pure from defilements..."
74:
Because they are the dwelling places of the Noble Ones (Ariyas) who possess pure minds, they bear purity (sucindharā). For the sake of ease in reciting the verse, it is expressed with the nasal sound (anunāsika). There is also a reading "sītavārisucindharā," which means those that bear cool and pure water, or those that possess ponds of cool and pure water. "Indagopakasanchannā" means well-covered by red insects of crimson hue named Indagopaka; this is said in reference to the power of the rainy season. Some teachers, however, say they are "red grasses named Indagopaka." Others say they are "Kaṇikāra trees." "Selā" means mountains made of rock, not mountains of earth. Therefore, it was said, "Just like a mountain made of rock" (Udāna 24). "Ramayanti maṃ" means they delight me; they increase my delight in seclusion (viveka). Thus, the Elder, wishing to make known his long-cultivated delight in the forest, illustrates the three kinds of delight in seclusion. Among those three, the declaration of the attainment of Arahantship is shown through the seclusion from the substrata of existence (upadhiviveka).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vanavaccha is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Novice Sivaka

The verse beginning with "Upajjhāyo" is the verse of the novice (sāmaṇera) Sivaka. What is the origin of this novice? It is said that thirty-one aeons ago from this present aeon, during the time of the Blessed One Vessabhū, he was born into a respectable family. One day, having entered the forest for some business, he saw the Blessed One Vessabhū sitting in a mountain cleft. With a heart full of faith, he approached, paid homage, and stood with joined palms. Again, seeing delightful kāsumārika fruits in that mountain cleft, he took them and offered them to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, out of compassion, accepted them. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, when his maternal uncle ordained, he ordained together with him and accumulated much merit that serves as a support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth (vivaṭṭūpanissaya). In this present Buddha's era, he was reborn as the nephew of Elder Vanavaccha, and his name was Sivaka. His mother, hearing that her elder brother Vanavaccha had ordained in the dispensation, completed the duties of a monk, and was living in the forest, said to her son: "Dear Sivaka, go and ordain in the presence of the Elder and attend to him; the Elder is now aged." That Sivaka...
75:
By the single word of his mother and because of his previously performed merit, the youth Sivaka went to the presence of his maternal uncle, the Elder, ordained, and lived in the forest while attending to him.

One day, while the novice Sivaka had gone to a village-precinct for some business, a severe illness arose in him. Although people provided medical treatment, the illness did not subside. As the novice was delayed, the Elder thought, "The novice is taking a long time; what could be the reason?" He went there, saw the sick novice, and after spending the day performing various necessary duties for him, he said at the time of dawn: "Sivaka, since the time I ordained, I have never stayed in a village; let us go from here to the forest alone."

Hearing those words, the novice Sivaka replied: "Venerable Sir, although my body is now in the village-precinct, my mind is established only in the forest. Therefore, even while lying down, I will go only to the forest." Hearing this, the Elder took him by the arm, led him to the forest, and gave him an exhortation. Established in the Elder's exhortation, the novice practiced insight meditation (vipassanā) and attained Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"Shining like a Kaṇikāra flower, sitting in a mountain cleft,
I saw the Buddha, free from dust, the Chief of the World, the Bull among Men.
With a heart of faith and a joyful mind, having made the añjali salutation,
Taking a kāsumārika fruit, I offered it to the Best of Buddhas.
Thirty-one aeons ago from now, because I gave that fruit then,
I do not know of any miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of offering fruit.
My defilements are burnt up... (etc.)... the Buddha's teaching has been done."

After attaining Arahantship, the novice Sivaka, comparing the meaning of what was said by his preceptor and himself, and wishing to make known his delight in seclusion and the completion of his task, spoke the verse beginning with "Upajjhāyo maṃ avaca."

In that verse, "Upajjhāyo" (preceptor) is so called because he closely contemplates (upanijjhāyati) what is a fault and what is not, and because he looks with the eye of wisdom, desiring the pupil's welfare. "Maṃ" refers to himself. "Avaca" means he spoke. "Ito gacchāma Sivaka" is a demonstration of the manner in which it was said: "Sivaka, come from this village-precinct to the forest place; let us go. That forest place alone is our..."
76:
It means a place suitable for living. Thus spoken to by his preceptor, Sivaka Sāmaṇera, like a noble thoroughbred horse struck by a whip, was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and, expressing his desire to go only to the forest, said:

"Though my body dwells in the village, my mind has gone to the forest. Even lying down I shall go; for one who knows, there is no attachment."

The meaning of those words is: "Even though my body is now situated near the village, my intention has gone only to the forest. Therefore, even if I am unable to stand, sit, or walk due to illness, I shall go even while lying down. In this lying posture, crawling like a reptile, I mean to say, 'Venerable Sir, let us go only to the forest.' Why? 'For one who knows, there is no attachment'—because for one who truly knows the danger in sense pleasures and saṃsāra, and the benefits in renunciation and Nibbāna according to the nature of things, there is no attachment to any object. Thus, with a single statement, he showed that he had followed his preceptor's command and, under that pretext, declared his attainment of the fruit of Arahantship."

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sivaka Sāmaṇera is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kuṇḍadhāna

"Cut off the five, abandon the five..." and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna. As for its origin—in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī. When he came of age, as mentioned above, he approached the Blessed One and, while listening to the Dhamma, saw the Teacher appoint a monk to the foremost position among those who first receive the voting tickets (salāka). He aspired for that position and lived performing meritorious deeds appropriate for it.

One day, he offered a large bunch of bananas, yellow like realgar (manosilā) powder, to the Blessed One Padumuttara who was seated after emerging from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). The Blessed One accepted and consumed it. By the power of that merit, he became a king of devas eleven times and a universal monarch (cakkavatti) twenty-four times. Thus, repeatedly performing meritorious deeds and wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he was reborn as a terrestrial deity (bhumma-devatā) in the time of Kassapa Buddha. For long-lived Buddhas, such as the Blessed One Vipassī, the Uposatha was held once every six years. The Blessed One Kassapa also recited the Pātimokkha once every six months. At the time of the Blessed One Kassapa's Pātimokkha recitation, two monks who were friends living in different regions went to perform the Uposatha. At that time, the future Elder Kuṇḍadhāna was a terrestrial deity. The love between those monks was so firm that it seemed inseparable. That deity, thinking, "Will these monks split or not?" followed them at a short distance, watching for an opportunity. Then, one monk handed his bowl and robes to the other monk to attend to his bodily needs and for the sake of washing...
77:
For long-lived Buddhas, there is no Uposatha once every fortnight. For this reason, for the Blessed One Vipassī, the Uposatha was held once every six years. But the Blessed One Kassapa recited the Pātimokkha once every six months. At the time of the Blessed One Kassapa's Pātimokkha recitation, two monks who were friends living in different regions went, saying, "We shall perform the Uposatha."

This terrestrial deity thought, "The love between these two monks is extremely firm. If there were a cause for division, would they split or not?" Watching for an opportunity, the deity followed them at a short distance. Then, one elder handed his bowl and robes to the other elder and went to a place with water to attend to his bodily needs. Having washed his hands and feet, he emerged from near a bush. The terrestrial deity, behind the elder who was emerging, manifested in the form of a very beautiful woman. She appeared as if she were shaking out and arranging her hair to tie it, as if she were brushing dust off her back, and as if she were properly adjusting and wearing her undergarment. Following closely in the elder's footsteps, she emerged from the bush.

The companion elder, standing in a suitable place, as soon as he saw this, became displeased and thought: "Now my love for this monk, which has lasted for a long time, is destroyed. If I had known such a nature, I would not have associated with this monk for so long." To the elder who was approaching, he said, "Friend, here are your bowl and robes. I will no longer travel the same path with such a wicked person." Hearing those words, the heart of that conscientious monk felt as if it were pierced by a sharp sword. Then he said to that monk, "Friend, what kind of words are you saying? For so long, I am not aware of having committed even a minor (dukkaṭa) offense. Yet today you call me a 'wicked person.' What did you see?" "What need is there for any other seeing? Did you not emerge from the same place with such an adorned woman?" "Friend, this is not so for me. I did not see such a woman." Although he spoke thus up to three times, the other elder did not believe his words. Taking only what he himself had seen as the truth, he did not travel the same path with that monk...
78: He went to the presence of the Teacher by another path. The other monk also went to the presence of the Teacher by a different path. Then, at the time of entering the Uposatha hall for the Saṅgha, that monk recognized the other monk at the Uposatha hall and, thinking, 'There is such a sinful monk in this Uposatha hall; I will not perform the Uposatha with him,' he went outside and stood there. Then, a terrestrial deity (bhummadeva), thinking, 'I have committed a grave deed,' approached the Elder in the guise of an elderly lay follower and asked, 'Venerable sir, why are you standing in this place?' 'Lay follower, a sinful monk has entered this Uposatha hall; I am standing outside because I do not wish to perform the Uposatha with him.' 'Venerable sir, do not think so; this monk is of pure virtue. The woman you saw was actually me; I did that deed to test whether the loving-kindness (mettā) of these Elders was firm or not, and to see if it would break.' 'Who are you, good man?' When asked, the deity replied, 'Venerable sir, I am a terrestrial deity.' Revealing himself through divine power, the deity prostrated at the Elder's feet and pleaded, 'Venerable sir, please forgive me for this fault; the Elder does not know (the truth). Please perform the Uposatha.' Thus entreating him, he led him into the Uposatha hall. Although that Elder performed the Uposatha in the same place at that time, he no longer stayed in the same place with the other monk due to the loss of intimacy. The story of this Elder is not further told; however, the accused Elder, practicing insight meditation (vipassanā) repeatedly, attained Arahatship. Due to the consequence of that deed, the terrestrial deity did not escape the danger of the lower realms for the duration of one Buddha-interval. If at any time he were to reach the human state, the fault committed by someone else would fall upon him alone. In the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī and was named Dhāna. When he came of age, he learned the three Vedas, and in his old age, having heard the Dhamma from the Teacher and gained faith, he ordained. From the day of his higher ordination, an adorned woman...
79: ...whenever he entered the village, she entered the village with him; whenever he left, she left. Even when he entered the monastery, she entered with him; when he stood, she stood. Thus, her constant following was evident. The Elder did not see her. Due to the consequence of his past karma, she appeared only to others. Women giving gruel and alms-food in the village would mock him, saying, 'Venerable sir, this ladle of gruel is for you, and this one is for this woman, our companion.' The Elder suffered great distress. Even when he went to the monastery, novices and young monks would surround him and mock him, saying, 'Dhāna has become a rogue (koṇḍa).' Then, for that very reason, he became known as the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna. The Elder, repeatedly getting up and unable to endure their mockery, became as if mad and said, 'You are rogues! Your preceptor is a rogue! Your teacher is a rogue!' Then they reported the matter to the Blessed One, saying, 'Venerable sir, Kuṇḍadhāna speaks such harsh words to the young monks and novices.' The Blessed One had him summoned and asked, 'Dhāna, is it true that you speak harsh words to the novices?' When he replied, 'It is true, Blessed One,' the Buddha asked, 'Why do you speak thus?' 'Blessed One, I speak thus because I cannot endure the constant harassment.' 'You have not been able to wear out the karma committed in the past until this very day. Monks, do not speak such harsh words again.' Saying this, he spoke these verses: 'Do not speak harshly to anyone; those spoken to might answer you back. Indeed, arrogant talk is painful, and retaliatory blows might touch you. If you can keep yourself as still as a broken bronze gong, then you have reached Nibbāna; arrogance is no longer found in you.' They also reported to King Kosala about this Elder wandering around with a woman. The King sent men, saying, 'Friends, go and investigate.' He himself, with a small retinue, went to the Elder's dwelling and stood watching from a suitable place. At that moment, the Elder was sitting and doing needlework, and that woman appeared to be standing not far away. Seeing this, the King said, 'There is indeed a reason for this,' and went toward where the woman was. When the King approached, she seemed to enter the Elder's leaf-hut. The King also entered that same hut with her and, looking everywhere...
80:
(The King), not seeing (the woman), thought, "This is not a woman, but only a kind of result of the Elder's karma," and though he first went near the Elder, he did not pay homage. Having learned the falsity of that matter, he returned, paid homage to the Elder, and sitting in a suitable place, asked, "Venerable Sir, are you not weary for lack of almsfood?" The Elder replied, "Great King, it is well." "Venerable Sir, I know your condition; who indeed could have faith in you as you wander about with such defilement? From today onwards, there is no need for you to go anywhere; I will support you with the four requisites. Do not be negligent in wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra)," he said, and arranged a permanent supply of alms.

Having received the King's support, the Elder, with a concentrated mind due to the suitability of food, developed insight (vipassanā) and attained the fruit of Arahantship. From that time on, that woman disappeared.

At that time, Mahāsubhaddā, living in a family of wrong view in the city of Ugga, thinking, "May the Blessed One have compassion on me," observed the Uposatha, and being free from the scent of defilements, stood on the upper terrace of the palace and made an act of truth: "May these flowers not scatter in the air but remain as a canopy over the head of the One of Ten Powers; by this sign, may the One of Ten Powers accept my alms tomorrow together with five hundred monks." She then threw eight handfuls of jasmine flowers. The flowers went and stood like a canopy over the head of the Blessed One at the time of the Dhamma teaching. The Blessed One, seeing that canopy of jasmine flowers, accepted Subhaddā's alms with his mind alone. 

The next day at dawn, he said to the Elder Ānanda, "Ānanda, today we shall go for alms to a distant place; do not give the voting tickets (salākā) to worldlings (puthujjanas), but give them only to the Noble Ones (Ariyas)." The Elder informed the monks, "Sirs, today the Blessed One will go for alms to a distant place; let worldlings not take them, let only the Noble Ones take the voting tickets." 

The Elder Kuṇḍadhāna said, "Friend Ānanda, bring the ticket," and was the first to stretch out his hand. The Elder Ānanda thought, "The Blessed One does not have the tickets given to such monks; he has them given only to the Noble Ones," and went to inform the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "Give the ticket to the one who asks." The Elder thought, "If it were not proper to give the ticket to Kuṇḍadhāna, the Blessed One would have forbidden it; there must be a reason for this," and went to give the ticket to Kuṇḍadhāna. 

Before the Elder Ānanda arrived, the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for direct knowledge, and standing in the air by psychic power, said, "Friend Ānanda, bring it; the Blessed One knows me; the Blessed One does not forbid a monk like me from taking the first ticket," and stretching out his hand, he took the ticket. Based on that incident, the Blessed One placed the Elder in the foremost (etadagga) position among the monks who take the first ticket in this Dispensation. This is because this Elder, having received the King's support and having a concentrated mind due to the suitability of food, became one who possessed the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā) due to the perfection of his supporting conditions (upanissaya) while practicing insight.
81:
(Venerable Ānanda) intended to "give the ticket" and set out. Before the Elder Ānanda arrived, the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for direct knowledge, and standing in the air by psychic power, said, "Friend Ānanda, bring it; the Blessed One knows me; the Blessed One does not forbid a monk like me from taking the first ticket," and stretching out his hand, he took the ticket. Based on that incident, the Blessed One placed the Elder in the foremost position among the monks who take the first ticket in this Dispensation. This is because this Elder, having received the King's support and having obtained suitable food, had a concentrated mind, and while striving in the work of insight, became one possessed of the six direct knowledges because he was endowed with the necessary supporting conditions. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"With a clear and happy mind, I served the Excellent Buddha, the Self-Enlightened One, the Supreme Person, who had been in seclusion for seven days.

Knowing the time he emerged (from cessation), I approached the Great Sage Padumuttara, carrying a large bunch of bananas.

The Blessed One, the All-Knowing Lord of the World, accepted it and, gladdening my heart, the Great Sage partook of it.

Having partaken, the Fully Enlightened One, the Unsurpassed Caravan Leader, sat on his seat and spoke these verses:

'Let the yakkhas who reside on this mountain, and the beings present and future in the forest, listen to my words.

I shall praise the one who served the Buddha, who is like a lion, the king of beasts; listen as I speak.

He will be the king of devas eleven times, and he will be a wheel-turning monarch twenty-four times.

In a hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka line, will arise in the world.

Due to the result of the evil deed of having insulted virtuous monks who were free from taints, he will receive a (notorious) name.'"
82:
He will be a disciple named Kuṇḍadhāna, a true heir to the Dhamma, born of the Dhamma, and created by the Dhamma, in the teaching of that Gautama Buddha.

I dwell devoted to the three kinds of seclusion, practicing meditation, delighting in Jhana, pleasing the Teacher, and remaining free from taints.

Surrounded by disciples and preceded by the community of monks, the Victorious Buddha, sitting in the midst of the Sangha, had the voting tickets taken.

Arranging my robe over one shoulder and paying homage to the Lord of the World, I was the first to take the ticket in the presence of the Best of Speakers.

By that meritorious deed, the Blessed One, who causes the ten thousand world systems to tremble, sitting in the midst of the Sangha, placed me in the foremost position.

My energy is like a beast of burden, leading to Nibbāna, the end of the four bonds; I bear this final body in the Dispensation of the Fully Enlightened One.

My defilements have been burned... (p)... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

Worldly monks, unaware of the virtues of this elder who possessed such qualities, collectively wondered at that time during the first taking of the voting tickets, "What is this?" To dispel their doubt, the elder ascended into the air, performed a miracle of psychic power, and wishing to declare his attainment of the fruit of Arahantship through another means, recited the verse beginning with "Pañca chinde".

In that verse, "Pañca chinde" means one should cut the five lower fetters that cause rebirth in the lower realms, just as a man cuts the ropes binding his feet with a weapon, using the three lower paths; one should abandon them. "Pañca jahe" means one should abandon the five higher fetters that are the cause of rebirth in the higher celestial realms, just as a man cuts the rope binding his neck, using the Path of Arahantship; or it means one should cut them. "Pañca cuttari bhāvaye" means to abandon those five higher fetters, one should further develop the five faculties such as faith, etc., after attaining the Path of Non-Returning, by means of attaining the highest Path (Arahantship). "Pañcasaṅgātigo" means such a monk, by transcending and abandoning the five attachments of lust, hatred, delusion, pride, and views, is called one who has transcended the five attachments. (He is also called one who has crossed the four floods of sense-desire, existence, views, and ignorance, and stands in Nibbāna.)

The explanation of the verses of Kuṇḍadhāna Thera is finished.

1-Ekanipāta-2-Dutiyavagga-16-Belatthasīsatheragāthā.

The verse beginning with "Yathābi ājaññam" is the verse of the Venerable Belatthasīsa Thera. The origin of that verse is as follows: When that Belatthasīsa Thera was born in a respectable family during the time of Padumuttara Buddha...
83:
Because he has completely destroyed the defilements, he is called a 'Bhikkhu'. Because he has crossed the floods of sense-desire, existence, views, and ignorance, and stands in Nibbāna, which is the other shore of those floods, he is called 'Oghatiṇṇa' (One who has crossed the flood).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Kuṇḍadhāna Thera is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Verses of Belatthasīsa Thera

The verse beginning with 'Yathāpi bhaddo ājañño' is the verse of the Venerable Belatthasīsa Thera. What is the origin of that verse? It is said that the elder was born in a respectable family during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Having approached the Blessed One and heard the Dhamma, he gained faith and ordained. Although he practiced the recluse's Dhamma, he was unable to attain the special distinction of the paths and fruits because his supporting conditions were not yet mature. However, having accumulated much merit as a supporting condition for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya), he wandered through the realms of gods and humans. Thirty-one aeons ago from this present age, he saw Vessabhū Buddha and, with a devout heart, offered a citron fruit (mātuluṅga) to him. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the heavens, and after performing further merits and passing from one happy state to another, he was born into a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī during the time of this Buddha's appearance. Even before the Blessed One's Great Enlightenment, he ordained as an ascetic under Uruvela Kassapa and tended the sacrificial fire. During the preaching of the Ādittapariyāya Sutta, which was the means of taming Uruvela Kassapa, he attained Arahantship along with the thousand former matted-hair ascetics. That account is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

'I saw the Lord of the World, shining like a Kaṇikāra flower, like the full moon, and like a blazing lamp-tree.'
'Having taken a citron fruit, I offered it to the Teacher, the Hero worthy of offerings, with my own hands and a devout heart.'
'Thirty-one aeons ago from now, because I gave that fruit then, I have not known a miserable rebirth since. This is the fruit of giving fruit.'
'My defilements have been burned... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.'

The Venerable Belatthasīsa Thera, who had thus attained Arahantship, one day rose from the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). Reflecting on the peaceful and noble bliss of seclusion and his past efforts, he recited the verse beginning with 'Yathāpi bhaddo ājañño' with a surge of rapture. In that verse, 'Yathāpi' is a particle used in the sense of a simile. 'Bhaddo' means being endowed with courage, strength, and power. 'Ājañño' (thoroughbred) means one who has the nature of knowing well what is a cause and what is not; it means 'noble' because of such knowledge.
84: The Elder Belaṭṭhasīsa, the preceptor of the Venerable Treasurer of the Dhamma (Ānanda), having thus attained Arahantship, emerged one day from the attainment of fruition. Having reflected on that peaceful, sublime, and spiritual bliss, as well as his own previous efforts (pubba-yoga), he spoke the verse beginning with 'Yathāpi bhaddo ājañño' through the power of a surge of joy. In that verse, 'yathāpi' is a particle used for the purpose of comparison. 'Bhaddo' means excellent, endowed with courage, strength, power, speed, effort, and so on. 'Ājañño' means a thoroughbred, one who knows well what is a cause and what is not. There are three types of thoroughbreds: the noble bull, the noble horse, and the noble elephant; here, the noble bull is intended. That noble bull is also one yoked to the task of ploughing. Therefore, he said 'naṅgalāvattanī'. It is called 'naṅgalāvatta' because it turns the ploughshare here and there; it means one who ploughs according to the furrows in the field. Alternatively, the place where the ploughshare is turned is called 'naṅgalāvatta', meaning the furrows in the field; it means (moving) in those furrows. For the sake of the verse's euphony, it is said here as 'vattanī' with a long vowel (dīgha). 'Sikhī' means one who has horns called 'sikhā' because they are like flames due to their position on the head. Other teachers, however, say that 'sikhā' here refers to the hump (kakudha). In either case, 'sikhī' is a mention of a primary feature. 'Appakasirena' means without difficulty (easily). 'Rattindivā' means nights and days. The connection is: thus the (times) pass for me without difficulty. This is what is meant: 'Just as a noble thoroughbred bull yoked to ploughing goes about turning here and there without difficulty, even in furrows with thick grass, roots, and so on, without minding them, until it shows exhaustion from the grass and ploughing; even so, the days and nights pass for me easily and without difficulty.' He stated the reason for this as 'sukhe laddhe nirāmise'. It means because of having obtained the peaceful and sublime bliss of the attainment of fruition, which is unmixed with the baits of sensuality, the baits of the world, and the baits of the round of rebirth. Here, the locative case (sattamī) in 'sukhe' and so on is a locative used in the sense of the nominative (paccatta), as in 'vanappagumbe' and 'tena vata re vattabbe'. Alternatively, he spoke 'sukhe laddhe nirāmise' after reflecting that from that day onwards, the nights and days pass without difficulty. It means when the spiritual bliss is obtained, starting from the time it was obtained. ## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Belaṭṭhasīsa is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Verse of Dāsaka Thera

The verse beginning with "Middhī yadā" is the verse of the venerable Elder Dāsaka. What is its origin? It is said that ninety-one aeons ago from this present aeon (before the appearance of Vipassī Buddha), he descended from Mount Gandhamādana to the human realm and offered delightful mangoes to a Paccekabuddha named Ajita, who was wandering for alms in a certain village. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in the time of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha, he ordained in the Dispensation and performed much merit as a support for the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭūpanissaya). Having thus been devoted to wholesome deeds and passing from one happy destination to another, he was reborn in this Buddha's era in a good family in Sāvatthī. His name was Dāsaka. He was appointed by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika to the task of looking after the monastery. While respectfully looking after the monastery, he gained faith through frequently seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dhamma, and he ordained.

Some teachers, however, say: "In the time of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha, he was born in a good family and, upon reaching maturity, while serving a certain Arahant Thera, he ordered the Thera to do some work, wishing to have it done. Due to that [bad] deed, in the time of our Blessed Buddha, he was reborn in the womb of a slave woman of Anāthapiṇḍika in Sāvatthī. When he reached maturity, the merchant appointed him to look after the monastery, and he gained faith in the same manner as previously mentioned. The great merchant, knowing his virtuous conduct and his inclination, freed him from slavery and said, 'Ordain as you wish.' Then the monks ordained him."

From the time of his ordination, he became lazy and lacked energy, performing no duties great or small; how then could he perform the recluse's Dhamma (samaṇadhamma)? He lived eating as much as he desired and indulging in much sleep. Even at the time of hearing the Dhamma, he would enter a corner, sit at the edge of the assembly, and fall asleep, breathing with a snoring sound (ghuru-ghuru). Then the Blessed Buddha, seeing his past potential (upanissaya), uttered the verse beginning with "Middhī yadā hoti mahagghaso ca" to arouse spiritual urgency (saṃvega).

In that verse, "middhī" means one overcome by sloth and torpor (thina-middha). For when torpor (middha) overcomes someone, sloth (thina) also overcomes them. "Yadā" means at which time. "Mahagghaso" means a great eater (glutton), like one of the following: an āharahatthaka, an alaṃsāṭaka, a tatthavaṭṭaka, a kākamāsaka, or a bhuttavamitaka. "Niddāyitā" means one who has the habit of sleeping. "Samparivattasāyī" means one who, lying down and rolling from here to there, repeatedly indulges in the pleasure of lying on the back, the pleasure of lying on the side, and the pleasure of dozing.
86:
He shows the repeated practice of the pleasure arising from drowsiness. "Nivāpapuṭṭho" means one who is plump and fed with pig-fodder such as broken rice. Indeed, a domestic pig, being raised from a young age, when it has a fat body and is unable to go out of the house, just lies down turning this way and that under a couch and so on. The meaning intended here is: when a man is oppressed by drowsiness (middha) and is a glutton, like a great hog fattened on food, unable to maintain any other posture and having the habit of sleeping, he lies turning this way and that. At that time, he is unable to contemplate the three characteristics: "impermanence, suffering, and non-self." Because of the inability to contemplate these three characteristics, that person of dull wisdom repeatedly undergoes rebirth; he is not liberated from the round of rebirths. Having heard these words of the Buddha, Elder Dāsaka was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), developed insight (vipassanā), and before long realized the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"The Buddha named Ajita, who was endowed with conduct (caraṇa) and skilled in concentration (samādhi), lived in the Himalayas at that time.
While the Buddha, who was of golden hue and worthy of receiving offerings, was walking on the road, I offered him a mango fruit.
In the ninety-one aeons from this Bhadda-kappa, because of the merit of offering that mango fruit, I have not known the four woeful states; this is the result of offering the fruit.
My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

After reaching the fruit of Arahantship, Elder Dāsaka reflected, "The Blessed One admonished me with this verse; this verse is like a goad to me," and he recited that very verse again. This was the Elder's declaration of his attainment of Arahantship (aññābyākaraṇa) by way of repeating the instruction.

## The Commentary on the Verse of Elder Dāsaka is finished.

## 8. Singālapituttheragāthāvaṇṇanā

"Ahu buddhassa dāyādo" and so forth is the verse of Elder Singālapitu. What is its origin? It is said that ninety-four aeons from this Bhadda-kappa, he saw the Paccekabuddha named Sataraṃsi wandering for alms. With a devoted mind, he paid homage and offered a palmyra fruit that was in his hand. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the celestial realm.
87:
Having performed meritorious deeds here and there and wandering only in the happy realms, he was born in a human family during the time of Buddha Kassapa. Having gained faith in the Dispensation, he ordained and developed the perception of a skeleton (aṭṭhikasaññā). Again, when our Buddha appeared, he was born in a noble family in Sāvatthī. Upon reaching maturity, he married and had a son, whom he named "Singālaka." Therefore, people called him "Singālapitu" (the father of Singālaka). Later, he abandoned the bond of the household and ordained in the Dispensation. The Blessed One, seeing his inclination, gave him the meditation subject of the perception of a skeleton. Taking that meditation subject, he resided in the Bhesakaḷāvana forest at Susumāragiri in the Bhagga country. Then, a deity residing in that forest, wishing to arouse effort in him and to reveal the meaning that "the fruit of meditation will soon be in his hand" by way of referring to another, spoke the verse: "He is an heir of the Buddha."

In that verse, "ahu" means "is"; this past tense form is used in the sense of the present. "Buddhassa" means of the Omniscient Buddha. "Dāyādo" means an heir of the Dhamma, one who receives the ninefold supramundane Dhamma as an inheritance through his own right practice (sammā-paṭipatti). Alternatively, "ahu" means "will be." The meaning is that any obstacle to becoming an heir of the Buddha of such a name will be removed right now. Therefore, it is said: "I think that he will quickly abandon sensual lust (kāmarāga)." "Bhesakaḷāvane" is so called either because it was obtained and possessed by a yakkha named Bhesaka, or because of the abundance of pigeon pea plants (bhesakaḷā) and wood; thus the forest received the name "Bhesakaḷāvana." Stating the reason for that monk being an heir of the Buddha, it is said: "Merely by the perception of a skeleton, he pervaded this earth." In that verse, "kevalaṃ" means entirely, without remainder. "Aṭṭhisaññāya" means by the meditation on the skeleton. "Aphari" means he pervaded by way of directing the mind to "skeleton." "Pathaviṃ" refers to the ground of his own individual existence (attabhāva). Here, the individual existence is called "pathavī" (earth), as in the verses such as "Who shall overcome this earth?" "Manyehaṃ" should be split as "manye ahaṃ." There is also a reading "manyāhaṃ." "So" refers to that monk. I think that monk will soon abandon sensual lust. Why? Because the perception of a skeleton is the direct opposite of sensual lust. The intended meaning is this: a person who, through the perception of a skeleton obtained in one place, [pervades] his own or all others'...
88:
That monk, having established himself by pervading his own body as just "bones", and taking that meditation on bones (atthika-jhāna) as a basis for insight, will before long abandon sensual lust (kāmarāga) through the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga), or abandon all craving—named "kāma" because it is desired and "rāga" because it attaches—through the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga). Hearing this verse, the Elder thought, "This deity spoke thus to inspire my effort," and having resolved upon unwavering energy and developing insight, he attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

"The Blessed One named Sataraṃsī, self-enlightened and unconquered, having arisen from the three types of seclusion, came forth for alms.
Seeing the Best of Men, I, holding a fruit in my hand, approached Him; with a confident and joyful mind, I offered a palm fruit.
Ninety-four aeons ago, I gave that fruit; because of that gift of fruit, I do not know of (have not reached) any woeful state.
My defilements are burnt away... I have followed the Buddha's teaching."

Upon reaching Arahantship, out of appreciation for the deity's words, he recited that very verse as an inspired utterance (udāna). That became the Elder's declaration of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Siṅgālapitu is finished.

## 9. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kula

"Udakañhi nayanti" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Elder Kula. What is its origin? This elder, having accumulated much merit in the past which is a condition for liberation from the cycle of suffering, and being possessed of sufficient requisites, saw the Blessed One Vipassī traveling through the air. With a confident mind and desiring to offer a coconut, he stood there. The Teacher, knowing his mind, descended and accepted the offering. With an extremely confident mind and the faith gained therefrom, he approached the Teacher and requested ordination. The Teacher [commanded] another...
89:
(The Blessed One) commanded a certain monk, "Ordain this man." Having been ordained and received the higher ordination, he practiced the recluse's Dhamma. After passing away from that life, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans during the interval between six Buddhas. In this Buddha's era, he was reborn in a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī. He was named Kula. When he came of age, having gained faith in the Dispensation, he ordained in the presence of the Blessed One, but due to much distraction (vikkhepa), he was unable to achieve distinction.

Then one day, while entering the village for alms, he saw men on the way digging the earth to make a channel and leading water to wherever they desired, and he noted that. Entering the village, he saw a fletcher putting an arrow shaft into a straightening tool, closing one eye and looking to make it straight, and he noted that too. Going further, he saw carpenters hewing parts of a chariot wheel such as the rim, the hub, and so on, and he noted that as well. Returning to the monastery, after finishing his meal and putting away his bowl and robes, he sat for the day's abiding. Taking the signs he had seen as similes, he reflected on taming his own mind:

"People can lead even inanimate water to wherever they desire. Likewise, they can make even an inanimate crooked arrow shaft straight by means of a device. Likewise, carpenters can make inanimate pieces of wood, such as the rim and so on, crooked or straight. Why then should I not make my own mind straight?" Thinking thus, he developed insight, and by striving and exerting himself, he attained Arahantship before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

"In the city of Bandhumatī, I was then a gardener. I saw the stainless Buddha Vipassī traveling through the air.
Taking a coconut, I offered it to the Best of Buddhas. The Greatly Renowned One, standing in the air, accepted it.
By offering the coconut to the Buddha with an especially clear mind, I obtained the benefit that brings joy and happiness in the present life.
At that time, I obtained abundant rapture and supreme happiness. Wherever I am reborn in various lives, treasures always arise for me."
90:
“Ninety-one aeons ago, I gave a fruit as an offering; because of that meritorious deed, I do not know of any rebirth in the four states of misery. This is the fruit of offering a fruit.

My divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) is exceptionally purified; I am skilled in concentration (samādhi); I have reached the far shore of supernormal knowledge (abhiññā). This is the fruit of offering a fruit.

My defilements have been burnt away... the teaching of the Buddha has been carried out.” (Thus he spoke).

In this way, by taking the signs he had seen as objects and developing insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahatship. Upon reaching that state, comparing it with the discipline of his own mind and wishing to explain another matter, he spoke the verse beginning with: “Irrigators lead the water.”

In that verse, in the phrase “udakañhi,” the word “hi” is a mere particle. “Nayanti” means they dig here and there in the earth, remove obstacles, fill it with water, and by making a canal or using a wooden trough, they lead the water to wherever they desire. Because they lead it in such a way, they are called “nettikā” (irrigators/canal-makers). “Tejanaṃ” refers to an arrow-shaft. The meaning is: irrigators lead the water to their desired place; fletchers also straighten the arrow-shaft by heating it over a fire. Carpenters (tacchakā), for the sake of making rims and so on, plane the wood and bend it according to their wish, making it straight or curved. In this way, by making such things their object, the wise ones of good practice, through the excellent practice of virtue (sīla) and so forth which they have undertaken, bring about the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) and so on, thus disciplining themselves. When they reach the fruit of Arahatship, they are truly called those who are perfectly disciplined.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Kulatthera is finished.

## 10. Ajitattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

“I have no fear of death,” and so on, is the verse of the Venerable Ajita Thera. What is its origin? It is said that ninety-one aeons ago, having seen Vipassī Buddha and with a confident mind, he offered a wood-apple (kapittha) fruit. After that, performing various meritorious deeds and wandering through the realms of devas and humans, in this aeon, even before our Buddha had appeared, he was reborn in Sāvatthī as the son of the Brahmin Aggāsanīya, the chief chaplain of King Mahākosala. His name was Ajita. At that time, a Brahmin named Bāvarī, who lived in Sāvatthī, was endowed with three marks of a Great Man and had reached the far shore of the three Vedas. That Brahmin left Sāvatthī, became an ascetic, and lived in a wood-apple grove (Kapitthārāma) on the banks of the Godhāvarī River. Then Ajita was ordained as a pupil under that Brahmin Bāvarī. Urged by a deity who desired his welfare, Bāvarī sent Ajita to the Buddha. Along with Tissa Metteyya and others, he approached the Buddha and asked questions only with his mind. When those questions were answered, with a confident mind, he was ordained in the presence of the Buddha, took a subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), developed insight, and reached the fruit of Arahatship...
91:
At one time, a Brahmin named Bāvarī, who lived in Sāvatthī, was endowed with three marks of a Great Man and had reached the far shore of the three Vedas. He left Sāvatthī, became an ascetic, and lived in a wood-apple grove (Kapitthārāma) on the banks of the Godhāvarī River. Then Ajita was ordained as a pupil under that Brahmin Bāvarī. Urged and prompted by a deity who desired his welfare, Bāvarī sent Ajita to the Buddha. Along with Tissa Metteyya and others, he approached the Buddha and asked questions only with his mind. When those questions were answered, with a confident mind, he was ordained in the presence of the Buddha, took a subject of meditation, developed insight, and reached the fruit of Arahatship. Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna:

“To the Buddha of golden hue, worthy of receiving offerings, as He was walking on the road, I gave a wood-apple fruit.

Because of the merit of giving that wood-apple fruit ninety-one aeons ago, I have never known rebirth in the four states of misery. This is the fruit of offering a wood-apple fruit.

My defilements have been burnt away... the teaching of the Buddha has been carried out.”

Upon reaching the fruit of Arahatship, uttering a lion's roar, he recited the verse: “I have no fear of death.”

In that verse, ‘maraṇe’ means because of the cause of death. ‘Me’ means for me. There is no fear because the root of existence has been cut and rebirth has been exhausted. Only for those who have not yet abandoned the root of existence would there be fear of death, thinking, “What will my future rebirth be like?” ‘Nikantī’ means the craving of longing. That craving no longer exists because the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā) are clearly seen as suffering, essence-less, and so forth, and because the formations (saṅkhāra) have been thoroughly suppressed. I, having reached such a state, shall lay down this burden of suffering called the body. In laying it down, I shall do so with the wisdom of reflection due to the abundance of wisdom, and with the mindfulness of clear perception due to the abundance of mindfulness, thinking: “The purpose to be achieved with this body has been achieved; now this body must certainly be discarded.” After saying this verse, the Elder entered into meditative absorption (jhāna) and immediately thereafter attained Parinibbāna.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Ajita Thera is finished.

## The Commentary on the Second Vagga is finished.

## 3. Third Chapter (Tatiyavagga)
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Nigrodha

"I do not fear danger"—this verse is that of the Venerable Elder Nigrodha. What is its origin? It is said that one thousand eight hundred aeons ago, this elder was born into a wealthy Brahmin family (Brāhmaṇamahāsāla). Upon reaching maturity, seeing the disadvantages of sensual pleasures and the benefits of renunciation, he abandoned the bonds of household life and entered the forest. Having built a leaf-hut in a certain Sal forest, he was ordained as an ascetic and lived consuming forest roots and fruits.

At that time, the Buddha named Piyadassī appeared in the world. While quenching the heat of defilements for the world including the devas by raining down the nectar of the Dhamma, one day, out of compassion for the ascetic, he entered that Sal forest and entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). While going out to search for forest roots and fruits, the ascetic saw the Blessed One and, with a devout mind, took blossoming Sal branches and constructed a Sal pavilion. Covering that pavilion entirely with Sal flowers, he paid homage to the Blessed One. Due to the power of joy and happiness, he did not even go for food but remained there paying homage.

Emerging from the attainment of cessation, the Blessed One, out of compassion for that ascetic, thought, "Let the community of monks arrive," intending to "inspire faith in the community of monks as well." At that very moment, the community of monks arrived. Seeing the community of monks, the ascetic, with a devout mind, paid homage and stood with palms joined in reverence. The Blessed One, by means of a smile, revealed the ascetic's future prosperity, preached the Dhamma, and then departed together with the community of monks.

Through that meritorious deed, wandering only among devas and humans and accumulating much merit as a support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya), he was born into a wealthy Brahmin family in Sāvatthī during the time of this Buddha's appearance and was named Nigrodhatissa. On the day the Jetavana monastery was accepted, he gained faith upon seeing the Buddha's power, was ordained, and after striving in insight meditation (vipassanā), soon became an possessor of the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā). Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

"Having entered the Sal forest, my hermitage was well-prepared;
Covered with Sal flowers, I lived in the forest then."
