93:
"The Blessed One Piyadassī, the Self-Enlightened, the Supreme Person,
Desiring seclusion, the Fully Enlightened One approached the Sal forest.

Leaving the hermitage, I went to the forest,
Searching for roots and fruits, I was wandering in the forest then.

There I saw the Fully Enlightened One, Piyadassī of great fame,
Seated well in attainment, shining in the great forest.

Having set up four posts above the Buddha,
I made a well-constructed pavilion and covered it with Sal flowers.

Maintaining that Sal-covered pavilion for seven days,
With a clear mind in that pavilion, I paid homage to the Best of Buddhas.

At that time, the Blessed One, emerging from concentration,
The Supreme Man sat looking a yoke's length ahead.

A disciple named Varuṇa of the Teacher Piyadassī,
Approached the Leader with a hundred thousand masters of the senses (Arahants).

The Blessed One Piyadassī, the Elder of the world, the Bull among men,
The Conqueror, seated in the midst of the community of monks, manifested a smile.

The Elder Anuruddha, the attendant of the Teacher Piyadassī,
Arranging his robe over one shoulder, questioned the Great Sage:

'What, O Blessed One, is the cause for the Teacher's smile?
When there is a reason, the Teacher manifests a smile.'

'The youth who maintained the Sal-flower roof over me for seven days,
Remembering his deed, I manifested a smile.

I see no place where this merit will not ripen;
Whether in the deva world or the human world, the opportunity does not cease.

For him who dwells in the deva world, endowed with meritorious deeds,
As far as his retinue extends, it will be covered by Sal flowers.'"
94:
"In that deva world, with divine dances, songs, and instrumental music,
That person, endowed with meritorious deeds, will always rejoice in peace.

As far as his retinue extends, they will be fragrant with the scent of Sal flowers.
While dwelling in that deva world, a rain of Sal flowers will fall.

When this person passes away from that deva world, he will come to the human world;
In this human world too, a roof of Sal flowers will remain at all times.

In this human world too, dancing and singing accompanied by gongs and cymbals
Will always surround me; this is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.

When the sun rises, a rain of Sal flowers falls;
Joined with meritorious deeds, it rains at all times.

One thousand eight hundred aeons from now, born in the Okkāka dynasty,
A Teacher named Gotama by name will appear in the world.

Being a true heir to his Dhamma, a breast-born son, created by the Dhamma,
Fully understanding all taints (āsava), he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.

When penetrating the Four Noble Truths, there will be a roof of Sal flowers;
When being cremated on the funeral pyre, there will be a roof of flowers there.

Having praised the ripening of the deed, the Great Sage Piyadassī
Preached the Dhamma to the assembly, satisfying them with the rain of Dhamma.

For thirty aeons, I exercised sovereignty among the devas;
Sixty and seven times, I was a Wheel-turning Monarch.

Coming from the deva world to this human world, I obtain extensive happiness;
In this human world too, the occurrence of the Sal-flower roof is the fruit of the Sal pavilion.

This is my last existence, my final birth;
In this final birth too, there will be a roof of Sal flowers at all times.

Having pleased the Great Sage Gotama, the Bull of the Sakyans,
I have reached the unshakable state (Nibbāna), abandoning victory and defeat."
95:
One thousand eight hundred aeons ago, I worshiped the Buddha. Due to the merit of that worship, I do not know of any unhappy rebirth (duggati).

My defilements are burnt; all existences are uprooted. Like an elephant that has broken its bonds, I live without taints (āsavas).

My coming to the presence of the Excellent Buddha was indeed a good coming. The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

The four analytical insights, the eight liberations, and the six superknowledges have been realized. The Buddha's teaching has been followed and carried out.

Thus, being one who possesses the six superknowledges and spending time in the bliss of fruition (phalasukha), he spoke the verse beginning with "I do not fear fear" by way of declaring his attainment (aññābyākaraṇa) to clarify the liberating nature of the Dispensation.

In that verse, "fear" (bhaya) refers to birth, aging, and so on, because one fears from these. In the word "bhayassa", the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative. The meaning is: "I do not fear because of the causes of fear such as birth, aging, and death." He stated the reason for not fearing: "Our Teacher is skilled in the Deathless." Our Teacher is proficient in the Deathless (Nibbāna) and is expert in giving the Deathless to those to be tamed. "Where fear does not remain" means that in that Nibbāna, the aforementioned fear does not stay or find an opportunity. "Tena" means because of that Nibbāna. "Vajanti" means they go only to the place of safety (fearlessness). Nibbāna is indeed called the place of safety. By what means do they go? He said, "Monks go by the path." Monks who follow the Teacher's advice go by the Eightfold Noble Path; "bhikkhu" means those who see danger in Saṃsāra. Or, "yattha" means because of the attainment of the Noble Path, the twenty-five kinds of fear, such as self-reproach, find no footing. By that Noble Path, monks in the Buddha's Dispensation go to the place of safety. "I too have gone by that path; therefore, I do not fear fear," thus the Elder declared his attainment.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Nigrodha Thera is finished.
96:
By this verse, the Elder declared his attainment of Arahatship. The commentary on the verses of Nigrodha Thera is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Cittaka Thera

The verse beginning with "Nīlāsugīvā" is that of the Venerable Cittaka Thera. What is its origin? It is said that since the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he accumulated merit which is a support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya). Ninety-one aeons ago, he was born into a human family. Upon reaching maturity, he saw Vipassī Buddha and, with a heart full of faith, made an offering of flowers and paid homage. He resolved in his heart toward the Buddha and Nibbāna, thinking, "There must surely be a peaceful Dhamma in this Dispensation." Due to that meritorious deed, he passed away from that life and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. After performing various merits and wandering through the rounds of rebirth among gods and humans, in this Buddha's era, he was born in Rājagaha as the son of a wealthy Brahmin and was named Cittaka.

When the Buddha arrived at Rājagaha and was staying at the Veḷuvana monastery, Cittaka approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and ordained. Taking a meditation subject suitable for his temperament, he entered the forest and, devoted to meditation, attained Jhana. Developing insight (vipassanā) based on Jhana, he soon attained Arahatship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"I saw the Buddha Vipassī, the Leader of the World, free from dust,
Glowing like a Kaṇikāra flower, seated within a mountain range.

Having raised three Kiṅkaṇi flowers, I offered them;
After worshiping the Fully Enlightened One, I departed facing south.

Due to that well-performed deed and the aspiration of my volition,
I abandoned the human body and went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Ninety-one aeons ago, I worshiped the Buddha;
Due to the merit of that worship, I do not know of any unhappy rebirth.

My defilements are burnt... (as before) ... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

After attaining Arahatship, he went to Rājagaha to pay homage to the Teacher. Then the monks asked him, "Friend, did you live diligently in the forest?" To inform them of his diligent living and to declare his attainment of Arahatship, he recited the verse beginning with "Nīlāsugīvā".
97: In that verse, 'nīlāsugīvā' means blue-necked; a long vowel is used here for the sake of the verse's euphony; it means endowed with a beautiful neck because of its folds. Those peacocks are called 'nīla' (blue/dark) because they are mostly blue in color. They are called 'sugīvā' because of their beautiful necks. 'Sikhino' means crested ones, because they are majestic with the crests grown on their heads. 'Morā' means peacocks (mayūra). 'Kārambhiyaṃ' means in the Karamba tree. Or 'Kārambhiya' is the name of that forest. Therefore, 'Kārambhiyaṃ' means in the forest named Kārambha. 'Abhinadanti' means that in the rainy season, upon hearing the thunder of the clouds, the peacocks make the 'kekā' sound and cry out as if surpassing the swans and others with the voice produced by the perfection of the season. 'Te' refers to those peacocks. 'Sītavātakīḷitā' means those (peacocks) who cry out with a melodious sound while playing due to the cool rain-wind. 'Suttaṃ' means sleeping to dispel the drowsiness that occurs after a meal, or sleeping at the permitted time to relieve physical fatigue. 'Jhāyanti' means the habit of meditating through the meditations of Samatha and Vipassanā, being devoted to mental development. 'Nibodhenti' means they awaken. The meaning is that they make one rise from sleep by arousing clear comprehension (sampajañña) in this way: 'Even these peacocks, without falling into sleep, remain awake and perform their own duties; what then of me?' ## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Citta is finished. ## 3. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Gosāla. The verse beginning with 'Ahaṃ kho veḷugumbasmiṃ' is the verse of the Venerable Elder Gosāla. What is the origin? He too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated wholesome merit which is a strong support for the ending of the round of rebirth in various lives. Ninety-one aeons ago from this one, on a certain mountain, he saw a rag-robe of a Paccekabuddha hanging from a tree branch. With a devoted mind, thinking 'This is indeed the banner of the Arahants,' he worshipped it with flowers. Because of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. From then on, wandering only among devas and humans, he was born in this Buddha's era in the kingdom of Magadha, in a wealthy family, with the name Gosāla. Because of his friendship with Soṇa Koṭikaṇṇa, when he heard about the latter's ordination, he thought: 'Even that Soṇa Koṭikaṇṇa, despite having such great wealth...'
98:
"...will go forth as a monk, what then of me?" With such spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arisen, he ordained in the presence of the Blessed One. Taking a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable for his temperament and seeking a favorable dwelling place, he lived in a mountain range not far from his native village. His mother gave him alms-food every day. Then one day, when he entered the village for alms, his mother offered him milk-rice (pāyāsa) prepared with honey and sugar. He took that milk-rice, sat at the foot of a certain bamboo thicket in the shade of that mountain, and after eating, with his bowl and hands washed, he began to practice insight (vipassanā). Due to the attainment of suitable food, his body and mind were healthy and concentrated. As the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa) and other insights arose sharply and courageously, he applied himself to insight without difficulty. Progressing through the stages of the path, he brought his meditation to its peak and realized Arahatship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

'Not far from the Himalayas, there is a mountain named Udaṅgaṇa;
There I saw a rag-robe hanging from the top of a tree.

Having picked three kiṅkaṇi flowers at that time,
With a joyful heart, I honored that rag-robe from below.

Through that well-performed deed and through my intentions and aspirations,
Having abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Ninety-one aeons ago from this age, I performed that deed at that time;
I have not known a miserable rebirth since honoring the banner of the Arahats.

My defilements have been burned away... I have followed the teaching of the Buddha.'

Having attained Arahatship, wishing to go to the mountain range for the sake of living happily in this present life (diṭṭhadhamma-sukhavihāra), and desiring to make known his practice, he spoke the verse: 'Ahaṃ kho veḷugumbasmiṃ'.

In that verse, 'veḷugumbasmiṃ' means near the bamboo thicket, in the shade of that thicket. 'Bhuttvāna madhupāyāsaṃ' means having consumed the milk-rice mixed with honey. 'Padakkhiṇaṃ' means with right acceptance, by properly receiving the instruction of the Teacher. 'Sammasanto khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ' means contemplating with insight the rise and fall of the five aggregates of clinging; even if...
99:
The meaning is that, having now completed what was to be done, he wishes to practice insight (vipassanā) again for the sake of attaining fruition (phalasamāpatti). “I will return to the mountain range” means that he will go specifically to the mountain range where he had previously resided. “I will cultivate seclusion” means that he wishes to cultivate the seclusion of fruition, known as the seclusion of tranquility (paṭipassaddhiviveka), and physical seclusion (kāyaviveka); or it should be understood as meaning he will go to the mountain range which is the cause for cultivating those two types of seclusion. Having spoken thus, the Elder went to that very mountain range. This verse itself was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Gosāla Thera is Finished.

## 4. The Commentary on the Verses of Sugandha Thera

“Anuvassiko pabbajito” is the verse of the Venerable Sugandha Thera. What is its origin? It is said that ninety-two aeons ago, during the time of the Tissa Buddha, he was born in the human world. When he reached the age of discretion, he lived wandering in the forest, killing animals as a hunter. Out of compassion for him, the Teacher (the Buddha) left a footprint and departed. When he saw the shrine of the Teacher’s footprint, due to the merit he had performed under previous Buddhas, he realized, “These are the footprints of the Supreme Person in the world including the devas.” Filled with joy and happiness, he offered Koraṇḍaka flowers and gained confidence in his heart.

Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world. Passing away from there, he performed various merits repeatedly and wandered through the worlds of devas and humans. During the time of the Kassapa Buddha, he became a householder and offered a great gift to the Teacher and the Saṅgha of monks. He ground expensive Gosīta sandalwood to make a paste for the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) and made a prayer: “In every place I am born, may my body have such a fragrance.” Thus, having performed many meritorious deeds in other various lives, he wandered only in the happy realms (sugati). In this Buddha’s era, he was born in Sāvatthī in the home of a wealthy Brahmin.

From the time he was conceived in his mother’s womb, his mother’s body and the entire house were filled with a fragrant scent. On the day he was born, an exceptionally superior fragrance spread even to the neighboring houses. His parents, saying, “Our son has come bringing his own name,” named him “Sugandha” (Fragrant). As he gradually...
100:
...reached the proper age, he saw the Elder Mahāsela. Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of that Elder, he went forth (ordained). While practicing the work of insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahatship within seven days. Thus it is stated in the Apadāna:

“In the past, I was a forest worker. When my father and mother died, I lived by killing animals; I had no wholesome merit.
Near my dwelling, the Tissa Buddha, the Eye of the World, the Supreme Leader, showed three footprints out of compassion.
Seeing the footprints trodden by the Teacher named Tissa, with a joyful heart, I gained confidence in the footprints.
Seeing a blooming Koraṇḍaka tree growing on the earth, I took the flowers along with the buds and honored the noble footprints.
Through that well-performed deed and through my intentions and prayers, I abandoned the human body and went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
In whatever womb I am born, whether as a deva or a human, I have a complexion like the Koraṇḍaka flower and I am possessed of a beautiful radiance.
Ninety-two aeons ago, I performed that deed. Due to the fruit of honoring the footprints, I have never known a miserable rebirth (duggati).
My defilements are burnt away... I have fulfilled the Buddha’s teaching.”

Having attained Arahatship and wishing to declare his final knowledge, he spoke this verse: “Anuvassiko pabbajito.”

In that verse, “anuvassiko” means entering the rains (vassa) is “anuvassa,” and “anuvassa” itself is “anuvassiko.” “Pabbajito” means one who has gone forth. The meaning is one who has just entered the rains after becoming a monk, a monk of one year. Alternatively, a past rains retreat is called “anuvassa,” and one who has that rains is “anuvassiko.” If a monk’s rains are not yet complete and thus not yet counted, he is described in this way.
101:
"Anuvassiko pabbajito" means one who has entered the rainy season retreat (vassa); thus, he is called "anuvassa." This "anuvassa" itself is called "anuvassika." "Pabbajito" refers to the attainment of monkhood. It means one who has become a monk and has just reached one rainy season retreat. Alternatively, a completed rainy season is called "anuvassa," and one who has that rainy season is called "anuvassika." If a monk's rainy seasons are not yet complete and cannot be counted, he is called "avassika" (one without a vassa). Therefore, it means "one who has no vassa." Behold the excellence of the Dhamma of your Teacher, the Blessed One—its well-expounded nature and its certain leading to liberation—in which Dhamma you were ordained having just reached one rainy season. You have reached, attained, and realized the three knowledges: the knowledge of recollecting past lives, the knowledge of the divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of taints. Because of this realization, you have properly followed and practiced the instruction and advice of the Dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha. Thus, based on the fact that the task of the Path and Fruit has been completed, the Elder, filled with joy and happiness, speaks of himself as if he were another person.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sugandha Thera is finished.

## 5. The Commentary on the Verses of Nandiya Thera

"Obhāsajātaṃ" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Nandiya Thera. What is its origin? It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, he [Nandiya] constructed a railing of sandalwood at the shrine (cetiya) and performed a grand offering and honor. From then on, being endowed with noble intention and accumulating many meritorious deeds that are the basis for liberation from the cycle of rebirths in various existences, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn in the Sakyan royal family in Kapilavatthu. Because his parents were filled with joy at his birth, they named him "Nandiya." When he reached maturity, while Sakyan princes like Anuruddha were ordaining in the presence of the Teacher, he himself also ordained. While practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), due to his previous meritorious deeds, he attained Arahatship before long.

Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"The Victor named Padumuttara, the Chief of the World, the Best of Men, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having shone like a great mass of fire, attained Parinibbāna.

When the Great Hero had attained Nibbāna, there was a widespread shrine; people from afar came to attend at the excellent and noble relic chamber.

With a confident and joyful mind, I made a sandalwood railing; at that time, the mass of the shrine and what was suitable for the shrine were clearly visible."
102:
"Whether being reborn in the world of devas or humans, I do not see any inferiority in myself; this is the fruit of my past deeds.

One thousand five hundred aeons ago from this present age, there were eight wheel-turning monarchs (cakkavatti) of the same name and great power.

My defilements have been burnt away... I have followed the Dispensation of the Buddha."

After attaining Arahatship, while residing in the Pācīnavamsamigadāya (Eastern Bamboo Grove Deer Park) together with Elders such as Venerable Anuruddha, one day Māra the Evil One, wishing to frighten Venerable Nandiya, displayed a terrifying form. The Elder, knowing that "This is Māra," and wishing to show, "O Evil One, what can your actions do to those who have transcended the realm of Māra? By doing so, you alone will meet with exhaustion and misfortune," spoke the verse beginning with "Obhāsajātaṃ phalagaṃ."

In that verse, "Obhāsajātaṃ" means having a radiance that has arisen through the light of knowledge, because of the attainment of the knowledge of the highest Path (arahattamagga-ñāṇa). It means having an exceedingly brilliant radiance because the darkness of defilements has been entirely destroyed and dispelled by that Path-knowledge. "Phalagaṃ" means having reached the Fruit (arahattaphala), meaning being endowed with the highest Fruit-knowledge. The word "cittaṃ" refers generally to the mind of an Arahant. Therefore, he said "abhiṇhaso" (constantly). Because their minds incline toward cessation (nirodha), Arahants constantly enter the attainment of the Fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala-samāpatti); thus, it is worthy to be called "a mind endowed with the Fruit." "Tādisaṃ" means an Arahant of such a nature. "Āsajja" means by harassing, oppressing, or assaulting. The word "Kaṇha" is an address to Māra. Māra is called "Kaṇha" (The Dark One) because he has dark unwholesome deeds and because he is born in the dark states of deprivation (apāya). "Dukkhaṃ nigacchasi" means that in this life, you will encounter the suffering of useless physical exhaustion, such as entering the belly, etc., and in the future life, you will encounter the suffering of the states of deprivation that cannot be remedied. Upon hearing these words, Māra, saying "The recluse knows me," vanished right there.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Nandiya Thera is finished.

"Subhāsitaṃ vācaṃ vadanti" and so forth is the verse of Venerable Abhaya Thera. This Venerable Abhaya Thera became a preaching monk after ordaining in the Dispensation of Padumuttara Buddha. When preaching the Dhamma, he used to first praise the Blessed One with verses before preaching. Due to the fruit of that meritorious deed, he did not reach the states of deprivation for a hundred thousand aeons. This statement is true. Because Venerable Abhaya Thera praised the self-enlightened Padumuttara Buddha with a confident mind and noble faith, he did not have to go to the four states of deprivation for a hundred thousand aeons, and was endowed with [favorable] regions and so forth...
103:
## 6. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Abhaya

The verse beginning with "Sutvā subhāsitaṃ vācaṃ" belongs to the Venerable Elder Abhaya. How did it arise? It is said that in the dispensation of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he went forth and became a Dhamma preacher. When preaching the Dhamma, he first praised the Blessed One with four verses and later preached the Dhamma. By the power of that meritorious deed, for a hundred thousand aeons, he was never reborn in the lower realms. Thus it was said:

"With a heart full of faith, Abhaya praised the Self-Awakened One, the Conqueror Padumuttara;
Having noble faith, he did not go to the lower realms for a hundred thousand aeons."

Due to the excellence of the field (the recipient) and other factors, and because of the extreme nobility of the Elder's preceding and succeeding volitions, that immeasurable flood of merit and flood of wholesome deeds occurred. Is it not said: "For those who have faith in the inconceivable, the result is inconceivable"? The merit accumulated in various lives became a support for Prince Abhaya. This is true: that Elder once made an offering of Ketaka flowers to the Blessed One Vipassī. Due to such noble and special merits, he wandered only in the happy realms and, in the time of our Buddha's appearance, was reborn as the son of King Bimbisāra. His name was Abhaya. His story will become clear later.

Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta taught Prince Abhaya a two-pronged question and sent him, saying, "Ask this question and refute the doctrine of the Ascetic Gotama." He approached the Blessed One and asked that question. When the Blessed One answered the question with a multi-faceted explanation, he realized the defeat of the Nigaṇṭhas and the Sammāsambuddha status of the Teacher, and declared himself a lay follower. Later, when King Bimbisāra passed away, he felt spiritual urgency (saṃvega), went forth in the dispensation, and became a Stream-enterer through the teaching of the Tālacchiggaḷūpama Sutta (the Discourse on the Simile of the Hole in the Yoke). Again, he practiced insight meditation (vipassanā) and realized Arahatship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"On the bank of the Vinatā River, the Best of Men (Vipassī) resided;
I saw the Buddha, free from dust, one-pointed, and well-composed."
104:
"At that time, with a heart of faith and joy, I worshipped the Greatest Buddha with a Ketaka flower of sweet fragrance.

In the ninety-one aeons since I worshipped with that flower, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

Having reached Arahatship, the Elder spoke the verse beginning with "Sutvā subhāsitaṃ vācaṃ," declaring his attainment by praising his own practice.

In that verse, "sutvā" means having listened and attended through the ear-door. "Subhāsitaṃ" means well-spoken, perfectly spoken; because of being a Sammāsambuddha and having great compassion, it is a Dhamma talk explaining the Four Noble Truths, spoken in a way that unfailingly achieves the intended meaning without any deviation. Indeed, there is no Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One that is devoid of the Four Truths. "Buddhassa" means of the Omniscient Buddha. "Ādiccabandhuno": because he was born in the solar lineage, the Sun is his kinsman, thus the Blessed One is called Ādiccabandhu (Kinsman of the Sun). Or, he is Ādiccabandhu because he is a kinsman of the Sun. This is also because he is the Blessed One's true-born son. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"The one who makes light in the dark gloom, the radiant one, the circular one of fierce heat—
O Rāhu, do not swallow that Sun wandering in the sky;
O Rāhu, release the Sun, my son."

"Paccavyadhiṃ" means I have penetrated and realized. The word "hi" is a mere particle. "Nipuṇaṃ" means the extremely subtle Truth of Cessation, or the Four Noble Truths themselves. The word "hi" is also used in the sense of cause (hetu). Because I have penetrated the extremely subtle Four Noble Truths, there is now nothing further to be penetrated; this is the meaning. How did he penetrate? He said, "Vālaggaṃ usunā yathā" (Like a hair-tip with an arrow). Just as a well-trained, skilled archer would pierce the tip of a hair split seven times with an arrow without missing, so too did he penetrate the subtle Noble Truths; thus the meaning should be connected.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Abhaya is finished.
105:
## 7. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Lomasakangiya

The verse beginning with "Dabbaṃ kusaṃ" is that of the Venerable Elder Lomasakangiya. What is the origin of this elder? It is said that ninety-one aeons ago, having seen the Buddha Vipassī, he was filled with devotion and made an offering of various flowers. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the celestial realm, and after performing further merits here and there, he wandered only through the happy realms. In the dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa, he went forth and practiced the ascetic life. At that time, while the Teacher was teaching the practice of Bhaddhekaratta, another monk engaged in a discussion with him based on the Bhaddhekaratta Sutta. He was unable to grasp that discussion with his wisdom. Because he could not grasp it, he made a resolution: "In the future, may I be able to teach the practice of Bhaddhekaratta to you." The other monk also made a resolution: "May I be able to ask [about it]."

Among those two, the first monk wandered through the celestial and human realms for the interval between two Buddhas, and in the time of our Buddha, he was reborn in the Sakyan royal family in the city of Kapilavatthu. Because of his delicacy, hair grew on the soles of his feet, just like the Venerable Soṇa. Because of that hair growth, he was given the name Lomasakangiya. The other person was reborn in the celestial realm and became known as the deity Candana.

The prince Lomasakangiya did not wish to go forth even when other Sakyan princes such as Anuruddha went forth. Then, the young deity Candana approached him to stir his sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and asked him about the Bhaddhekaratta practice. The prince replied, "I do not know." Then the deity urged him, saying, "If so, why did you make an agreement saying, 'May I be able to teach the Bhaddhekaratta practice'? Now, you do not even know its name."

The prince, together with that deity, approached the Buddha and asked, "Venerable Sir, is it true that I previously made an agreement saying, 'I shall teach the Bhaddhekaratta practice to this person'?" The Buddha replied, "Yes, young man, it is true; you made such an agreement in the time of the Buddha Kassapa." This matter should be understood in detail as it appears in the Uparipaṇṇāsa Pali.

Then the prince Lomasakangiya said, "If that is so, Venerable Sir, please let me go forth." The Buddha refused, saying, "The Tathāgatas do not ordain a son who has not been permitted by his parents." The prince went to his mother and said, "Mother, please permit me to go forth; I shall go forth." When his mother said, "Dear son, you are very delicate, how will you be able to live as a monk?", he recited the verse beginning with "Dabbaṃ kusaṃ poṭakilaṃ" to reveal his ability to endure hardships.
106:
In that verse, "dabba" refers to dabba-grass, which is also called "saddūla". "Kusa" refers to kusa-grass, which is called "kāsa". "Poṭakila" refers to both thorny and non-thorny bushes, but here, only thorny bushes are intended. Usīra (fragrant root grass) and others are easily understood. Grasses such as dabba are vīraṇa-grasses, which cause suffering to those who tread on them with their feet and hinder travel. "I shall push aside those grasses with my chest; I shall remove them even with my chest." By thus removing them and enduring the suffering caused by that reason, I shall be able to enter the thickets in the forest and practice the ascetic life. This is shown to mean: "What need is there to speak of treading with the feet?"

"Vivekamanubrūhayaṃ" means cultivating physical seclusion (kāya-viveka), mental seclusion (citta-viveka), and seclusion from acquisitions (upadhi-viveka). For one who abandons the company of the crowd and cultivates physical seclusion, if he can concentrate his mind on any of the thirty-eight meditation objects, that is mental seclusion; it is not possible for one who delights in company. Only one who is concentrated can perform the work of insight (vipassanā), and by practicing serenity (samatha) and insight in tandem, one attains seclusion from acquisitions through the destruction of defilements; it is not possible for one who is not concentrated. Therefore, it is said, "cultivating physical seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion from acquisitions."

When the son spoke thus, the mother permitted him, saying, "Dear son, if that is so, then go forth." He approached the Buddha and requested ordination, and the Teacher ordained him. After going forth, having performed the preliminary duties and taking a meditation subject, he entered the forest. The monks asked him, "Friend, you are so delicate, how will you be able to live in the forest?" He recited the same verse to those monks as well, and having entered the forest and devoted himself to meditation, he soon became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal powers. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"I worshipped the Buddha of golden hue, worthy of offerings,
As He was walking on the road, with various flowers.
In the ninety-first aeon ago, because of the flowers I offered,
I have not known any woeful state; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
My defilements are burnt away... (etc.) ... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

Upon reaching Arahantship, the elder recited that very same verse to declare his attainment of the fruit of Arahantship.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Lomasakangiya is finished.
107:
## 8. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Jambugāmiyaputta

The verse beginning with "Kacci no vatthapasuto" is that of the Venerable Elder Jambugāmiyaputta. What is the story of its origin? This elder, having performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome deeds that serve as a support for liberation (vivaṭṭanissaya) in various lives, saw kiṃsuka flowers one day during the time of the Blessed One Vessabhū, thirty-one aeons ago from this present Bhadda-kappa. Taking those flowers and repeatedly recollecting the virtues of the Buddha, he offered them by tossing them into the air, dedicating them to the Blessed One. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. After that, performing further merits and wandering through the rounds of rebirth among gods and humans, he was reborn in this Buddha-dispensation as the son of a lay devotee named Jambugāmiya in the city of Campā. Therefore, he was known simply as "Jambugāmiyaputta" (the son of Jambugāmiya).

When he reached the age of maturity, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One and, gaining a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he ordained as a monk. After performing the preliminary duties (pubbakicca), he took a meditation subject and resided in the Añjanavana forest in the city of Sāketa. At that time, his father, wishing to test him, thought, "Is my son delighting in the Dispensation, or is he not?" and sent him a written verse beginning with "Kacci no vatthapasuto."

When the elder read that verse, he felt a sense of urgency, thinking, "My father suspects that I am living in negligence, and even now, I have not yet transcended the state of a worldling (puthujjana)." Striving and exerting himself, he soon became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā). This matter is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

"Seeing a kiṃsuka tree in bloom, I raised my hands in salutation,
Recollecting the Most Excellent Buddha, I offered them in the air.
By that well-performed deed, and by my intention and aspiration,
I abandoned the human body and reached Tāvatiṃsa.
Because of the deed I performed then, thirty-one aeons ago,
I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.
My defilements have been burned away... (and so forth) ... I have followed the Dispensation of the Buddha."

After reaching the fruit of Arahantship, he went to the city where his relatives lived and displayed miracles to make manifest the fact that the Dispensation leads out of suffering. Seeing those miracles, the relatives were filled with faith and built many monasteries (saṅghārāma). The elder, together with his father...
109: Having seen the Paccekabuddha named Sudassana and with a heart full of devotion, he made an offering of Kutaja flowers. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered only through the happy realms (sugati) and, in the time of this Buddha, was reborn in Sāvatthī in a wealthy Brahmin family. His name was Harita. When he came of age, his parents brought him a Brahmin maiden suitable in lineage and appearance. While enjoying sensual pleasures with her, one day, looking at his own physical perfection and hers, and being urged by the nature of things (dhammatā), he attained spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking: 'Such beauty will soon be oppressed by old age and death.' After a few days, his wife was bitten by a black cobra and died. Because of that, he felt even greater spiritual urgency, went to the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, severed the bonds of the household, and ordained. Although he lived taking a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable for his temperament, the meditation did not succeed, and his mind was not straight. While entering the village for alms, he saw a fletcher (usukāra) putting an arrow shaft into a machine and straightening it. He thought: 'These people can straighten even inanimate things; why should I not be able to straighten my mind?' He turned back from there, sat in a place for the day's stay, and began insight meditation (vipassanā). Then the Blessed One, sitting in the air above him, gave him advice by reciting the verse: 'Exalt yourself...' Some say the Elder himself spoke this, advising himself as if he were another. In that verse, 'Exalt yourself' (samunnamaya) means exalting well; not allowing the mind to fall into the side of sloth (kosajja) by the power of attainment (samāpatti), but lifting it up from there and applying balanced energy (vīriya). 'Yourself' (attānaṃ) means the mind. Alternatively, 'samunnamaya' means 'exalt yourself from the side of sloth.' The letter 'ma' is a euphonic junction. The meaning is: if your mind does not enter the path of meditation due to weak energy, exalt it well by initiating energy; make it neither bent down nor bent away. When doing this, one is like a fletcher with an arrow. 'Harita, having made the mind straight, break through ignorance (avijjā),' he said. For example, just as a fletcher removes even a slight downward or outward bend of an arrow shaft to make it straight for the purpose of piercing the target, so too, by removing the mind that is bent down due to lack of protection from falling into sloth, and the mind that is bent away due to lack of protection from falling into restlessness (uddhacca), and by reaching absorption (appanā), the mind...
110:
(Just as a fletcher straightens an arrow,) make the mind straight, and with a concentrated mind, exert yourself in insight (vipassanā) and quickly pierce and destroy ignorance with the knowledge of the highest path (Arahatta-magga-ñāṇa). Hearing these words, the Elder Harita developed insight and soon became an Arahat. This matter is stated in the Apadāna—

"Not far from the Himavanta mountains, there is a mountain named Vasala. In the valley of that mountain, the Exalted Paccekabuddha named Sudassana resided.

"Taking a kuṭaja flower from the Himavanta mountains, I traveled through the air. At that time, I saw the Fully Awakened One, Sudassana the Paccekabuddha, who had crossed the flood and was free from taints.

"Then, taking the kuṭaja flower and placing it upon my head, I offered it to that Exalted One, the Self-Enlightened, the Great Seeker.

"In the thirty-one aeons since I offered that flower, I have not known a woeful state; this is the fruit of offering a flower.

"My defilements have been burned away ... (l) ... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

Even when declaring his attainment of the fruit of Arahatship, he recited that very verse.

## The Commentary on the Verse of Venerable Harita is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Verse of Venerable Uttiya

"Ābādhe me samuppanne" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Uttiya. What is the origin of this verse? It is said that the Venerable Uttiya had performed special merit under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit which is a support for Nibbāna in various births. Ninety-four aeons ago from now, in the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was reborn as a large-bodied crocodile in the Candabhāgā River.

Seeing the Blessed One who had come to the riverbank, that crocodile, with a confident mind and wishing to convey Him to the other side, lay down near the bank. Out of compassion for the crocodile, the Blessed One placed His feet upon its back. With a joyful and elated mind, and with double the effort due to the surge of rapture, the crocodile cut through the current and conveyed the Blessed One to the other side with great speed. The Blessed One, seeing the clarity of the crocodile's mind, [thought], "When this crocodile passes away from here..."
111:
Having been reborn in the celestial realm, and from then on wandering only in the happy realms, the Buddha prophesied, "Ninety-four aeons from now, you will reach the Deathless Nibbāna," and then departed.

That person, wandering only in the happy realms according to that prophecy, was reborn in this Buddha-era in the city of Sāvatthī as the son of a certain Brahmin, named Uttiya. When he came of age, thinking, "I will search for the Deathless Nibbāna," he became a wanderer and traveled about. One day, he approached the Blessed One, heard the Dhamma, and ordained in the Dispensation. However, because his virtue and other qualities were not purified, he was unable to attain any distinction. Seeing other monks attaining distinction and declaring their attainment of Arahantship, he approached the Blessed One and requested an instruction in brief. The Blessed One gave him a brief instruction, saying, "Therefore, Uttiya, you should purify the very beginning" (SN 5.369). The Elder Uttiya, established in that instruction, began to practice insight meditation (vipassanā). While he was practicing insight meditation, an illness arose. When the illness arose, a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) was born in him. Making that the basis for arousing effort, he performed the work of insight meditation. By striving in insight meditation, he attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"At that time, on the bank of the Candabhāgā River, I was a crocodile. While wandering in my hunting ground, I reached the river landing."
"At that time, the Buddha Siddhattha, the Self-Awakened One, the Supreme Person, desiring to cross the river, arrived at the river landing."
"When the Fully Enlightened One arrived, I also approached that landing. Having approached the Fully Enlightened One, I spoke these words:"
"'Ascend, O Great Hero! I will carry you across. O Great Sage, have compassion on me in this river, which is my ancestral domain.'"
"Hearing my roar, the Great Sage ascended. With a joyful heart, I carried the Leader of the World across."
"On the far bank of the river, the Leader of the World, Siddhattha, comforted me there, saying, 'You will reach the Deathless Nibbāna.'"
112:
"Passing away from that body, I went to the celestial realm. Surrounded by celestial nymphs, I experienced divine bliss."

"Seven times I ruled the celestial realm as the King of Gods. Three times I was a Wheel-turning Monarch, a ruler of the earth."

"Devoted to the three kinds of seclusion (viveka), prudent, and well-restrained, I bear my final body in the Dispensation of the Fully Enlightened One."

"Ninety-four aeons ago, I carried that Best of Men across the river. Because of that deed of carrying him across, I do not know any woeful state. This is the fruit of carrying him across."

"My defilements have been burned away... (pe)... the Buddha's bidding has been done."

Upon reaching Arahantship, wishing to declare his attainment by manifesting the perfection of his own right practice, he recited the verse beginning with "Ābādhe me samuppanne."

In that verse, "Ābādhe me samuppanne" means: when a disease caused by the disturbance of disproportionate elements, which is called "affliction" (ābādha) because it oppresses the body, arose in me. "Sati me udapajjathā" means: "An illness has indeed arisen in me. This is a situation where this illness might increase. While this illness has not yet increased, let me begin to arouse effort for the sake of reaching the unreached, for the sake of attaining the unattained, and for the sake of realizing the unrealized Nibbāna." Thus, mindfulness, which is the basis for arousing effort, arose in me who was being oppressed by painful feeling due to that very illness. Therefore, he said, "An illness has arisen in me; it is time for me to be diligent." Thus, making the mindfulness that had arisen like a goad, this Elder reached Arahantship.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Uttiya Thera is finished.
## The Commentary on the Third Group (Vagga) is finished.
113:
## 4. The Fourth Group (Catuttha Vagga)
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Gahwaratīriya Thera

The verse beginning with "Phuṭṭho ḍaṃsehi" is that of the Venerable Gahwaratīriya Thera. What is its origin? It is said that he had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas. Thirty-one aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, he was a hunter wandering in the forest. He saw the Blessed One Sikhī teaching the Dhamma to devas, nāgas, and yakkhas at the foot of a certain tree. Having seen him, with a heart full of faith, he grasped the sign in the sound, thinking, "This is the Dhamma being spoken." Due to that faith in his heart, he was reborn in the celestial realm. After wandering repeatedly only in the happy realms, he was reborn in this Buddha-era in a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī and was given the name "Aggidatta." When he came of age, he saw the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya) of the Blessed One and, faith having arisen, he ordained in the Dispensation. Taking a meditation subject, he lived in a forest area called Gahwaratīra. Therefore, he became known by the name "Gahwaratīriya." He developed insight meditation and before long reached Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"In the past, I was a hunter in a dense forest. I saw the Buddha, free from dust, surrounded by a host of devas."
"While he was revealing the Four Noble Truths and teaching the Deathless State, I heard the sweet Dhamma of Sikhī, the Kinsman of the World."
"I settled my heart with faith in the voice of that Peerless Person. Having settled my heart there, I crossed over the existence that is difficult to cross."
"Thirty-one aeons ago, because of the perception (saññā) I gained then, I have not known a woeful state. This is the fruit of the perception of the voice."
"My defilements have been burned away... (la)... the Buddha's bidding has been done."

After reaching Arahantship, he went to Sāvatthī to pay homage to the Blessed One. Hearing of his arrival, his relatives approached and offered a great gift of alms. After staying for a few days, he desired to return to the forest. Then his relatives said, "Venerable Sir, the forest is full of dangers such as mosquitoes and gadflies. Stay right here..."
114:
"Please stay," they requested. Hearing this, the Elder, wishing to declare the fruit of Arahantship by praising his delight in seclusion, said, "The forest life alone is pleasing to me," and recited the verse beginning with "Phuṭṭho ḍaṃsehi."

In that verse, "Phuṭṭho ḍaṃsehi makasehi" means being touched or bitten by gadflies, named "ḍaṃsa" because of their habit of biting, and by mosquitoes and other needle-mouthed creatures called "makasa." "Araññasmim" refers to a forest that possesses the characteristics of a forest, described as being "at least five hundred bow-lengths away." "Brahāvane" refers to a large forest or a great woodland because it is dense with trees and bushes. "Nāgo saṅgāmasīseva" means like a great elephant experienced in battle who endures the attack of the enemy's army at the front of the battle. Being one who is energetic and mindful, thinking, "The forest life has been praised and lauded by the Buddhas and other noble ones," one should endure when such contact with mosquitoes and gadflies arises in that forest. It means one should not abandon the forest life, saying, "Mosquitoes and gadflies are harassing me."

## The Commentary on the Verse of Elder Gahvaratīriya is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Verse of Elder Suppiya

The verse beginning with "Ajaraṃ jīramānena" is the verse of the Venerable Suppiya. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed Padumuttara, he was born into a respectable family. Having gone forth as an ascetic and living in a forest, he saw the Blessed One and, with a devoted mind, offered large and small fruits. He did the same for the Saṅgha of monks. Through that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was born into a royal family in the time of the Kassapa Buddha. Gradually reaching the age of discretion, he gained urgency (saṃvega) by relying on a good friend (kalyāṇamitta), went forth in the Dispensation, and became very learned. However, he lived exalting himself and disparaging others due to pride in his birth and pride in his learning. In this Buddha-arising, as a result of that unwholesome karma, he was born in Sāvatthī into a family of cemetery keepers of unattractive appearance. His name was Suppiya. Later, when he reached the age of discretion, he approached his friend, the Elder Sopāka, and having heard the Dhamma from him, he gained urgency (saṃvega), went forth, fulfilled the noble practice, and recited the verse beginning with "Ajaraṃ jīramānena."

In that verse, "Ajaraṃ" refers to the ageless Nibbāna. In truth, there is no aging in that Nibbāna. Or, there is no aging for the person who has reached that Nibbāna. Thus, because it is devoid of the nature of aging, it is called "Ajaraṃ." "Jīramānena" means by that which is aging, reaching old age moment by moment [referring to the body]. "Tappamānena" means being burned, being scorched by the heat of defilements such as lust (rāga)...
115:
That Suppiya approached the Elder Sopāka, and having heard the Dhamma from him, he gained urgency (saṃvega), went forth, fulfilled the noble practice, and recited the verse beginning with "Ajaraṃ jīramānena."

In that verse, "Ajaraṃ" refers to the ageless Nibbāna. Because it is unarisen, there is no aging there; or, because there is no aging for the person who has attained that Nibbāna, it is called "Ajaraṃ" due to the absence of aging. "Jīramānena" means by that which is aging, reaching old age moment by moment. "Tappamānena" means being burned, being scorched by the eleven fires such as lust (rāga). "Nibbutiṃ" refers to Nibbāna, which is peaceful in nature because of the absence of the aforementioned burnings. "Nimiyam" means exchanging or bartering. "Paramaṃ santiṃ" refers to the supreme peace because it is the nature of the stilling of the burnings of all defilements and volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra). It is called "Yogakkhema" (security from bonds) because it is not bound by the four bonds (yogas). It is called "Anuttara" (unsurpassed) because there is no other state superior to it.

The summary of the meaning here is: By means of this [body] which is aging because it is oppressed by old age moment by moment, and likewise being scorched by the fire of lust and so on—thus being impermanent, suffering, without essence, unpeaceful in every way, and accompanied by danger—one should barter for Nibbāna, which is the opposite of those dangers: ageless, supremely peaceful, unassailed by any danger, and unsurpassed, thinking, "Great indeed is my gain! A great benefit has come into my hands!"

Just as when people exchange any goods, they are without regret [for what they give] and have great regard for the goods they receive; in the same way, this Elder, living with a resolute mind, wishing to manifest his lack of regard for his own body and life, and his state of having directed his mind toward Nibbāna, said, "Nimiyaṃ paramaṃ santiṃ, yogakkhemaṃ anuttaraṃ," and while developing that very practice and applying himself to insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"A Brahmin named Varuṇa, a master of the Vedas, then abandoned ten sons and entered the forest."
"Having built a well-constructed, well-proportioned, and delightful hermitage, and having made a leaf-hut, I lived in the woodland."
"The Buddha Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, the Recipient of Offerings, wishing to deliver me, came to my hermitage."
116:
Throughout the extent of the forest grove, a vast radiance appeared; at that time, by the power of the Buddha, the great forest shone brilliantly.

Seeing that miracle of the Buddha, who is endowed with such qualities, I took a basket of fruit and made an offering of fruit.

Approaching the Sambuddha, I offered a carrying-pole of fruit; out of compassion for me, the Buddha spoke these words:

"Take this carrying-pole of fruit and follow behind me; when the Saṅgha has partaken of it, there will be merit for you."

Taking that basket, I offered it to the Bhikkhu-Saṅgha; with a mind full of faith in that deed, I was reborn in the Tusita realm.

In that Tusita realm, I always enjoyed happiness associated with meritorious deeds through divine dances, songs, and instrumental music.

Whether reborn as a deva or a human, in whatever existence I arise, there is no deficiency in my wealth and pleasures; this is the result of the offering of fruit.

Throughout the extent of the four great islands together with the oceans and mountains, because I offered fruit to the Buddha, I exercised sovereign rule.

All the flocks of birds that fly in the sky also follow my will; this is the result of the offering of fruit.

The Yakkhas, Bhūtas, Rakkhasas, Kumbhaṇḍas, and Garuḷas that dwell in the forest also come to me as attendants.

Turtles, dogs, bees, gadflies, and both types of mosquitoes also follow my will; this is the result of the offering of fruit.

The birds named Supaṇṇas, who possess great strength, also come to me for refuge; this is the result of the offering of fruit.

The Nāgas of great power, great fame, and long life also follow my will; this is the result of the offering of fruit.
117:
Lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, jackals, and wolves also exist. These creatures also constantly follow my will; this is the result of the offering of fruit.

The Osaḍhī star, the deities dwelling in the grass, and those deities who usually dwell in the sky also exist. All of them come to me for refuge; this is the result of the offering of fruit.

I dwell having touched and experienced the Dhamma which is very difficult to see, very subtle, deep, and well-proclaimed; this is the result of the offering of fruit.

I dwell without taints (āsavas), having touched and experienced the eight liberations (vimokkhas). I am energetic and wise; this is the result of the offering of fruit.

There are sons of the Buddha who are established in the fruition, whose taints are destroyed, and who have great fame. I am one among them; this is the result of the offering of fruit.

Urged by the root of merit, I have reached the pinnacle of supernormal knowledges (abhiññās); understanding all taints, I dwell free from taints.

Among the sons of the Buddha who possess the three knowledges, who have attained supernormal powers, who have great fame, and who have attained the divine ear, I am one of them.

In the hundred thousandth aeon past, I gave that fruit. Due to the merit of that offering, I do not know of any rebirth in the four woeful states; this is the result of the offering of fruit.

My defilements have been burned away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

Even after reaching the fruit of Arahantship, he spoke this very verse as a declaration of his attainment.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Suppiya Thera is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Verses of Sopāka Thera

"Just as for an only son" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Sopāka Thera. What is its origin? It is said that he had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and was accumulating wholesome states that serve as a support for liberation in various births. In the time of Kakusandha Buddha, he was born as the son of a householder. One day, having seen the Teacher, with a mind full of faith, he offered citron fruits (bījapura) to the Teacher. The Blessed One accepted them out of compassion.
118:
Out of compassion, (he accepted the offering). That son of a merchant, being greatly devoted to the Saṅgha of monks, prepared ticket-food (salāka-bhatta) and, according to the order of the Saṅgha, offered milk-rice to three monks for as long as he lived. Due to that meritorious deed, he repeatedly experienced prosperity in the celestial and human realms. Once, reborn in the human realm, he offered milk-rice to a Paccekabuddha. Thus, performing meritorious deeds in various realms, he wandered only within the happy destinations (sugati). In this Buddha's era, due to the result of his past karma, he was conceived in the womb of a poor woman in Sāvatthī.

After carrying him in her womb for ten months, when the pregnancy was mature and it was time to give birth, his mother was unable to deliver. She fell into a swoon and lay as if dead for a long time. Her relatives, thinking she was dead, took her to the cemetery and placed her on a funeral pyre. However, due to the power of the devas, a storm of wind and rain arose, so they departed without lighting the fire. Because the child was in his final existence, he emerged from his mother's womb without any illness through the power of the devas. The mother, however, passed away. The devas took the child and, appearing in human form, placed him in the house of the cemetery keeper and nourished him with suitable food for some time. Thereafter, the cemetery keeper raised the child as his own son. As he grew up, he wandered about playing with the cemetery keeper's son named Supiya. Because he was born and raised in the cemetery, he became known by the name 'Sopāka'.

Then one day, when the boy was seven years old, the Blessed One, at the time of dawn, spread his net of knowledge and, while surveying beings to be tamed, saw him within the net of his knowledge and went to the cemetery. The boy, prompted by the causes of his past merit, approached the Teacher with a clear mind, paid homage, and stood there. The Teacher preached the Dhamma to him. Having heard the Dhamma, he requested ordination. When told, 'Have you been permitted by your father?', he brought his father to the Teacher. His father approached the Teacher, paid homage, and gave permission, saying, 'Venerable Sir, please ordain this boy.'

After ordaining the boy, the Teacher urged him to practice the meditation on loving-kindness (metta-bhāvanā). While Sopāka dwelt in the cemetery practicing the meditation on loving-kindness, he soon attained the jhānas of loving-kindness. Based on those jhānas, he developed insight (vipassanā) and realized the fruit of Arahantship. This matter is stated in the Apadāna as follows:
119:
## 
'The Great Hero named Kakusandha, who reached the end of all phenomena,
Being secluded from the group, went into the forest.

I took the seed-kernels (bījamiñja) and strung them with a creeper;
At that time, the Blessed One was absorbed in jhāna between the mountains.

Seeing that God of gods with a particularly clear mind,
I offered the seed-kernels to the Great Hero Kakusandha, who is worthy of offerings.

In this very aeon, because of the seed-kernels I offered then,
I do not know of any woeful state; this is the fruit of offering seed-kernels.

My defilements have been burned away by the fire of the Path... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.'

After becoming an Arahant, wishing to show the method of practicing the meditation on loving-kindness to other monks who were cemetery-dwellers, Elder Sopāka spoke this verse: 'Yathāpi ekaputtasmiṃ'.

In that verse, 'yathā' is a particle used in the sense of a simile. 'Ekaputtasmiṃ' means 'putta' (son) because he cleanses and protects his own lineage; it refers to an only son among various kinds of sons such as those born of oneself. Here, the locative case is used in the sense of the object (visaya). 'Piyasmiṃ' means in a beloved son, because of being worthy of love, being an only son, and being a cause for love due to his appearance, virtue, and conduct. 'Kusalī' means 'kusala' is said to be safety and well-being; because he has such safety and well-being, he is called 'kusalī', meaning one who has a disposition of loving-kindness and desires the welfare of beings. 'Sabbesu pāṇesu' means towards all living beings. 'Sabbattha' means in all directions, or in all realms of existence, or in all conditions.

This is what is meant: Just as parents would be truly desirous of the welfare and safety of a beloved and pleasant only son, so too should one be skilled in being truly desirous of the welfare of all beings situated in all directions such as the east, in all realms of existence such as the sensual realm, and in all conditions such as youth. Without making a boundary as 'friend, neutral, or enemy', one should develop loving-kindness of a single flavor everywhere by way of the breaking of boundaries (sīmā-sambheda). After speaking this verse, he said, 'If you, venerable sirs, thus...'
120: "Practice the meditation on loving-kindness repeatedly. May you truly be those who receive and enjoy the eleven benefits of loving-kindness taught by the Blessed One, beginning with 'one sleeps happily' (sukhaṃ supati)," he gave this advice. ## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sopāka is finished. ## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Posiya The verse beginning with "Anāsannavarā" is that of the Venerable Posiya Thera. What is the story of its origin? It is said that this Elder, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating much merit as a support for liberation in various lives, was wandering in the cycle of rebirths only in happy realms. Ninety-two aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Tissa, he was a deer hunter wandering in the forest. At that time, the Blessed One, in order to show him favor, went to the forest and appeared within his sight. Seeing the Blessed One, the hunter, with a heart full of faith, laid down his weapon, approached, and stood with his hands raised in salutation. The Blessed One showed his desire to sit. At that moment, the hunter took handfuls of grass, spread them carefully on a level piece of ground, and offered them. Out of compassion, the Blessed One sat on that grass mat. While the Blessed One was seated, the hunter, experiencing great joy and happiness, paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down himself in a suitable place. Then the Blessed One, reflecting, "This much seed of merit is sufficient for this noble son," rose from his seat and departed. Not long after the Blessed One had left, a king of lions killed him. When he passed away, he was reborn in the celestial realm. It is heard that if the Blessed One had not come, that hunter would have been reborn in hell after being killed by the lion. The Blessed One, seeing this, approached him to ensure his rebirth in a happy realm and to plant the seed of merit. Having remained there for the full lifespan of a deity, he passed away from that celestial realm and, wandering only in happy realms, was reborn in this Buddha-era in Sāvatthī as the son of a very wealthy merchant and the younger brother of the Venerable Saṅgāmajita Thera. He was named Posiya. When he reached adulthood, he married and had a son. Then, urged by the natural law of those in their final existence, he felt spiritual urgency (saṃvega) regarding birth and so on, ordained, entered the forest, and lived in seclusion from the crowd...
121: ...and while repeatedly practicing the meditation on the Four Noble Truths, he soon developed insight and attained Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna: "Not far from the Himālaya mountains, there is a mountain named Lambaka. There, the Fully Enlightened Tissa was walking in meditation in the open air. "At that time, I was a deer hunter in the forest. Seeing that God of gods, I offered a handful of grass. "I offered it for the Buddha to sit upon and gladdened my heart. Having paid homage to the Fully Enlightened One, I departed facing the north. "Not long after I had gone, a king of lions struck me down. Being struck by the lion, I passed away right there. "I had performed a good deed toward the Supreme Buddha, the Taintless One. Like the speed of a well-shot arrow, I went to the celestial realm. "There, a beautiful pillar (palace) was created by my meritorious deeds. It had a thousand sections, a hundred spheres, was decorated with banners, and was made of gold. "Its radiance shone like the rising sun with a hundred rays. Surrounded by celestial nymphs, I enjoyed sensual pleasures as I desired. "Having passed away from the celestial realm, urged by that pure root of merit, I came to the human state and reached the destruction of the taints (Arahantship). "Ninety-four aeons ago, I offered a seat. Since then, I have not known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of a handful of grass. "My defilements are burned away... the teaching of the Buddha has been carried out." After attaining Arahantship, when he came to Sāvatthī to pay homage to the Blessed One, he went to his relatives' house out of compassion for them. There, his former wife paid homage to him and at first showed her devotion like a lay follower by providing a seat and so on. However, not understanding the Elder's disposition, she later desired to entice him with feminine gestures and such. The Venerable Posiya thought, "Oh, how foolish she is! She behaves in such a manner even toward one like me (an Arahant)." Without saying a single word, he rose from his seat and returned to the forest. The monks living in the forest asked him, "Friend, why have you returned so quickly? Did you not meet your relatives?" The Venerable Posiya, wishing to explain what had happened, recited the verse beginning with "Anāsannavarā etā." In that verse, "Anāsannavarā" means that those women are best for men when they are not approached but remain at a distance; it means they bring about welfare. One who knows that it is best (not to approach) not only at night, during the day, or in seclusion, but at all times, (says this). There is also a Pali reading "Anāsannaparā," which has the same meaning. The meaning of this verse is: Even fierce elephants, horses, buffaloes, lions, tigers, ogres, demons, and hungry ghosts...
122:
(That woman intended to seduce him with feminine gestures). The Elder thought, "Oh, how foolish she is; she acts in such a manner even toward one like me," and without saying a single word, he rose from his seat and went back to the forest. The forest-dwelling monks asked him, "Friend, why have you returned so quickly? Did you not see your relatives?" The Elder, wishing to explain what had happened, recited the verse beginning with "Anāsannavarā etā."

In that verse, "Anāsannavarā" means that these women are best for a man and bring him welfare only when they are not near, not approached, but stay far away. Such excellence exists at all times—not only at night, during the day, or in private, but always. "Vijānatā" means by one who knows. There is also a Pāḷi reading "Anāsannaparā," which has the same meaning. The meaning here is this: even fierce elephants, horses, buffaloes, lions, tigers, yakkhas, rakkhasas, and pisācas are best when they do not approach humans; they do not bring harm then. If those creatures do approach, they might cause harm only in this present life. Women, however, if approached, destroy one's welfare in this life and the next, including the benefit associated with liberation (vimokkha), which is the Path and Fruit of Arahantship, and thus cause great harm. Therefore, it means that for one who knows, "these women are always best only when they are not near but stay far away."

Now, wishing to show that meaning by applying it to himself, he spoke the words beginning with "Gāmā." In that verse, "Gāmā" means to the village. Here, the ablative case is used in the sense of the accusative. "Araṇyamāgamma" means having come from the forest. The letter "ma" is inserted for euphonic combination (sandhi), and here the accusative case is used in the sense of the ablative. "Tato" means from the couch. "Anāmantetvā" means without speaking, without even saying as much as "Be heedful" to his former wife. In saying "Posiya," he refers to himself as if he were another person. For those teachers who read "pakkāmiṃ," the construction should be "I, Posiya, have departed."

Some teachers, however, say: That woman, having fed the Elder who came to the house, felt a desire to seduce him. Seeing that behavior, the Elder immediately left the house, went to the monastery, and sat on the couch in his dwelling place. That woman also, after the meal, having adorned and prepared herself, followed him to the Elder's dwelling in the monastery. Seeing her, the Elder, without saying anything, rose from his seat and went to his daytime retreat. According to those teachers, the meaning of the verse "Gāmā araṇyamāgamma" should be taken exactly as it is recited. This is because in this context, the monastery itself is intended by the word "arañña" (forest).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Posiya is Finished.
123:
## 5. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sāmaññakāni

The verse beginning with "Sukhaṃ sukhattho" is that of the Venerable Sāmaññakāni. What is its origin? It is said that this Elder had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and was accumulating merit in various births. Ninety-one aeons ago, during the time of Buddha Vipassī, he was born into a human family. Seeing Buddha Vipassī, he gained a settled faith and offered a couch. Due to that meritorious deed, while wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he was born as the son of a certain wanderer (paribbājaka) during the time of this Buddha's appearance. His name was Sāmaññakāni. When he reached the age of wisdom, he saw the Buddha's Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) and, with a settled faith, ordained in the Dispensation. Taking a meditation subject suitable for his temperament, he attained jhāna. Making that jhāna the basis, he developed insight and reached the Fruit of Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

"To the Buddha Vipassī, the Foremost of the World, the Such-like One, a couch was given by me with a faithful heart and my own hands.

I obtained elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, and divine vehicles. By that gift of a couch, I have reached the destruction of the taints (āsavas).

In the ninety-first aeon from now, I gave that couch then. Since then, I have not known any woeful state; this is the fruit of the gift of a couch.

My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled."

The Elder had a friend from his lay life, a wanderer named Kātiyāna. Since the Buddha's appearance, because the gains and honor of the sectarians had declined, he did not even receive enough food and clothing. Being oppressed by the Ājīvakas, he approached the Elder and asked, "You who are called the sons of the Sakyans have reached the pinnacle of great gain and fame and live happily. We, however, are miserable and live with difficulty. By practicing in what way may one be endowed with happiness in this life and in the life to come?"

Then the Elder, wishing to explain to him by way of a figure that "In the absolute sense, what is called happiness is only supramundane (lokuttara) happiness, and it is attained only by one who practices the practice suitable for it," and that he himself had attained that supramundane happiness, recited the verse beginning with "Sukhaṃ sukhattho labhate tadācaraṃ."
125:
## 6. Commentary on the Verse of Kumāputta Thera

The verse beginning with "Sādhu sutaṃ" is the verse of the Venerable Kumāputta Thera. As for the account of his origin: It is said that he had performed meritorious deeds of aspiration (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas. Ninety-one aeons ago from this present aeon, he was an ascetic wearing an antelope skin, living in the royal garden in the city of Bandhumatī. Seeing the Blessed One Vipassī, with a confident mind, he offered oil for anointing the feet. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the heavenly world. From then on, he wandered only in the happy realms (sugati). In the time of this Buddha's appearance, he was reborn in a householder's family in the city of Veḷukaṇṭaka in the country of Avanti.

They gave him the name "Nanda." Since his mother's name was "Kumā," he became known as "Kumāputta" (son of Kumā). This young man Nanda, having heard the Dhamma from the Venerable Sāriputta and gained confidence, went forth. Having performed the preliminary duties, he practiced the ascetic life (samaṇa-dhamma) on a remote mountain slope, but being unable to produce the distinction (of the Path and Fruit), he approached the Blessed One, heard the Dhamma, and purified his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Living in a suitable place, he developed insight (vipassanā) and realized the fruit of Arahatship. This matter is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

"In the city of Bandhumatī, I lived before. At that time, I was an ascetic wearing an antelope skin and carrying a water pot.

I saw the stainless Buddha, the Self-awakened One, the Unconquered, who was supreme, with a directed mind, a meditator delighting in jhāna, a master of himself.

Having seen that Blessed One, whose every wish was fulfilled, who had crossed the flood, and who was free from taints (āsava), with a confident and joyful mind, I offered anointing oil.

Since I offered anointing oil ninety-one aeons ago, I have not known a woeful state; this is the result of offering anointing oil.

My defilements have been burnt away... (pe) ... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

After attaining Arahatship, seeing monks in the forest who were diligent in physical endurance, he exhorted them, and wishing to manifest the liberating nature of the Dispensation, he recited the verse beginning with "Sādhu sutaṃ sādhu caritakaṃ."
126:
In this verse, 'sādhu' means excellent. 'Sutaṃ' means hearing. Here, the hearing that is desired is the hearing of the ten subjects of discourse (kathāvatthu), which is supportive of liberation from the cycle of rebirth (vivaṭṭūpanissita) and specifically associated with fewness of wishes (appicchatā) and so on. 'Sādhu caritakaṃ' means that practicing that very conduct of fewness of wishes and so on is very excellent; the excellent conduct itself is called 'caritaka'. By these two words, it is shown that great learning (bāhusacca) and the practice corresponding to that learning are 'excellent'. 'Sadā' means at all times—whether at the time of being a junior monk, a middle-ranking monk, or a senior monk—or it means in all moments of the postures (iriyāpathakkhaṇa). 'Aniketavihāra' means that the five cords of sensual pleasure (pañca kāmaguṇa) are called 'niketa' (home/dwelling) because they are the dwelling places of the defilements; or the six mundane sense objects are called 'niketa'. As it was said: "Householder, one who dwells and frequents the home of the sign of forms (rūpanimitta) is called a 'dweller in a home' (niketasārī)," and so on. The practice for the sake of abandoning those 'niketas' is called 'aniketavihāra' (homeless dwelling). 'Atthapucchana' means that one who desires to know the meaning approaches a good friend (kalyāṇamitta) and inquires about the distinctions of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal (Nibbāna); or it is the inquiry into the nature of things (sabhāva-dhamma) distinguished as wholesome and so on, in such a way as: "Venerable sir, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy? What is blameless?" and so on. 'Padakkhiṇakamma' means, after inquiring about that meaning, the firm establishment in his advice and the right practice by way of accepting that advice respectfully. Here also, the word 'sādhu' should be brought and applied. 'Etaṃ sāmaññaṃ' means that all—the hearing, the conduct, the homeless dwelling, the inquiry into the meaning, and the right practice—mentioned starting with 'sādhu sutaṃ' constitute the state of a recluse (sāmañña). Because the state of a recluse is possible only through this practice and not by any other means, the name 'sāmañña' is a direct designation for the Path and Fruit (magga-phala). Or else, this practice is the unerring practice (apaṇṇaka-paṭipadā), and to show to what kind of person that recluseship (sāmañña) can occur, it is said 'akiñcanassa'. It means for one who is free from possessing and accepting fields, land, gold, silver, female slaves, male slaves, and so on.

## The Commentary on the Verse of Kumāputta Thera is finished.
127:
## 7. Commentary on the Verse of Kumāputtasahāya Thera
The verse beginning with "Nānājanapadaṃ yanti" is the verse of the Venerable Kumāputtasahāya Thera. As for the origin of this Thera: he had made an aspiration in the presence of former Buddhas and had accumulated wholesome merit that is a support for liberation from the cycle of suffering (vivaṭṭa) in various births. More than ninety-four aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, during the time of Siddhattha Buddha, he was born into a noble family. When he reached the age of discretion, he entered the forest, cut many pieces of wood, made walking sticks (kattarayāṭṭhi), and offered them to the Saṅgha. He also performed other meritorious deeds according to his wealth and was reborn in the deva realm. From then on, he wandered only in the happy destinations (sugati) and was born into a wealthy family in the city of Veḷukaṇṭaka during the time of our Buddha. His name was Sudanta. Some call him Vāsula. He was a dear friend of the youth Kumāputta. While wandering about, he heard that "Kumāputta has gone forth as a monk." He thought, "This Dispensation (sāsana) in which Kumāputta has gone forth is certainly not an inferior teaching," and following after him, desiring to go forth himself, he approached the Teacher. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. He developed an intense desire for the monkhood, went forth, and lived together with Kumāputta at the edge of a forest mountain, devoted to meditation (bhāvanā). At that time, many monks, while wandering on a walking tour (cārika) through various regions (janapada), arrived at that place. Because of that, a great commotion and noise occurred there. Seeing that situation, the Elder Sudanta was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking: "These monks, having gone forth in the Dispensation that leads out of suffering, follow after thoughts (vitakka) concerning the regions and fail in the concentration of the mind (samādhi)." Wishing to make that very spiritual urgency a goad for taming his own mind, he recited the verse beginning with "Nānājanapadaṃ yanti."

In that verse, "nānājanapadaṃ" means various and different regions, many countries such as Kāsi and Kosala. "Yanti" means they go. "Vicarantā" means wandering on a walking tour through the regions by the power of thoughts such as "Such a region has plenty of food and alms are easily obtained; such a region is safe and free from disease." "Asaññatā" means being unrestrained in mind because those thoughts concerning the regions have not yet been abandoned. "Samādhiဉ္စ virādhenti" means they fail in access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and fixed concentration (appanā-samādhi), which are the foundation of all superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), namely the Path and Fruit.
128:
In the word "virādhenti", the particle "ca" is used in the sense of commendation.
