Because of wandering to other places, there is no opportunity to practice meditation; thus, they do not attain the concentration (samādhi) not yet attained, and they cause the concentration already attained to decline and perish due to the lack of mastery. Therefore, it is said "virādhenti" (they fail or miss).

In the sentence "kiṃsu raṭṭhacariyā karissati", the word "su" is merely a particle. He speaks by way of reproach, saying: "For those who have thus failed in concentration, what benefit can wandering throughout the country bring? What purpose can it achieve? It is indeed useless." Therefore (tasmā) means: because such wandering to other places does not bring benefit to a monk, but rather brings harm by causing the loss of attainments, therefore (tasmā).

"Vineyya sārambhaṃ" means: having removed and calmed the impetuosity (sārambha), which is the defilement of the mind arising from dissatisfaction with one's place of residence, through suitable reflective wisdom. "Jhāyeyya" means: one should meditate with the two kinds of jhāna, namely, meditation by scrutinizing the object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and meditation by scrutinizing the characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). "Apurakkhato" means: not being led by wrong thoughts or by craving, etc.; not following their influence, one should only attend to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).

After saying this, Elder Kumāputtasahāya made that very sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) like a goad, developed insight (vipassanā), and attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"Having entered the forest at that time, I cut bamboo,
And having made a staff, I gave many to the Saṅgha.

With that clarity of mind, having paid homage to the well-behaved ones,
And having given the staff, I departed facing the north.

In the ninety-four aeons since I gave that staff,
I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of giving a staff.

My defilements are burned away... [pe]... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Making that meaning like a goad, this Elder attained Arahantship. Keeping that very meaning in his heart, even after attaining Arahantship, he recited this very verse: "nānājanapadaṃ yanti". Therefore, that verse became his declaration of Arahantship (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kumāputtasahāya is finished.
129:
## 8. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Gavampati

The verse beginning with "Yo iddhiyā sarabhuṃ" is that of the Venerable Elder Gavampati. What is its origin? It is said that he had made an aspiration (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas. Thirty-one aeons ago, having seen Sikhī Buddha, with a clear mind, he made an offering of flowers. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the celestial realm. Performing merits repeatedly, he had a parasol and a railing (vedikā) made for the shrine (cetiya) of Koṇāgamana Buddha.

During the time of Kassapa Buddha, he was born in a certain family. In that family, there was a large herd of cattle, which were looked after by cowherds. This noble son wandered among the herd, considering what was proper and improper. He saw an Arahant Elder who, after wandering for alms in the village, would take his daily meal at a certain spot outside the village. Thinking, "The Venerable One will be exhausted by the heat of the sun," he set up four acacia (sirīsa) posts, placed acacia branches on top of them, and made a leaf-pavilion (maṇḍapa) as an offering. Some also say, "He planted an acacia tree near the pavilion." Out of compassion for him, the Elder sat there daily.

Due to that meritorious deed, he passed away from that life and was reborn in the Cātumahārājikā heaven. As a sign of his past deed, a large acacia grove appeared at the gate of his mansion, which was always beautiful with other flowers endowed with color and fragrance. Therefore, that mansion was known as "Serīsaka". That deva-son wandered through the celestial and human realms for the interval between two Buddhas. In this Buddha's era, he was born as Gavampati, one of the four lay friends of Elder Yasa. Hearing that Venerable Yasa had gone forth, he went to the Buddha's presence along with his friends.

The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. At the end of the teaching, he, along with his friends, was established in Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"In the past, I was a hunter wandering in the forest,
I saw the stainless Buddha, who had reached the far shore of all dhammas.

To that Great Compassionate One, who delights in the welfare of all beings,
With a clear mind and joy, I offered Nela flowers."
130:
Thirty-one aeons ago from now, I worshipped with flowers. Due to the merit of that offering to the Buddha, I have never known a miserable rebirth.

My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled. (He spoke thus).

After attaining the fruit of Arahantship, the Elder, experiencing the bliss of liberation (vimuttisukha), resided in the Anjana Wood in the city of Sāketa. At that time, the Blessed One, together with a large community of monks, arrived at Sāketa and stayed in the Anjana Wood. As the lodgings were insufficient, many monks slept on the sandy banks of the Sarabhū River near the monastery. Then, at midnight, as a flood of water came down the river, the novices and others made a loud noise. The Blessed One, knowing this, commanded the Venerable Gavampati: "Gavampati, go and restrain the flood of water so that the monks may live in comfort." The Elder replied, "Very well, Bhante," and by the power of his psychic ability, he restrained the river's current, and from afar, it stood like a mountain peak. From that day on, the Elder's supernatural power became well-known in the world. Furthermore, one day, while the Teacher was sitting in the midst of a great assembly of deities, he saw the Elder preaching the Dhamma. Out of compassion for the world and to make the Elder's virtues known, he praised him by reciting the verse beginning with "Yo iddhiyā sarabhu."

In that verse, "iddhiyā" means by the power of resolve (adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi). "Sarabhu" refers to the river of that name, known in the world as the Sarabhū. "Aṭṭhapesi" means not allowing the water to flow, turning back the current and making it stand as a great mass of water like a mountain peak. "Asito" means one who is unattached, free from the dependence of craving and views; or, because all fetters (saṃyojana) have been completely cut off, he is not bound by any bond. Because he is free from such bonds, he is "anejo" (unshaken), as he lacks the trembling defilements. To that Gavampati, who has "gone beyond all attachments" (sabbasaṅgātigato) because he stands having transcended the five attachments of greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, and views; who is a "Great Sage" (mahāmuniṃ) because he is an Arahant sage (asekkha-muni); and who has "gone to the further shore of existence" (bhavassa pāraguṃ) because he has reached Nibbāna, the further shore of all existence consisting of sense-desire, kamma, and becoming—"the gods pay homage" (devā namassanti). If even the gods pay homage, what need is there to mention other beings? (They certainly do). At the end of the verse and the teaching, the realization of the Four Noble Truths (dhammābhisamaya) occurred for the great multitude of people. When the Elder Gavampati attained the fruit of Arahantship, wishing to worship the Blessed One, he uttered this very verse.
132:
It is to be done; they reach death or suffering as bitter as death itself. 'Ḍayhamāne' means being burnt by fire. 'Matthake' means on the head (at the top of the head). The intended meaning is this: Just as a man pierced by a spear exerts effort, makes an attempt, and strives for the removal of the barb and the treatment of the wound; and just as a man whose head is on fire exerts effort and makes an attempt to extinguish that fire; even so, O monk, for the sake of abandoning sensual desire (kāmarāga), one should dwell mindful, diligent, and possessed of extreme effort.

In this way, the Blessed One, giving advice to that Elder for the subsiding of his anger and distress, concluded the teaching by focusing on the abandonment of sensual desire, as it shares the same basis with that anger and distress. Having heard this verse, the Elder, with a mind full of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), remained constantly devoted to the practice of insight (vipassanā). Knowing his inclination, the Teacher taught the Tissatthera Sutta from the Saṃyutta Nikāya (Saṃ. Ni. 3.84). At the conclusion of the teaching, he was established in the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 2.53.66-73):

"Having experienced both types of glory in the deva world and the human world,
In the end, I reached the peerless Nibbāna, which is secure and peaceful.

For one who increases merit by dedicating it to the Buddha
Or to the Bodhi tree of that Teacher, what kind of wealth would be hard to obtain?

In the Path, the Fruit, the Scriptures (Āgama), and the qualities of Jhana and Supernormal Knowledge,
Being superior to others, I attain Nibbāna, free from taints (anāsava).

Formerly, I abandoned other things for the sake of attaining the knowledge of the Four Truths; with a joyful mind,
I am fully endowed with these twenty factors in every way.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Upon reaching the fruit of Arahantship, the Elder, wishing to declare his attainment and to honor the Teacher, recited that very same verse.

## The Commentary on the Verse of Tissa Thera is finished.
133:
## 10. Vaḍḍhamānattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with "Sattiyā viya omaṭṭho" is the verse of the Venerable Vaḍḍhamāna Thera. What is the story of its origin? This Elder also had made a meritorious resolution (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas. Ninety-two aeons ago, during the time of Tissa Buddha, he was born into a respectable family. When he reached the age of discretion, he saw Tissa Buddha walking for alms and, with a clear and confident mind, offered well-ripened mangoes that had fallen from their stems. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world. Accumulating other meritorious deeds, he was born into the Licchavī royal family in the city of Vesālī during the time of this Buddha's appearance, and was named Vaḍḍhamāna Tissa.

When he reached adulthood, he became a lay follower who was faithful, confident, helpful, and a supporter of the Saṅgha. Due to a certain fault, when the Teacher had the Saṅgha perform the act of overturning the alms-bowl (pattanikkujjana-kamma) against him, he was as terrified as one who had stepped on fire. He asked for forgiveness from the Saṅgha, had the act revoked, and, being moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he ordained. After ordaining, however, he lived overcome by sloth and torpor (thīna-middha). Wishing to inspire him with urgency, the Teacher spoke the verse beginning with "Sattiyā viya omaṭṭho."

In that verse, "bhavarāgap pahānāya" means for the sake of abandoning lust for existence (bhavarāga), lust for material existence (rūparāga), and lust for immaterial existence (arūparāga). Although there is no such thing as abandoning external fetters (bahiddha-saṃyojana) without abandoning internal fetters (ajjhatta-saṃyojana), by mentioning the abandonment of the higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana) due to their sequential nature, the abandonment of the lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana) is also implied. Alternatively, for some noble ones (ariyas) who have already cut off the lower fetters, the higher fetters are still difficult to abandon. Therefore, to show the difficult task rather than the easy one, the Blessed One taught the abandonment of all higher fetters, taking the abandonment of lust for existence (bhavarāga) as the primary focus. Or otherwise, it was taught in this way according to the Elder's own inclination. The remaining words are to be understood in the same manner as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verse of Vaḍḍhamāna Thera is finished.

## The Commentary on the Fourth Group (Catuttha Vagga) is finished.
134:
## 5. Pañcama Vagga
## 1. Sirivaḍḍhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

"Vivaramanupatanti vijjutā" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sirivaḍḍha. What is its origin? This elder, too, having made aspirations under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome merit that is a strong support for Nibbāna in various existences, was reborn in a good family ninety-one aeons ago during the time of Buddha Vipassī. Upon reaching maturity, he saw Buddha Vipassī and made an offering with kiṅkaṇi flowers. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the celestial realm and, after performing further merits, wandered only through the happy realms. In this Buddha's era, he was reborn in the house of a wealthy Brahmin in the city of Rājagaha and was named Sirivaḍḍha. When he reached maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher and the True Dhamma at the assembly where King Bimbisāra met the Buddha, and being endowed with sufficient supporting conditions, he went forth into monkhood. After going forth and performing the preliminary duties, he resided in a mountain cave in a forest area not far from Mount Vebhāra and Mount Paṇḍava, devoted to his meditation subject. At that time, a great unseasonable rain fell. Flashes of lightning moved about as if entering the mountain clefts. For the elder, who was oppressed by the heat, the heat was extinguished by the cool and substantial rain-winds. By obtaining a suitable climate, his mind became one-pointed. With a concentrated mind, he applied himself to insight (vipassanā) and attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is stated in the Apadāna:

"The Buddha, the Supreme Person, resembling a golden pillar, the All-Knowing Leader of the World, descended into the lake and bathed.

Taking a kiṅkaṇi flower, I offered it to Buddha Vipassī, the Lord of bipeds, the Such-like One, with an uplifted and joyful mind.

In the ninety-one aeons since I offered that flower, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.

In the twenty-seventh aeon, I was a Cakkavatti King named Bhīmaratha, endowed with the seven treasures and great power.

My defilements have been burned away... (and so forth) I have fulfilled the Buddha's teaching."

Wishing to make known his qualities such as the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), he uttered the verse beginning with "Vivaramanupatanti". In that verse, "vivaraṃ" means...
135:
Having reached the fruit of Arahantship, wishing to express an inspired utterance based on himself by way of declaring his attainment, he spoke the verse beginning with "Vivaramanupatanti vijjutā".

In that verse, "vivaraṃ" means the gap or the middle. "Anupatanti" means they strike, occur, or shine with reference to a mark. Indeed, the occurrence of lightning is its very shining. Here, because of the association with the word "anu", the accusative case is used, as in "rukkhamanuvijjotanti" (they shine with reference to the tree). "Vijjutā" refers to flashes of lightning. The connection is that they strike with reference to the gap between Mount Vebhāra and Mount Paṇḍava. "Nagavivara-gato" means one who has reached a mountain cave, which is a mountain cleft. "Jhāyati" means he meditates by way of meditation on the object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and meditation on the characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna), developing Samatha and Vipassanā with diligence. "Putto appaṭimassa tādino" means the breast-born son of the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is peerless and incomparable due to his perfection of the Dhamma-body (such as the aggregate of virtue) and the Form-body, and who is "Such-like" (tādi) due to his perfection of the quality of being such-like amidst desirable and undesirable objects. By the word "putta" (son) itself, it should be understood that the elder declared his attainment of Arahantship by illustrating that he is a son born after (anujāta) the Teacher.

## The Commentary on the Verse of Elder Sirivaḍḍha is finished.

## 2. Khadiravaniyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

"Cāle upacāle" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Elder Khadiravaniya Revata. How did it arise? It is said that in the time of Buddha Padumuttara, this elder was reborn in a family of ferrymen in the city of Haṃsavatī. While working as a ferryman at the Payāga ferry on the great Ganges River, he saw the Blessed One together with the community of disciples approaching the bank of the Ganges. With a faithful heart, he joined boats together to form a raft and, with great honor and offerings, ferried them to the other side. Seeing the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among forest-dwellers, he made an aspiration for that position and performed a great almsgiving to the Buddha and the community of monks. The Blessed One also prophesied that his aspiration would not fail. From that time on, in various existences, he performed merit which is a strong support for Nibbāna...
136:
Having performed merit and wandering through the realms of devas and humans, during the time of our Buddha's appearance, he was reborn in the womb of the noble brahmin lady Rūpasārī in the village of Nālaka in the kingdom of Magadha. When he reached the age of maturity, his parents desired to bind him with the fetters of a householder's life. Upon hearing of the renunciation of the Elder Sāriputta, he thought: "My elder brother Upatissa has renounced such great wealth; why should I swallow again the wealth that he has discarded like a lump of spit?" Feeling a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), like a wild animal fleeing to safety without approaching a snare, he deceived his relatives. Urged by the force of his past merits, he went to the monks, informed them that he was the younger brother of the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), and expressed his desire to ordain. The monks ordained him as a novice and, when he reached the age of twenty, granted him full ordination (upasampadā) and instructed him in meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). Taking the meditation subject, he entered the Khadiravana (Acacia Forest) and strove with the thought, "I will see the Blessed One and the General of the Dhamma only after attaining Arahatship." Due to the maturity of his knowledge, he soon attained the six supernormal powers (chalabhiññā). Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna:

There is a river named Gaṅgā Bhāgīrathī, flowing from the Himavanta mountains; at that river crossing, I was a ferryman and I transported people across.

The Buddha Padumuttara, the Leader, the Supreme among men, arrived at the bank of the Gaṅgā with a hundred thousand disciplined ones (arahants).

Having brought many boats and having them well-prepared by carpenters, I made a canopy over the boat and honored the Buddha, the Bull among men.

The Buddha came and boarded that boat; standing in the middle of the water, the Teacher spoke these verses:

"He who has transported the Buddha and the Saṅgha free from taints (āsavas), through that clarity of mind, he will rejoice in the deva realm.

A well-constructed celestial mansion in the shape of a boat will arise for you; a canopy of flowers will always shade you in the sky.

Fifty-eight aeons from now, he will be a kshatriya named Tāraka, a victorious world-turning monarch (cakkavatti) ruling over the four islands."
137:
"Fifty-seven aeons from now, a king named Cammaka, possessing great power and majesty, will shine like the rising sun.

One hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka dynasty, will appear in the world.

Passing away from the Tāvatiṃsa deva realm, he will reach the human state and will be a brahmin by the name of Revata.

Urged by his root of merit, he will leave the household life and ordain in the dispensation (sāsana) of the Blessed One Gotama.

After ordaining, that noble son, devoted to meditation and practicing insight (vipassanā), will fully understand all taints (āsavas) and, becoming taintless, will attain Parinibbāna.

My energy is like a beast of burden, carrying me to the security from bondage (yogakkhema); I bear this final body in the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One.

The deed performed a hundred thousand aeons ago shows its fruit to me here; like the speed of a well-released arrow, it has burnt away my defilements.

Then, seeing me delighting in the forest, the Sage who has reached the end of the world, the Great Wise One, declared me the foremost among the monks who dwell in the forest."

My defilements have been burnt away; the Buddha's bidding has been done.

Having become one with the six supernormal powers, the Elder, wishing to pay homage to the Teacher and the General of the Dhamma, tidied his lodging, took his bowl and robes, and in due course reached Sāvatthī. Entering the Jetavana monastery, he paid homage to the Teacher and the General of the Dhamma and stayed in Jetavana for a few days. Then, the Teacher, seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones, placed him in the pre-eminent position (etadagga) among forest-dwelling monks: "Monks, among my monk disciples who dwell in the forest, Revata of the Acacia Forest (Khadiravaniya Revata) is the foremost." Later, the Elder Revata went to his home village and brought his three nephews—named Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsūpacālā, who were the sons of his three sisters Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsūpacālā—ordained them, and instructed them in meditation. Those nephews lived devoted to meditation. At that time, a certain illness arose in the Elder.
139:
## 3. Commentary on the Verses of the Venerable Sumangala

The verse beginning with "Sumuttiko" is that of the Venerable Sumangala. How did it arise? He, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit that serves as a strong support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various lives, was reborn as a tree deity during the time of the Buddha Siddhattha. One day, seeing the Teacher (the Buddha) standing with a single robe after bathing, he was filled with joy and clapped his hands. Due to that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in a poor family in a small village not far from Sāvatthī during the time of this Buddha's appearance, as a result of that kamma. That young man was named Sumangala.

When he reached adulthood, he made a living by farming, possessing tools such as a small sickle, a plow, and a spade. One day, while King Pasenadi of Kosala was offering a great alms-giving to the Buddha and the Sangha, he came along with people carrying offerings, carrying a jar of curds. Seeing the respectful honor and offerings given to the monks, he thought, "These recluses, sons of the Sakyans, dress well in delicate robes, eat good food, and dwell in dwellings protected from the wind. What if I, too, were to go forth?" He approached a certain Great Elder and informed him of his desire to ordain. Out of compassion, the elder ordained him and taught him a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).

While dwelling in the forest, he became weary and dissatisfied with living alone. Wishing to return to lay life, he was traveling to his relatives' village. On the way, he saw farmers with their waistbands tied, plowing fields, wearing soiled clothes, their bodies covered in dust, and suffering from the hot wind and sun. He was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking, "Indeed, these beings suffer great hardship repeatedly for the sake of a livelihood." Because his wisdom had matured, the meditation subject he had learned became clear to him. He approached the foot of a tree, attained seclusion, and by reflecting wisely (yoniso manasikāra) and developing insight (vipassanā), he reached the fruition of Arahantship through the sequence of the paths.

This account is stated in the Apadāna (Ap. i. 12. 11-19):
"The Buddha Atthadassī, the Best of Victors, the Chief of the World, the Bull among Men,
Having come out from the monastery, approached a pond.
Having bathed and drunk, the Awakened One, the Blessed One,
Stood there with a single robe, looking in all directions."
140:
Seeing the farmers with girded waists, plowing the fields, wearing soiled clothes, their bodies covered in dust from all sides, and touched by the hot wind and sun, he felt a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking: 'Alas, these beings experience great suffering for the sake of their livelihood!' Because his wisdom had matured, his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) became clear. That monk approached the foot of a tree, attained seclusion, and by reflecting through appropriate means (yoniso manasikāra) and developing insight (vipassanā), he reached the fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala) through the sequence of the paths. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

The Blessed One Atthadassī, the Great Being among men, the Supreme among men, departed from the monastery and approached a lake. After bathing and drinking, the Blessed One ascended, and while wearing a single robe, he stood there looking in all directions.

I, being in my celestial mansion, saw the Leader of the World, the Buddha, shining like pure gold with his own radiance. Then, with a joyful heart, I clapped my hands.

Shining like the sun with a thousand rays, and like glowing pure gold (while seeing the Buddha), I was engaged in dancing, singing, and the playing of the five-fold musical instruments.

In whatever birth I arose, whether as a deity or a human, I surpassed all beings, and my fame was vast.

Homage to you, O Noble Man! Homage to you, O Supreme Man! O Sage, having satisfied yourself, you satisfy others.

Living in the celestial mansion, having made joy and served the well-practiced Buddha, I was reborn in the Tusita realm.

In the sixteenth aeon from this one, there were eighteen universal monarchs (cakkavatti) named Ekacintita, endowed with the seven treasures and possessing great power.

My defilements are burnt... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Upon reaching Arahatship, while proclaiming his own attainment and liberation from suffering in the form of an inspired utterance (udāna), he spoke the verse beginning with 'Sumuttiko'.

In that verse, 'Sumuttiko' means one who has a good, final, and non-recurring liberation. Because of the praiseworthy and wonderful nature of that liberation, he spoke 'Sumuttiko' while clapping his hands. Again, to show the firmness of his faith in that liberation, he said, 'I am indeed well-freed.' The meaning is: 'I am truly and thoroughly freed.'

If it is asked, 'Why is there this state of being well-freed?', although this elder was well-freed from all the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha), he spoke the words beginning with 'from the three stoopings' (tīhi khujjakehi) to show the extremely undesirable suffering that was previously manifest to him. There, 'khujjakehi' means those having the nature of stooping or the manner of stooping. This word is in the ablative case (nissakka) in relation to the word 'mutta' (freed). For a farmer, even if he is not naturally stooped, shows himself stooping in three places: in harvesting, in plowing, and in hoeing. Those actions performed by a farmer, such as harvesting, are called 'khujja' (stooping) because they are done in a stooped manner. Therefore, the elder spoke the word 'khujjakehi'. Now, wishing to show those actions like harvesting himself, he spoke the verse beginning with 'Asitā su-muttikā'. In that verse, 'Asitā su-muttikā' means 'I am well-freed from the fatigues of the mind.' In the remaining words, the meaning of the cases should be understood in this same way.
141:
A farmer performs harvesting and so on; those sickles and such are also 'khujja' (crooked/stooped) because of their curved shape; thus it was said, 'by the three stoopings'.

Now, wishing to show those [actions] like harvesting in their actual form, he said: 'From sickles I (am well-freed), from plows I (am well-freed), from small hoes I (am well-freed).' Among those words, 'asitāsu mayā' means 'I am freed from sickles.' Here, the locative case (bhummavacana) is used in the sense of the ablative case (nissakka). In the remaining words, this same method applies. Other teachers, however, say that 'asitāsu mayā' means 'I was stooped because of the sickles which were the cause.' In their view, the locative case is used in the sense of instrument (karaṇa) or cause (hetu). The word 'nangalāsu' is spoken with a change of gender, meaning 'by the very laborious plows.' It is called 'khuddakuddālāsu' (small hoes) either because of the nature of the hoe used by himself being small, or because it has become short through frequent use. There is also a Pali reading 'kuṇṭhakuddālāsu'. It means 'among the hoes that are very sharp only through use.' In the word 'idham-eva', the letter 'm' is a euphonic junction (padasandhi). In the phrase 'atha vāpi', the word 'vā' is merely a particle. The meaning is that because they are located in the small village, even if those sickles and so on are near me, they are indeed rejected (by me). This repetition (of 'alam-eva') is an emphatic repetition (āmeḍita) spoken for the sake of haste.

'Jhāya' means 'meditate' (or 'contemplate') for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life by the power of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), and by the power of the divine abidings (dibbavihāra) and so on. 'Sumangala' is addressing himself as if he were another person. The repetition (āmeḍita) is made to show respect for meditation. 'Appamatto vihara' means: 'You have reached the fullness of mindfulness and wisdom, and thus you are not one who is negligent in any matter; therefore, Sumangala... now dwell in happiness.' Some teachers, however, say: 'Before reaching Arahatship, while on the path of insight (vipassanā), because of the delight that arose in the Dispensation, the elder spoke this verse while loathing the suffering of household life as he had experienced it, and later, having developed insight, he reached Arahatship.' In their view, the meaning of the words 'Jhāya appamatto vihara' is also appropriate by way of the path of insight.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sumangala Thera is finished.

The Verses of Sannu Thera. The verse 'Mataṃ me amma rodantī' is the verse of the Venerable Sannu Thera. That Sannu Thera, having performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) in the presence of former Buddhas...
142:
## 4. Sānuttheragāthāvaṇṇanā

'Matāṃ vā amma rodanti' and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sānu. How did it originate? This Venerable Sānu had also performed meritorious services (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that serves as a powerful support for Nibbāna, the liberation from the cycle of rebirth, in various existences. Ninety-four aeons ago from this Bhadda Kappa, he offered water to Buddha Siddhattha for washing his hands, feet, and face. Indeed, the Blessed One, when about to partake of his meal, had the intention to wash his hands and feet. That person, noticing the Blessed One's intention, offered water. After the Blessed One had washed his hands and feet and finished his meal, he again had the intention to rinse his mouth; that person, recognizing that intention as well, offered water for washing the face. The Blessed One rinsed his mouth and completed the task of washing his face. In this way, the Blessed One, out of compassion, accepted the service (veyyāvacca) performed by that person.

Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva realm and, performing merits here and there, wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the time of our Blessed One's appearance, he took rebirth in the house of an obscure lay devotee (upāsaka) in Sāvatthī. While the child was still in the mother's womb, the father went to another place. After ten months, the mother, a lay devotee (upāsikā), gave birth to a son and named him 'Sānu'. When the boy gradually grew up, at the age of seven, she had him ordained in the presence of the monks, thinking, 'In this way, he will grow up without obstacles and become a partaker of ultimate happiness.' He became famous as 'Sānu Sāmaṇera' (the novice Sānu). Being wise, dutiful, learned, an excellent Dhamma preacher, and possessing a heart of loving-kindness (mettā) toward all beings, he was dear and pleasing to devas and humans; all this should be understood according to the method mentioned in the Sānu Sutta.

In his past life, the mother of that novice had been reborn in the realm of Yakkhas. Other Yakkhas, thinking, 'This is the mother of Elder Sānu,' honored her with great respect and reverence. As time passed, as if to demonstrate the danger of being a worldling (puthujjana), one day, due to a lack of wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), Sānu Sāmaṇera developed unwise attention and a desire to disrobe (vibbhamitukāmatā) arose in him. His Yakkhiṇī mother, knowing this, informed his human mother: 'Your son Sānu has developed the thought, "I will disrobe"; therefore, you—

Tell the awakened Sānu, this is the word of the Yakkhas:
Do not commit an evil deed, whether in the open or in secret.'
143:
'If you do or will do an evil deed, there is no escape from suffering for you, even if you fly away and flee.' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.239; Dh. Pa. Aṭṭha. 2.325, Sānu Sāmaṇera Vatthu) — Tell him thus."

Having said this, the Yakkhiṇī mother vanished right there. The human mother, upon hearing those words, became overcome with lamentation and grief, as if pierced by mental suffering.

Then, in the morning, Sānu Sāmaṇera dressed in his undergarment, took his bowl and robes, and approached his mother. Seeing his mother weeping with tears flowing, he asked, "Mother, for what reason do you weep?" When she replied, "I weep because of you," he recited this verse to his mother:

"Mother, people weep for the dead, or for those who, though living, are not seen."

The meaning of that verse is: "Mother, those who weep, such as relatives or friends, weep for their own relative or friend who is dead, because they have gone to the next world. Or they weep for a relative or friend who, though living, is not seen because they have departed to another land. Neither of these two conditions applies to me. This being so, seeing me standing before you alive and well, why, mother, do you weep? There is truly no reason for your weeping on my account."

Hearing those words, Sānu Sāmaṇera's mother, in accordance with the Sutta passage, "Monks, this is death in the Discipline of the Noble Ones—when one gives up the training and returns to the lower life" (Ma. Ni. 3.63), wishing to show that disrobing is death in the Noble Discipline, recited these two verses:

"Son, they weep for the dead, or for those who, though living, are not seen.
And for him who, having abandoned sense pleasures, comes back here again.

Son, they weep for him too; for though living, he is indeed dead.
Dear son, having been pulled out of the hot embers, do you wish to fall back into the hot embers?" (Saṃ. Ni. 1.239; Dh. Pa. Aṭṭha. 2. Sānu Sāmaṇera Vatthu).

In those verses, "kāme cajitvāna" (having abandoned sense pleasures) means giving up the objects of sense pleasure (vatthu-kāma) with an inclination toward renunciation (nekkhamma). This abandonment should be understood as the temporary abandonment (tadaṅga-pahāna) of the defilement of sense pleasure (kilesa-kāma). Here, the abandonment of sense pleasure through ordination is intended. "Punāragacchate idha" (comes back here again) means coming back to this house again, referring to the return to the lower life of a layman. "Taṃ vāpīti" means that person who, having been ordained...
144:
People like me weep for such a person who has disrobed as if he were dead. Why? Because he is one who is dead while still alive. Even though he lives after disrobing, he is truly dead through the death of his virtues. Now, to arouse extraordinary sense of urgency (saṃvega) in him, she spoke the words beginning with "Kukkulā". The meaning of those words is: "O dear son Sānu, I, out of compassion, have pulled you out from the heap of hot ashes (the household life), which is like the Kukkula Hell because it burns day and night. Do you wish to fall back into that heap of hot ashes?"

Upon hearing those words, the novice Sānu was filled with a sense of urgency, developed insight (vipassanā), and before long attained the fruit of Arahatship. Regarding this, it is stated in the Apadāna:

"Seeing the noble monk eating, with a clear and undisturbed mind, I took water in a jar and offered it to the Buddha Siddhattha."
"Today, I am free from stains, free from defilements, and my doubts are exhausted. For me, who has been reborn in the cycle of existence, a beautiful result has arisen."
"In the ninety-four aeons since I offered that water, I have not known an unhappy rebirth; this is the fruit of the gift of water."
"Sixty-one aeons ago, there was a single powerful Wheel-Turning King named Vimala, endowed with the seven treasures."
"My defilements have been burnt away... (p) ... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Upon reaching the fruit of Arahatship, the Elder, by way of an inspired utterance (udāna), recited that very verse again, thinking, "The beginning of my insight and the attainment of Arahatship occurred through the power of this verse."

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sānu Thera is finished.
145:
## 5. Ramaṇīyavihārīttheiragāthāvaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with "Yathāpi bhaddo ājañño" is the verse of the Venerable Ramaṇīyavihārī Thera. What is its origin? This Elder had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merits in various existences. Ninety-one aeons ago, having seen the Buddha Vipassī and with a devoted mind, he paid homage with the fivefold prostration and made an offering of Koraṇḍa flowers. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the celestial realms and, performing merits here and there, wandered through the worlds of gods and humans. In this Buddha's era, he was reborn in Rājagaha as the son of a certain merchant, and lived intoxicated by the pride of youth, becoming infatuated with sensual pleasures.

One day, seeing a man being subjected to various royal punishments by the king's men for committing adultery, he was struck with a sense of urgency (saṃvega). He listened to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher and ordained. Even after ordaining, because he was of a lustful temperament, he used to live by constantly sweeping the precinct well, keeping the drinking and utility water well-placed, and arranging the couch and stool neatly. Because of living in such a manner, he became known as "Ramaṇīyavihārī" (one who dwells pleasantly).

Due to the abundance of lust, he attended to thoughts improperly and fell into the offense of intentional emission of semen. Feeling remorse, he thought, "Woe is me! Should one like me consume the food offered out of faith?" and being dissatisfied, he set out thinking, "I will disrobe." While walking, he sat down at the foot of a tree by the wayside. Along that road, carts were passing, and a bull yoked to a cart, being exhausted, slipped and fell on uneven ground. The carters unyoked it from the yoke, gave it grass and water, relieved its exhaustion, and then yoked it to the front of the cart again, and they proceeded.

The Elder, seeing that incident, reflected wisely: "Just as this bull, though it slipped once, rose again and can carry the load once more, so too should I, though I have slipped once through the power of defilements, rise again and practice the Dhamma of a recluse." He turned back, informed the Elder Upāli of his situation, and according to the procedure instructed by him, rehabilitated himself from the offense, purified his virtue, and by developing insight, attained Arahatship before long. Therefore, it was said in the Apadāna:

"Seeing the footprint stepped upon, adorned with the wheel mark,
Following the footprints of the Great Sage Vipassī."
146:
"Seeing the Koraṇḍa flower in bloom, I offered it with its roots; with a joyful and happy mind, I paid homage to the supreme footprint."

"In the ninety-one aeons since I made that offering of flowers, I have not known an unhappy rebirth; this is the fruit of the Buddha-pūjā."

"Fifty-seven aeons ago, there was a single powerful Wheel-Turning King named Vimala, endowed with the seven treasures."

"My defilements have been burnt away... I have fulfilled the Buddha's teaching."

Upon reaching Arahatship and experiencing the bliss of liberation (vimuttisukha), he recited the verse that illustrates his previous practice along with the attainment of the Noble Dhamma: "Just as a noble thoroughbred horse, even if it slips, stands firm again in its place."

In that verse, 'khalitvā' means having stumbled or slipped. 'Patitiṭṭhati' means it stands again in its original place; it stands once more in its established position. Thus, just as a noble thoroughbred bull, while carrying a load, becomes exhausted and, coming upon uneven ground, slips and falls once, yet does not abandon the load for that much, but because it is endowed with strength, speed, and effort, it stands firm again even after slipping, and staying true to its nature, it carries the load; in the same way, though one slips due to a lapse in conduct after being exhausted by defilements, one makes that slip as it was before (restores it) because of being endowed with the strength of energy. Then, through the right view of the Path, one is endowed with vision. Because of being endowed with that vision of Path-knowledge, at the end of hearing the teaching of the Fully Enlightened One, one is a disciple because of being born of the Noble Birth. One is a heart-born son because of the noble birth generated by the effort in the presence of the Buddha. One should be regarded as a 'thoroughbred' (ājañño) because of having tasks similar to a thoroughbred, quickly understanding the Buddha's will. This is the meaning.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Ramaṇīyavihārī Thera is finished.
147:
(End of the previous opening) "Know me as one who quickly understands the Buddha's will." The commentary on the verses of Elder Ramaṇīyavihārī is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Samiddhi

"I went forth out of faith" (Saddhāyāhaṃ pabbajito)—this verse belongs to the Venerable Elder Samiddhi. How did it originate? This Elder Samiddhi had also made an aspiration in the presence of previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various existences. Ninety-four aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, he saw the Blessed One Siddhattha and, with a clear mind, took flowers with their stalks and offered them. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the celestial realm and, performing merits alternately in the human and celestial realms, wandered only in happy states (sugati). When this Buddha appeared, he was born into a noble family in the city of Rājagaha. From the time of his birth, that family increased in wealth, grain, and so on. His body was also very beautiful, pleasant to look at, and endowed with good qualities. Thus, he became known as "Samiddhi" (Prosperity) because of his success in wealth and success in qualities.

This noble son Samiddhi, seeing the Buddha's power at the assembly of King Bimbisāra, gained faith and went forth. He lived devoted to the practice of meditation. One day, while the Blessed One was staying at the Tapodārāma monastery, he thought: "How fortunate I am! The Teacher, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One, is my teacher. I have gone forth in the well-expounded Dhamma-Vinaya. My fellow practitioners are virtuous and of good character." As he was thinking thus, great joy and happiness (pīti-somanassa) arose in him. Unable to bear that joy, the evil Māra made a terrifying sound near the Elder, as if the earth were splitting. The Elder reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "Māra is planning to blind your eye of wisdom. Go, monk, and stay there without thinking about it." The Elder went there and stayed, and before long, by exerting himself in insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"I saw the Blessed One Siddhattha, the incomparable leader of men, who was staying in the mountain cleft, shining like a Kaṇikāra flower, illuminating all directions.

At that time, I made a bow my support and prepared an arrow, then I cut a flower with its stalk and offered it to the Buddha.

Because of the merit of that offering to the Buddha, which I made ninety-four aeons ago, I have never known a miserable state (duggati).

Fifty-one aeons ago, I was once a powerful Wheel-turning King (Cakkavatti) named Jutindhara, endowed with the seven treasures.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."
148:
However, when the Elder, having reached Arahantship, was staying in that same place, Māra, not knowing his state as one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), made a great terrifying sound just as before. Hearing that sound, the Elder, without fear or trembling, declared his attainment of Arahantship, saying, "Even if there were a hundred or a thousand such Māras, they could not make even a single hair of mine shake," and spoke the verse beginning with "I went forth out of faith."

In that verse, "saddhāyā" means faith in kamma and its results (kamma-phala-saddhā) and faith in the Triple Gem (ratanattaya-saddhā) arising from the desire for the Dhamma (dhamma-chanda). By the word "ahaṃ," he refers to himself. "Pabbajito" means having reached the state of a monk. "Agārasmā" means from the house or from the household life. "Anagāriyaṃ" means the state of a monk; indeed, any work such as farming or trade that is "beneficial to the house" is called "agāriya," and because of the absence of such things, it is called "anagāriya" (homelessness). "Sati paññā ca me vuဍ္ဎā" means mindfulness, characterized by recollection, and wisdom, characterized by knowing in various ways, have been developed by me through the sequence of the paths from the moment of insight until Arahantship. It shows that now these mindfulness and wisdom have reached fullness and there is nothing further to develop. "Cittañca susamāhitaṃ" means my mind is well-concentrated by the power of the eight attainments and by the power of supramundane concentration (lokuttara-samādhi). It shows that now concentration has reached fullness and there is nothing further to concentrate.

Therefore, "Evil Māra, create whatever distorted forms you wish directed at me. You will not be able to afflict me with them; you will not even be able to make my body shake, so how could you make my mind distorted? Therefore, your action is like a gift given to one who does not accept it; it is of no use and will only result in the exhaustion of your own mind." Thus the Elder rebuked Māra. Hearing those words, Māra vanished right there, thinking, "The ascetic knows me."

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Samiddhi is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Ujjaya

The verse beginning with "Namo te buddha vīratthu" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Ujjaya. How did it originate? This Elder had also made an aspiration in the presence of previous Buddhas and had performed merits in various existences. Ninety-two aeons ago from this aeon, he saw the Blessed One Tissa and, with a clear mind, made an offering with Kaṇikāra flowers. Due to that meritorious deed...
149:
Having been reborn in the deva realm and repeatedly performing meritorious deeds, wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he was reborn in this Buddha-era in the city of Rājagaha as the son of a certain Sottiya Brahmin. His name was Ujjaya. Upon reaching maturity, although he had mastered the three Vedas, he saw no essence in them. Urged by his strong supporting conditions (upanissaya), he went to the Veḷuvana monastery, heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, gained faith, and ordained. Taking a meditation subject suitable for his temperament and living in the forest, he developed insight (vipassanā) and soon attained Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

“Seeing a Kaṇikāra flower in bloom, I picked it and then offered it to the Buddha Tissa, who had crossed the flood and was such a one (tādi).
In the ninety-two aeons since I offered that flower, I do not know of any woeful rebirth; this is the fruit of Buddha-pūjā.
Thirty-five aeons ago, I was a Cakkavatti king of great power, renowned as Aruṇapāṇi, endowed with the seven treasures.
My defilements have been burned away ... pe ... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

After attaining Arahantship, he went to the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. Wishing to make known his attainment of Arahantship by way of praising the Blessed One, he recited the verse beginning with “Namo te buddha vīratthu.”

In that verse, “Namo” signifies the act of paying homage. “Te” indicates the recipient of the act of homage, meaning “to you, the Blessed One.” “Buddha vīra” is an address to the Blessed One. The Blessed One is called “Buddha” because he has understood all aspects of things to be known, in their various ways, without remainder through his self-enlightened knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa). Likewise, he is called “Vīra” (Hero) because he is endowed with great energy, striving by way of crushing the five Maras. “Atthu” means “let it be,” and it is connected with the word “Namo.” “Vippamuttosi sabbadhī” means you are liberated and detached from all defilements and from all conditioned things (saṅkhāra). There is nothing from which you are not liberated. Because I dwell in your instruction (apadāna) and dwell free from taints (anāsava), it means I dwell in the practice of the path (magga) which is your instruction and advice.
150:
Practicing to the best of my ability and strength, having completely abandoned the four taints (āsava) such as the taint of sensual desire, I dwell free from taints. O Buddha of great heroism, may there be homage to you, who are endowed with such qualities.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Ujjaya Thera is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Verses of Sañjaya Thera

The verse beginning with “Yato ahaṃ” is that of the Venerable Sañjaya Thera. What is its origin? He too had performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and, accumulating merit that serves as a strong support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various births, he lived during the time of the Buddha Vipassī. By encouraging a large group of people, he collected materials and performed merit dedicated to the Triple Gem. Although he was poor himself, he was actively involved in the meritorious deeds of those groups. From time to time, he approached and paid homage to the Blessed One and, with a confident mind, performed various services (veyyāvacca) for the monks.

Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva realm. Performing merits in successive births and wandering only in the happy realms (sugati), he was reborn in this Buddha-era in Rājagaha in a wealthy Brahmin family with the name Sañjaya. When he reached maturity, seeing famous Brahmins such as Brahmāyu and Pokkharasāti having great faith in the Dispensation, he gained faith and approached the Teacher. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, he became a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna). Later, he ordained. At the very moment the shaving of his hair was completed, he became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal powers (chalabhiññā). This is stated in the Apadāna:

“In the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, there was a large group of people; I was a servant (veyyāvaccakara), busy in all tasks.

I had no material gift to give to the Buddha, the Great Sage, but with a clear mind, I paid homage at the Teacher's feet.

In the ninety-one aeons since I performed that service, I do not know of any woeful rebirth; this is the fruit of that service.”
151:
“Eight aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, I was a Universal Monarch named Sucintita, endowed with the seven treasures and possessed of great power.

My defilements have been burnt away ... (and so forth) ... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.” Thus he spoke.

Being one who possessed the six higher powers (abhiññā) and wishing to declare his attainment of Arahantship (to reveal his own virtues), he recited the verse beginning with “Yato ahaṃ pabbajito”.

In that verse, “Yato ahaṃ pabbajito” means: from the time I attained the state of a monk, from the time I became a monk, I do not recall having given rise to wrong thoughts (micchā-vitakka) such as sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka), which are associated with faults such as lust and are therefore base, which are not to be practiced by the Noble Ones (Ariyas) and are practiced by worldlings (puthujjanas) and thus are base, and which are called ‘thought’ (saṅkappa) because they imagine non-existent qualities in objects. He declared his attainment of Arahantship by saying, “At the very end of the shaving of my hair, I reached Arahantship.”

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sañjaya Thera is finished.

## 9. The Commentary on the Verses of Ramaṇeyyaka Thera

“Cihacihābhinadite” is the verse of the Venerable Ramaṇeyyaka Thera. What is its origin? This elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and, accumulating merit in various births, was born into a good family during the time of Sikhī Buddha. Upon reaching maturity, he saw the Blessed One and, with a heart full of faith, made an offering of flowers. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world. Performing merits repeatedly and wandering only through the happy realms (sugati), he was born into a wealthy family in Sāvatthī during the time of this Buddha. Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith during the acceptance of the Jetavana monastery, went forth as a monk, took a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable for his temperament, and lived in the forest. Because of his personal fulfillment and his practice which was appropriate for a monk, he was pleasing to behold, and thus he became known by the name “Ramaṇeyyaka” (The Delightful One).

Then one day, Mara, wishing to frighten the elder, made a terrifying sound. Hearing that sound, the elder, because of his courageous nature, was not startled and, knowing “This is the evil Mara,” wished to show his disregard for that terrifying sound, and thus recited the verse beginning with “Cihacihābhinadite”.

In that verse, “Cihacihābhinadite” refers to the sound produced by the loud crying of birds named “cihaciha” because they frequently make the sound “cihaciha”. In the phrases such as “sippikābhirutēhi”, deities are called “sippikā”. Or it refers to young animals (such as squirrels) with faces withered by hunger or afflicted by disease, or to large grasshoppers ...
152:
The elder, being of a firm and steady nature, was not frightened. Knowing “This is Mara,” and wishing to show his lack of respect toward Mara, he recited the verse beginning with “Cihacihābhinadite”.

In that verse, “Cihacihābhinadite” means the sound caused by the loud crying of birds named “cihaciha” because they repeatedly make the sound “cihaciha”. In “sippikābhirutēhi ca”, “sippikā” refers to deities; or it refers to young animals (black squirrels) with withered faces due to disease or hunger. Some teachers say they are large grasshoppers called “Mahākalanda”. It means because of the loud cries of those sippikās. Here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of cause (hetu). “Na me taṃ phandati cittaṃ” means my mind does not tremble, does not waver. The meaning is this: “O evil Mara, just as my mind does not tremble in this forest due to the chirping of birds or the cries of sippikās, so too my mind does not fall away from its meditation subject because of your making terrifying sounds.”

He stated the reason for not trembling with the words “Ekattaniratañhi me”. The word “hi” is in the sense of cause. Because my mind, having abandoned the company of groups, delights in solitude; or, having abandoned external distraction, delights in the one-pointedness of the meditation subject; or, delights in Nibbāna which is of a single nature; therefore, it does not tremble or waver from the meditation subject. It is said that while reciting this verse, the elder developed insight and reached Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

“The Blessed One Sikhī, golden-hued, with a thousand rays, majestic, and of loving-kindness, ascended the walking path.

With a confident and happy mind, having paid homage to the Buddha of supreme knowledge, I raised a Minela flower and offered it to the Buddha.

Thirty-one aeons ago from now, I offered that flower; because of this fruit of offering to the Buddha, I have not known a miserable rebirth.

Twenty-nine aeons ago, I was a Universal Monarch named Sumeghaghana, endowed with the seven treasures and possessed of great power.

My defilements have been burnt away ... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

This very verse was the elder’s declaration of Arahantship (aññā-byākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Ramaṇeyyaka Thera is finished.
153:
## 10. Vimalattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with "Dharaṇī ca siñcati" is that of the Venerable Elder Vimala. What is the origin of this Elder Vimala? He, too, having made aspirations under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome deeds that serve as a powerful support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various existences, was reborn into a family of conch-blowers during the time of Buddha Vipassī. Upon reaching maturity, he became proficient in that craft. One day, having seen Buddha Vipassī and with a mind full of devotion, he performed an offering by blowing the conch. From that day forward, he occasionally offered the sound of the conch to the Buddha.

Due to that meritorious deed, that noble son was reborn in the celestial realm and wandered between the celestial and human realms, performing further merits. During the time of Buddha Kassapa, he made the aspiration, "In the future, may my body be stainless and pure," and he bathed the Bodhi tree with scented water, washed the seating areas in the courtyards of the Cetiya and the Bodhi tree, and washed the soiled requisites of the monks.

After passing away from there and wandering through the celestial and human realms, he was reborn into a wealthy family (ibbhakula) in the city of Rājagaha during the time of this Buddha's appearance. While staying in his mother's womb and at the time of birth, his body was not defiled by bile, phlegm, or other impurities; it was as unstained as a drop of water on a lotus leaf. Because it was as exceptionally pure as that of a Bodhisatta in his final birth, they named him "Vimala" (Stainless). Upon reaching maturity, he saw the power of the Buddha as He entered Rājagaha, gained faith, and ordained. Having taken a meditation subject, he resided in a mountain cave in the Kosala country.

Then one day, a great cloud covering all four continents spread across the entire universe and rained down. It is said that such rain falls only during the lifetimes of Buddhas and Cakkavatti kings. Due to the cooling of the heat and the attainment of suitable weather (utu-sappāya), the Elder's mind became concentrated and one-pointed. With that concentrated mind, he immediately applied himself to insight (vipassanā) and, through the sequence of the Paths, attained Arahatship. This account is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

"In the time of Buddha Vipassī, I was a conch-blower. I was constantly devoted to serving the Sugata, the Great Sage."

"Behold the fruit of serving the Lord of the World, the Such-like One. Sixty thousand musical instruments always surround me."
155:
## 6. The Sixth Group (Chaṭṭhavagga)
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of the Four Elders Beginning with Godhika Thera

The four verses beginning with "Vassati devo" are the verses of these four elders: Godhika Thera, Subāhu Thera, Valliya Thera, and Uttiya Thera. What is their origin? These elders had also performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit in various existences. Ninety-four aeons ago, during the time of Siddhattha Buddha, they were born into noble families and, upon reaching maturity, became friends and traveled together. Among them, one saw Siddhattha Buddha wandering for alms and offered a spoonful of alms-food. The second, with a devoted heart, paid homage with the fivefold prostration and raised his hands in salutation. The third, with a devoted heart, offered a handful of flowers to the Buddha. The fourth offered jasmine flowers.

Thus, having clarified their minds toward the Buddha, they were reborn in the celestial realm due to that meritorious deed. Again and again, they performed merits and wandered through the realms of gods and humans. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, they were born into noble families, became friends, ordained in the Dispensation, and practiced the Dhamma of a recluse. In the time of our Buddha, they were born in the city of Pāvā as the sons of four Malla kings. They were named Godhika, Subāhu, Valliya, and Uttiya. They were dear friends to one another.

They went to the city of Kapilavatthu on some business. At that time, the Buddha had gone to Kapilavatthu and was staying at the Nigrodhārāma monastery. After demonstrating the Twin Miracle of water and fire, he disciplined the Sakyan kings, headed by King Suddhodana. Then, those four Malla princes also saw the miracle, gained faith, and ordained. While practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), they soon attained Arahatship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). This is stated in the Apadāna:

"(I saw) the Buddha, who is golden-hued, worthy of receiving offerings, who has made the noble renunciation, and who has reached Nibbāna, free from the forest of defilements.

I offered a spoonful of alms-food to Siddhattha, the Great Sage, who is calmed by wisdom, a Great Hero, and possessed of the quality of steadfastness (tādi).

As he walked step by step, bringing peace to the multitude, a great joy arose in me toward the Buddha, the kinsman of the Sun."
156:
"Ninety-four aeons ago, I gave that gift; because of that offering of alms-food, I have never known a woeful state.

Eighty-seven aeons ago, there were seven individuals named Mahāreṇu, endowed with the seven treasures, who became Universal Monarchs of great power.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled."

## Godhika Thera.

"(I saw) the Buddha, who is golden-hued, like a noble bull, like a great tusker in rut in three places, like a king elephant, the Great Sage who seeks the great aggregates of virtue and so on.

I saw the Buddha, the Chief of the World, who illuminates all directions like the full moon, as he was walking upon the road.

Having clarified my mind toward his knowledge, I raised my hands in salutation; with a devoted and joyful heart, I paid homage to Siddhattha Buddha.

Ninety-four aeons ago, I performed that deed; because of the merit of that perception of his knowledge, I have never known a woeful state.

Seventy-three aeons ago, there were sixteen Universal Monarchs, the best of men, endowed with the seven treasures and great power.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled."

## Subāhu Thera.

"I was once a florist living in the city of Tivara; then I saw Siddhattha Buddha, free from the dust of defilements, honored by the world.

With a devoted and joyful heart, I offered a handful of flowers; by the power of that deed, in whatever realm I am born,

I enjoy the desired fruits of my own previous good deeds; I am surrounded by beautiful flowers—this is the fruit of offering flowers.

Ninety-four aeons ago, I offered those flowers; because of that offering of flowers, I have never known a woeful state."
157:
Starting from ninety-four aeons ago, excluding the current existence, there were five hundred kings named Najjasama within those ninety-four aeons.

My defilements are burnt... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

## Elder Valliya

I once offered jasmine flowers to the Blessed One Siddhattha; with a joyful heart, I scattered and honored his feet with seven jasmine flowers.

Through that meritorious deed, I now surpass gods and humans; I bear my final body in the teaching of the Fully Enlightened One.

Ninety-four aeons ago, I offered those flowers; because of that offering, I have never known a miserable rebirth.

Five aeons ago, there were thirteen universal monarchs named Samantagandha, rulers of the four continents.

My defilements are burnt... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

## Elder Uttiya

Upon attaining Arahantship, these four elders became famous and well-known in the world. Honored and respected by kings and great ministers, they lived together in the forest. Once, when these four elders arrived at Rājagaha, King Bimbisāra approached and paid homage to them. He invited them to spend the three-month rains retreat and had individual small huts built for them. However, out of forgetfulness, he did not have them roofed. The elders lived in the unroofed huts. During the rainy season, it did not rain. The King, wondering "What is the reason it does not rain?", realized the cause. He had the huts roofed, plastered with clay, and decorated with paintings. While performing the dedication ceremony for the huts, he offered alms to a large community of monks. Out of compassion for the King, the elders entered their huts and attained the meditative state of loving-kindness (metta-samāpatti). Then, a great cloud rose from the northeast and, through the power of the elders' meditative attainment, prepared to rain.
158:
At the very moment the elders emerged from their meditative attainment, the rain began to fall. Among them, Elder Godhika, having emerged from meditation, spoke this verse along with the sound of thunder—

“The sky-god rains like a beautiful song; my little hut is roofed, pleasant, and sheltered from the wind. My mind is also well-concentrated. Therefore, O sky-god, rain if you wish!”

In that verse, ‘vassati’ means it pours down, it gives a stream of rain. ‘Devo’ refers to the rain cloud. ‘Yathā sugītaṃ’ means thundering like a beautiful song. Indeed, when it rains, the cloud is magnificent, rising with hundreds and thousands of layers, thundering and emitting lightning; it is not merely beautiful. Therefore, it is shown that it rains with a smooth, sweet, and deep sound. Referring to not being disturbed by that sound of rain, he said: “My little hut is roofed, pleasant, and sheltered from the wind.” Just as if it were not raining, this hut of mine, roofed with grass and such, is not disturbed by that downpour. It is called ‘sukhā’ (pleasant) because of the presence of the comfort of use and the comfort of suitable weather. It is ‘sheltered from the wind’ (nivātā) because the windows are closed with tight bolts, thus free from the danger of wind. He spoke of not being disturbed by these two kinds of suitable dwellings. ‘Cittaṃ susamāhitañca mayhaṃ’ means my mind is also well-fixed and well-concentrated on the object of Nibbāna through the unsurpassed concentration. By this, he shows his state of being free from anxiety due to the absence of internal dangers. ‘Atha ce patthayasi’ means if you now desire, if you wish. ‘Pavassa’ means pour down, let the water flow, give a stream of rain. ‘Devā’ is an address to the rain cloud.

## The Commentary on the Verse of Elder Godhika is Finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Verse of Elder Subāhu

Among the verses spoken by the other elders, there is a difference only in the third line. In the verse spoken by Subāhu, ‘cittaṃ susamāhitañca kāye’ means my mind is well-concentrated and well-fixed on the physical body through the power of mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati). This elder, having made the jhāna obtained through the power of mindfulness directed to the body...
160:
(All those events) occurred. All these matters should be understood according to the method stated in the commentaries on the Ratana Sutta in the Khuddakapāṭha and Suttanipāta. Specifically, when the Blessed One entered the city of Vesālī and the three dangers were appeased, many devas and humans realized the Four Noble Truths through the Buddha's Dhamma teaching. Seeing the Buddha's power, this prince gained faith and went forth. Just as this prince went forth, so did the four persons to be mentioned hereafter. They were Licchavi princes who were friends of this prince and went forth in the same manner. In the time of Kassapa Buddha, they were also friends and went forth together with this prince to practice the Dhamma of a recluse. At the feet of Padumuttara Buddha, they also planted the seeds of merit and so forth.

Among them, this Elder Anjanavaniya, having performed his preliminary duties, was staying in the cemetery area of Anjanavana in the city of Sāketa. As the time for the rains retreat approached, he found an old, decayed long-legged chair (āsandī) discarded by people. He placed it on four flat stones, covered the top and sides with grass and so on, attached a door, and entered the rains retreat. In the very first month, through diligent effort and striving, he attained Arahatship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“At that time, I was a florist named Sudassana. I saw the Buddha, free from the dust of defilements, the Foremost of the World, the Bull among Men.

Taking jasmine flowers, I worshipped Padumuttara Buddha. Being one of pure vision and joyful heart, I attained the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu).

Due to that offering of flowers and the resolution of my mind, I did not go to a miserable rebirth for a hundred thousand aeons.

Sixteen times I was a king named Devuttara; and thirty-six aeons ago, I was a Great Wheel-turning Monarch of great power.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.”

Having reached Arahatship and experiencing the bliss of liberation, upon emerging from meditative attainment, he reflected on his attainment. With a surge of joy, wishing to utter an inspired utterance, he spoke the verse beginning with “Āsandim kuṭikam katvā.”

In that verse, “Āsandim kuṭikam katvā” means: An āsandī is a long-legged square stool. There are also long rectangular ones. On such a stool, one can only sit, not (lie down).
161:
Having made a small hut from that long-legged chair for the purpose of sleeping and living, according to the method mentioned above, so that one sitting there could comfortably practice the Dhamma of a recluse without the danger of the elements—thus he made the hut. By this, he showed his supreme fewness of wishes and contentment regarding lodgings. This was also said by the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta:

“Rain falls on the knees
Of one sitting in the cross-legged position;
For a monk of resolute mind,
Even this much is enough for living in comfort.”

Other teachers, however, stating the reading “āsandikuṭikaṃ,” interpret it as “having made a hut the size of a long-legged chair.” Still others say, “An āsandī is a small house built above a couch for people who sit and so forth; having made a hut from that āsandī.” “Oggayha” means having entered or having gone into. “Anjanavana” is a forest of this name; because there are flowers with the color of collyrium (añjana), the creepers are called añjana. Due to the abundance of those creepers, the forest received the name “Anjanavana.” Other teachers say, “Añjana refers to large bushes.” The construction is: “I, who lived having entered that Anjanavana and having made a hut the size of a long-legged chair, have reached the three knowledges (tevijjā) and carried out the Buddha's teaching.” This itself was the Elder's declaration of final knowledge (aññā-byākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Anjanavaniya is Finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kutivihāri

“Ko kuṭikāyaṃ” and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Elder Kutivihāri. What is the background story? It is said that while the Blessed One Padumuttara was traveling through the air, he thought, “I will give an offering,” and taking cool water, with a heart full of joy and happiness, he looked upward and offered it by lifting it up. The Teacher, knowing his intention and to increase his faith, accepted it while remaining in the sky. He experienced great joy and happiness because of that offering. The rest is similar to what was said in the story of the Elder Anjanavaniya. The difference is this: Having gone forth in the manner mentioned and having performed his preliminary duties for meditation, while he was practicing insight (vipassanā), he was walking near a field in the evening. When it began to drizzle, he saw a grass hut, which was the small house of a field-watcher, and entered it. There, on a spread of grass...
162:
That Elder sat down. Just as he sat down, having obtained a suitable climate, he applied himself to insight (vipassanā) and attained Arahantship. In this regard, it is said in the Apadāna:

“I saw the Buddha, golden-hued, traveling through the air, shining like a blazing fire, like a kindled flame. Taking water in my hands, I threw it up into the sky as an offering. The Great Hero, the Compassionate Sage, the Buddha, accepted it. Standing in the air, the Teacher named Padumuttara, knowing my intention, spoke these verses: ‘By this gift of water and by the arising of joy, for a hundred thousand aeons, he shall not go to a state of misery.’ O Lord of bipeds, Foremost in the world, Bull among men, because of that meritorious deed, having abandoned victory and defeat, I have reached the unshakable state (Nibbāna). For sixty-five hundred aeons, I was a Cakkavatti king named Sahassarāja, a ruler of the four continents. My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.”

While the Elder was sitting in that hut after attaining Arahantship, a field-watcher came and asked, “Who is in the hut?” Hearing those words, the Elder said, “A monk is in the hut,” and so on. Combining the words of the field-watcher and the Elder:

“Who is in the hut? A monk is in the hut, free from lust, with a well-concentrated mind. Know this thus, friend; the hut you built is not in vain.”

It was thus included in the Recitation (Saṅgīti). In that verse, “Who is in the hut?” is the field-watcher's question, “Who is sitting in this hut?” “A monk is in the hut” is the Elder's reply to the field-watcher. Then, to show his state as an unsurpassed field of merit and to establish the donor in that noble merit through the use of the hut, he said “free from lust” (vītarāgo), and so on.
163:
To make the donor rejoice and to establish him in that noble merit, he spoke the words beginning with “Vītarāgo.” The meaning of that verse is: A monk who has destroyed defilements sits in your grass hut. Because of that, he is “free from lust” (vītarāgo) as lust has been completely cut off by the Path of Arahantship. He is “one with a well-concentrated mind” (susamāhitacitto) because his mind is perfectly steady, having Nibbāna as its object through unsurpassed concentration. Friend field-watcher, know this meaning as I say it; believe and be convinced. This grass hut built and offered by you is not in vain, not fruitless; it is beneficial and productive of results. Why? Because it is used by an Arahant, one who is worthy of offerings and whose taints are exhausted. If you rejoice, that rejoicing will be for your welfare and happiness for a long time.

Hearing those words, the field-watcher stood there rejoicing with a confident heart, thinking, “It is a gain for me, it is a great gain for me, that such a noble one has entered and sat in my grass hut.” The Blessed One heard this conversation with his divine ear (dibba-sota) and, knowing the donor's joy, wishing to reveal his future prosperity, addressed the field-watcher with these verses:

“A monk with a peaceful mind, free from taints, dwells in the hut. By the result of that action, you will become the Lord of Devas.

Thirty-six times you will be the Lord of Devas, ruling the kingdom of gods. Thirty-four times you will be a Cakkavatti king in the land. In your final life, you will be a Paccekabuddha named Ratanakuṭi, free from lust.”

Because he attained the special distinction in the grass hut, from that day on, the Elder became known as “Kuṭivihārī” (Hut-dweller). This verse was also the Elder's declaration of Arahantship (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verse of Kuṭivihārī Thera is Finished.
164:
## 7. Commentary on the Verses of the Second Elder Kuṭivihārī

"Ayamāhu purāṇiyā" and so forth—this verse belongs to the Venerable Kuṭivihārī. What is the account of its origin? It is said that, with a heart full of faith in the Blessed One Padumuttara, he offered a fan made of reeds and bamboo during a time of intense heat. The Teacher gladdened him with a verse of appreciation. The rest of what should be said here is just as stated in the story of the Elder Añjanavaniya.

However, this is the distinction: It is said that after ordaining in the manner described, while living in a certain old hut, he did not contemplate the recluse's Dhamma but gave rise to a thought of construction, thinking, "This small hut is dilapidated; it is proper to build another new hut." A deity, desiring his welfare, spoke this verse of clear light and profound meaning, beginning with "Ayamāhu," in order to arouse spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in him.

In that verse, the word "ayaṃ" is a term indicating what is near and present. "Āhu" means "was" (ahosi). It is spoken with a long vowel for the sake of metrical ease. "Purāṇiyā" means ancient, long-passed (dilapidated). "Aññaṃ patthayase navaṃ kuṭiṃ" means that because this hut is old and dilapidated, you now long for, desire, and wish for another new hut to be brought into existence. Relinquish all longing for a hut entirely. Just as with the old hut, relinquish longing, craving, and expectation for a new hut as well; be entirely detached in mind regarding it.

Why? Because, bhikkhu, a so-called new hut to be brought into existence again is painful because it brings suffering. Therefore, without giving rise to another new suffering, remain in this very old hut as it has arisen and perform the duty of a recluse that you ought to do.

This is the intention here: Bhikkhu, you wish to build another new grass hut, thinking, "This old grass hut is dilapidated," but you do not wish to practice the recluse's Dhamma. By wishing thus and not devoting yourself to meditation, you do not transcend the arising of renewed existence, and thus you are one who truly wishes to build and longs for the hut of a future physical existence (attabhāva). That hut of physical existence is not only painful due to the hardship of its construction, like a new grass hut, but even more so because it is intertwined with the sufferings of aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, and so on. Therefore, just as with the grass hut, relinquish longing and expectation for the hut of physical existence; be entirely detached in mind regarding that physical existence. In this way, the suffering of the round of rebirths will not occur for you.

Upon hearing the deity's words, the Elder was struck with spiritual urgency. Establishing insight (vipassanā) and striving with effort, he soon attained Arahatship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna:

To the Blessed One Padumuttara, who sat on a grass mat,
Who was peaceful and poised,
I took reed-flowers, made a fan, and honored him.
