I offered it to the Buddha, the Best of Men, the Poised One.
The All-Knowing One, the Leader of the World, accepted the fan,
And knowing my intention, he spoke this verse:
"Just as my body is cooled and no fever exists,
Even so, may your mind be liberated from the three fires."
165:
The Blessed One Padumuttara, the Eldest in the world, the Poised One, who was peaceful and poised, was sitting on a grass mat—

I took reed-flowers, made a fan, and offered it to the Buddha, the Lord of bipeds, the Poised One.

The All-Knowing One, the Leader of the World, accepted the fan, and knowing my intention, he spoke this verse—

“Just as my body is cooled and no fever exists, even so, may your mind be liberated from the three fires.”

All the deities who resided in the forest gathered, saying, “We shall hear the Buddha's words and the speech that gladdens the donor.”

The Blessed One, sitting there surrounded by the assembly of deities, spoke these verses to gladden the donor—

“Because of this gift of a fan and the aspiration of his mind, he will become a Universal Monarch named Subbata.

Driven by the remainder of that merit and that root of wholesome deeds, he will become a Universal Monarch named Māluta.

Because of this gift of a fan and this extensive honor, he will not go to a state of misery for a hundred thousand aeons.

Thirty-eight times he was a Universal Monarch named Subbata thirty thousand aeons ago. Eight times he was a Universal Monarch named Māluta twenty-nine thousand aeons ago.

My defilements are burnt... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.”

When he attained Arahatship, he reflected, “This verse was like a goad for my attainment of Arahatship,” and he recited that very verse. That itself became the Elder's verse declaring his final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa). And because he attained distinction through the instruction regarding the hut (kuṭi), he became known by the name Kuṭivihārī.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Second Elder Kuṭivihārī is finished.
166:
## 8. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ramaṇīyakuṭika

"Ramaṇīyā me kuṭikā" and so forth—this verse belongs to the Venerable Ramaṇīyakuṭika. What is the background (uppatti) of this Elder? He too, having planted the seeds of merit during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, was reborn into a noble family during the time of the Buddha Atthadassī, one thousand eight hundred (1,800) aeons ago. When he reached the age of discretion, he offered a seat worthy of a Buddha to the Blessed One. He also worshipped the Blessed One with flowers, paid homage with the five-point prostration, circumambulated him, and departed.

The rest of the story is just as stated in the account of the Elder Añjanavaniya. This, however, is the distinction: This Elder, having ordained in the manner described and having performed the preliminary duties, dwelt in a small village hut (kuṭi) in the Vajjī country. That hut was extremely beautiful, lovely to behold, and pleasing; its walls and floors were well-prepared and decorated; it was endowed with the delightfulness of gardens, ponds, and so forth; and the ground was strewn with sand resembling a net of pearls. Due to the Elder's perfection in his duties, such as having a well-swept courtyard, it remained exceedingly more delightful. Dwelling there, he developed insight (vipassanā) and before long was established in Arahantship.

Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"Having entered the quiet and undisturbed forest,
I offered a lion-throne (sīhāsana) to the Buddha Atthadassī, the Such-like One.

Taking a handful of flowers and circumambulating him,
I attended upon the Teacher and departed facing the north.

O Leader of the World, Best of Men, Lord of bipeds,
By that meritorious deed, I have quenched myself; all existences have been uprooted.

One thousand eight hundred (1,800) aeons ago, because of the gift I gave then,
I have known no miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of offering a lion-throne.

Seven hundred (700) aeons ago, I was a powerful Wheel-turning King (Cakkavatti),
Named Sannibbāpaka, endowed with the seven treasures.

My defilements have been burned away... [pe] ... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Having reached Arahantship, while the Elder was dwelling there, people who wished to see the monastery came from various places because of the delightfulness of the hut, and the hut...
167:
...they saw. Then one day, some women of a mischievous nature (dhutta-jātika) went there and, seeing the delightfulness of the small hut, thought: "We should be able to captivate the heart of this ascetic who lives here." Then they said, "Venerable, your dwelling place is delightful; we too are of delightful form and are in the prime of our youth," and they began to display feminine wiles and so forth. The Elder, manifesting his state of being free from passion, spoke the verse: "Delightful is my hut, a gift of faith, heart-pleasing..."

In that verse, "Ramaṇīyā me kuṭikā" means: "Venerable, your hut is delightful"—what you have said is true. This small dwelling hut of mine is of a pleasing form and is delightful. Furthermore, it is a "gift of faith" (saddhādeyya). It is called a gift of faith because it was given with faith and a desire for the Dhamma, believing in the fruit of kamma: "By making such a pleasing hut and giving it to those who have ordained, such-and-such a fruit will arise." It was not produced by mere wealth. And because it pleases the minds of those who see and use such gifts of faith, it is called "heart-pleasing" (manoramā). Indeed, it is heart-pleasing precisely because it is a gift of faith. Donors prepare the gift with respect through faith and so forth; and noble ones who use the gift of faith are endowed with the effort and intention that the donor's benefit is not lost. It means they are not lacking in effort and intention in the way you have imagined.

"Na me attho kumārīhi" means: Since my mind is entirely turned away from sensual pleasures, I have no need for young women. For even for the sake of performing allowable services (kappiya-kāraka), there is no need for women for someone like me, let alone for the sake of passion; therefore, he said, "I have no need for young women." Here, the word "young women" (kumārī) should be understood as a representative term (upalakkhaṇa). Showing that "In the presence of one like me, do not act thus," and that this behavior, which is improper and flawed by fault, would only be beautiful in front of those who share your own desires, he said: "O women, go to those who have need of you."

In that verse, "Yesaṃ" refers to those who are not yet free from passion for sensual pleasures. "Attho" means having a need or purpose. "Tahiṃ" means to them, to their presence. "Nāriyo" is an address. Hearing this, the women became crestfallen and, with their heads hanging down, returned by the same path they had come. In this context, by the Elder's statement of having no need for sensual pleasures through the words "I have no need for young women," it should be understood that he declared his Arahantship.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ramaṇīyakuṭika is finished.

"Saddhāyāhaṃ pabbajito" and so forth—this verse belongs to the Venerable Kosalavihāri. This Elder Kosalavihāri also planted the seeds of merit during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara and performed various meritorious deeds. The rest of the background is just the same as the story of the Elder Añjanavaniya. Specifically, this Elder Kosalavihāri, having ordained and performed the preliminary duties, dwelt in a forest in the Kosala country, depending on a donor's house. That donor, seeing the Elder living at the foot of a tree, built and offered a monastery. The Elder, dwelling in that monastery, attained concentration through the suitability of the dwelling and, by developing insight, reached Arahantship before long. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna: "In a leaf-roofed hut not far from the Himalayas, I dwelt; then I..."
168:
## 9. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kosalavihārī

"Saddhāyāhaṃ pabbajito" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Elder Kosalavihārī. How did it arise? This elder also planted the seeds of merit during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara and performed various meritorious deeds. The rest of the story is just like that of Elder Añjanavaniya.

This, however, is the distinction: This Elder Kosalavihārī, having gone forth in the manner mentioned and having performed the preliminary duties, lived in a forest near a village in the Kosala country, depending on a family of lay devotees. That lay devotee, seeing the elder living at the foot of a tree, built and offered a small hut. While living in that small hut, the elder gained concentration through the suitability of the dwelling, and while striving in insight meditation (vipassanā), he soon attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"Not far from the Himavanta, I lived in a leaf-thatched hut. At that time, I was possessed by greed for food and was habituated to sleep.

Digging up tubers such as ālu and kalamba, and biḷāli and takkala, and bringing fruits like kola, bhallātaka, and billa, I prepared them.

The Buddha Padumuttara, the Knower of the Worlds, the Recipient of Offerings, knowing my thought, came into my presence.

To the Great Hero who had approached, the God of gods, the Bull among men, I held up the biḷāli tuber and poured it into his bowl.

The Great Hero consumed it, then pleasing me. Having consumed it, the All-Knowing One spoke this verse:

'Having gladdened your own mind, you have given me the biḷāli tuber. For a hundred thousand aeons, you shall not go to a woeful state.'

This is my final existence; all births have been uprooted. I bear my last body in the Teaching of the Fully Enlightened One.

In the fifty-fourth aeon from this Bhadda-kappa, I was a powerful Universal Monarch named Sumekhaliya, endowed with the seven treasures.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's Teaching has been fulfilled."

Having reached Arahantship and experiencing the bliss of liberation, wishing to utter an exclamation of joy with the surge of rapture that had arisen, he recited the verse beginning with "Saddhāyāhaṃ pabbajito". In that verse, the meaning of the word "Saddhāyā" should be understood in the way it is explained. When the Buddha arrived at the city of Vesālī, seeing the Buddha's physical form, faith arose: "This Teaching is certainly the way out of the cycle of rebirth. Therefore, through this noble practice, I shall surely be liberated from aging and death." By the power of that faith, he attained monkhood. For me, who was accustomed to living in the forest, a small hut was built and offered; the person who had become a monk lived in seclusion in another forest dwelling.
169:
Having attained Arahantship and experiencing the bliss of liberation, wishing to utter an exclamation of joy with the surge of rapture that had arisen, he spoke the verse: "I went forth out of faith."

In that verse, "Saddhāyā" means that upon seeing the power and majesty of the Blessed One when he arrived at Vesālī, faith arose: "This Teaching is definitely the way out of the cycle of rebirth; therefore, by this practice, I shall surely be liberated from aging and death." By the power of that faith, he went forth and attained ordination. "A hut was built for me in the forest" means that a small hut was made for me as I lived in the forest in accordance with monkhood, showing that I live in seclusion as a forest-dweller fitting for a monk. Therefore, he said: "Being diligent and ardent, clearly comprehending and mindful."

This means that by the physical seclusion obtained through forest-dwelling, he applied himself to wakefulness, living diligently without losing mindfulness in that dwelling, being ardent because of his exerted energy, and having increased insight through the fulfillment of preliminary mindfulness and clear comprehension, he attained Arahantship. Thus, reaching the abundance of wisdom and mindfulness, he lives with clear comprehension and mindfulness. The praise of being diligent and so forth was indeed this elder's declaration of Arahantship (aññābyākaraṇa). Because he lived for a long time in the Kosala country, he became known by the name "Kosalavihārီ".

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kosalavihārī is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sīvali

"Those intentions of mine have been fulfilled" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sīvali. What is the background story? This elder also, during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, went to the monastery as mentioned above and, standing at the edge of the assembly while listening to the Dhamma, saw the Teacher appointing a certain monk to the foremost position (etadagga) among those of great gains. Thinking, "It would be good if I too could become such a person in the future," he invited the Ten-Powered One and for seven days gave a great offering (mahādāna) to the Sangha headed by the Buddha. Then he made an aspiration: "Blessed One, by this special meritorious deed, I do not wish for any other prosperity. In the future, in the Teaching of a Buddha, may I also be the foremost among those of great gains, just like the monk whom You have now placed in that foremost position." The Teacher, seeing that there would be no obstacles, prophesied: "This aspiration of yours will be fulfilled in the future in the presence of the Buddha Gotama," and then departed.
170:
That young man of good family, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of devas and humans, was reborn in a small village not far from the city of Bandhumatī during the time of the Buddha Vipassī. At that time, the citizens of Bandhumatī, after consulting with the King, were offering alms to the Buddha Vipassī. One day, while they were all together giving alms, they searched for what might be missing from their offering and found neither honey nor molasses-curd. Thinking, "We shall bring it from somewhere," they stationed men on the road leading from the countryside into the city.

At that time, that young man of good family took a jar of curd from his village and went towards the city, thinking, "I will bring something." While looking for a suitable place, thinking, "I will enter the city after washing my face, hands, and feet," he saw a honeycomb the size of a plow-head, free of flies. Thinking, "This has appeared due to my merit," he took it and entered the city. The man stationed by the citizens saw him and asked, "O man, for whom are you bringing this honey and curd?" He replied, "Sir, I am not bringing it for anyone; I have brought it to sell." The man said, "O man, if that is so, take this kahāpaṇa and give me that honey and molasses-curd."

The young man thought, "This honey and curd are not worth much, yet this man is offering a large price at once; it is worth investigating." Then he told the citizen, "I cannot sell it for one kahāpaṇa." When told, "If so, take two and give it," he said, "I cannot give it for two either." In this manner, he increased the price until it reached one thousand kahāpaṇas.

He thought, "It is not proper to increase it further. Let it be so, but first I will ask what he intends to do with it." Then he asked him, "Why do you buy this for such a high price when this molasses-curd is not worth much?" The man replied, "O man, the citizens here are competing with the King to give alms to the Buddha Vipassī, and they are searching because they do not have these two items, honey and curd, in their offering. If they do not get these two, the citizens will be defeated. Therefore, I am buying them for a thousand kahāpaṇas." He asked, "Is it only the citizens who have the right to offer this molasses-curd? Is it not proper for others to offer it?" The man replied, "There is no restriction on anyone offering it." He asked, "Is there anyone in the citizens' offering who gives an item worth a thousand kahāpaṇas in a single day?" They replied, "Friend, there is no such person." He asked, "Do you know that these two items are worth a thousand kahāpaṇas?" He said, "Yes, I know."

"If so, go and tell the citizens: 'A man does not wish to sell these two items for a price; he wishes to offer them with his own hands. Do not worry about these two things.' You shall be the witness of my seniority in this offering." He instructed thus. That countryman bought five pungent spices with the money he had brought for travel expenses, ground them into powder, mixed them with a little salt, squeezed the honeycomb into the curd, wrapped it well in a lotus leaf, and went to sit near the Buddha. Watching the people performing acts of veneration and waiting for his opportunity to make an offering, when the opportunity arose, he approached the Buddha Vipassī and said, "Venerable Sir, please accept this gift."
171:
(Tell the citizens,) "Do not be anxious about these things." (He said,) "You shall be the witness of my being the chief in this offering." That man bought five kinds of pungent spices with the money he had brought for travel, made them into powder, squeezed the honeycomb into the curd, mixed it with the pungent powders, placed it in a lotus leaf, prepared it well, and sat in a place not far from the Buddha. While waiting for his turn near the offerings brought by the multitude, and knowing the opportunity was right, he approached the Buddha and said, "Venerable Sir, this is a gift from a poor man that has arisen; please accept this gift out of compassion for me." The Buddha, out of compassion for him, accepted the gift in a stone bowl offered by the Four Great Kings and resolved that it would not be exhausted even when given to six million eight hundred thousand monks. That young man of good family, having paid homage to the Buddha who had finished his meal, stood at a respectful distance and said, "Venerable Sir, today I have seen the offerings brought to you by the citizens of Bandhumatī. By the result of this deed, may I reach the pinnacle of gain, fame, and retinue in every life I am reborn." (A. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.1.207). The Buddha said, "Young man, may it be so," and after performing the thanksgiving for the meal to him and the citizens, he departed.

That young man of good family, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of devas and humans, was reborn in the womb of Princess Suppavāsā during the time of our Buddha. From the time of his conception, hundreds of gifts were brought to Princess Suppavāsā in carts every evening and morning. Then, wishing to test his merit, they had her touch a basket of seeds with her hand. From each single seed, hundreds and thousands of stalks of rice grew. From a single field of one karīsa, about fifty or sixty cartloads of grain were produced. Even when filling the granaries, they had her touch the door of the granary with her hand. Due to the merit of the princess, the places from which grain was taken were filled again. Even from a bowl full of rice, when giving to anyone while saying, "This is the merit of the princess," the rice was not exhausted as long as they did not rise from their seats. While the child was in his mother's womb, seven years passed.
172:
When the pregnancy reached full term, (Princess Suppavāsā) experienced great suffering for seven days. She called her husband and said, "Before I die, while I am still alive, let me give an offering," and sent him to the Buddha. She instructed him, "Go, report this matter to the Blessed One and invite Him. Whatever the Blessed One says, remember it well and come back to tell me."

That prince went and reported the princess's message to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "May Suppavāsā, the daughter of the Koliyans, be happy, free from disease, and give birth to a healthy son."

Having heard these words, the prince paid homage to the Blessed One and set out for his home. Even before the prince arrived, the child came out easily from Suppavāsā's womb, like water flowing from a water-strainer. The people surrounding her, though their eyes were filled with tears, began to smile. Greatly rejoiced and delighted, the people went to report the news to the prince.

As soon as the prince saw them coming, he thought, "I think the words spoken by the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala) have been fulfilled." He arrived and told the princess the words of the Blessed One. The princess said, "The 'life-sustaining meal' (jīvita-bhatta) invited by you will indeed be an 'auspicious meal' (maṅgala-bhatta). Go and invite the Blessed One for seven days." The prince did as she said. For seven days, they provided a great offering to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.

Because the young boy was born while cooling the burning hearts of all his relatives, they named him "Prince Sīvali." Because he had lived in his mother's womb for seven years, he was capable of performing all tasks from the time of his birth. On the seventh day, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, engaged in conversation with the boy. The Blessed One also recited this verse in the Dhammapada:

"He who has crossed over this difficult path, the thorny road of saṃsāra and delusion;
Who has crossed to the other shore, a meditator, free from craving, free from doubt;
Who is cooled, not clinging to anything through grasping—him I call a Brahman."

Then the Elder asked the boy, "After suffering such a mass of misery, is it not proper for you to ordain?" The boy replied, "Venerable Sir, if I receive permission, I would ordain." Princess Suppavāsā, seeing her son talking with the Elder, wondered, "What is my son talking about with the General of the Dhamma?" She approached the Elder and asked, "Venerable Sir, what is my son talking about with you?" The Elder replied, "He is telling me about the suffering of living in the womb that he himself experienced, and says, 'If you give permission, I will ordain.'"
173:
"It is well, Venerable Sir, please ordain him," she requested. The Elder took the boy to the monastery, gave him the meditation on the five parts of the body ending with the skin (taca-pañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna), and while ordaining him, said, "Sīvali, there is no need for other instructions for you; just contemplate the very suffering you experienced for seven years." Sīvali replied, "Venerable Sir, your responsibility is only to ordain me; as for what I must do, I shall know it myself."

At the very moment the first lock of hair was shaved, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). At the moment the second lock was shaved, in the fruit of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmi-phala). At the moment the third lock was shaved, in the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala). The completion of shaving all the hair and the realization of the fruit of Arahantship (Arahatta-phala) occurred simultaneously, without before or after. From the day of Venerable Sīvali's ordination, the four requisites arose in abundance for the Saṅgha of monks as much as they desired. Thus, the story originated in this matter.

Later, the Blessed One went to Sāvatthī. The Elder paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir, I wish to test my merit; please give me five hundred monks." The Blessed One said, "Take them, Sīvali." Taking the five hundred monks and heading towards the Himalayas, he traveled by a forest path. The deity residing in the first banyan tree he saw offered alms for seven days. Thus, he:

"First saw the banyan tree, second the Paṇḍava mountain,
Third the Aciravatī river, fourth the noble ocean.
Fifth he reached the Himalayas, sixth the Chaddanta lake,
Seventh the Gandhamādana mountain, and eighth the presence of Revata."

In all places, they offered alms for seven days each. At the Gandhamādana mountain, a king of deities named Nagadatta offered milk-rice on one of the seven days and ghee-rice on another. The monks asked, "Great Deity, no cows being milked are seen for this king of deities, nor is the churning of curds seen. From where do these arise?" The king of deities replied, "Venerable Sirs, this is the result of offering milk-rice by lottery (salāka-bhatta) during the time of Kassapa Buddha."

Later, the Blessed One, making the welcoming of Khadiravaniya Revata the occasion, placed the Elder in the foremost position (etadagga) among those in His dispensation who are supreme in receiving gains and followers.

Regarding the attainment of Arahantship by this Elder who reached the pinnacle of gains and followers, some teachers say: "As mentioned below, when the General of the Dhamma gave the instruction, he replied, 'I shall know what I must do,' and after ordaining, he took the insight meditation (vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna). On that very day, seeing a secluded small hut, he entered it and repeatedly contemplated the suffering he had experienced for seven years in his mother's womb. By the power of that contemplation, as he looked at the past and future, the three realms of existence appeared to him like a burning house. As his knowledge matured, he entered the path of insight and, at that very moment, through the sequence of the paths, he exhausted all taints (āsava) and reached the fruit of Arahantship." In both ways, the Elder indeed reached the fruit of Arahantship.
174:
Later, the Blessed One, based on the occasion of the welcoming by the Elder Khadiravaniya Revata, placed the Elder Sīvali in the foremost position among those who are pre-eminent in receiving gains and followers in his Dispensation. Regarding the attainment of Arahantship by this Elder who reached the pinnacle of gains and followers, some teachers say this: When instructed by the Elder Sāriputta in the manner mentioned above, he said, "I shall know the task that I can perform," and after ordaining, he took up a subject of meditation for insight (vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna). On that very day, seeing a certain secluded small hut, he entered it and repeatedly reflected on the suffering he had personally endured for seven years in his mother's womb. By the power of reflecting on that suffering, as he contemplated the past and the future, the three realms of existence appeared to him like a house on fire. Because his knowledge had matured, he entered the path of insight, and at that very moment, through the sequence of the Paths, exhausting all cankers (āsavas), he attained Arahantship.

In both ways, only the Elder's attainment of Arahantship is manifested. However, the Elder Sīvali was one who possessed the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and the six higher powers (abhiññā). Therefore, it is stated in the Apadāna:

"At that time, I was a king of devas named Varuṇa, and I possessed chariots, troops, and a retinue.
When the Lord of the World, Atthadassī, the Supreme Man, attained Parinibbāna, I took all kinds of musical instruments and went to the supreme Bodhi tree.
With music and dance, accompanied by cymbals and gongs, I attended upon the supreme Bodhi tree as if I were in the presence of the Buddha himself.
Having attended upon that Bodhi tree, a tree grown from the earth, I sat down cross-legged and passed away right there.
Delighting in my own deed and having confidence in the supreme Bodhi tree, through that clarity of mind, I was reborn in the Nimmānarati realm.
Sixty thousand musical instruments always surround me wherever I am reborn in the worlds of devas and humans, in various states of existence.
The three fires [of lust, hatred, and delusion] are extinguished for me; all existences are uprooted. I bear my final body in the Dispensation of the Fully Enlightened One.
Thirty-four khattiya kings named Subāhu, endowed with the seven treasures, existed five hundred aeons ago from now.
My defilements are burned away... the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled."

Having attained Arahantship and experiencing the bliss of liberation, due to the surge of rapture, he uttered the inspired verses beginning with "My intentions have been fulfilled." In those verses, the meaning of the words "My intentions have been fulfilled; for which purpose I entered the hut; they will reach knowledge and liberation" should be understood as follows: Previously, I had longed for the thoughts of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa) and so forth, which absolutely cut off sensual thoughts (kāma-saṅkappa) and so forth, thinking, "When shall I dwell having attained that state which the Noble Ones now dwell having attained?" Thus, with a mind desiring Arahantship, having intentions aimed at Arahantship, and being repeatedly heedful...
175:
Furthermore, having reached Arahantship and experiencing the bliss of liberation, he uttered the inspired verse beginning with "My intentions have been fulfilled" due to the surge of rapture.

In that verse, the meaning of the words "Te me ijjhiṃsu saṅkappā, yadattho pāvisiṃ kuṭiṃ, vijjāvimuttiṃ pacesanti" should be understood as follows: In the past, I had indeed longed for those thoughts of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa) and so forth, which absolutely cut off sensual thoughts (kāma-saṅkappa) and so forth, thinking, "The Noble Ones now dwell fully endowed with such thoughts of renunciation; when shall I also dwell fully endowed with those thoughts of renunciation and so forth, which are the basis for Arahantship?" Thus, with a mind desiring Arahantship, I had intentions conceived through repeated and unremitting mindfulness directed toward Arahantship. For the purpose of achieving the three knowledges (vijjā) and the fruit of Arahantship, I entered the hut, called a secluded dwelling, to practice insight. All those intentions of mine, who sought the three knowledges and the fruit of Arahantship, have now reached fulfillment. The meaning is that I have become one whose wholesome intentions are accomplished and whose desires are fulfilled. To show the fulfillment of those intentions, he said, "mānānusayamyjjahaṃ" (abandoning the latent tendency of conceit). Because I have abandoned and cut off the latent tendency of conceit, therefore my intentions have been fulfilled—thus the connection should be viewed. Indeed, when the latent tendency of conceit is abandoned, there is no such thing as an unabandoned latent tendency, and Arahantship is already attained. Therefore, the abandonment of the latent tendency of conceit is mentioned as the cause for the fulfillment of the aforementioned intentions.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sīvali is finished.

## The Commentary on the Sixth Chapter is finished.

## 7. The Seventh Chapter

## 1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vappa

The verse beginning with "Passati passo" is the verse of the Venerable Vappa. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in a family home in the city of Haṃsavatī. When he reached the age of discretion, he heard the praise: "Such and such an Elder was the first to receive the Dhamma from the Teacher." He then approached the Blessed One and made an aspiration: "O Blessed One, may I also be one of those who are the first to receive the Dhamma from such a Fully Enlightened One in the future." He also took refuge in the Triple Gem in the presence of the Blessed One Padumuttara. He performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and, after passing away from that life, wandered only through the realms of devas and humans. When our Buddha appeared, he was reborn in the city of Kapilavatthu as the son of a Brahmin named Vāseṭṭha. They gave him the name Vappa. That Vappa, along with the hermit Asita...
176:
He also announced his taking of refuge in the presence of the Teacher. Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, he passed away and wandered only through the realms of gods and humans. During the time of this Buddha's appearance, he was reborn in Kapilavatthu as the son of a Brahmin named Vāseṭṭha, and his name was Vappa. Having been prophesied by the hermit Asita that "Prince Siddhattha will become an Omniscient Buddha," he renounced the household life along with the Brahmin youths led by Koṇḍañña and became an ascetic. Thinking, "When that prince attains omniscience, I shall hear the Dhamma in his presence and reach the Deathless," he attended to the Great Being (Bodhisatta) who was striving for six years in the Uruvelā forest. However, becoming disillusioned when the Bodhisatta partook of solid food, he went to Isipatana. After the Teacher attained Enlightenment and spent the seven weeks, He went to Isipatana and set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion. On the day following the full moon of Āsāḷha (the day of the first sermon), Vappa was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. On the fifth day of the waning fortnight, he attained Arahantship along with the elders led by Aññāsi Koṇḍañña. Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna:

"A battle was imminent between two kings of the devas.
A fierce army was arrayed, and a great roar arose.
The Padumuttara Buddha, the Knower of the World, the Recipient of Offerings, stood in the air and caused the great multitude to be stirred with awe.
All the devas, being delighted, laid down their armor and weapons, and having paid homage to the Buddha, remained with one-pointed minds at that moment.
Knowing my intention, He uttered noble words.
The Compassionate One, the Knower of the World, calmed the great multitude.
If a man with a corrupted mind harms even a single living being, he may fall into a state of misery because of that mental corruption.
Like an elephant on the battlefield, do not harm many living beings.
Calm your own minds; do not harm again and again.
Those armies of the two kings of the devas, being filled with wonder, approached the Buddha, the Foremost in the World, the Renowned One, as their refuge.
Having made the multitude understand, the One with Vision (the Buddha) raised His foot.
While the devas were watching, He departed, facing the north."
177:
"First, I went for refuge to the Buddha (Padumuttara), the Supreme among two-footed beings, who is of such nature. Because of that refuge, for a hundred thousand aeons, I have never been reborn in a state of misery.

Thirty thousand aeons ago, there were sixteen Universal Monarchs named Mahādundubhi.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

After reaching the fruit of Arahantship, reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher's virtues by way of reviewing his own attained supramundane bliss, he thought: "We once addressed such a Teacher with words like 'Bāhulika' (one who lives in abundance). Oh, the state of a worldling indeed causes blindness and lack of the eye of wisdom. Only the state of a Noble One (Ariya) provides the eye of wisdom." Wishing to show this, he spoke the verse beginning with "Passati passo" (The seer sees).

In that verse, "Passati passo" means: One who sees things rightly through Right View (Sammādiṭṭhi) and understands the Dhamma without distortion is called "Passo" (the seer). Such a Noble One, endowed with vision, sees one who has undistorted vision with the eye of wisdom, knowing "This person has undistorted vision," and understands the nature of Dhamma and non-Dhamma as they truly are. Not only does he see the one who sees, but he also sees the one who does not see. A worldling (puthujjana) who lacks the eye of wisdom and does not see the Dhamma as it truly is—the Noble One sees that unseeing worldling with his own eye of wisdom, thinking, "Alas, this person is blind and lacks vision." "Apassati apassantaṃ, passantañca na passati" means: A blind fool (andhabāla) who lacks the eye of wisdom does not see or know another such blind fool, thinking "This person does not see the Dhamma as it truly is." Similarly, he cannot see or know a wise person who sees the Dhamma as it truly is with the eye of wisdom, thinking "This person is of such a nature." Therefore, I too, previously lacking vision, did not see the Blessed One who sees all knowable things as clearly as an emblic myrobalan in the palm of the hand, nor did I see Pūraṇa Kassapa and others as they truly were. But now, being endowed with vision through the power of the Buddha, I see both types of persons as they truly are. Thus, he showed his own undistorted practice regarding what should and should not be associated with.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vappa is finished.
178:
## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vajjiputta

The verse beginning with "Ekakā mayaṃ araññေ" is that of the Venerable Elder Vajjiputta. What is its origin? This Elder had also performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that is a powerful support for liberation from the cycle of rebirths (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various existences. Ninety-one aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was born into a respectable family. Upon reaching the age of discretion, he saw the Blessed One Vipassī one day and, with a heart full of faith, made an offering of ironwood (nāgapuppha) pollen.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha's era, he was born into a minister's family in the city of Vesālī and was named Vajjiputtatissa. When the Blessed One visited Vesālī, he saw the Buddha's power and majesty, gained faith, and ordained. Having performed the preliminary duties, he took a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and resided in a forest grove not far from Vesālī. At that time, a festival was being held in Vesālī. Dancing, singing, and music were taking place everywhere, and the people were joyfully enjoying the festivities. Hearing those sounds, the monk attended to them unwisely (ayoniso manasikāra), abandoned his seclusion, let go of his meditation subject, and, wishing to express his discontent (anabhirati) with the Dispensation, spoke this verse:

"We live alone in the forest, like a piece of wood discarded in the woods.
On such a night as this, who indeed could be more wretched than us?"

Hearing this, a deity residing in that forest grove, wishing to show compassion to the monk, thought: "Monk, although you speak disparagingly of living in the forest, the wise who desire seclusion value it greatly." Wishing to show this meaning, the deity spoke this verse:

"You live alone in the forest, like a piece of wood discarded in the woods.
Many envy you, just as those in hell envy those going to heaven."

Having spoken this verse, the deity admonished him: "Monk, having ordained in the liberating Dispensation of the Fully Enlightened One, why do you harbor unwholesome thoughts that do not lead to liberation?"
179:
The deity caused that monk to feel spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Thus, stirred by that deity like a noble thoroughbred horse struck by a whip, he entered the path of insight (vipassanā). Before long, having applied himself to insight, he attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

'I saw the Fully Enlightened One, golden-hued, radiant like the sun with a thousand rays, illuminating all directions, like the full moon.

Surrounded by his disciples as the earth is by the oceans, I raised ironwood flowers and offered the pollen to the Buddha Vipassī.

In the ninety-one aeons since I offered that pollen, I have not known a bad rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.

Forty-five aeons ago, there was a kshatriya named Reṇu, a Universal Monarch endowed with the seven treasures and great power.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.'

Upon attaining Arahantship, thinking, 'This deity's words became like a goad for my attainment of Arahantship,' he combined his own words and those spoken by the deity and recited this verse:

"We live alone in the forest, like a piece of wood discarded in the woods.
Many envy me, just as those in hell envy those going to heaven."

The meaning of that verse is: Even if we live alone and without companions in this forest, like a piece of wood thrown away in the woods without regard, many noble sons who desire their own welfare envy me so living, thinking, 'Oh, if only we too could abandon the bonds of the household and live in the forest like Elder Vajjiputta!' How so? Just as those in hell envy those going to heaven. For example, beings born in hell due to their own evil deeds envy those who have gone to heaven, thinking, 'Oh, if only we too could abandon the suffering of hell and enjoy the bliss of heaven!' This is how the fulfillment of the meaning should be understood. This is the explanation.

In this verse, because he desired the plural (we) out of self-respect, he said 'Ekakā mayaṃ viharāma' in the plural; however, regarding the singular nature of that meaning, he used the singular 'tassa me' (of me). Both the words 'me' and 'saggagāminaṃ' should be understood in the dative sense (sampadāna) in connection with the word 'pihayanti' (they envy). Because they envy such qualities as living in the forest, I, the commentator, say 'abhipatthenti' (they greatly desire). Alternatively, 'tassa me' means 'they desire the virtues within me.' The commentary on the verse of Elder Vajjiputta is finished.
180:
In this context, because of the desire to use the plural form as a mark of self-respect, although it is said, "We dwell alone," later, referring to the singular nature of that meaning, the singular form "of that me" (tassa me) is used. Both the terms "tassa me" and "saggagāminaṃ" (going to heaven) should be understood as having the sense of the accusative case within the dative construction, in relation to the word "pihayanti" (they envy). It is said with the intention that "they envy" (abhipatthenti) means they are those who long for such qualities as forest-dwelling and so on. Alternatively, "tassa me" means "(they long for) the qualities that exist in me."

## The Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Vajjiputta is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Pakkha

The verse beginning with "Cutā patanti" is that of the Venerable Pakkha. What is its origin? He also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and, while performing merits in various existences, ninety-one aeons ago from this present age, he became a general of the Yakkhas. Having seen the Blessed One Vipassī, with a heart full of devotion, he made an offering of a divine cloth. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this Buddha-era, he was reborn in the royal family of the Sakyans in the market town of Devadaha, and was named "Sammoda Kumāra."

In his youth, due to a wind ailment, his feet could not move. For some time, he moved about like a cripple. Therefore, the name "Pakkha" (the lame) became well-known for him. Later, even when he was free from the disease, people still recognized him by that name. Having seen the miracle performed by the Blessed One at the assembly of his relatives, he gained faith and ordained. Having performed the preliminary duties and taking a subject of meditation, he dwelt in the forest.

Then one day, while going to enter the village for alms, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree along the way. At that time, a certain hawk was flying through the sky carrying a piece of meat. Many other hawks followed it and struck it down. Another hawk picked up the piece of meat that had been dropped. Yet another hawk snatched it away. Seeing this incident, the Elder reflected, "Just as this piece of meat is common to many, full of suffering, and full of distress, so too are sensual pleasures common to many, full of suffering, and full of distress." Thus, contemplating the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefits in renunciation, he initiated insight (vipassanā). While attending to it as "impermanent" (anicca) and so on, he went for alms and,
181:
having finished his meal, he sat in a place for the day-rest, developed insight, and attained Arahatship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"The Blessed One named Vipassī, the Eldest in the world, the Bull among men, then entered the city of Bandhumatī with sixty-eight thousand monks.
Leaving the city and proceeding to the Dīpa Cetiya, I saw the Buddha Vipassī, free from the dust of defilements, worthy of receiving offerings.
Eighty-four thousand Yakkhas attended upon me respectfully, just as the hosts of devas attend upon Sakka.
Leaving my palace then, I raised a cloth, paid homage with my head, and offered that cloth to the Great Sage.
Ah, the Buddha! Ah, the Dhamma! Ah, the perfection of our Teacher! By the power of the Buddha, this earth trembled.
Seeing that wonder, that extraordinary and hair-raising event, I gained devotion in the Buddha, the Lord of bipeds, such as He is.
Having gained devotion and offered the cloth to the Teacher, I, along with my ministers and retinue, went for refuge.
Because of the deed I performed ninety-one aeons ago, I do not know (have not experienced) any miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.
Fifteen aeons ago from now, there were sixteen universal monarchs named Suvāhana, endowed with the seven treasures and great power.
My defilements have been burnt away... the teaching of the Buddha has been carried out."

Upon reaching Arahatship, because he had attained knowledge by making that very object of spiritual urgency (saṃvegavatthu) his goad and developing insight, he spoke the verse beginning with "Cutā patanti" to declare his attainment of Arahatship by way of praising it.

In that verse, "cutā" means fallen away. "Patanti" means they drop down. "Patitā" refers to those who have fallen to the ground by way of passing away, or fallen by way of dropping from the sky. "Giddhā" means towards greed...
182:
...arrived. 'Punāgatā' means they have returned or arrived again. The word 'ca' (and) should be understood as being connected to all the terms. The meaning is this: In this world, hawks fall, and they fall in succession. A piece of meat falls from the beak of another hawk, and that piece of meat falls to the ground; all those hawks, overcome by greed for it, return again. Just like these hawks, beings wandering in Saṃsāra, when they fall away from wholesome Dhamma, fall into hell and so forth. Those who have thus fallen, as well as those who have not yet fallen but remain in a prosperous existence, return again to the suffering called 'this or that existence' through the karma that leads to those existences, because they are not yet liberated from existence, being attached to the sensual realm through the repeated pursuit of sensual pleasures, and to the fine-material and immaterial realms through attachment to existence. Such is the nature of these beings. As for me, I have completed the sixteen-fold task, such as full understanding (pariññā) and so on; now, there is nothing more of that task to be done. Nibbāna, which is delighted in by the Noble Ones and is liberated from all conditioned things, is delightful, exceedingly delightful, and pleasant. It should be understood that one reaches Nibbāna, which is absolute bliss and is attained through the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti-sukha), or one reaches the bliss of fruition and the bliss of Nibbāna, which are attained through the bliss of insight (vipassanā-sukha) and the bliss of the path (magga-sukha), which constitute the pleasant practice (sukhāpaṭipadā).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Pakkha is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vimalakoṇḍañña

The verse beginning with 'Dumavhayāya uppanno' is that of Elder Vimalakoṇḍañña. How did it arise? This Elder also had performed meritorious service under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit, which is a powerful support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth in various existences. Ninety-one aeons ago, during the time of Vipassī Buddha, he was born into a wealthy family. When he reached the age of discretion, one day he saw Vipassī Buddha preaching the Dhamma surrounded by a large assembly, and with a devoted heart, he worshipped with four golden flowers. To increase his devotion, the Blessed One performed a psychic feat such that a golden light pervaded that entire area. Seeing that wonder, his heart became exceedingly devoted; he paid homage to the Blessed One, took that sign as his object, went to his home, and without letting go of the joy (pīti) centered on the Buddha, he passed away from a certain disease and was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Having performed merits repeatedly and wandered through the realms of gods and humans, in this Buddha's era, he took conception in the womb of the courtesan Ambapālī, depending on King Bimbisāra. King Bimbisāra, having heard of Ambapālī's beauty in his youth, developed a strong desire for her. Accompanied by a few men and in disguise, he went to the city of Vesālī and spent a night with that courtesan. At that time, this Elder Vimalakoṇḍañña took conception in her womb. That courtesan also informed the King of her pregnancy. King Bimbisāra, having made himself known and giving a suitable gift, departed. When the pregnancy reached full term, she gave birth to a son...
183:
...depending on King Bimbisāra, he took conception in the womb of Ambapālī. Indeed, King Bimbisāra, having heard of Ambapālī's physical beauty in his youth, felt a strong desire and, with a few attendants in disguise, went to Vesālī and spent a night with her. At that time, this Venerable One took conception in her womb. Ambapālī informed the King of the pregnancy. The King made his identity known, gave a suitable gift, and departed. When the pregnancy matured, Ambapālī gave birth to a son and named him 'Vimala'; later he became known as 'Vimalakoṇḍañña'. When he reached adulthood, he saw the Buddha's power during the Blessed One's visit to Vesālī and, with a devoted heart, he ordained. Having performed the preliminary duties and developing insight, he attained Arahantship before long. For that reason, it is said in the Apadāna:

'The Blessed One named Vipassī, the Foremost in the world, the Bull among men, was seated in the midst of a crowd and preached the state of the Deathless.
Having heard the Dhamma of that Leader of bipeds, the Such-like One, I offered four golden flowers to the Buddha.
At that time, there was a canopy of golden flowers as far as the assembly extended; due to the Buddha's radiance and the golden radiance, there was an extensive light.
With an uplifted and happy mind, filled with awe and with hands joined in reverence, I created joy for them, which brings happiness in the present life.
Having requested leave from the Sambuddha and paid homage to the One of good conduct, and having generated joy, I returned to my own home.
While sitting in my home, I recollected the Buddha, the Best of Beings; with that devotion of heart, I was reborn in Tusita.
In the ninety-first aeon from this one, because of the flowers I offered, I do not know of any rebirth in a woeful state; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
There were sixteen kings named Nemisammata, and forty-three aeons ago from now, there were powerful Universal Monarchs.
My defilements have been burned away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.'
184:
Having attained the fruit of Arahantship, and wishing to declare his attainment by referring to another, he recited the verse beginning with “Dumavhayāya.”

In that verse, “Dumavhayāya” refers to the courtesan Ambapālī, whose name is associated with the mango tree (duma). In this word, the dative case ending is used in the sense of the locative (ādhāra). “Uppanno” refers to one who was born or is being born in the womb of that courtesan. “Jāto Paṇḍaraketunā” means born because of King Bimbisāra, who was well-known as “Paṇḍaraketu” (White Banner) due to his white garments and banners; it means he was born depending on that king. Alternatively, the word “Uppanno” shows the initial conception. Following that, the word “Jāto” shows the birth (jāti). This is because in the world, the term “born (jāta)” is used only from the time of birth.

In this verse, by the words “Dumavhayāya uppanno,” he removes the nature of self-exaltation and shows that many noble sons can also achieve the extraordinary Dhamma. By the words “Jāto Paṇḍaraketunā,” he removes the contempt of others by showing that he has a well-known father. “Ketuhā” means one who has abandoned pride. Pride is called “ketu” (banner) because it has the characteristic of loftiness, similar to a banner. Thus, it is said of that pride, “It has the manifestation of desiring a banner.” “Ketunāyeva” means only by wisdom. Wisdom is called the banner (dhaja) of the Noble Ones because of its supreme loftiness among faultless wholesome states, because it crushes the army of Māra, and because of its nature of being a precursor. Therefore, it was said, “The Dhamma is the banner of the seers.”

“Mahāketuṃ padhaṃsayī” means that because he has a vast range of objects, he is great; and because of the various types of pride such as the pride of superiority and the pride of birth, as well as other defilements, he is like a raised banner; thus the evil Māra is called “Mahāketu.” He has conquered that Māra by destroying his power and transcending his domain, making him harmless (like one without poison). By the words “Mahāketuṃ padhaṃsayī,” wishing to present himself as if he were another, he declared his attainment of Arahantship by referring to another cause.

## The commentary on the verses of Venerable Vimalakoṇḍañña is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Ukkhepakata-vaccha

The verse beginning with “Ukkhepakatavacchassa” is that of the Venerable Ukkhepakata-vaccha. What is its origin (uppatti)? It is said that he, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit that serves as a support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth in various existences, was born into a good family ninety-four aeons ago from this present Bhadda-kappa, during the time of Siddhāttha Buddha. When he reached the age of discretion, wishing to make a great offering to the Teacher but being unable to obtain an umbrella, he made a canopy (umbrella) out of branches at the place where the Buddha resided. Due to that meritorious deed, that noble son was born in the celestial realm and, after performing merit repeatedly and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was born as the son of a Brahmin in Sāvatthī when our Buddha appeared. His name was “Vaccha,” derived from his lineage (gotta). Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher and gaining faith, he ordained. While living in a village dwelling in the Kingdom of Kosala, he learned the Dhamma from the monks who came and went. However, he did not know the divisions such as “This is the Vinaya, this is the Sutta, this is the Abhidhamma.”
185:
A group of people who were building a pavilion (māḷa) dedicated to the Buddha could not find a pillar (thamba). He gave them a pillar and performed the duty of a companion. Due to that meritorious deed, he was born in the celestial realm and, after performing merit repeatedly and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was born as the son of a certain Brahmin in Sāvatthī when our Buddha appeared. The name Vaccha is a name derived from his lineage. Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher and gaining faith, he ordained. While living in a village dwelling in the Kingdom of Kosala, he learned the Dhamma from the monks who came and went. However, he did not know the divisions such as “This is the Vinaya, this is the Sutta, this is the Abhidhamma.” One day, he inquired of Venerable Sāriputta and noted all the divisions of the Piṭaka according to their classifications. Even before the formal Recitation of the Dhamma (Saṅgīti), names such as “Piṭaka” were already established in the Dhamma of learning (pariyatti-saddhamma). Therefore, terms such as “Bearer of the Vinaya” (Vinayadhara) arose among the monks. That monk, while learning the Word of the Buddha known as the Tipitaka and inquiring repeatedly, noted the phenomena of materiality and mentality (rūpa-arūpa) taught in those Piṭakas. Establishing insight (vipassanā) and contemplating them, he attained Arahantship before long. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“In the time of Siddhāttha Buddha, there was a large group of people (performing merit).
They went to the Buddha for refuge and had faith in the Tathāgata.

All of them, having met and consulted together, were building a pavilion for the Teacher.
Being unable to find a single pillar, they searched in the great forest.

Then, seeing that group in the forest, I approached them.
Raising my hands in salutation, I questioned that group.

Those virtuous lay devotees, being questioned by me, replied:
‘We wish to build a pavilion, but a single pillar cannot be found.’

‘Give the task of one pillar to me; I will offer it to the Teacher.
I will bring the pillar; may you all be free from worry.’

Those devotees, with clear and joyful minds, gave the task of the pillar to me.
After giving it, they turned back and went to their own homes.

Not long after the group had left, I brought the pillar at that time.
Being joyful and with a happy heart, I was the first to erect it.”
186:
Because of that clarity of mind, I reached a celestial mansion. My abode is high, rising up with seven stories.

When the large drums are beaten, I always enjoy myself. Fifty-five aeons ago, I was a king named Yasodhara.

Even then, my abode had seven stories, rising high. It was a delightful single-columned palace, complete with gabled chambers.

Twenty-one aeons ago, I was a khattiya named Udena. Even then, my abode had seven stories, rising high.

In whatever birth I arose, whether as a deva or a human, I experienced all happiness. This is the fruit of donating a single pillar.

Ninety-four aeons ago, when the Buddha Siddhattha appeared, I donated a pillar. Since then, I have not known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of donating a single pillar.

My defilements are burnt away... (etc.). The Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

Having reached Arahantship and being established in the state of having done what was to be done, without weariness, out of compassion for the laypeople and monastics who came to him, he investigated the word of the Buddha called the Tipiṭaka and taught the Dhamma. While teaching, one day, wishing to show himself as if he were another, he spoke this verse:

"The Elder Ukkhepakatavaccha, who has sat well with great joy, speaks to laypeople the word of the Buddha that has been gathered and kept in the heart for many years."

In that verse, "Ukkhepakatavaccha" means: the Elder named Vaccha who has "done the lifting" (ukkhepa). This refers to the portions of Vinaya, Sutta, and Abhidhamma learned separately in the presence of a monk, which he placed above the respective Vinaya, Sutta, and Abhidhamma according to their divisions, and by the power of recitation, he inserted them right there. This is the meaning. Here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrument. "Saṅkalitaṃ bahūhi vassehi" means: kept in the heart by way of accumulation over many years. There is also a reading "saṅkhalitaṃ", meaning made like a chain...
187:
...made like a chain, or made to occur by way of being continuous. "The word of the Buddha" (vacanasesa) refers to that Dhamma of scriptures (pariyattidhamma) which he speaks or tells. "Gahatthānaṃ" (to laypeople) is said because they were the majority. "Sunisinno" (well-seated) means sitting firmly and immovably in that Dhamma, not longing for gain or honor, but preaching while established solely at the head of the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, it is said "uḷārapāmojjo" (with great joy), meaning having great joy and delight arisen by way of the happiness of the attainment of the fruit and by way of the Dhamma teaching.

To clearly show this: "Friends, in whatever way a monk teaches the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard it and as he has learned it, in that very way, he gains the inspiration of the meaning, gains the inspiration of the Dhamma, and gains the joy associated with the Dhamma" (DN 3.355), and so on.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Ukkhepakatavaccha is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Meghiya

"The Great Hero has exhorted" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Meghiya. What is its origin? This one also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, planting the seeds of merit in various births. Ninety-one aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was born in a respectable family and reached the age of discretion. At that time, the Blessed One Vipassī, having reached the end of his Buddha-duties, relinquished his life-force. Consequently, when earthquakes and such occurred, the great multitude became terrified. Then the Great King Vessavaṇa explained the matter and reassured them. Hearing this, the great multitude was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Among them, this clansman, hearing of the Buddha's power, felt great respect and reverence for the Teacher and experienced sublime rapture and joy. Due to that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he was born in this Buddha-dispensation into the Sakyan royal family in Kapilavatthu. His name was Meghiya. When he came of age, he ordained in the presence of the Teacher and served the Blessed One. While the Blessed One was staying at Cālikā, he saw a delightful mango grove on the bank of the Kimikālā river, and there...
188:
The Elder Meghiya, wishing to stay (in the mango grove), was twice forbidden by the Blessed One, but on the third time, he was given permission. While staying there, he was harassed by the flies of wrong thoughts (micchāvitakka) and, failing to attain concentration of mind (cittasamādhi), he returned to the Blessed One and reported the matter. Then the Blessed One gave him this advice: "Meghiya, for the immature liberation of mind (cetovimutti), five things lead to its maturity," and so forth (Udāna 31). Established in that advice, the Elder developed insight (vipassanā) and attained Arahatship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"When Vipassī, the Foremost of the World, renounced the life-force (āyusaṅkhāra),
The earth, with the ocean as its girdle, trembled violently.

At the end of the life of the Buddha Vipassī,
My mansion, with its well-arranged crest-ornaments, also trembled.

When the mansion trembled, terror arose in me;
'For what reason has this upheaval occurred?' A great light also appeared.

King Vessavaṇa, having come here, calmed the multitude;
'There is no danger for living beings; be one-pointed and restrained.'

'How wonderful is the Buddha! How wonderful is the Dhamma! How wonderful is the perfection of our Teacher,
At whose birth the earth trembles violently!'

Having praised the power of the Buddha, I rejoiced in heaven for an aeon;
In the remaining aeons, I performed meritorious deeds.

In the ninety-first aeon ago, when I obtained that perception (of the Buddha),
Since then, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of the perception of the Buddha (buddhasaññā).

Fourteen aeons ago, I was a powerful king,
A Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti) of great strength, named Samita.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's bidding has been done."

Having attained Arahatship and receiving advice in the presence of the Blessed One, wishing to declare his attainment of Arahatship, saying, "I have attained Arahatship":
190:
## 7. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Ekadhammasavanīya

The verse beginning with "Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ" is that of the Venerable Elder Ekadhammasavanīya. What is the origin of this verse? It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn as a tree deity. Seeing some monks (three) who had lost their way and were wandering in a great forest, he was moved by compassion, descended from his mansion, comforted them, provided them with food, and guided them to their desired destination. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. When the Blessed One Kassapa appeared in the world, completed the Buddha's work, and attained Parinibbāna, he was a king named Kikī in Bārāṇasī. When that king passed away, his son was King Puthuvinda. His son was named Susāma. His son, named Kikī-Brahmadatta, became king. While he was ruling, the Sasana disappeared, and he had no opportunity to hear the Dhamma. He proclaimed, "Whoever can preach the Dhamma, I shall give him a thousand pieces of gold." However, not finding even a single Dhamma preacher, he thought, "In the time of my ancestors, the Dhamma existed and preachers were easy to find. Now, even one who can preach a single four-line verse is rare. Before the perception of Dhamma vanishes, I shall ordain." He renounced the kingdom and set out for the Himalayas. Sakka, the king of devas, came and preached the Dhamma with the verse "Aniccā vata saṅkhārā..." and caused him to return.

Returning, he performed many meritorious deeds and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha-era, he was born into a wealthy family in the city of Setavya. When he came of age, while the Blessed One was staying in the Siṃsapā forest near Setavya, he approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat at a respectful distance. The Teacher, observing his inclination (ajjhāsaya), preached the Dhamma with this verse: "Aniccā vata saṅkhārā." Because of his past merit regarding this verse, the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā) became very clear to him. Gaining spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he ordained and began contemplating the Dhamma. Applying his mind to the perception of suffering (dukkha-saññā) and the perception of non-self (anatta-saññā), he developed insight (vipassanā) and attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"The disciples of the Buddha Padumuttara, wandering in the forest,
Lost their way in the great wilderness and wandered like the blind.
Constantly remembering the Buddha Padumuttara, the Leader,
Those sons of the Sage were lost in the great forest."
191:
"Descending from my mansion, I went to the presence of the monks;
I told them the way and gave them food.

O Lord of bipeds, Chief of the world, Best of men, by that deed,
At the age of seven from birth, I attained Arahantship.

Five hundred aeons ago from now, there were twelve
Wheel-turning kings named Sacakkhu, endowed with the seven treasures.

My defilements are burnt... the Buddha's teaching is done."

Because his task was completed by hearing the Dhamma just once, he became known as "Ekadhammasavanīya". Having become an Arahant, while declaring his attainment, he spoke this verse:

"My defilements are burnt, all existences are uprooted;
The cycle of rebirth is completely exhausted, now there is no more renewed existence."

In that verse, "kilesā" (defilements) refers to greed (rāga) and so on, because when they arise in a continuity, they afflict, torment, or distress that person. "Jhāpitā" (burnt) means they are burnt together with their roots by the fire of the Noble Path Knowledge, just as trees and bushes are burnt by Indra's fire (lightning). "Mayhaṃ" means by me, or in my continuity. "Bhavā sabbe samūhatā" means all existences such as sensual existence and kamma-existence are uprooted because the defilements have been burnt. Indeed, if the round of defilements exists, the round of kamma must follow. Because kamma-existences are uprooted, rebirth-existences (upapatti-bhava) are also uprooted, as they are rendered incapable of arising. "Vikkhīṇo jāti-saṃsāro" means the cycle of rebirth, characterized by the uninterrupted continuity of aggregates, elements, and sense bases starting with birth, is especially exhausted. Therefore, there is now no more renewed existence. Because there is no renewed existence in the future, the cycle of rebirth is exhausted; and because all existences are uprooted, there is no more renewed existence—this should be understood by alternating the terms. Alternatively, it should be connected as: the cycle of rebirth is exhausted, and for that very reason, there is now no more renewed existence.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Ekadhammasavanīya is finished.
192:
## 8. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Ekudāniya

The verse beginning with "Adhicetaso appamajjato" is that of the Venerable Elder Ekudāniya. What is the account of his origin? This elder, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit that serves as a support for liberation from Saṃsāra in various existences, was reborn as a Yakkha general during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī. When the Teacher attained Parinibbāna, he fell into lamentation and grief, thinking, "Alas, I have suffered a loss! I have missed a rare opportunity, for I did not get the chance to perform meritorious deeds such as giving alms while the Teacher was still alive."

Then, a disciple of the Teacher named Sāgara dispelled the Yakkha's grief and urged him to worship the Teacher's stupa. That Yakkha worshipped the stupa for five years, and after passing away from that life, he wandered only through the realms of devas and humans due to that merit. In the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was born into a respectable family and, upon reaching maturity, approached the Teacher from time to time. At that time, the Teacher frequently exhorted his disciples with the verse beginning with "Adhicetaso". Hearing it, faith arose in him, and he ordained. After ordaining, he used to recite that very same verse repeatedly.

Although he practiced the duties of a recluse (samaṇadhamma) for twenty thousand years in that dispensation, he was unable to attain any special distinction because his knowledge was not yet mature. Passing away from that life, he was reborn in the deva realm and wandered only through the happy destinations (sugati). When this Buddha appeared, he was born as the son of a wealthy Brahmin in the city of Sāvatthī. Upon reaching maturity, he saw the majesty of the Buddha at the time of the acceptance of the Jetavana Monastery, gained faith, and ordained. Having performed the preliminary duties and while living in the forest, he came to the Teacher.

At that time, the Teacher, seeing the Venerable Sāriputta nearby devoted to the higher mind (adhicitta), uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) beginning with "Adhicetaso". Hearing this, the elder, though living in the forest for a long time practicing meditation, would also utter that same verse from time to time; thus, the name "Ekudāniya" (One-Verse Reciter) became well-known for him. Furthermore, one day, the elder attained one-pointedness of mind, developed insight (vipassanā), and reached Arahatship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"Immediately after the Blessed One Atthadassī, the One Gone to Well-being, had attained Parinibbāna,
I was reborn in the realm of Yakkhas, and at that time I attained great fame and wealth."
193:
"Indeed, my acquisition (of human life) was poor; it was a bad dawn, a bad rising. For while my wealth existed, the One with Vision (the Buddha) attained Parinibbāna. Knowing my intention, the disciple named Sāgara, desiring to rescue me (from the whirlpool of Saṃsāra), came to me. 'O wise one, why do you grieve? Do not fear; practice the Dhamma. The Buddha has bestowed the fulfillment of the seed (for reaching Nibbāna) upon all beings. Whether one honors the living Buddha, the Lord of the World, or honors even a mustard-seed-sized relic of the One who has attained Parinibbāna—if the devotion of the heart is equal, the noble merit has an equal result. Therefore, build a stupa and worship the relics of the Conqueror.'

Hearing the words of Sāgara, I built a Buddha-stupa. For five years, I served and worshipped the supreme stupa of the Sage. O Buddha, supreme among bipeds, foremost in the world, bull among men! Having enjoyed prosperity through that meritorious deed, I have now attained Arahatship. Seven hundred aeons ago from this era, there were four powerful Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti) endowed with the seven treasures and wisdom as vast as the earth. My defilements have been burnt away... I have followed the teaching of the Buddha."

Having attained Arahatship and dwelling in the bliss of liberation, one day, the Venerable Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, wishing to test his wisdom, urged him, saying, "Friend, preach the Dhamma to me." Because he had been familiar with it for a long time, he recited this very same verse:

"For the sage of lofty mind, diligent, training in the paths of silence, peaceful, and ever mindful, sorrows do not exist for such a one."
194:
In that verse, 'adhicetaso' means one who possesses higher mind (adhicitta), endowed with the fruition-mind of Arahantship which is superior to all minds. 'Appamazzato' means one who is diligent, endowed with constant practice in blameless wholesome states through diligence (appamāda). 'Munino' means a sage; as it is said, 'He who knows both worlds is called a sage,' or because he is endowed with 'mona', which is the wisdom of the fruition of Arahantship, an Arahant whose taints are destroyed is called a sage; it refers to that sage. 'Monapathesu sikkhato' means one who trains in the paths of 'mona' (Arahantship knowledge), which are the means—the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—or in the three trainings. This is said by taking the preliminary stage of practice (pubbabhāgapatipadā). Indeed, an Arahant is one who has completed the training; therefore, it should be understood as referring to the sage who has reached the state of a sage through this training.

Therefore, the meaning of these terms is appropriate: 'adhicetaso' by virtue of the path and fruition minds of the lower stages, 'appamazzato' by virtue of diligence in the practice of realizing the Four Noble Truths, and 'munino' by virtue of being endowed with the knowledge of the highest path. Alternatively, the words 'appamazzato sikkhato' should be regarded as the primary causes (padhāna-hetu). Thus, it means one is 'adhicetaso' (having a superior mind) because of the cause of diligence and the cause of training.

'Sokā na bhavanti tādino' means that for such an Arahant sage, sorrows and mental distress caused by separation from the loved and so on do not occur. Alternatively, it means sorrows do not occur for the asekha sage who has reached the quality of being 'such' (tādi). 'Upasantassa' means for one who is peaceful due to the absolute subsiding of lust and so on. 'Sadā satīmato' means for one who is never without mindfulness, having reached the fullness of mindfulness.

Here, by the word 'adhicetaso', the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā) is shown; by 'appamazzato', the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā); and by 'munino monapathesu sikkhato', the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). Or, by 'munino', the training in higher wisdom is shown; by 'monapathesu sikkhato', the preliminary practice of those supramundane trainings; and by 'sokā na bhavanti' etc., the benefits of the fulfillment of the trainings are shown. This very verse was the Elder's declaration of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verse of Ekudāniya Thera is Finished.

8. Commentary on the Verse of Chanda Thera.
The verse beginning with 'Yena dhammaṃ mahāsayaṃ' is that of the venerable Chanda Thera. This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulating merits such as generosity and virtue which are supportive of liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various lives. He was born into a family during the time of the Buddha Siddhattha and became wise upon reaching maturity. On one occasion, seeing the Buddha Siddhattha approaching the foot of a tree, with a clear mind, with a soft cloth, and with a clear mind, for seven days...
195:
## 9. Commentary on the Verse of Channa Thera

"Sutvāna dhammaṃ mahato mahārasaṃ" etc. This verse is that of the venerable Channa Thera. What is its origin? This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulating merits which are supportive of liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various lives. He was born into a family during the time of the Buddha Siddhattha and, upon reaching maturity, one day saw the Buddha Siddhattha approaching the foot of a tree. With a clear mind, he prepared and offered a bed of leaves (paṇṇasanthara) that was soft to the touch. He also performed worship by scattering flowers all around.

Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world and, again performing merits repeatedly, wandered only in happy realms. In the time of our Buddha, he was born in the womb of a slave woman in the house of King Suddhodana. He was named Channa and was born on the same day (sahajāta) as the Bodhisatta. This Channa gained faith during the Buddha's meeting with his relatives and ordained. Out of affection for the Blessed One, he developed a sense of possessiveness, thinking "Our Buddha, our Dhamma," and being unable to cut the bond of affection, he lived without practicing the recluse's Dhamma. When the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, he was threatened with the Brahma-punishment (brahmadaṇḍa) carried out according to the Blessed One's instructions. He then attained spiritual urgency (saṃvega), cut his affection, and while practicing insight, attained Arahantship before long. This matter is stated in the Apadāna:

"I offered a leaf-bed to the Blessed One Siddhattha;
And I scattered flowers as an offering all around.
I enjoyed a delightful and precious excellence like a palace;
And costly flowers flowed onto my bed.
I lay upon a bed spread with variegated flowers;
At that moment, a rain of flowers fell upon my bed.
Since I offered the leaf-bed ninety-four aeons ago,
I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of the bedding.
In the fifth aeon from now, there were seven lords of men,
Cakravartins named Tiṇasantharaka.
My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

Then, having attained Arahantship and delighting in the bliss of liberation, wishing to utter an inspired utterance (udāna) with a surge of joy, he spoke the verse beginning with "Sutvāna dhammaṃ mahato mahārasaṃ." Having heard the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, who is endowed with supreme qualities such as virtue, who gives the noble taste of liberation, who is the means to reach the deathless Nibbāna, and who possesses sharp omniscient knowledge...
197:
## 10. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Puṇṇa

The verse beginning with "Sīlameva" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Puṇṇa. The account of his origin is as follows: He too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated wholesome roots as a support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various births. Ninety-one aeons ago, in a world empty of Buddhas, he was born into a Brahmin family. Upon reaching maturity, he achieved perfection in the Brahmin arts. Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he abandoned the household life, became an ascetic, and lived in a leaf-hut in the Himalayan region.

In a mountain cleft not far from the ascetic’s dwelling, a Paccekabuddha, being afflicted by disease, attained Parinibbāna. At the time of that Paccekabuddha’s Parinibbāna, a great light appeared. Seeing that light and wishing to investigate, "How did this light arise?", he wandered here and there and saw the Paccekabuddha who had attained Parinibbāna in the mountain cleft. He gathered sandalwood, cremated the body, and honored it by pouring scented water.
