At that time, a deity standing in the sky said, "Excellent, excellent, virtuous man! By increasing merit, you have fulfilled the meritorious kamma that leads to a happy destination. Because of that merit, you will be reborn only in happy destinations, and your name will be 'Puṇṇa'." Due to that meritorious kamma, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this Buddha-era, he was born into a householder’s family in the port of Suppāraka in the Sunāparanta country, and he received the name Puṇṇa.

When he reached maturity, he went to Sāvatthī with a large caravan for the purpose of trade. At that time, the Blessed One was residing in Sāvatthī. Then Puṇṇa went to the monastery with the lay followers living in Sāvatthī, and having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith and ordained. He lived performing the major and minor duties for his teachers and preceptors.

One day, he approached the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One instruct me with a brief instruction, having heard which I may dwell in the Sunāparanta country." The Blessed One gave him instruction beginning with, "Puṇṇa, there are forms cognizable by the eye..." (Majjhima Nikāya 3.395, Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.88), and after making him roar a lion's roar, dismissed him. The Venerable Puṇṇa paid homage to the Blessed One, went to the Sunāparanta country, and while residing at the Suppāraka port, he applied himself to Samatha and Vipassanā and realized the Three Knowledges (tevijjā). This is stated in the Apadāna:

"Depending on the mountain peak, the self-become, unconquered,
And that Buddha, afflicted by disease, dwelt in the mountain cleft."
198:
Having gone to the monastery with lay devotees and heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I gained faith and was ordained. I lived pleasing my teachers and preceptors with great and small duties. One day, that Elder approached the Blessed One and requested: "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One exhort me with a brief instruction. Having heard that instruction, it would be well if I could dwell in the Sunāparanta country." The Blessed One gave him the instruction, starting with, "Punna, there are forms cognizable by the eye..." and sent him off after he spoke courageous words. That Elder Punna, having paid homage to the Blessed One, went to the Sunāparanta country. While staying at the Suppāraka port and striving in tranquility and insight meditation, he realized the three knowledges. Therefore, it is stated in the Apadāna Pali:

Near my hermitage, there dwelt in a mountain cleft a Paccekabuddha, a self-enlightened one, unconquered by the five Māras, who was afflicted by illness. At the very moment that the Exalted One attained Parinibbāna near my hermitage, a radiance arose and light appeared.

At that moment, all the wolves and leopards in that forest grove, as well as the fierce wild beasts and lions, roared.

Seeing that wondrous omen, I went to the mountain valley. There, I beheld the Paccekabuddha, the conqueror of enemies and pride, who had attained Parinibbāna.

I beheld that Noble One, who had attained Parinibbāna and conquered enemies and pride, appearing like a royal Sal tree in full bloom, like the rising sun with its thousand rays, or like an ember whose flame has been extinguished.

Having gathered grass and wood, I built a pyre there. After properly preparing the pyre, I cremated the body.

After cremating the body, I poured scented water. Then, a deity standing in the sky gave me a name.

"O hermit, you have completed the cremation duties for the self-enlightened Paccekabuddha of noble conduct. Therefore, may you always be known by the name Puṇṇaka," said the deity.

Passing away from that life, I went to the celestial realm. In that heaven, divine scents constantly rain down from the sky.

Even in that celestial realm, my name was Puṇṇaka. Whether as a deity or a human, I was able to fulfill my wishes.

This is my final birth; the last existence is proceeding. In this life too, the name Puṇṇaka remains well-known.

Having pleased the Blessed One Gotama, the Bull of the Sakyans, and having fully understood all the Āsavas, I dwell free from taints.

Because of the meritorious deed I performed ninety-one aeons ago, I have not known any woeful states. This is the fruit of that small meritorious act.

My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

That Elder Punna, having reached the fruit of Arahantship, inspired great faith in the Buddha's Dispensation among many people. Because of this, about five hundred men understood the status of a lay follower (Upāsaka), and about five hundred women understood the status of a female lay follower (Upāsikā). That Elder dwelt in the Sunāparanta country, abiding in the bliss of meditative absorption (jhāna).
200:
## 8. Eighth Group (Aṭṭhamavagga)
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vacchapāla

The verse beginning with 'Susukhumanipuṇatthadassinā' is that of the Venerable Elder Vacchapāla. What is the origin of this elder? This elder, having performed meritorious service under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various existences, wandered through the realms of gods and humans. Ninety-one aeons ago, he was born into a Brahmin family, attained mastery in Brahmin arts, and was serving the sacrificial fire. One day, while carrying milk-rice in a large golden bowl and searching for a worthy recipient, he saw the Blessed One Vipassī walking in the air. Filled with wonder and joy, he paid homage to the Blessed One and showed his desire to make an offering. Out of compassion, the Blessed One accepted it.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans, and in this Buddha’s era, he was born in Rājagaha as the son of a wealthy Brahmin and was named Vacchapāla. At the assembly where King Bimbisāra met the Buddha, he saw the Elder Uruvela Kassapa perform miracles and show supreme humility towards the Teacher. Gaining faith from this, he ordained. Just seven days after his ordination, he developed insight and attained the six higher powers. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"The All-knowing Buddha, golden-hued, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, came out from the forest, preceded by the community of monks.

Having filled a large golden platter with milk-rice, I, desiring to make an offering, presented that sacrificial gift.

At that time, the Blessed One, the Chief of the World, the Bull among Men, was walking well-composed in the air, the path of the winds.

Seeing that wonder, marvelous and hair-raising, I set down the golden bowl and paid homage to Vipassī.

'You are the God of gods, the All-knowing One in the world with its gods and humans; out of compassion, O Great Sage, please accept this.'"
201:
"The All-knowing One, the Leader of the World, the Teacher, the Great Sage in the world, knowing my intention, accepted it.

In the ninety-one aeons since I gave that gift, I have not known a woeful state; this is the fruit of the milk-rice.

Forty-one aeons ago, there was a Cakkavatti king named Buddha, endowed with the seven treasures and great power.

My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Having attained Arahantship and wishing to clarify his own peaceful attainment of Nibbāna, he spoke this verse:

"For one who sees the extremely subtle and profound meaning, who is skilled in wisdom, humble in conduct, and has cultivated the virtue of the elders—for such a one, Nibbāna is not difficult to attain."

In that verse, 'susukhumanipuṇatthadassī' means one who sees meanings such as the Four Truths and Dependent Origination—which are subtle because they are extremely difficult to see, and profound because of their delicate nature—by applying the characteristics of impermanence and so on. By such a person. 'Matikusala' means skilled in wisdom; skilled in producing the wisdom known as the investigation of states enlightenment factor (dhamma-vicaya-sambojjhaṅga), thinking, "Wisdom increases for one who acts thus, and does not increase for one who acts thus." 'Nivātavutti' means one who has a humble manner towards fellow practitioners, behaving appropriately towards both seniors and juniors. 'Saṃsevitavuddhasīlī' means one who has the virtue of the elders that has been repeatedly practiced. Or, one by whom virtuous and wise elders have been associated with. The word 'hi' has a causal meaning. The meaning is: because Nibbāna is not difficult to attain for one who is humble in conduct, possesses the virtue of the elders, is skilled in wisdom, and sees subtle meanings. Because of his humble conduct and possession of the virtue of the elders, wise people consider that he should be exhorted and repeatedly instructed. Standing in the instruction of the wise, if he performs the work of insight with his own skill in wisdom and ability to see subtle meanings, it should be understood that he reaches Nibbāna before long. This very verse was the elder's inspired utterance (udāna) upon reaching the fruit of Arahantship. Thus should the conclusion be understood. The commentary on the verses of Elder Vacchapāla is finished.
202:
Because of his own skill in wisdom and his seeing of subtle and profound meanings, while performing the work of insight, he reached Nibbāna in no long time. This very verse was the elder's declaration of gnosis (aññābyākaraṇa) upon reaching the fruit of Arahantship.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vacchapāla is Finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Ātuma

"Yathā kaḷīro susu vaḍḍhitaggo"—this verse is that of the Venerable Elder Ātuma. What is its origin? This Elder Ātuma also had a strong aspiration made under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit that is a powerful support for the fruit of Arahantship in various existences. Ninety-one aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, he was born in a respectable family. When he reached maturity, he saw the Blessed One Vipassī walking along the road and, with a confident mind, made an offering of scented water and scented powder. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world. Wandering only in happy destinies, he ordained in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa and performed the duties of a recluse, but because his knowledge was not yet mature, he was unable to attain distinction.

Then, when our Buddha Gotama appeared, he was born in Sāvatthī as the son of a merchant and was named Ātuma. When he reached maturity, his mother consulted with relatives, saying, "We shall bring a wife for my son." Knowing of this consultation and being urged by the perfection of his causes, he thought, "What is the use of household life to me? I shall ordain right now," and went to the monks and ordained. Even after he had ordained, his mother, wishing to make him disrobe, enticed him in various ways. Without giving her an opportunity and wishing to make clear his own intention, he spoke this verse:

"Just as a young bamboo shoot with a growing tip is difficult to pull out once it has produced branches,

So too, if a wife is brought for me, I would grow (with children and grandchildren) and it would be difficult to escape.

Therefore, please give me permission now; I have already ordained."

This verse he spoke.
203:
In this verse, 'kaḷīro' means a sprout; however, in this context, a bamboo shoot is intended. 'Susu' means a young person. 'Vaḍḍhitaggo' means one with grown branches. 'Susuvaḍḍhitaggo' also means one with well-grown branches and leaves. 'Dunnikkhamo' means the inability (difficulty) to be extracted from a bamboo thicket. 'Pasākhajāto' means one in whom branches have appeared, with small branchlets growing at every joint of the branches.

'Evaṃ ahaṃ bhariyāyānītāya' means: Just as a bamboo tree with a grown top is difficult to extract from a bamboo thicket because of the small branches and branchlets intertwined among the bamboo trees, so too, if I were to bring a wife, I would grow with children and so on, and it would be difficult to escape from the household life due to the power of attachment. Just as a bamboo shoot that has not yet developed the entanglement of branches is easy to extract from a bamboo thicket, so too, I am one who is easy to escape because I do not yet have the entanglements of wife and children. Therefore, even before bringing a wife, please give me permission—thus he made [his mother] give permission herself.

'Pabbajitomhi dāni' means: "Now I have gone forth; it is good," thus expressing his delight in renunciation; or it is saying to his mother, "Now I have gone forth, please give me your permission." The meaning here is: Although you did not give permission before, now I have become a monk; therefore, give me permission to remain in the state of a recluse; do not make me return to lay life. Speaking thus, while remaining as he was, he developed insight, exhausted the defilements through the path-sequence, and became an Arahat endowed with the six supernormal powers. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"Sitting in a noble palace, I saw the Conqueror Vipassī, the All-knowing One, free from taints, shining like a great peak.

"Not far from the palace, the Leader of the World was walking; his radiance streamed forth like that of the sun.

"Taking scented water, I poured it over the Excellent Buddha; with that clarity of mind, I passed away right there.

"Ninety-one aeons ago, because of that merit of pouring scented water, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.

"Thirty-one aeons from now, I was a powerful Universal Monarch named Sugandha, endowed with the seven treasures.

"My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

After attaining the six supernormal powers, he asked his mother's permission and, while she was watching, departed through the air. After reaching the fruit of Arahatship, this Elder used to frequently recite this very verse from time to time. In that verse, by the word 'pabbajitomhi dāni', this verse is also the Elder's declaration of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa), because it shows the subsiding of stains such as lust in his own continuity. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Because he has banished his own stain, he is called a 'pabbajita' (one who has gone forth)." The explanation of the verse of Elder Anuma is finished.

## Commentary on the Verses of Elder Mahāvaṇṇavaccha
'Jiṇṇañca sudukkhitaṃ byādhitaṃ' and so on—this verse is that of the Venerable Mahāvaṇṇavaccha. This Elder also had made a resolution in the presence of former Buddhas and had a strong support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various births...
205:
When that Bodhisatta was born, the ten thousand world systems shook; that Blessed One, the Teacher, endowed with the five eyes, now teaches the Dhamma.

When that Bodhisatta was born, a great light appeared; that Blessed One, the Teacher, endowed with the five eyes, now teaches the Dhamma.

When that Bodhisatta was born, the rivers did not flow; that Blessed One, the Teacher, endowed with the five eyes, now teaches the Dhamma.

When that Bodhisatta was born, the fires of Avīci Hell did not burn; that Blessed One, the Teacher, endowed with the five eyes, now teaches the Dhamma.

When that Bodhisatta was born, the flocks of birds did not fly; that Blessed One, the Teacher, endowed with the five eyes, now teaches the Dhamma.

When that Bodhisatta was born, the masses of wind did not blow; that Blessed One, the Teacher, endowed with the five eyes, now teaches the Dhamma.

When that Bodhisatta was born, all the gems shone brightly; that Blessed One, the Teacher, endowed with the five eyes, now teaches the Dhamma.

When that Bodhisatta was born, seven steps were taken; that Blessed One, the Teacher, endowed with the five eyes, now teaches the Dhamma.

As soon as he was born, the Bodhisatta Vipassī looked towards all directions and uttered a noble speech; such is the nature of the Buddhas.

Having caused spiritual urgency among the people, having praised the Lord of the World, the Buddha Vipassī, and having paid homage to him, I departed facing the East.

In the ninety-one aeons since I praised the Buddha Vipassī, I have not known a miserable state; this is the fruit of that praise.

Ninety aeons ago from this auspicious aeon, there was a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch) named Sammukhāthavika, endowed with the seven gems and possessed of great power.

Eighty-nine aeons ago from this auspicious aeon, there was a Cakkavatti named Pathavīdundubhi, endowed with the seven gems and possessed of great power.
206:
Eighty-eight aeons ago from this auspicious aeon, there was a Cakkavatti named Obhāsa, endowed with the seven gems and possessed of great power.

Eighty-seven aeons ago from this auspicious aeon, there was a Cakkavatti named Saritacchedana, endowed with the seven gems and possessed of great power.

Eighty-six aeons ago, there was a Cakkavatti named Agginibbāpana, endowed with the seven gems and possessed of great power.

Eighty-five aeons ago, there was a Cakkavatti named Gatipacchedana, endowed with the seven gems and possessed of great power.

Eighty-four aeons ago, there was a king named Vātasama, a Cakkavatti endowed with the seven gems and possessed of great power.

Eighty-three aeons ago, there was a Cakkavatti named Ratanpajjala, endowed with the seven gems and possessed of great power.

Eighty-two aeons ago, there was a Cakkavatti named Padavikkamana, endowed with the seven gems and possessed of great power.

Eighty-one aeons ago, there was a king named Vilokana, a Cakkavatti endowed with the seven gems and possessed of great power.

Eighty aeons ago, there was a king by the name of Girasāra, a Cakkavatti endowed with the seven gems and possessed of great power.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

When that monk, who had attained Arahantship, was asked by other monks, "Friend, because of what spiritual urgency (saṃvega) did you ordain while still so very young?", he replied by way of declaring his attainment of Arahantship through the reason for his ordination:

"Having seen an old person, a suffering person, and a sick person,
And having seen a dead person whose life-force had come to an end,
Because of seeing these, I renounced the delightful sensual pleasures,
Departed for the forest, and became a monk."

Thus, he recited this verse.
207:
In that verse, 'jiṇṇaṃ' refers to one overcome by old age, possessing such features as broken teeth, grey hair, and wrinkled skin. 'Dukhitaṃ' means one who has reached suffering. 'Byādhitaṃ' means a sick person (an invalid). Here, although 'byādhita' is mentioned, the state of having reached suffering is already established; the use of 'dukhita' is to highlight the severity of that person's illness. 'Mataṃ' means the deceased. Since a deceased person is one who has reached the exhaustion, destruction, and dissolution of life, it is said, 'reached the end of the life-span.' Therefore, because of seeing the old, the sick, and the dead, [he thought,] 'These states such as old age do not belong to these people alone; indeed, they are common to all beings. Therefore, I too am not exempt from old age and so forth.' Thus, out of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), [he ordained]. 'Nikkhameitūna' means 'having gone forth'; or this 'nikkhamitūna' itself is the original text. It means having left the house with the intention of ordaining. 'Pabbajiṃ' means he entered the state of a monk in the Teacher's Dispensation. 'Pahāya kāmāni manoramāni' means having abandoned the delightful objects of sensuality (vatthukāma) which, due to being desirable and pleasant, delight the minds of those not yet free from lust; it means discarding them without lingering concern, having completely cut off the lustful desire (chandarāga) associated with those sensual objects by means of the Noble Path. By way of proclaiming the abandonment of sensual pleasures, this was the Elder's declaration of Arahantship (aññābyākaraṇa). Because he ordained while still a youth (māṇava), the name 'Māṇava' became well-known for this Elder.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Māṇava Thera is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Suyāmana Thera

The verse beginning with 'kāmacchando ca byāpādo' is that of the Venerable Suyāmana Thera. What is its origin? This Elder also had made an aspiration under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merits in various births. Ninety-one aeons ago, during the time of Vipassī Buddha, he was born into a Brahmin family in the city of Dhaññavatī. Upon reaching maturity, he attained mastery in the Brahmin arts and taught the Vedic hymns. At that time, the Blessed One Vipassī entered the city of Dhaññavatī for alms together with a large community of monks. Seeing the Buddha, the Brahmin, with a clear and confident mind, led Him to his house, prepared a seat, and having spread a carpet of flowers upon that seat, offered it. While the Teacher sat there, he satisfied Him with choice food. After the meal, he also honored Him with fragrant flowers. The Teacher, having given a talk of appreciation (anumodanā), departed. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world and repeatedly [performed] merits...
208:
...having performed [merits] and wandering through the worlds of devas and humans, during the time of this Buddha's appearance, he was born as the son of a certain Brahmin in the city of Vesālī; his name was Suyāmana. When he reached maturity, he became a master of the three Vedas and was endowed with extremely distinguished views. Loathing the enjoyment of sensual pleasures of household life, his mind inclined towards Jhana. When the Blessed One visited Vesālī, he gained faith and ordained. He attained Arahantship even while his hair was being shaved (at the tip of the razor). This matter is stated in the Apadāna:

"In the city of Dhaññavatī, I was then a Brahmin, (proficient) in the science of marks, in history, and in the glossaries together with the rituals."
"I was an expert in words, a grammarian, and skilled in the science of omens. I taught the hymns to students, being a master of the three Vedas."
"Five handfuls of lotuses were placed on my back, as I desired to make an offering at the gathering of my parents."
"Then the Blessed One Vipassī, the Bull among Men, came illuminating all directions, preceded by the community of monks."
"Having prepared a seat and invited the Great Sage, and having spread those flowers, I led Him to my own house."
"Whatever material gift was ready in my own house, that I gave to the Buddha with my own hands, with a clear mind."
"Knowing the time when He had finished His meal, I gave the five handfuls of flowers. The All-Knowing One, having given thanks, departed facing the north."
"In the ninety-one aeons since I gave those flowers then, I have not known a bad rebirth; this is the fruit of the offering of flowers."
"In the aeon immediately preceding this one, I was a powerful Universal Monarch named Varadassana, endowed with the seven jewels."
"My defilements are burnt away... [as before]... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Having attained Arahantship, by way of proclaiming the abandonment of the hindrances, and desiring to clearly declare his own Arahantship—
209:
“Sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor of a monk, restlessness and doubt—these do not exist in any way at all.” Thus he spoke this verse.

In that verse, 'kāmacchanda' means desire for sensual pleasures. Because it is both the sense-object (kāma) and that desire (chanda), it is called 'kāmacchanda' (sensual lust). In this context, however, since it refers to the defilements to be abandoned by the Path of Arahantship, 'kāmacchanda' is intended to mean all forms of lust (rāga). Therefore, it was said, "they do not exist in any way at all." Indeed, all things belonging to the three planes of existence are called 'kāma' in the sense of being desirable. The lust that arises for those things is 'kāmacchanda'. Thus the Blessed One said: "In the formless realm, depending on the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness, and the hindrance of ignorance arise" (Paṭṭhāna 3.8.8).

'Byāpāda' (ill will) is so called because by it the mind becomes corrupted (byāpajjati) or reaches a state of putrefaction; it is the malice (āghāta) that arises in such ways as "He has done me harm," etc. 'Thina' (sloth) is the sickness of the mind, the lack of exertion and shrinking. 'Middha' (torpor) is the sickness of the mental body (the cetasika aggregate), the inability, obstruction, and fatigue. Both of these together are called 'thina-middha' (sloth and torpor). They are spoken of as one because they are similar in opposing activity and nutriment. 'Uddhacca' (restlessness) is the state of being scattered; it is the distraction of the mind by which the mind becomes agitated and unpeaceful. Here, by the inclusion of restlessness, it should be understood that 'kukkucca' (remorse) is also included, as they are similar in opposing activity and nutriment. That remorse has the characteristic of subsequent regret. The unhappiness (vippaṭisāra) that arises depending on the performed or unperformed wholesome and unwholesome deeds is called 'kukkucca'.

'Vicikicchā' (doubt) is so called because one falls into uncertainty such as "Is it thus, or is it not thus?" or because one becomes weary and fatigued (kicchati) by it while investigating the nature of things. It is doubt rooted in the Buddha and so forth. 'Sabbaso' means without remainder. 'Na vijjati' means it does not exist; it is not found because it has been utterly uprooted by the Path.

These two words should be applied to each of the hindrances. The connection here is as follows: For whichever monk sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt do not exist in any way at all because they have been utterly uprooted by the respective Noble Paths, for that monk there is nothing further to be done, or there is no need to add to what has been done. Thus, by referring to another, he declares his own Fruition of Arahantship. For when the five hindrances are uprooted by the Path, all defilements that reside together with them are also uprooted. Therefore, it was said: "All those Blessed Ones, having abandoned the five hindrances, the defilements of the mind..." (Dīgha Nikāya 2.146).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Suyāmana Thera is finished.
210:
## 5. Commentary on the Verses of Susārada Thera

"Sādhu suvihitāna dassanaṃ"—this verse belongs to the Venerable Susārada Thera. The background story is as follows: It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a Brahmin family. Having reached the completion of his studies in the sciences and seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he abandoned the household life, ordained as an ascetic, and lived in a hermitage in a forest region of the Himalayas. Then, the Blessed One Padumuttara, wishing to show him favor, approached him at the time of the alms-round. Seeing the Buddha from afar, the ascetic, with a devoted mind, went out to meet Him, took His bowl, and offered sweet fruits into it. The Blessed One, having accepted the fruits and given a blessing (anumodanā), departed.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha-dispensation, he was born into a Brahmin family related to the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta). Because of his dull wisdom, he was given the name "Susārada." Later, having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the General of the Dhamma, he gained faith and ordained. Developing insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna (Ap. Thera 1.13.75-83):

"I was a reciter of the Vedas, a master of mantras, one who had reached the further shore of the three Vedas. I lived in a hermitage not far from the Himalayas.

I had a fire sacrifice, and I also had Puṇḍarīka fruits. I placed them in a basket and hung them on the top of a tree.

Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, the Recipient of Offerings, wishing to lift me up (from saṃsāra), approached me while seeking alms.

With a devoted and joyful mind, I gave the fruit to the Buddha. That gift produced joy in me and brought happiness in the present life.

The Golden-hued Buddha, the Fully Enlightened One, the Recipient of Offerings, the Teacher, standing in the air, spoke this verse:

'By this gift of fruit and by his volition and aspiration, for a hundred thousand aeons, he shall not go to a state of woe.'

Due to that very root of merit, having enjoyed prosperity, I have reached the unshakable state (Nibbāna), having abandoned victory and defeat."
211:
Seven hundred aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, I was a Wheel-Turning Monarch named Sumangala, endowed with the seven treasures and possessed of great power.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

After reaching the fruit of Arahantship, while praising the benefits of associating with and relying on a good person (sappurisa) and thereby declaring his attainment of Arahantship—

'Seeing the virtuous who are well-behaved is excellent; doubt is severed, wisdom increases; they make even a fool a wise person; therefore, association with the virtuous is truly good.' He spoke this verse.

In that verse, 'sādhu' means excellent or beautiful. 'Suvihitāna dassanaṃ' means seeing the Noble Ones (Ariyas) whose physical existence is well-ordered by virtues such as morality (sīla). The nasal (niggahīta) is dropped for metrical ease in the verse. The construction is: seeing the Noble Ones, whose bodies are well-ordered by virtues like morality and whose Dhamma teachings are well-delivered out of compassion for others, is good. 'Dassana' (seeing) should be understood as a mere indication, as hearing and other actions are also very beneficial. As the Blessed One said—

'Monks, I say that seeing those monks who are accomplished in virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, who are advisers, instructors, demonstrators, encouragers, inspirers, gladdeners, and capable of explaining the True Dhamma, is of great benefit. Hearing... approaching... attending to... recollecting... and following them into monkhood, I say, monks, is of great benefit to those monks.' (Itivuttaka 104).

Alternatively, 'seeing' is mentioned here because it is the root of the others. The phrase 'doubt is severed' etc., states the reason for that seeing. When one sees such good friends (kalyāṇamitta), a wise person of good family who desires his own welfare approaches and attends to them, asking questions like, 'Venerable sir, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome?' They dispel his doubts regarding various doubtful matters; hence it is said, 'doubt is severed.' By dispelling their doubts through Dhamma teaching, they first cause the arising of the Right View of the Path of Action (kammapatha-sammādiṭṭhi) and the Right View of Insight (vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi); thus their wisdom increases. When they develop insight and penetrate the Four Noble Truths, they understand them. At that time, the sixteen-fold and eight-fold doubts (vicikicchā) are completely and well severed. Wisdom, which is 'buddhi', increases. Transcending the state of a fool...
212:
...having dispelled doubt, they first cause the arising of the Right View of the Path of Action and the Right View of Insight; thus their wisdom increases. When they develop insight and penetrate the Four Noble Truths, the sixteen-fold and eight-fold doubts are severed, completely severed; wisdom, which is knowledge without remainder, increases. Because they transcend the state of a fool, they become wise. Those virtuous ones increase wisdom in that person; they make even a fool a wise person. The word "Tasmā" (therefore) etc., is the conclusion. Because by seeing the virtuous, in the manner described, doubt is severed and wisdom increases, and those virtuous ones make a fool wise, for that reason, association (samāgama) with the virtuous (sataṃ), the Noble Ones, is good and excellent; it means associating with them is a proper growth.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Susārada is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Piyanjaha

The verse beginning with "Uppatantesu nipateti" is the verse of the Venerable Piyanjaha Thera. What is its origin? This Piyanjaha Thera had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit that serves as a support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various lives. Ninety-one aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, during the time of Buddha Vipassī, he was a tree-deity in the Himālaya. While living in a mountain cleft, because he had little power, he stood at the edge of the assembly during gatherings of deities and heard the Dhamma, thereby gaining faith in the Teacher. One day, seeing a very pure and delightful sandbank in the Ganges, he recollected the qualities of the Teacher: "Even purer than this sandbank are the Teacher's qualities, which are infinite and immeasurable." Thus, focusing on the Teacher's qualities, he gladdened his mind. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this Buddha's era, he was reborn in the Licchavī royal family in Vesālī. When he reached maturity, he was fond of war and undefeated in battle; he became known as 'Piyanjaha' because he destroyed the affection (piya) of his enemies. When the Teacher came to Vesālī, he gained faith, ordained, and while living in the forest, he developed insight and attained Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"Living in a mountain cleft in the Himālaya mountains,
Seeing the beautiful sand,
I recollected the Excellent Buddha."
213:
In the knowledge of the Buddha, there is no comparison; for the Buddha, there are no conditioned things (saṅkhāra). Having known all things through higher knowledge, He is resolved through knowledge.

Homage to You, O Thoroughbred of Men! Homage to You, O Supreme among Men! There is no one equal to You in knowledge; how supreme is Your knowledge!

Having gladdened my mind in the knowledge of the Buddha Vipassī, I rejoiced in heaven for an aeon. In the remaining aeons, I practiced wholesome deeds.

Ninety-one aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, I obtained that perception (saññā) at that time. Because of that perception, I have never known a miserable rebirth (duggati). This is the fruit of the perception of the knowledge of the Buddha Vipassī.

Seventy aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, I was once a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) named Pulinapupphiya, endowed with the seven treasures and great power.

My defilements have been burnt away... (pe)... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out. Thus he spoke.

Upon reaching Arahantship, wanting to explain another aspect of Arahantship by showing the meaning: "The practice of the Noble Ones is far removed from the practice of the blind worldlings," he recited this verse:

"One should be humble among those who are restless; one should uplift those who are lowly. One should practice among those who do not practice the Path; one should not delight among those who delight in sensual pleasures."

In those verse-parts, "uppatantesu" means among beings who are not peaceful, exalting themselves through conceit (māna), restlessness (uddhacca), stubbornness (thambha), and arrogance (sārambha). "Nipate" means one should be humble; one should live a life of humility by avoiding those unwholesome states. "Nipatantesu" means among beings who are declining and falling away from virtue due to improper attention and laziness. "Uppate" means one should uplift; one should strive in virtue through noble inclination and the arousal of energy.

Alternatively, "uppatantesu" means defilements (kilesas) that raise their heads through obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna). "Nipate" means one should suppress them through the power of reflection so they do not arise, using appropriate contemplation; one should both distance oneself from them and eradicate them completely. "Nipatantesu" means the decline of the practiced states of tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) due to either improper attention or weak energy..."
214:
...one should establish, produce, and increase them through proper attention (yoniso manasikāra) and the accomplishment of energy. "Vase avasamānesu" means that although beings do not live the life of the Path (magga-brahmacariya) or the Noble Life (ariyavāsa), one should live that life oneself. Or, just as Noble Ones are free from living with defilements or living with companions, one should live in that way. "Ramamānesu no rame" means that although beings delight in sensual pleasures or defilements, one should not delight in that way. Or, just as Noble Ones delight in the joy of jhāna etc. which is free from worldly bait (nirāmisa), one should also delight in that way. Otherwise, one should never delight or take pleasure in anything else.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Piyanjaha is finished.

## 7. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Hatthārohaputta

"This mind formerly wandered as it liked"—this is the verse of the Venerable Hatthārohaputta. As for its origin: This Elder had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit that serves as a support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various births. In the time of the Buddha Vipassī, he was born in a good family. Upon reaching maturity, one day, seeing the Teacher leaving the monastery surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, he felt a gladdened mind, offered flowers, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and circumambulated before departing. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha's era, he was born in a family of elephant trainers in Sāvatthī. Upon reaching maturity, he became an expert in the art of elephant training. One day, while going to the riverbank to train an elephant, being prompted by his past merits, he thought, "What is the use of taming this elephant? Taming oneself is better." He approached the Blessed One, heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and ordained. Taking a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable for his temperament, while practicing insight (vipassanā), his mind wandered outside the meditation subject due to long habit. Like a skilled elephant trainer taming a wild elephant in rut with a hook, he restrained his mind with the hook of reflection and recited the verse: "This mind formerly wandered as it liked."

In that verse, "this" (idaṃ) is said because the mind is perceived directly by himself. "Formerly" (pure) means before the time of restraint. "Wandered" (acāri) means it moved about; because of instability, it wandered among various objects. "Wandering" (cārikaṃ) means going as it liked. Therefore, it is said "as it liked, where it liked, as it pleased." "That" (taṃ) refers to that very mind. "Today" (ajja) means at this time. "I shall restrain" (niggahessāmi) means I shall suppress and discipline it, making it free from irritation. "Wisely" (yoniso) means through method. How? Like a man holding a hook restrains a wild elephant in rut. This is the intended meaning. My mind, before being restrained, wandered among objects like sights as it liked, in whatever object it desired, as it pleased. Now, that mind, like a wild elephant in rut, by a skilled elephant trainer...
215:
(That mind) wandered about among various objects without a fixed place. 'Cārikaṃ' means wandering as one wishes. Therefore, it is said, 'wherever it wished, as it desired, as it pleased.' 'Taṃ' refers to that mind. 'Ajja' means at this time. 'Niggahessāmi' means I will restrain and discipline it, I will make it free from indulgence. 'Yoniso' means by a proper means. How? Just as a man holding a goad restrains and disciplines a great elephant in rut with secretions flowing from both temples.

The meaning is this: Before being restrained and disciplined, this mind of mine wandered for a long time among objects such as visible forms, according to whatever object it wished to delight in, whatever it desired, and in whatever way it traveled pleasantly. Now, I will restrain and discipline that mind through wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), just as a skilled elephant trainer holding a goad restrains and disciplines an untamed great elephant in rut with secretions flowing from both temples; I will no longer allow it to overstep.

While saying this, that Elder developed insight (vipassanā) and realized the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Ap. Thera 1.13.91-96):

"The Buddha Vipassī, who has a complexion like gold and is worthy of offerings, departed from the monastery surrounded by his disciples.
Seeing that Buddha, the best, the All-Knowing One, the Dispeller of Darkness, I, with a confident mind and full of joy, offered a gaṇṭhi flower.
With that confidence of mind toward the Lord of bipeds, who is endowed with such qualities, I, with a joyful heart, paid homage to the Tathāgata once again.
Because of that intention of offering flowers ninety-one aeons ago, I have never known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
Forty-one aeons ago, I was a powerful Universal Monarch named Caraṇa, endowed with the seven treasures.
My defilements have been burnt away... (and so on) ... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

This very verse was the Elder's declaration of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Hatthārohaputta is finished.
